The 1520–21 letters of Cardinal Ippolito d’Este’s secretary in Hungary, in a homophonic cipher of graphic signs. One postscript had been deciphered by Judit W. Somogyi in 2025; the key was rebuilt by aligning the ciphertext with her text. It deciphers 161 of the 166 cipher signs of a letter of 25 February 1521 and most of two more (89.7% and 66.9%). Somogyi (key or decipherment used) external text At a glance Key from external plaintext · partial (12% of the cipher) The letters Giuliano Caprile, canon of Eger and secretary of Cardinal Ippolito d’Este, to the ducal secretary Bonaventura Pistofilo and to Duke Alfonso I, March 1520 to April 1521: five texts in one cipher. Where Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4; DECODE R1136, R1138, R1139 (catalogue item 157), and the Hungarian database Vestigia, where the letters of 16 and 25 February 1521 (Vestigia 1920, 1921) are not on DECODE. The cipher A homophonic cipher of invented signs with no word division, crossed ligatures for s and q . How it was deciphered One postscript of 16 February 1521, in both its versions, was deciphered by Judit W. Somogyi in 2025. Her two printed texts, aligned against a transcription of the signs, gave the key. On 2 October 2026 the letter of 25 February 1521 added five values, and second transcriptions of R1139 and R1136 at full resolution were deciphered with them. What it says Ippolito’s estate at Eger after he left Hungary: the custode , the governor, the see, money and debts. On 25 February 1521 Caprile reports that il custode è stato quel ch’à persuaso others to say Eger had been given away before the new bishop came, and advises the Duke to reclaim what is due sopra soi beni . Measured V1921: 161 of 166 cipher signs give sense (97.0%), 147 at grade C. R1139: 453 of 505 decoded letters inside deciphered phrases (89.7%, 3 October 2026). R1136: 378 of 565 (66.9%). These are shares of decoded letters inside phrases: R1139 and R1136 still have holes in most lines, so they are decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026). Still open Stretches of R1139 and a third of R1136, limited by doubtful sign separations. Other ciphers Caprile’s 1519 letters use a different two-tier cipher, with its own page ; Alfonso Cistarelli’s numerical cipher of July 1520, in the same box, also has its own page . R1139, the slip of 6 April 1521, in the cipher of graphic signs. Phrases are deciphered here; no earlier decipherment was found. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, Caprili 1520–21 no. 13, via DECODE R1139.

The Vestigia records flagged as cipher in the 1519–21 files are these five, Caprile’s 1519 letters and Cistarelli’s: no other letter uses the 1520–21 key. Caprile’s 1519 letters are in a different, two-tier cipher, most of them deciphered in 1882; the one left without a decipherment, R1128, is on its own page .

The cipher is a run of invented signs with no word division: φ, ψ, λ, ÷, ss, ff, a crossed b, m and n with a cross, an inverted T, and some forty more. There are 49 labels in all, over 2,278 signs in five texts, transcribed from the DECODE and Vestigia images. Somogyi calls it homophonic, and it is. The key was built in two steps: A ciphertext-only solver run (simulated annealing) over all five texts, scored with a sixteenth-century Italian n-gram model. It gave a rough key in which scritti , regno , signore and Ungaria could already be recognised. That key seeded a monotone alignment (Viterbi with gaps, re-estimated until stable) of the transcription against Somogyi’s two texts. 714 letters align, and 90% of alignments agree with the majority value of their sign. The values: a = q, T, ⊥ · c = φ, θ · d = ψ, r · e = y, ss · g = w, u · i = ƀ, ɔ, L · l = ff, n · m = z, Ħ · n = ÷, p · o = ɛ, the stacked q/b, oσo · p = & and its looped variant · r = *, x · s = m+, n+ · t = h, f · u = λ, a The letter of 25 February 1521 corrected and extended these values (2 October 2026). The lone o, taken at first for a null, is a homophone for h and u (“ha”, “ch’à”, “qui”, “suo”), as the alignment counts had already shown; two lone o together are b (“beni”, and R1139’s “debito”); z and x with a cross, and x with the looped p, are q (“qui”, “quel”, “quantunque”); the looped p doubles for f (“oficio”); and K is et once. The second transcriptions of R1139 and R1136 added o with a cross = s , the crossed 3 and 3 with the looped p = q , the triangle = b or x , plain c = o , and o with a lead-in = h . The figure 8 is a null in one place. A statistical check on the letter of 25 February (161 tokens, 42 sign types) scores the reading well above random keys (z 6.6), but a key annealed onto the shuffled ciphertext reaches the same score, so the test alone cannot confirm the key on so short a text: verdict underdetermined . The key’s support is the alignment with Somogyi’s two texts and the sense of the three letters it deciphers.

Caprile to Duke Alfonso I from Esztergom, 25 February 1521 (Caprili 1520–21 no. 12). It is not on DECODE; Vestigia has it as item 1921, flagged as containing cipher. The letter is in clear until its last third, where six cipher runs are set inside clear sentences. They were transcribed sign by sign on the Vestigia image, with four corrections to the first transcription, and deciphered with the key on 2 October 2026. The letter of 25 February 1521, lines 15–22: the cipher runs begin at the left of the second line (“E me dicixe ha un omo qui”) and continue between the clear phrases “qual oltra che fa mille pacie”, “e ha ditto haver scritto al suo mazo che” and “a dire che”. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, Caprili 1520–21 no. 12, p. 1, via Vestigia 1921. 161 of the 166 cipher signs give sense (97.0%); 147 of them (88.6%) at grade C , with every sign at its key value. On a sixteenth-century Italian model the reading scores −1.79 per character, against −4.12 for the same letters shuffled. Clear text in roman, the deciphered runs in bold: … il tutto per adviso e scarico di chi ne ha colpa. E me dicixe [= disse?] ha un omo qui qual oltra che fa mille pacie & da poca riputation ale cose del patron, dice ogni cosa e revelta [?] , e ha ditto haver scritto al suo mazo che il custode è stato quel ch'à persuaso [..] a dire che [.] Agria era data d'anti il suo advento, e[t] che lo toglia in oficio , e molto sturbato le sue cose, e chi l'ha messo in gran disgratia di suo signore ; il che quando cossi sia, como mi acerta alcuno ch'à veduto le lettere, a V. Ex.a sera poca fatica i cominciar a repeter il suo sopra soi beni, quantunque siano in reg[no?] . E S. V. Ex.a a questo modo … “And he told me there is a man here who, besides committing a thousand follies and bringing little credit to the master’s affairs, tells everything and [gives it away]; and he has said he wrote to his [messenger] that it was the custode who persuaded [them] to say that Eger had been given away before his arrival, and that he should take him into office … and put him in great disgrace with his lord. If that is so, as someone who has seen the letters assures me, it will be little trouble for Your Excellency to begin reclaiming what is his from his goods, even though they are in the kingdom.” The patron and the claim are Ippolito d’Este’s Eger bishopric, the subject of R1136, R1138 and R1139. Dicixe (for disse ?) and revelta are grade M. Open: two minim strokes after persuaso with no key value, one sign before Agria (probably a slip), and two signs at the torn edge after in reg .

A slip pasted into the letter of 6 April. Nine lines of cipher, then the clear text “Expettamo sino a S. Georgio…”. It is the estate business of Somogyi’s article: the keeper ( custode ) and the governor of Eger, the money of the late bishop’s debt, and someone who says he wants to go to Italy. Six passes since September 2026 have worked on it: the signs re-checked on the image wherever the decrypt did not read (three transcription errors found, among them the tall-stem r of custode ), letters proposed from the key’s sign counts with an Italian model, a second transcription from the DECODE image at full resolution, the values from the letter of 25 February, a table of look-alike sign pairs over all five texts, and a study of pen shapes. After them 453 of the 505 decoded letters fell inside phrases (89.7%, 3 October 2026). The reading audit of 22 October 2026 asked whether the slip builds sentences: it does not, and it is decoded, not read. On 22–23 October the cipher was re-read on strips of the native image at 2.2 times, five sign labels were corrected, and every token was decoded again with the key; no new value holds across every occurrence (4 = e , 1 = v , 1 7 = ve were tested and rejected). The partial reading, aligned word by word with the signs ( R1139_reading.md ; two of its eleven sentences are clean): Post. Il custode, quando a Buda, com[?e] i' scrisi, et è tornato gubernator de [4817]. […] decime, et fa ogni cosa per […] io [17] […]; a si tenuto Agria in oficio. [?E] credo dia ogni [?ato] e qualche cosa a le ma […] custode; per anchora si n'è intrato [?ci] in castelo. Et cosi la venuta sua in Italia, [?a] de che vi scrivi, qua[…] li teneva per ferma, è andata in [?vero]. Il che vedendo io, bel belo li go fato moto deli danari del suo debito, come mi dise meser [?a] Alfonso. Lui m'ha resposto, dice [?te] voler andar in Italia quando al dare te […]. […] Milan […] andiate. Parlaremo a longo sopra ciò, et se i bisionran danari in [?presto], per andar ve ne darò. Vedrò quel mi darà, [?e] il tut[o] reportarò a V. Ex. “Postscript. The custode, when [he was] at Buda, as I wrote, has also come back as governor of [4817]. […] tithes, and he does everything for […]; [he] has thus held Eger in office. [?And] I believe he gives every [?act] and something into the hands […] custode; as yet he has not entered [?there] into the castle. … Seeing this, I gently raised with him the money of his debt, as messer [?a] Alfonso told me. He answered me, saying he wants to go to Italy … We shall talk at length about it, and if they need money on [?loan], I will give you some for the journey. I shall see what he gives me, [?and] I shall report the whole to Your Excellency.” Go is the Venetian-Ferrarese gh’ò (I have); fato moto is fatto motto (mentioned). The groups 4817 and 17 look like figures or code signs and have no key value.

Twelve lines after a clear opening (“e la susseguente matina”), written the day after Ippolito crossed out of Hungary for the last time (7 March 1520). A second transcription at full resolution (2 October 2026) put 378 of the 565 decoded letters inside phrases (66.9%), but the lines do not build sentences. The 22–23 October re-read confirmed the sign labels at twice the size on contrast-stretched strips; the breaks turn on signs the key cannot separate or value, and a stain covers about six signs at the left of lines 1–3. The partial reading ( R1136_reading.md ; none of its nine sentences is clean): [?Asi] transferse a Buda il custode […]. […] [?altro] li a in oficio questo episcopato, et a epso custode […]. […] gu[…]ernator […] Lactantio, ho inteso, qual […] a in gran presia […]amato a Buda, et dicono eser conclusi […] congregati […] Bachiensis, che ogni episcopa[…] […] il man[…] […] cosi [17] ne tenir […]. […] et l'altro in titulo, [?ma] questo modo excluderà […]. […] li daran poco […] vo[…]stra Excelentia, quel si […] potrà far al custode par questa via de Ungaria sopra il su[…] […]. […] secondo patrone, […] in questo loco niente […]. […] tornato el sia […] canto, e vedrò intendere il […] pensier suo […] sopra tal debito. The custode moves to Buda; the see of Eger, its custode and governor, Lactantio, the prelates gathered ( Bachiensis is taken here to be the archbishop of Kalocsa-Bács; this identification is not from the sources and was not checked here), and the advice that the Duke “potrà far al custode par questa via de Ungaria” on his goods, the claim Caprile repeats a year later on 25 February 1521.

R1139 and R1136, decoded, not read. After second transcriptions at full resolution, two more passes on 3 October 2026 and the re-read of 22–23 October, 10% of R1139’s decoded letters and 33% of R1136’s fall outside phrases, and neither builds sentences. In R1139 these are the figure-like groups 4 8 1 7 and 1 7 and short stretches of lines 2, 4–5 and 8; in R1136, a stain over about six signs at lines 1–2 and the stretches limited by doubtful sign separations. A table of the look-alike sign pairs over all five texts (pass 5) settled only two of them ( CE = o, crossed xp = q), and added mi per Milan in R1139 line 8; a study of the pen shapes (pass 6) found no shape class with a consistent value. 4 8 1 7 and 1 7 fit neither as letters nor as numerals, and are probably nomenclator codes with no list. V1921. Five of 166 signs stay open (no key value, a slip, the torn edge); dicixe and revelta are grade M. What would finish it. Hand-placed crops of every occurrence of the doubtful sign pairs, or more text in the same key. No further letter in this cipher exists in the file.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. R1139, slip of 6 Apr 1521 decoded, not read Postscript slip from Giuliano Caprile to Ferrara about the custode (castellan) of Eger, the governor's return, money of the late bishop's estate, and someone's wish to go to Italy: the Ippolito d'Este estate business of Somogyi's article. About 90 % of decoded letters fall inside read phrases; two numeral-like groups are open. A mechanical decode with holes in most sentences: shown so that the transcription and the key can be checked and improved, not as a reading. Where The Francia 346 dossier; DECODE R75 and R84, among eleven records that carry George Lasry’s key of 24 October 2020. The cipher Homophonic and syllabic on two-digit figures: every pair begins with a null 2, and the single figure 6 separates words. The only ambiguity is whether the next code is two digits or a three-digit nomenclator element. How it was read Lasry’s key was applied. Busta 346 of the Francia series of the Segreteria di Stato holds the originals and ciphers sent from Rome to Ceva during his extraordinary nunciature, 1632 to 1634. DECODE catalogued eleven ciphertexts from it, R74 to R84. The catalogue entry here named five (R75, R77, R78, R82, R84) and scored them by rule from the metadata, unviewed. Opening the records changed the problem. Every one of the eleven carries, as an attachment, a key marked #KEY: reconstructed , #TRANSCRIBER NAME: George Lasry , #DATE OF TRANSCRIPTION: October 24, 2020 . Every one also carries the same 29,050-byte file of aligned decipherments, covering four letters. So the state of the dossier before this session was: DECODE Item Date Pages Before R74 346-1 7 Sept 1632 1 read by Lasry R75 346-2 25 Sept 1632 2 not read R76 346-3 1632 3 marked decrypted R77 346-4 1632 2 read by Lasry R78 346-5 1632 2 read by Lasry R79–R81, R83 346-6 to -8, -10 1632–34 7 marked decrypted R82 346-9 27 [Oct] 1632 1 read by Lasry R84 346-11 18 Dec 1632 2 not read Three of the five ciphertexts the catalogue named were therefore already deciphered by Lasry, and two were not. R75 and R84 carry a raw ciphertext transcription and nothing else. Lasry, for his part, left every one of the ninety-five nomenclator elements he met printed as <xxx> ; none was given a value.

The key is Lasry’s. It was re-derived here from his four aligned decipherments, parsed into 104 line pairs and 179 distinct tokens, which confirms it and settles three points the key note leaves open. Token Value 6 word separator 2x null — no pair beginning 2 ever carries plaintext XY letter or syllable, 61 codes: three homophones for each vowel, two for most consonants, and groups for al, che, chi, con, da, de, di, et, il, in, io, la, ma, mi, no, per, qu, quel, se, si, st pXY nomenclator element: one prefix digit followed by an ordinary two-digit code First, the figure 6 occurs inside no code , neither in a key pair nor in any of the ninety-five nomenclator elements. Word boundaries in this cipher are therefore certain, which is unusual and is what makes the rest tractable. Second, the DECODE key note says the nomenclator elements “have 4 digits starting with prefix 4”. They have three . Concatenating Lasry’s own token stream for 346:1 and diffing it against the original transcription of the same leaf gives a 99.7% match with no dropped prefix; the elements are three digits as they stand. The prefix is 4 in twenty-seven of the ninety-five, but it is also 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 8 or 9. Third, in ninety-one of the ninety-five the two digits after the prefix are themselves a valid key code. The element is a prefix plus an ordinary code, which is exactly why the parse is ambiguous: at most positions a two-digit and a three-digit reading are both legal. Twenty-nine of the hundred pairs are dead ( 02 05 06 12 16 32 33 36 42 46 52 56 60–69 72 76 82 86 92 96 99 ), and meeting one forces the three-digit reading, but that is not enough on its own.

The decoder works along the digit stream and keeps the several hundred most probable partial decryptions at each position. Every 6 is taken as a separator; elsewhere the decoder chooses between a two-digit code, a two-digit null and a three-digit element, scored by a character model. Scoring is incremental: the shared lang package’s dense model is a flat table of log P(c | previous four characters), so each emitted character costs one array lookup and several hundred candidates are cheap to keep. The model matters more than the search. it-cinquecento is Renaissance diplomatic Italian but stops around 1620 and knows nothing of this clerk’s hand: one sign for u and v, doubled letters dropped, word division his own. It was interpolated with a model built on 7,693 characters from the dossier itself: the passages the clerk wrote in clear, plus Lasry’s plaintext of whichever letters were not under test. Calibration is leave-one-document-out against Lasry’s four letters: the nomenclator inventory offered for a document is built from the other three only, which is the situation of R75 and R84. Agreement with his own segmentation: Model Tokens Nomenclator recall Precision it-cinquecento alone 0.945 0.52 0.70 interpolated, w = 0.6 0.958 0.70 0.79 Per letter, interpolated: 346:1 0.871, 346/4 0.928, 346/5 0.905, 346/9 0.951. The figure to keep in view is the nomenclator recall. Three elements in ten are still missed, and a missed element comes out as two or three plausible Italian letters, with no gap to mark it. Errors in the decipherments below are concentrated there. The one independent check is R75’s own leaf. A decipherer in 1632 wrote his decipherment between the cipher lines, and the DECODE transcriber copied what was legible of it. It was used for nothing else: neither for the key, the model nor the decoder. On the twenty-four lines where enough survives, 1,105 letters, 77.5% agreement , ignoring word division; the last line agrees at 100%. The residue is shared between errors in this decryption and the witness’s own illegibility, since the transcriber flagged much of the faded interlinear with ? and * . R75 (25 September 1632), f. 81r, left half of four lines in the lower part of the page: the 1632 decipherer’s interlinear, … di guerra saranno sempre in pericolo … a conoscere quanto sia pericolosa alla Francia … cominciano hormai a pensar a … , the witness this decryption was checked against. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 346 f. 81r, via DECODE R75.

Two pages, 1,446 code groups. The reading follows the figures, decoded with Lasry’s key and the adopted values, against the contemporary decipherment on f. 82r (DECODE attachment “082r.jpg [cleartext]”) and the 1632 interlinear; where the decipherer and the figures differ, the figures are followed (fifteen places, listed in R75_reading.md ). Code words such as Schombergh , Cardinale Richelieu and Religione Catolica are carried by the decipherment alone. Spelling as the figures give it, the clerk writing doubled letters once; […] marks the three short runs left open. Le vitorie di Schombergh e della forza renderano per aventura più facile a V.S. il negotio del acomodamento di Monsieur, ma più dificile asai quello del unione. Però è necessario ch'ella si sbraci a trovar motivi di persuadere che ancora a detto compla per gli interessi di Francia l'unione. Io ne acennerò alcuni, et ella se ne serva secondo li stimi […]. Il Cardinale Richelieu è avido di gloria, della quale non farà minor acquisto con l'unir le armi di Francia vitoriose per asicurar la Religione Catolica di quello che sia stato portar le medesime armi alla vitoria. È tempo che S.E. cominci a conoscere quanto sia pericolosa alla Francia la potenza d'Olandesi, che cominciano hor mai a pensar a cose grandi et ad indrizar la […] loro a gli Imperi. Consideri quanto sia oportuno alli vastisimi pensieri di quella natione estendere il loro dominio sino al Mediteraneo con acquisto d'una piazza, e con quanto buon fondamento lo posono sperare in una revolutione del Regno di Francia, alla quale è tanto sotoposto mentre hano tanto forze maritime e terestri. Consideri ancora S.E. che la vitoria del Sueco è altretanto formidabile alla Francia quanto alla Germania. “The victories of Schomberg and of the [royal] forces will perhaps make Your Lordship’s business of the accommodation of Monsieur easier, but that of the union much more difficult. So it is necessary that you exert yourself to find reasons to persuade [them] that the union also suits the said [Cardinal] for the interests of France. … Cardinal Richelieu is greedy for glory, and he will win no less of it by joining the victorious arms of France to secure the Catholic religion than he did by carrying those same arms to victory. … It is time that His Eminence began to see how dangerous to France is the power of the Dutch, who are now beginning to think of great things and to turn their […] towards the Empires. Let him consider how well it suits the vast designs of that nation to extend their dominion to the Mediterranean by acquiring a stronghold … Let His Eminence consider too that the victory of the Swede is as formidable to France as to Germany.” The letter goes on to Monsieur, who “sarà sempre al medesimo”, and ends by urging Richelieu to seek glory in the arts of peace or in war against the infidels. The September decryption had made the victories and the rising power Swedish; the decipherer on f. 82r wrote “di Gostavo lo Svedese quella natione” where the figures give only “di quella natione”, and the 1632 interlinear “di Goto natione”, but 104 is Olandesi in the figures.

Two pages, 954 code groups, written a month after Lützen (16 November 1632). The first folio is largely in clear: Barberini acknowledges Ceva’s despatch of the 8th, says he has nothing further to answer, and refers him to Mons. Bichi at court. The cipher was deciphered on the figures and compared with the contemporary decipherment on f. 136r; the figures are followed where they differ ( Vega , gelosie , vol , tengano ). … ricordando a V.S. che si vaglia della vitoria contro Gostavo, però con la sua consueta prudenza, ad indur S.M.tà a facilitar il trattato. E sappi lei che gli affari che bolivano in Francia dopo la mia partenza, pure de pensieri torbidi di Monsieur, furono cagione che li Francesi concludesero la pace di Valtellina. … Si avisa da per tutto la fuga di Monsieur. Non so quanto sia stato a proposito con insoliti rigori nella Francia meter in disperatione quel Prencipe, potendo da questo nascere consegvenze che tengano disunita per un pezzo la Francia e sotoposta alle esterne violenze, o almeno impotente a socorer li suoi aliati. “… reminding Your Lordship to make use of the victory over Gustavus, though with your usual prudence, to induce His Majesty to ease the treaty. And you should know that the affairs that were seething in France after my departure, and the troubled designs of Monsieur too, were the reason the French concluded the peace of the Valtellina. … The flight of Monsieur is reported everywhere. I do not know how wise it was to drive that Prince to despair with unaccustomed severity in France, since from this consequences may arise that keep France disunited for a long time and exposed to violence from outside, or at least unable to help her allies.” One word is uncertain in both witnesses: “da [?N.S.re]”.

Lasry gave no value to any of the ninety-five elements he met. Deciphering R75 puts a placeholder at each element; aligning that decryption against the 1632 interlinear shows which word of the contemporary decipherment stands at the placeholder. Twenty-two elements caught a witness fragment, and six survive checking against Lasry’s four letters, where they were not fitted: Code Reading Evidence 474 mente piena~, principal~, non sola~ per il solo proprio, malacomoda~; witness fragment met 495 quanto “e ~ al proporre arbitrare”; pairs with 498 498 tanto “che ~ in <347> quanto in <857> si sappia la cagione” 830 Francia four times out of four in Lasry’s letters, always after a feminine article: “render la ~ più poderosa”, “valere a danno quella ~”, “hoggi la ~ in a di dar legge” 854 guerra R75 interlinear, twice 149 piazza R75 interlinear, “acquisto d’una ~” Adding the six raised the control agreement on R75 from 0.737 to 0.775. That test is partly circular for 854 and 149 , which came from the witness itself; the independent evidence for 474 , 495 , 498 and 830 is that they fit the four letters Lasry read, which the witness never touched. The pairing of 498 and 495 as tanto…quanto around two undecoded place codes is the best supported of them. One element was rejected at the time. 491 drew the fragment goto , but it does not fit its four contexts in Lasry’s letters. The complete decipherments of October 2026 settle it as quell- , and add seven more values that hold at every occurrence: 88 del (keyed quel ), 33 gli , 541 armi , 171 Regno , 473 mentre , 497 tutt- , 104 Olandesi (not Svedesi ).

R75 : three short runs: “se ne serva 494 li stimi v4” (one word after stimi ; the decipherer paraphrases “se ne servirà secondo che giudicherà necessario”), “diolavse 1” at the head of line 21, and “la e8 loro”. No value of the key gives a word. R84 : “da [?N.S.re]” (figures c 5 ): the abbreviation in the decipherer’s hand on f. 136r is cramped and the figures give no word. Values carried by one decipherment only (357 Schomberg, 581 Cardinale Richelieu, 197 Religione Cattolica, 844 Gostavo, 930/957 Mons.r Nuntio and others): there is no nomenclator for the dossier on DECODE, and confirming them across the dossier needs the Vatican key. The other six letters. R74 was deciphered by Lasry; R76, R79, R80, R81 and R83 are marked decrypted on DECODE. None of them is touched here.

DECODE transcriptions: R75 by IB, 25 July 2020 (with the 1632 interlinear copied as far as legible); R84 by MEG, 3 April 2020. The cipher copy of Commodore Knowles’s neutrality notice to the inhabitants of Dominica, enclosed by Governor Champigny in a letter whose inventory says part was never deciphered (ANOM, COL C8 A 56 fols. 57–57v). Brice Dudout rebuilt the Navy code of the Windward Islands from the interlinear glosses of six letters of 1744, froze it and tested it on a seventh (0.894 of characters against 0.578 at most for shuffled keys), and read the notice: 154 of 155 words. Knowles offers protection to those who stay neutral and four louis d’or for each deserter returned. Jacques-Charles Bochart de Champigny, governor general of the Windward Islands, enclosed it with his letter of 17 August 1744 to Maurepas, the Navy minister. Where Archives nationales d'outre-mer, Aix-en-Provence, COL C8 A 56 fols. 57–57v (images FRANOM23_C8A_056_0103–0104). The inventory says of the letter that part of it was not decrypted. Not on DECODE. The cipher The Navy code of the Windward Islands: about 500 numbers for syllables, letters and a few words, with several numbers for common syllables, in no alphabetical order. How it was deciphered Brice Dudout aligned the code against the interlinear glosses of six letters of Champigny of 1744, froze it, and tested it on a seventh, which it reproduced at 0.894 of characters, against 0.578 at most for shuffled keys. Applied to the enclosure, it gives sentences. What it says Knowles promises protection to the inhabitants of Dominica "as if they were of his own nation" as long as they stay neutral, demands the return of his deserters at four louis d'or a head, and threatens to treat anyone who hides them as an enemy. Still open One word of 155 (group 320, "agissent" or "obéissent"); 5 words restored from the sense and 7 probable. In the summer of 1744 the war between France and Britain reached the West Indies. Commodore Charles Knowles anchored at Dominica, an island that both powers treated as neutral, and circulated a notice to its inhabitants. Champigny's letter of 17 August, glossed between the lines in Versailles, tells of Knowles's arrival at the Grande Anse with the Superbe , two 50-gun ships and frigates, of his sailors deserting to Martinique, and of an attack on Saint Lucia that was feared. It announces a copy of the writing Knowles had circulated "to offer the inhabitants of that island a neutrality, which they did not accept". That copy is the enclosure on fols. 57–57v: 48 manuscript lines of numbers, 381 groups in all, with a few numbers underlined for figures that are meant as figures. The letter was deciphered at the ministry; the enclosure never was, and the ANOM inventory records that part of the letter "has not been decrypted". The key sheet is not in the file. No image of the leaf is reproduced here: the ANOM viewer states no reuse licence and could not be reached by script, so the strip at the top is set from Brice Dudout's transcription.

The code is a numerical nomenclator of about 500 values (1–500), two-part, so that nothing in the order of the numbers tells you what they mean. Most values are syllables and letters, spelling the text out in pieces ( 276 187 = ch - ef ), and a few are words: 205 is Dominique , 474 Royal , 3 trois . Frequent syllables have several numbers each. Numbers written in clear and underlined stand for themselves, as the "4 louis d'or" of the notice does. It is not the code of 1761 rebuilt by Daniel Bourdeau ( Mercier 1761 ), nor the d'Ennery form of 1765, nor the Guiana code of 1744–1762: the three agree with it on none, one and none of the numbers they share with it.

The key, called K5 in the notes, was built only from the contemporary interlinear glosses of six letters of Champigny of 1744 in the same volume (C8 A 56 fols. 40, 44, 54–56v, 59, 63 and 67), about 4,900 groups aligned automatically to their glosses, with four written decisions on ambiguous groups (393 = i , 296 = ro , 465 = qu , 300 = fa ). It was frozen, its SHA-256 recorded, before the validation letter was opened. The test was a seventh glossed letter never used before the freeze, fol. 79 of 17 November 1744: 566 groups and 263 words of gloss. Against the gloss, with a measure fixed in advance, the key reaches 0.894 of characters and 0.814 of words; 200 control keys, with the values shuffled between groups, reach 0.578 and 0.122 at most. The criterion (0.85 and 0.75, above every control) was met. Three earlier tests with poorer keys on other letters had stayed below it, at 0.76–0.81 and 0.65–0.74.

The 381 groups give 155 words of French: M. [Knowles], chef d'escadre de Sa [Majesté] {Britannique}, fait savoir à tous les {habitans} de l'isle de la Dominique que, pendant qu'ils demeureront dans une parfaite neutralité, qu'ils peuvent être assurés de sa protection en toute manière, comme s'ils étoient de sa propre nation, ayant bien soin d'{empêcher} toute insulte et pillage qui pourroient leur [arriver] par les corsaires ou autres vaisseaux {armés} ; mais aussi de la part des habitans de l'isle de la Dominique, il demande [absolument] [d'eux] la restitution de tous les gens de son équipage qui ont déjà ou pourront déserter des vaisseaux, et pour comble de récompense il promet de donner pour chaque homme déserté du bord de son escadre 4 louis d'or ; mais si d'autre manière ils cachent aucun de ses gens pour {empêcher} leur restitution, ils peuvent être assurés qu'ils seront {traités} comme des ennemis ; mais s'ils ‹320›issent comme il {demande}, ils peuvent être assurés de sa protection. Braces mark a probable reading, square brackets a word restored from the sense, angle quotes a group left unresolved. Mr Knowles, commodore of His Britannic Majesty, makes known to all the inhabitants of Dominica that while they stay perfectly neutral they may count on his protection in every way, as if they were of his own nation, and that he will see to it that privateers and other armed ships do them no harm. In return he demands that they give back every man of his crew who has deserted or may desert, and promises, "as a crowning reward", four louis d'or for each man deserted from his squadron. Those who hide his men to prevent their return will be treated as enemies; those who do as he asks keep his protection. To Brice Dudout's knowledge this is the first published decipherment of the enclosure.

Unresolved, 1 word. "s'ils ‹320›issent comme il demande": agissent (act) or obéissent (obey). Group 320 occurs in none of the seven glossed letters examined. Either reading gives the same sense. Restored from the sense, 5 words. Knowles : 381 251 326 110 217 301 (elsewhere the name is 381 25 326 110 217, with 25 = K, so 251 is probably a malformed 25). Majesté : number 222, absent from every glossed letter, the only word that fits "Sa … Britannique". arriver : 300 ( fa ) written for 303 ( ve ), neighbouring numbers. absolument : 470, not in the glosses. d'eux : 336 306 428 = ce eu x , which would make "il demande absolument ce eux la restitution" ungrammatical. Probable, 7 words. Britannique (391 standing for -mbr- in "nombre"), habitans (253 followed by 436 instead of 435, neighbours), empêcher twice (296 = ro in 35 of 35 glossed cases, so the sense is relied on), armés (254 with a number seen once), traités (204 = tr in a September letter) and demande (433, one doubtful alignment). Control. The held-out test is on a letter of the same year and volume. The enclosure has no gloss of its own, so the reading itself is checked by the sense and by the four louis d'or, the neutrality and the deserters that Champigny's glossed letter reports.

Translation translation.md # English translation Mr Knowles, commodore of His Britannic Majesty, makes known to all the inhabitants of the island of Dominica that, as long as they remain in perfect neutrality, they may be assured of his protection in every way, as if they were of his own nation; he will take good care to prevent any insult and plunder that privateers or other armed ships might inflict on them. But on the part of the inhabitants of the island of Dominica, he absolutely demands of them the return of all the men of his crew who have already deserted, or may desert, from the ships; and as a crowning reward he promises to give four louis d’or for every man deserted from on board his squadron. But if in any other way they hide any of his men to prevent their return, they may be assured that they will be treated as enemies; if they [act / obey] as he demands, they may be assured of his protection. Three lines of strokes, dots and digits found behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general, 107 characters, with no known solution. Two transcriptions were attacked as a simple substitution in ten languages under six conventions; the same solver recovers matched controls almost completely, and the cryptogram never comes close. It is not a simple substitution of any language tested. Copenhagen · strokes, dots and digits, system undetermined · found probably in the late 1950s The Copenhagen cryptogram Three lines of strokes, dots, carets and digits found behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum, no. 23 on Klaus Schmeh’s Top 50. In September 2026 it was attacked as a simple substitution in ten languages, under two transcriptions and six conventions, with matched controls. No key was recovered, and no decipherment has been published. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 · Sources: Klaus Schmeh’s Cipherbrain posts of January 2015, August 2017 and October 2021 and their comments; the 614 × 147 px scan Danish-General-Cryptogram.jpg Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The object A slip with three lines of strokes, dots, carets and digits, found (probably in the late 1950s) behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum. It is no. 23 on Klaus Schmeh’s Top 50. Where Sent to the American Cryptogram Association, which recorded no solution. The only image in circulation is a 614 by 147 pixel scan from Kent Ramliden, published by Schmeh in 2015, 2017 and 2021. The cipher Unknown. The merged reading has 107 tokens: 103 symbols of 20 kinds plus 4 long strokes used as dividers. ShadowWolf’s reading splits them into 25 symbols. How it was tried Both transcriptions were attacked as a simple substitution in ten languages by simulated annealing scored with a 5-gram model. The best score was −2.69 nats per letter, and 300 restarts did not move it. The same solver recovers twelve of fifteen random 103-letter control passages. Why it resists Genuine text of this length scores between −1.4 and −2.1. Either the slip is not a simple substitution in these languages, or both readings share a transcription error. Still open A better scan or the original slip (the ACA archive, Ramliden’s papers), the identity of the general, or a shorthand or private code, which nothing here tests.

The slip carries three short lines. It was found, probably in the late 1950s, behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum, and sent to the American Cryptogram Association. The ACA recorded no solution and never wrote it up. The museum, the general and the finder are all unrecorded. Klaus Schmeh received a scan from ACA member Kent Ramliden, a Swede living in Florida who died in 2016. He published it three times: in German in January 2015, as no. 23 of his Top 50 in August 2017, and as German and English “cold case” posts in October 2021. The only image in circulation is that scan, 614 by 147 pixels. Two reader contributions from the 2021 comments matter here: a 25-symbol transcription by “ShadowWolf”, and a Danish quadgram hill-climb by Matthew Brown that found nothing.

Two transcriptions were used. cipher.txt is this project’s, made from the scan upscaled four and six times, half a line at a time. cipher_sw.txt is ShadowWolf’s 25-symbol reading from the comments of the German post of 7 October 2021. This is the merged reading, one token per symbol, space separated: 7 N F n F B 3 A D B n o 3 D B P 6 3 B 3 P 8 D F 2 n 3 | 2 3 A W R F 0 3 A n 2 0 B n o 9 P n P 9 2 B 3 v v 3 D B | 0 A B v 3 D B P n o F 3 8 0 D B P X 0 3 B n o n F 9 n D B v n | 1 3 | n o n 3 F D B 3 F B A 1 2 3 A That is 107 tokens: 103 symbols of 20 kinds, plus 4 long vertical strokes written | and treated as sentence dividers. Digits 4 and 5 never occur. token mark on the slip count 3 digit 3 16 n plain n 13 B backslash with its trailing dot (\.) 14 F slash with its trailing dot (/.) 8 P plus sign 6 A caret or lambda (^) 6 D free-standing dot that precedes a stroke 8 o small round letter o 5 2 digit 2 5 0 tall zero 5 v as written 4 9 digit 9 3 1 digit 1 2 8 digit 8 2 7 6 X as written 1 each N n with two dots above 1 R small “or”-like glyph at the end of line 1 1 W caret with a double accent above 1 | long vertical stroke, sentence divider, not counted among the 103 4 Where the two readings differ The two readings agree symbol for symbol except that ShadowWolf splits what is merged here. He separates the backslash with a dot after it from the backslash with dots on both sides, which here is a free dot D followed by B . He separates the slash with a trailing dot from the slash with a leading dot, here D followed by F . He gives the small raised double tick after the first caret pair its own symbol. He distinguishes four caret shapes: a tall lambda-like one, which is the first caret of line 1 and the last symbol of line 3; a small one; one with a trailing dot opening line 2; and one after the zero in line 2. And he reads the second tall stroke around 1 3 in line 3 as the digit 1 rather than a divider. With those splits the symbol count is 25, which is Schmeh’s figure; merged it is 20. Both readings were attacked. Two internal regularities The letter o occurs five times and every time directly after n : no3 , no9 , +no , non and non3 , with non twice in line 3. The doubled pair vv occurs once, in line 2. Section 06 shows how far they go.

solve.py builds character 5-gram language models from Project Gutenberg texts in ten languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, German, Dutch, French, English, Latin, Icelandic and Finnish, 0.6 to 2.4 million letters each. The corpus is not in the repository; it is fetched through the Gutendex API with the ids in the session log. The solver is simulated annealing over an injective symbol-to-letter map, 60 to 80 restarts per run, with the long strokes treated as sentence boundaries. The solver optimises the 5-gram score alone; its top candidates are then re-ranked by dictionary coverage, which it does not optimise. Six token conventions were tested on the merged reading: the free dot as a letter, dropped, as a boundary, or fused to the following stroke; the long stroke as a letter; and the dotted n merged with plain n. The 25-symbol reading was run as it stands. A separate script, solve_sp.py , tests the hypothesis that the two dotted strokes are word separators, which would make the text 22 words averaging 3.7 letters, using a space-aware model and scoring whole-word hits. Nothing readable came out in any language under any convention. Best per-letter scores, with what the best key produced: language best score per letter, any convention what it looked like Latin −2.69 fxsisted tine togeteom scie ... Danish −2.77 junindel dige dskedesf ... / ... udstødes ... velsigne ... Norwegian −2.81 bærersag sena stjasatm ... Swedish −2.81 honensam sera stfasatv ... English −2.88 cydidsea sine stbesetf ... German −2.93 uchthien itze irbeierm ... French −2.97 chiailes lape ltbeletr ... Dutch, Icelandic, Finnish −3.07 to −3.30 The word-separator hypothesis scores −4.6 per letter under the spaced model, where real text scores about −2.3. It yields only isolated Danish words: er , elle , unge , død , døde . The last two are the fragment discussed in section 06.

A failed search proves nothing on its own, so the solver was calibrated on texts it should solve. control.py draws passages of 103 letters with three sentence breaks at random from the same corpora, enciphers each with a random simple substitution of about 20 symbols, and attacks it with the identical solver. Three trials per language, 40 restarts each; the real cryptogram got 60 to 80, then 300. Accuracy is the share of the passage recovered. language trial letters in key accuracy score found score of true text outcome Danish 1 19 0.99 −1.99 −1.85 recovered Danish 2 19 0.99 −1.93 −1.96 recovered Danish 3 18 0.99 −1.85 −1.76 recovered German 1 22 0.96 −1.88 −1.78 recovered German 2 19 0.79 −2.64 −1.75 partial German 3 22 0.14 −3.42 −1.81 search failed English 1 20 1.00 −1.44 −1.44 recovered English 2 21 0.99 −1.99 −1.85 recovered English 3 20 1.00 −1.67 −1.67 recovered Latin 1 18 1.00 −2.09 −2.09 recovered Latin 2 18 1.00 −1.74 −1.74 recovered Latin 3 19 0.99 −1.87 −1.72 recovered Swedish 1 22 1.00 −1.95 −1.95 recovered Swedish 2 22 0.05 −3.49 −1.59 search failed Swedish 3 22 1.00 −1.99 −1.99 recovered Twelve of fifteen passages are recovered essentially completely, and the true text always scores between −1.4 and −2.1 per letter. Two trials fail outright and one partly. In each case the true key would have scored far better than what the solver found: −1.81 against −3.42, −1.59 against −3.49, −1.75 against −2.64. These are search failures at 40 restarts, most likely tied to 22-letter keys, and they mean that a single failed run on the real text would prove nothing. That is why the strongest candidate languages were rerun with 300 restarts on both readings. Against that calibration the cryptogram never scores better than −2.7 in any language or under any reading. So either it is not a simple substitution of a text in these ten languages, or the transcription conflates or splits letters in a way that both independent readings share. Danish, the default assumption since 2015, fits no better than Latin or Norwegian. Matthew Brown’s Danish quadgram hill-climb in the 2021 comments came to the same nothing.

Best per-letter score with 300 restarts from seed 5, for the merged reading in the full and nodot conventions and for the 25-symbol reading. The dotattach runs were still going when the notes were written and had not beaten these. language merged, full merged, no dot 25-symbol reading Latin −2.90 −2.82 −3.16 Danish −3.04 −2.90 −3.16 Swedish −3.17 −2.99 −3.20 Norwegian −3.12 −3.01 −3.17 English −3.20 −3.13 −3.28 German −3.29 −3.32 −3.46 Five times the restarts move nothing; section 03 took the best of six conventions, these runs fix the convention and the seed, and no cell improves on it. The ceiling is the same, 0.7 to 1.4 nats per letter below what genuine text of this length scores in every one of these languages. Search failure is excluded as the explanation.

non as død Under n = d, o = ø, 3 = e, the n-o-n pattern gives Danish død (dead, death), non3 gives døde (died, the dead), and no3 gives døe , the pre-1900 spelling of dø (to die). It is the one suggestive fragment in the whole search. It surfaced in the word-separator run, whose only other whole-word hits were er , elle and unge . The three symbols involved account for 34 of the 103 tokens, so this assignment fixes a third of the text. It does not extend. The rest of that decryption is noise, and the run as a whole scores −4.6 per letter where real text under the same model scores about −2.3.

not solved Closed from the scan that exists. Three routes would reopen it. The original slip or a better scan. The ACA received the slip from the museum, so the ACA archive or Kent Ramliden’s papers are the places to ask. A second image would settle the split-versus-merged question in section 02. The painting. An 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum points to the Tøjhusmuseet, now the Danish War Museum. Identifying the general would give a name, a date and a language. Shorthand or a private code. If the strokes and dots are a shorthand or a private code rather than letters, no substitution model applies, and nothing here tests that possibility.

Everything is in targets/copenhagen/ in the project repository. cipher.txt is the merged 20-symbol reading with its token conventions in the header; cipher_sw.txt is ShadowWolf’s 25-symbol reading aligned to it. solve.py is the 5-gram solver (simulated annealing) with dictionary re-ranking, solve_sp.py the word-separator test, control.py the matched-control harness. NOTES.md holds the full record of the attempt. The Gutenberg corpus is not in the repository; the Gutendex ids are in the session log.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 4 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (86% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Daniel Bourdeau (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (86% of the cipher) The despatch Antoni Augustyn Deboli, the Commonwealth’s envoy at the Russian court, to King Stanisław August, “St Petersbourg ce 13 May 1788”, no. 038 of his cipher despatches. Where Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych, Warsaw, Zbiór Popielów (zesp. 12), no. 428, k. 74–75v: 943 groups. Of Deboli’s 112 cipher despatches of 1788, this and no. 039, also of 13 May, are the only ones with no same-date decipherment in ZbPop 417. The cipher A numerical code of the 1789–91 type, in groups of 1–4 digits that write stems and syllables, with nulls. The writer makes 0 and 8 alike, which the transcription marks. How it was deciphered The key is Daniel Bourdeau’s 1789 key (see Deboli 1789 ), completed in three frozen stages on 1788 despatches aligned with their cabinet decipherments. On a pair never used for learning (11 November 1788, 341 groups) it reads 0.862 of groups as sense, against a best of 0.199 for 200 shuffled keys. What it says A great dinner given for the famous privateer lately taken into Russian service, very probably John Paul Jones. Stackelberg at table, and Deboli voicing Polish unease at the King of Prussia’s designs. The reply is that the project of alliance is to be concluded at the Diet, “which we shall try to turn into a Confederation”, and Russian aid is promised when it is needed. An arrangement with Ostermann about Gdańsk. Still open 32 groups have no value in the key and 11 more have unsettled alternatives, so the share actually read is nearer 0.86 than the 96.6% of groups that have a value. The details are less secure than the gist. The images were not seen here. Credit Brice Dudout transcribed the despatch, extended the key and read it, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. Daniel Bourdeau’s 1789 key is the starting point.

The volume holds 112 cipher despatches of Deboli to the King, 4 January to 26 December 1788. The cabinet’s Polish decipherments are the same-date texts in ZbPop 417; every despatch has one except nos. 038 and 039, because the 417 volume jumps from 9 to 16 May. A decipherment of 3 June (417 k. 139) refers back to this letter: “the words of Bezborodko to me, which I reported to Your Majesty in my letter of 13 May”. Despatch 039 opens in a different table (the French 9933 table) and belongs in its own entry; it is not read here. The older code is deciphered too: the 4 and 11 January despatches align with their texts in 417, and the two codes alternate through the year, so the older-code despatches are existing decipherments.

Key K4 is the 1789 key with additions learned only on 1788 pairs: 12 values and 3 nulls (for example 1085 Osterman and 1420 Stackelberg), 6 values attested at least twice, and 11 automatic alternatives. Each stage was frozen, with its SHA-256 in the key header, before its validation pair was opened. The learning pairs are 20 and 30 May, 3 June, 29 August and 4 November; 8 August and 11 November 1788 are held out. The measure was written before it was computed: the cipher groups are aligned on the cabinet’s decipherment, and a group counts as read as sense if it is a null or its value equals the aligned stretch of clear text, to within two letters of ending or one of spelling. On 11 November K4 gives 0.862 of groups, 0.750 of exact words and 0.882 of characters, against shuffled-key maxima of 0.199, 0.131 and 0.289. The earlier key K3 gives 0.859 on the same pair and 0.836 on 8 August. The score plateaus near 0.86 even on learning pairs, partly because of the alignment and partly because the code writes stems and syllables while the cabinet supplied the endings from the sense. On 2 November 2026 we re-ran the contributor’s measure script on the 11 November pair and reproduced 0.750 of words and 0.882 of characters, with the same shuffled-key maxima; the groups-as-sense figure (0.862) was not re-run.

All 943 groups were transcribed, 911 of them (96.6%) with a key value. On the held-out measure the share read is lower, so this is a partial reading. The Polish text, with word division, endings and punctuation added and unread groups marked, and an English translation are under Full texts. A reader’s review of the Polish as sentences gave grade B: the first two thirds build a coherent account, and the last part has unread groups in most sentences.

32 groups have no value in K4, and 11 groups have alternatives (for example 637 list or ła , 360 ie or nie ) that the learning pairs do not settle. The end of the despatch is the weakest part, with unread groups in most sentences. A group-by-group human review of the despatch and of the held-out pair has not been done, and the images were not seen here. No printed edition of the 1788 despatches was found in a web search; the Institute of History’s Korespondencja polityczna Stanisława Augusta has Deboli volumes for 1781, 1782 and a 2015 volume, but none for 1788.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method · 3 despatches with no clear text (25 Mar, 10 May, 14 Dec 1789): key recovered based on adjacent plaintext (partial) · 103 despatches with a clear text in ZbPop 419/417: read from existing decipherment (complete) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial · 5,094 of 5,903 groups The letters 106 cipher despatches from Antoni Augustyn Deboli, the King’s envoy at St Petersburg, to Stanisław August, 2 January to 29 December 1789: the first year of the Four-Year Sejm. Where AGAD Warsaw, Zbiór Popielów 17, catalogued as letters in cipher with no decipherment. The clear texts are Zbiór Popielów 419, and for 22–29 December Zbiór Popielów 417, which is catalogued as 1788. The cipher A Polish syllabary of about 2,200 numbered groups in alphabetical order, with a band of punctuation groups (1775–1788) and a separate table, framed by 4000 9933, for French phrases. How it was deciphered 103 despatches have a clear text of the same date. Eleven pairs were aligned group by group and the code rebuilt from them; a blind test on a held-out pair confirmed the key. The key then deciphered most of the three despatches without a clear text (86.3% of their groups). What it says Potemkin, Branicki, the rumoured Ukrainian rising, Prussia’s offer to Poland, and Deboli asking to be recalled: “Śmiam o tym namienić WKrMci”. Still open In the three despatches without a clear text, 809 groups (13.7%) have no value that fits. The other 92 paired despatches were not transcribed; their clear texts exist.

Zbiór Popielów 17 holds Deboli’s despatches of 1789 in cipher: dotted number groups under a clear “Sire!”, closed by the French formula “Je suis avec le plus profond Respect” and the date. AGAD lists all 106 as “język: szyfr” with no decipherment, and none is written between the lines. Zbiór Popielów 419, “Deboli do króla 1789”, holds 105 Polish despatches of the same year, fair copies in a secretary’s hand signed “Deboli” and docketed with the day they arrived (“reçue le 17. / rep.”). 100 of the 106 cipher despatches have a piece of the same date there. The clear texts of 22, 25 and 29 December are filed with the January 1790 despatches at the end of Zbiór Popielów 417, a unit catalogued as 1788. That leaves three cipher despatches with no clear text: an addition of 25 March, and the despatches of 10 May and 14 December. “Ajouté au Duplicata seul, le 25. Mars.” The addition sent only with the duplicate, one of the three despatches with no clear text. It opens 1175 (Postscriptum) 453 1092 782 1145 931 637 … “Już po napisaniu listu”. Image: Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych, Warsaw, Zbiór Popielów 17 k. 77r, via the AGAD image server.

Eleven cipher despatches and their clear texts were transcribed in full (6 January, 1 and 12 May, 4, 8, 11, 15, 18, 22, 25 and 29 December; 22,161 cipher groups) and aligned group by group. Each cipher reads as its clear letter from the first word to the last, at a steady 1.9 groups per clear word. Repeats line up: in the 6 January letter “lokacya” is 623 461 2150 both times, “aby” is 1900 three times in one sentence, and “warunkami” and “warunkow” share 1560 1262 780. Latin and Italian words left in clear inside the cipher (“vulgo”, “Vederemo”, “per consequens”, “Qui vult finem vult media”) stand where they stand in the clear letters. The 15 May pair does not fit: its clear letter is far longer than the cipher, which carries only part of it. Whether the fair copies are clear duplicates or the cabinet’s decipherments is not settled here. The sessions on the 1790 and 1791 volumes of the same series, run the same day, read them as the cabinet’s decipherments, and the 1782 edition shows the cabinet deciphering Deboli’s letters on separate sheets. Either way the text of 103 despatches has been in the archive since 1789–90. The key was tested blind. Rebuilt from seven other pairs without the 18 December one, it gave a value to 95.6% of that despatch’s groups, and 91.4% of the decoded letters fall in the order of the real clear text: “Pisałem do WKMci pod dniem 15. currentis przez Pana du Hamela, który tegoż dnia z tąd wyiechał”. A second test failed, and its method was dropped: filling unknown groups from a Polish language model, inside their alphabetical bracket, got 5 to 8 of 171 hidden groups right.

A one-part syllabary: groups stand for letters, syllables and common words (8 do, 895 nie, 1353 się, 1489 tym, 1681 że, 2004 będzie, 1216 przez), and for some names and formulas (1182 posła, 1578 WKMci, 551 króla, 1307 Rossya). The numbers follow the alphabet in two runs: from 1 to about 1770 the values run a to z (461 ka < 466 ko < 623 lo < 692 mi < 780 n < 895 nie < 961 on < 1262 ru < 1559 w < 1560 wa), and from about 1870 a second run starts again at a (1873 a, 1900 aby, 1926 ale, 1988 bo, 2059 by, 2150 cya). The whole band 1775–1788 carries no letters: 1786 alone occurs 649 times in the transcriptions and is the commonest group in December, though it never appears on 6 January. The 1791 decipherment shows it is punctuation (1786 a comma, 1775 a full stop). A letter written under a group (355a, 873c) marks a variant. In the despatches of 22 and 29 December, runs of groups between 2300 and 3409 are framed by 4000 9933. The alignment puts French text exactly inside each frame: “quoiqu’il crie avant qu’on l’ecorche”, “droit au solide alloit Bartholomée” and “insinuez à Sa Majesté le Roi qu’il prenne confiance dans l’Abassadeur relativement à cette affaire d’Alliance”. So the frame switches to a French table for quoted French. It is not the second Polish code of 1791. The keys filed in the same fonds, the “Cyfra polska” sent to Deboli in 1783 (Zbiór Popielów 444) and the French cipher of 1780 (451), are not online. The key rebuilt from the eleven pairs anchors 630 groups. The 1791 session’s tables for the same code, built independently, agree with it where both have a group, up to accents and syllable breaks.

Już po napisaniu listu przychodzi mi na myśl następuiaca uwaga, to iest, że we zwyczay to u siebie wprowadzę, często w listach moich po{wta}[?]ć te zapytanie: co robi Hetman Branicki. […] Przy tym wszystkim, w czym proszę WKMci o sekret: Xże de Nassau tu pisze, że Branicki iest ieden z nayprzywiązańszych do Rossyi. Przebóg! Te[n] Xże de Nassau, który {1407} {672b} odebraniu WKMci, nie miał czasu respons WKMci na odprawie […] A co do Rossyi w ogólności, to ia {437}ie wiem, że {108} nowey woyny nie życzy. “It has just occurred to me, having written the letter, to make it a habit to ask in my letters what Hetman Branicki is doing. […] With all that, about which I beg Your Majesty for secrecy: the Prince of Nassau writes here that Branicki is one of the most devoted to Russia. Good God! […] As for Russia in general, I know that she wishes no new war.” 10 May 1789 Potemkin has left for the army (“Już tedy dnia wczorayszego z rana X[iążę] Potemkin puścił się w podroż”). Deboli reports long talks with the Prince of Nassau-Siegen about the rumoured rising in Ukraine (“bunt”), about Branicki, and about the withdrawal of the Russian commissariats from Poland. He has seen a letter of Potemkin to Markov “w którym wyraża, że ofiaruie”. Stackelberg reported “że król pruski ofiaruie swoią pomoc Polsce”. Someone had written to Potemkin “że WKMci chciałeś Branickiego otruć”. The King’s past dealings with Repnin, the Primate and the see of Kraków are rehearsed, and Deboli closes a paragraph: “że to teraz pora, aby się Polska podźwignęła, a resztę Panie Boże robi”. 14 December 1789 This despatch, in another hand, mixes cipher with 39 clear Polish phrases. Potemkin had his courier tell the Empress “że przeieżdżaiac przez nasz kray” he met rudeness and had to fight for horses; Russian couriers had been given escorts in Poland “dla bezpiecznieyszego przeiazdu”; Stackelberg kept reporting against Deboli. Deboli asks to be recalled: “iuż od roku prawie będąc tu … Śmiam o tym namienić WKrMci, abyś zawczasu … kogo na zastąpienie mię destynował in petto”. He asks the King to burn the letter and to answer in a separate packet “abym go sam desz[yfr]ował”.

10 May: 666 of 4,393 groups unread. Groups with no value in the eleven pairs, or whose aligned value does not fit in place. The hand writes 0 and 8 alike, and 154 groups were transcribed with a doubt. 14 December: 130 of 1,222 groups unread, for the same reasons, in another hand. 25 March: 13 of 288 groups unread (1407, 518, 437, 108, 2140b and a few fragments), each once. The 92 paired despatches not transcribed: their clear texts exist in Zbiór Popielów 419. Grades: values from the key are C (from known-plaintext letters); readings from context and the alphabetical bracket are I (1175 Postscriptum, 2161 często, 1287 respons, 2094 czy, 1369 śl-, 1711 zal-, 2009 bie, and 1586 wiadomość, 48 dość, 1612 wyraż- from the 1791 tables). More pairs near May and a second look at the doubtful digits would narrow the gaps.

Do ostatniego listu mego, w ktorym opisałem daną z tąd na insynuacyą Posła Hiszpańskiego odpowiedź, przydać potrzeba, że względem Porty Rossya domaga się od Hiszpanii aby wyiednała nayprzod wypuszczenie P. Bułhakowa, y że zagadzaiąc tym sposobem obrazę uczynioną Rossyi, Porta zrobi sobie wstęp do dalszych negocyacyi. W tych dniach kilku kuryerow przybiegło z Wiednia wkrotce ieden po drugim. Kobentzl był wczoray zatrudniony wysłaniem iednego od siebie. Pruska partya widząc tu cieszących się z wzięcia Oczakowa, dogryza ucinkami, że na wiosnę da się widzieć, kto się będzie cieszył. Sam na swoie uszy słyszał[em] mowiącego o tym Sekretarza Pruskiego. Uczyniłem podług rozkazu WKMci względem Posła Angielskiego, ktorego widziałem zmartwienie z mego opowiedzenia o Jego następcy. Domyślił się zaraz że wina Haylesa w tym, że się dał wciągnąć przez drugich. Obiaśniłem mu że to tak iest. Moie przywiązanie do Krola Jmci, rzekł on, niebędzie zmnieyszone przez konnexyą interessow, y przyrzekł, że będzie pisał do Haylesa: co mienił bydź przyzwoitszym, niż pisanie do Dworu. Po odebraniu listu WKMci de 24. elapsi, nie zdarzyło mi się z nikim mowić o interessach, bo moie teraz iest prawidło nie narażać się na to: Będęć ia wiedział, iakie maią wiadomości o Branickim, ale ia pierwszy rozgłaszać nie będę moich. Jam się z tego mocno radował, że z Strony WKMci nikt się nieodezwał do wszczętey przez Biskupa Płockiego materyi na Sessyi 22. Xbris, bo też prawdziwie nie dobrze ten Prałat, tym ktorzy brali pensye dał zasadę, czerpiąc ią w słowach przysięgi 1776. przepisaney. Ta restrykcya nikomu służyć niemoże, za ulgę sumnienia. Jeżeliby tylko nie więcey, iak w tym przypisać Oppozycyi zapał, że tych sięga, ktorzy pensye (: pod co Biskupa Naruszewicza podciągać niemożna; bo drugim Litterata tytuł niesłuży:) zagraniczne brali, to by niebyło w Oppozycyi żadney winy. Ja Boga proszę, żeby innych dziwactw poprzestała, a wzięła się do tego, co iest nayg[ł]ownieyszym, y bez czego Polska szczęśliwą bydź niezdoła, to iest: do ustanowienia podatkow y Woyska przez połowę tego, co Woiewoda Sieradzki podał w proiekcie. Przyięcie legionu od Radziwiłła niebędzie złe z następuiącemi warunkami: aby nie on, ale Kommissya Officyerow kreowała; aby dziecko niebyło Generałem, aby lokacya w dobrach Radziwiłła w ten czas była, kiedy służba wyciągać niebędzie postania gdzie indziey Legionu całkiem lub częściami. Zabespieczona przez tych warunkow lokacya, pod Szefostwem iednego z Radziwiłłow, iuż iest wielkie beneficium za Ofiarę. Armat; że po Swiętach, Sapieha wielką wszczął burzę przeciwko Rossyi, ale że Hetman zachował się w milczeniu. # k.143v (image 0168, left) Z tego opowiedzenia, iuż obeymuiącego co się stało po swiętach, wniosłem, że musiał nadeyść Kuryer, lub sztafeta: o czym Krzyżanowski nieumiał mi powiedzieć. Tuszył mi o bliskim swoim wysłaniu, że miał bydź tegoż dnia prezentowanym Imperatorowey, od ktorey to rozkazanym było; y był ow Krzyżanowski _bonae spei_, że za przybyciem Jego Branicki upamięta się. Jezeli się to ziści, czysta będzie konkluzya, że wszystko zebrawszy, musiała bydź iakaś taiemnica, niewiadoma może nikomu więcey, iak Xciu Potemkinowi, y że co Branicki czynił, była iedna komedya, ktorą znać mu kazą porzucić, z przyczyny iż się może wiele scen w nią wchodzących nieudało. Samo tedy ustanie tey Komedyi, ieżeli nastąpi po przyiezdzie Krzyżanowskiego /: na ktory należy się mieć baczność:/ będzie dowod do suspicyi y do dalszey ostrożności. Ostermann powiedał we Wtorek Ministrowi Neapolitańskiemu, iż tego dnia odebrali wiadomość o dwudniowych sprzeczkach, ktore trwały na Seymie; że to klika Sapiehy, y że nic nieskonkludowano. Rozszerzył się Ostermann z pochwałami dla WKMci, wielbiąc Jego rostropność y zręczność, ktorą nadrabiasz, y żeś ią mianowicie w tym razie pokazał. W mowie Ostermana niezbywało na nadziei, iż się to postaremu dobrze skończy; a na to wszystko Minister Neapolitański twierdził mu, iż to będzie skutek moderacyi, ktorey z[?] # k.144r (image 0168, right) używaią. To tedy, co wyżey wyraiam, wiem o naszym Seymie, czekaiąc co mi poczta przyniesie. Z Szwedami na tym tu przestaią, co do krokow Nieprzyiacielskich, że im oddaią wet za wet. Oni byli dawniey zachwycili pikietę Rossyiską, za to im odpłacono, y takowy ma bydź plan, to iest odporny. Że trzy stany ciągle Krolowi sprzyiaią, maią tu pewne wiadomości; on przeto swoie zrobił, co do formy rządu; choć się stan szlachecki będzie protestował, ale też wiedzą, że przygotowania Woienne zwolniały; a Pruski Poseł powiedział im w tych dniach iż Krol Szwedzki zdaie się bardziey słuchać perswazyi Ministrow Hiszpańskiego y Pruskiego. Oni tu dobrze pozmuią[?] że to są lenitiva, a że finalnie pokoy z Szwecyą będzie wstrzymywany, aby go ułożyć razem z Tureckim. Jakiem iuż doniosł WKMci, że Xże Potemkin życzący pokoju, zaczął od przymilania się Anglii, tak y teraz to potwierdzam, przydaiąc, iż iuż w tym, z czym się tu przed Anglią, zbliżaiąc się niby do niey, oswiadczano, miała się Anglia porozumieć z Dworem Berlinskim, y czekaią tu Kuryera z Londynu, do przybycia ktorego zwleka Xże Potemkin swoy wyiazd. Wszystko to ma się dotąd utrzymywać w granicach partycypacyi żądaney do pokoju, z Strony Dworow Londyńskiego # k.144v (image 0169, left) y Berlińskiego, a nie żeby rozeyść się miał alians z Cesarzem, czego Imperatorowa niechce. Są poznaki, że iuż w insynuacyach Dwory zakroiły na demoliowanie Oczakowa; na co tu podobno przystaną. Zgoła są to ieszcze z Strony Dworow maiaczenia, tu się okazuie co raz większa nuda z okazyi teraznieyszey Woyny, a z resztą kampania za pasem. Maią tu mieć wiadomość od Dunaju, że Tureckie Woysko zbliża się przeciw Korpusowi Rossyiskiemu. Ow list o ktorym doniosłem ostatnią Pocztą, był pisany nie do Imperatorowy, lecz do Potemkina, przez ktorego był iey podsunięty, bywszy zapewne ułożonym na ten koniec. Branicki ma się użalać, iż go zostawiono bez kommendy. Powiedziała w prawdzie Imperatorowa czytaiąc: Ten pisał niewart y iednym żołnierzem kommenderować, y że to dziwna iest rzecz, iakie czyni protestacye przywiązania do Rossyi, a wszystko na wspak robi. Dowodzą te słowa, iak pierwsze pokuszenie udało się; ale mię to ieszcze niewywodzi z obawy aby ich więcey takich niebyło. Już tedy y tu y w Warszawie wychodzi prawda na wierzch, że Branickiemu chce się dopaść Kommendy. Bog wie, co za dalszy układ. W tym prawdy # k.145r (image 0169, right) dociekać potrzeba; ale ani się iey WKMość domacasz od Stackelberga, ani się ona tu nie wysuwie[?] przez Jego depesze. W nie prędzey wnidzie Xże Stanisław, lub kto inny, za iaki uczynek mowy, niżeli Branicki za nayszkodliwsze samemu interessowi Rossyi kabały. O tych się odemnie nayprędzey[?] dowiaduią, iako też y o drugich anekdotach; a w moich oczach, co raz więcey stawia się obiektow, w ktorych widzę, że Stackelberg rozumi się z Potemkinem, y że to co w początkach Seymu robione przez Partyzantow Branickiego uchodziło w myslach WKMci /: iakeś Mi to wyraził:/ za narzędzone przez Potemkina dla zmartwienia Stackelberga, miało inną zasadę, ktorą rożne gradacye, często mi, nawet przez Posła Duńskiego wytykane, oznaczały, to iest: że się Stackelberg rozumiał z Branickim. Teraz tu Potemkin iest Protektorem Synow Stackelberga. Starszego bierze z sobą, a młodszy ma bydź Kamerjunkrem. Krzyżanowski chełpił się wczoray przedemną, iż to on iest ten, ktory ich wkręcił do Xięcia. Temie wygadywał przedemną, iż Xże Potemkin chciałby nawet, aby Jabłonowscy trafili do Lisianki &c. Kiedym był zakiem, to takowe powieści dobre byby były do łudzenia mię. # k.145r catchword "Zgoła" (= first word of k.145v), kept in the text below. # k.145v (image 0170, left) Zgoła ia się teraz nie do Ministerium uwodzę podeyrzliwością, ale ku Potemkinowi y Stackelbergowi. Miey go WKMć za Ambassadora to dosyć będzie do systematycznych układow; ale niemiey go WKMć za Konfidenta, chyba że masz o tego dla siebie szczerości przeważaiące dowody, nad te, z ktorych ia wnoszę, że w nim na niey schodzi względem WKMci y Xcia Prymasa. Serce mi się kraie widząc, iż z iedney strony tu malował, że WKMość dążysz koniecznie do powiększenia swoiey władzy; że Xże Prymas chcąc zatrzymać Biskupstwo Krakowskie z Prymasowstwem, daie przyczynę do niechęci; a z drugiey strony wciągał Xcia Prymasa, aby do tego celował. Na wszystkie wczorayszę mowy Krzyżanowskiego bijące na Hetmana, powiedziałem grzecznie z obowiązkiem doniesienia o tym Xięciu, że Pa Hetmanowi będą dogadzali, gdy niebędzie chciał wynosić się nad drugich; że Oginski człowiek zacny, a niedrze się do Kommendy; że Radziwiłł iuż po zmodyfikowaniu swoich kondycyi, widząc, że przez obawę, aby się niestał mocnym, niechcą przyiąć Jego ofiary, pokazał się skłonnym; a za cożby ieden Branicki miał mieć przywiley, przeciwko ktoremu sam będę animował WKMość. Przyiazd tego Krzyżanowskiego do Warszawy strasznie ciekawy. Niema iechać aż po Niedzieli, y powiedział # k.146r (image 0170, right) mi, że wszystkie listy gotowe, a chodzi tylko o ieden, ktory Xże ma pisać swoią ręką. Miłościwy Panie! Znoś się WKMość dobrze w tym punkcie nie z Stackelbergiem, ale z Narodem; bo bez stałości WKMci będzie domowa woyna, y te konsekwencye, ktore wyłuszczyłem w liscie moim de 6. Febrii. Do Systema Rossyi /: rozumie się ogulnie wziętey:) dość będzie, aby Polska przeciwko niey niepowstała. Ja się boię akcessorow, przeciwko ktorym niezabespieczy się WKMość inaczey, iak tylko strzegąc się podeyscia, y iednocząc się z tym wszystkim, co nie iest partyą Branickiego. Wczoray /: we Czwartek:) przyiechał Kuryer z Wiednia do Cobenzla, donoszący o niebespieczeństwie Cesarza. Jam zaś wiedział co Noailles pisał do Segura, iż choć Doktorowie taili, niebyło prawie więcey nadziei. Ktory z Nas /: bo to sobie ieszcze powiadano po cichu:) o tym wiedział, mocno był tym strwożony, y iest czym. Takowego uprzedzenia zbiiać formalnie niemożna było, boć Pruski y Angielski Ministrowie maią swoie o tym wiadomości, na ktorych polegaią. Ponieważ konwersacya moia z Kellerem była w oczach Podkanclerzego, gdym się został u niego na wieczor, pytał mię się o czym była kwestya w tey konwersacyi. Those who [...] thought to themselves what sort of [...] Prince Potemkin [is] before us, and how cunningly he made shift to set the Empress against us. Stackelberg, having formerly written here through me (*as I have already reported*), lately, two posts running, repeated his [complaints] about me, accusing me *not only of this, that he can [tell] many things (as he judges)*, but [that I] report to Your Majesty [...], and that even to the Deputation he writes [...] that I had gone over to Russia from the opposition [?], hoping that Stackelberg would be [...] by this means. [...] He was answered the first time that if he reports anything of the kind, in which he [...] distorted what they could tell me here *ministerially*, they could then accuse me of [mischief]. **k. 297r.** And the second time he was expressly forbidden to write anything about me, for they here [have] noticed nothing [to suggest] that I do anything bad, and know me of old. When I learned all this privately, I [stifled] it in myself, *and not even in thought* [...], remembering well that all [...] subject [...]; to show it would *have been to step outside the caution by which I must constantly proceed in my department*. I have won myself a good opinion [...]; this he cannot impair by writing to the Deputation that the Sejm [...]. Had I written otherwise, I would have been a traitor to my country. And so for our [...] nobody can draw anything out of me. With the help, then, of the good opinion they have of me, maintaining myself so far, I shall try not to lose it. **k. 297v.** To that end secrecy is needed, and on my side [...]. I have been here nearly a year beyond my wish, *but for this one consideration, that* my [position?] does not allow me to ask for my recall in these times, when now, with God's help, [...] the Sejm [...]; then [...] my personal affairs, *which absolutely require* that I leave this post. *I make bold to mention it to Your Royal Majesty*, so that you may in good time [...] *destine* someone to replace me *in petto*. That will be enough [for now], for I shall keep this intention of mine secret until there is [occasion] *to reveal it*. [...] Your Majesty, every [...] which [...] in naming to my post such a one as Your Majesty would not wish; I always counsel [...] persons *whom Your Majesty could fully satisfy*. **k. 298r.** Whether I shall succeed, with caution and skill, as I have so far, in freeing Your Majesty from all importunity from here of the Prince, who is not liked here, and his intrigues, in which [...]. *It is impossible, Most Gracious Lord, that* in my post [...] without making [...]; *and I contented myself with assuring myself* [...] the secret [...] which did not reach me in this.
