Transcribed from the scans 27 Oct 2026. # k.390r My tu mamy za rzeczy pewne, 1o że zawsze zakładaiąc za kondycyą wypuszczenie Bułhakowa, Rossya ma wszelką względem kondycyi pokoju moderacyą, y że będzie się kontentowała Oczakowem. 2o że Xże Potemkin /: co iest postaremu duszonym w sekrecie:/ ma zamiar wynieść na Hospodara Moldawskiego hołdującą iednak Porcie, ale z warunkiem nieodmienności siebie na tym Urzędzie, y przyścia onego do swoich Sukcessorow. Kogo z nich obierze, to kwestya. Może dzieci Branickiego; albo też tym łudzić będzie Oyca. 3o mamy także za pewne, że Cesarz oprocz Belgradu chce zatrzymać Wołoszczyznę. Partya Pruska rozumi, że tym wzbudzi zazdrość w tuteyszym Dworze; ia zaś iescze dotąd pokombinować niemogę, czyli # k.390v względem nabycia Moldawii Xże Potemkin rozumi się z Cesarzem, czyli też że szuka inney pomocy, ktorą, iest to zdanie niektorych, że mu pod ręką obiecuie Anglia; są zaś poznali że Imperatorowa sprzyia temu Hospodarstwu. 4o zaprzeczaią tu stale, żeby dotąd miały wyiść od Porty iakowe względem pokoiu propozycye. Trzeba zobaczyć na co się Porta determinować będzie, po odebraniu wiadomości o poniesionych klęskach. 5o Tu same Ministerium iest w tym mniemaniu, że nietak przez zazdrość przeciwko Moskwie, iak przez zazdroszczenie Cesarzowi, będą drugie potencye używały wszelkich sposobow do oddalenia pokoiu; y z tąd w Ministerium nawet pochodzi wątpliwość, czyli pokoy stanie tey Zimy. 6o Rozumieią iednak, że Łatwieyszym[?] uczynią Cesarza zamieszki Brabanckie; ktore pod wszelkiemi uważaią widokami, na tym się postaremu skończą, że się w tamtych Prowincyach zostanie Cesarzowi cień samowładztwa; bo Anglia, a w Hollandyi Partya Stathouderska są potrwożone, y boią się aby zamieszki Brabanckie nie sięgnęły do Hollandyi, gdzie iest wiele malkontentow. W Anglii miano uczynić Rewitzkiemu takową w materyi zamieszkow Brabanckich deklaracyą, z ktorey Dwor Wiedeński może # k.391r bydź kontent, y wnosić, że tylko do pewnego punktu da Anglia doyść tym zamieszkom, a że iey polityka niedozwala zakrawać iey nato, aby te Prowincye wyrwać z pod Panowania Domu Austryackiego. To zdanie słyszałem od Podkanclerzego Ostermana. 7o Zastanawia Nas negocyacya Alopeusa; wyglądamy iey skutku, y u wielu widzę te mniemanie, że nieuniknięmy straty Gdańska: czego niebędziemy mieli przyczyny załować, ieżeli ta ofiara doprowadzi do pożądanego skutku te obroty Nasze, ktore WKMć wyszczegulniasz w liscie de 2. Xbris. Ja zawsze wracam się do swego argumentu, iż dla uskuteczniania tych obrotow, trzeba wzmocnienia Polski woyskiem, bez czego daremne będzie celowanie do uszczęśliwienia iey. Qui vult finem, vult media, a to iest iedyny srzodek; drugi utrzymania teraz u Nas wewnętrzney spokoyności. Przy każdey okazyi wmawiam w Xcia de Nassau, mianowicie że my rostropnością[?] się rządzić będziemy, y niedamy się wciągnąć w Woynę. Odpowiedział mi na to w przeszłą Srzodę, iż przez wdzięczność ktorą ma Polszcze, życzy mocno tego. Prawda, rzekł on, moglibyście mieć z początku, iakowe sukcessa, ale naczym by się to skończyło? W tym trafił w moie zdanie. Juzem WKMci doniosł, że po odebraniu tu wiadomości, o tym # k.391v (image 0468) powtornym reskrypcie do Kurlandyi, nie są wcale z niego kontenci, boby radzi byli, żeby za pierwszym reskryptem rzeczy zostały się in statu quo. Howen pisał przeszłą pocztą do Derpera, że ich ten reskrypt mocno potrwożył; że niewiedzą dokąd się udać o aggrawacye, ktore im czyni Xże; że on Howen niedząc łaskawość WKMci dla Szlachty Kurlandzkiey wstrzymuie umysły od rezolucyi udania się do Seymu; że on Howen wie, że go czernią przed WKMcią. Że smie iednak supplikować WKMci, abyś, gdy zachodzą na niego skargi, raczył kazać się go zapytać o explikacyą; że on ią da na wszystko przekonywaiącą, że wszystkie swoie kroki do tego stosuie, aby umysły w Kurlandyi naywiększą dla WKMci okazywały powolność. Podiąłem się donieść to wszystko WKMci. A nieźle będzie, że WKMć wiedzieć będziesz, iż się do Mnie udaią, znaiąc mię, że nieiestem parcyalny, a tandem w sprzyianiu teraz Szlachcie, muszę się stosować do teraznieyszego geniuszu tuteyszego u wielu przeważaiącego. Powiadano Mi, że Xiążę, ktorego Oycu dane było pozwolenie używania dla swoich Zołnierzy feldzeigu y kokardy Rossyiskiey odmienił teraz iedno y drugie na kolory Pruskie. Passe # k.392r (image 0469) gdyby na Polskie. Już po napisanym liście pewna Osoba chciała we mnie, pod postacią przestrogi, wmowić, że WKMć za posrzednictwem Xcia de Nassau, masz sekretną z Imperatorową korrespondencyą y żeś niedawno odebrał list od tey Monarchini; tudzież że WKMć czynisz iakieś Osobom Rossyiskim dary: niedodano, czy tu, czy w Warszawie. Ja na tę poufałą niby przestrogę nic więcey nieodpowiedziałem, iak tylko że temu niewierzę; że niemam śladow korrespondencyi WKMci z Imperatorową; y przydałem dla tym większego okazania przeświadczenia mego w tey mierze, iż gdybym wpadł na te ślady, nie zostawało by mi się nic, iak widząc, że nie mam ufności u WKMci prosić o Moy rappel. Miarkuiąc po gatunku Osoby od ktorey mam tę konfidencyą, mogę się domyślać, iż iest przygotowana dla szepnienia nie iednemu w ucho u Nas, aby wzniecić diffidencyą w kraju przeciwko WKMci. Więc mam sobie za powinność ostrzedz o tym Deboli. # Notes: secretary's hand, signed "Deboli" by the writer. Trzeba zobaczyć na co się Porta determinować będzie, po odebraniu wiadomości o poniesionych klęskach. 5o Tu same Ministerium iest w tym mniemaniu, że nietak przez zazdrość przeciwko Moskwie, iak przez zazdroszczenie Cesarzowi, będą drugie potencye używały wszelkich sposobow do oddalenia pokoiu; y z tąd w Ministerium nawet pochodzi wątpliwość, czyli pokoy stanie tey Zimy. 6o Rozumieią iednak, że Łatwieyszym[?] uczynią Cesarza zamieszki Brabanckie; ktore pod wszelkiemi uważaią widokami, na tym się postaremu skończą, że się w tamtych Prowincyach zostanie Cesarzowi cień samowładztwa; bo Anglia, a w Hollandyi Partya Stathouderska są potrwożone, y boią się aby zamieszki Brabanckie nie sięgnęły do Hollandyi, gdzie iest wiele malkontentow. W Anglii miano uczynić Rewitzkiemu takową w materyi zamieszkow Brabanckich deklaracyą, z ktorey Dwor Wiedeński może # k.391r bydź kontent, y wnosić, że tylko do pewnego punktu da Anglia doyść tym zamieszkom, a że iey polityka niedozwala zakrawać iey nato, aby te Prowincye wyrwać z pod Panowania Domu Austryackiego. To zdanie słyszałem od Podkanclerzego Ostermana. 7o Zastanawia Nas negocyacya Alopeusa; wyglądamy iey skutku, y u wielu widzę te mniemanie, że nieuniknięmy straty Gdańska: czego niebędziemy mieli przyczyny załować, ieżeli ta ofiara doprowadzi do pożądanego skutku te obroty Nasze, ktore WKMć wyszczegulniasz w liscie de 2. Xbris. Ja zawsze wracam się do swego argumentu, iż dla uskuteczniania tych obrotow, trzeba wzmocnienia Polski woyskiem, bez czego daremne będzie celowanie do uszczęśliwienia iey. Qui vult finem, vult media, a to iest iedyny srzodek; drugi utrzymania teraz u Nas wewnętrzney spokoyności. Przy każdey okazyi wmawiam w Xcia de Nassau, mianowicie że my rostropnością[?] się rządzić będziemy, y niedamy się wciągnąć w Woynę. Odpowiedział mi na to w przeszłą Srzodę, iż przez wdzięczność ktorą ma Polszcze, życzy mocno tego. Prawda, rzekł on, moglibyście mieć z początku, iakowe sukcessa, ale naczym by się to skończyło? W tym trafił w moie zdanie. Juzem WKMci doniosł, że po odebraniu tu wiadomości, o tym # k.391v (image 0468) powtornym reskrypcie do Kurlandyi, nie są wcale z niego kontenci, boby radzi byli, żeby za pierwszym reskryptem rzeczy zostały się in statu quo. Howen pisał przeszłą pocztą do Derpera, że ich ten reskrypt mocno potrwożył; że niewiedzą dokąd się udać o aggrawacye, ktore im czyni Xże; że on Howen niedząc łaskawość WKMci dla Szlachty Kurlandzkiey wstrzymuie umysły od rezolucyi udania się do Seymu; że on Howen wie, że go czernią przed WKMcią. Że smie iednak supplikować WKMci, abyś, gdy zachodzą na niego skargi, raczył kazać się go zapytać o explikacyą; że on ią da na wszystko przekonywaiącą, że wszystkie swoie kroki do tego stosuie, aby umysły w Kurlandyi naywiększą dla WKMci okazywały powolność. Podiąłem się donieść to wszystko WKMci. A nieźle będzie, że WKMć wiedzieć będziesz, iż się do Mnie udaią, znaiąc mię, że nieiestem parcyalny, a tandem w sprzyianiu teraz Szlachcie, muszę się stosować do teraznieyszego geniuszu tuteyszego u wielu przeważaiącego. Powiadano Mi, że Xiążę, ktorego Oycu dane było pozwolenie używania dla swoich Zołnierzy feldzeigu y kokardy Rossyiskiey odmienił teraz iedno y drugie na kolory Pruskie. Passe # k.392r (image 0469) gdyby na Polskie. Już po napisanym liście pewna Osoba chciała we mnie, pod postacią przestrogi, wmowić, że WKMć za posrzednictwem Xcia de Nassau, masz sekretną z Imperatorową korrespondencyą y żeś niedawno odebrał list od tey Monarchini; tudzież że WKMć czynisz iakieś Osobom Rossyiskim dary: niedodano, czy tu, czy w Warszawie. Ja na tę poufałą niby przestrogę nic więcey nieodpowiedziałem, iak tylko że temu niewierzę; że niemam śladow korrespondencyi WKMci z Imperatorową; y przydałem dla tym większego okazania przeświadczenia mego w tey mierze, iż gdybym wpadł na te ślady, nie zostawało by mi się nic, iak widząc, że nie mam ufności u WKMci prosić o Moy rappel. Miarkuiąc po gatunku Osoby od ktorey mam tę konfidencyą, mogę się domyślać, iż iest przygotowana dla szepnienia nie iednemu w ucho u Nas, aby wzniecić diffidencyą w kraju przeciwko WKMci. Więc mam sobie za powinność ostrzedz o tym Deboli. # Notes: secretary's hand, signed "Deboli" by the writer. No. 3 on Klaus Schmeh’s Top 50. Where Originals at the Brewster Memorial Library, Essex County Historical Society. Three passages (969 glyphs of 333 types) were transcribed here in September 2026. The cipher Probably a French syllabary, one glyph per spoken syllable. The cipher poem is twenty lines of rhyming couplets, and the last glyph of each line is identical within 9 of the 10 couplets. How it was tried Searches were tested first on planted texts. No match in 7,821 couplet windows of French verse; the four lines of No. 10 do not encode the poem written under them; Moore and Debosnys’s own English copies were excluded; a syllable-model solver recovers nothing at this length. Why it resists Pinning a key for this many glyphs needs roughly 800 to 2,000 glyphs; the whole surviving corpus is about 1,200. Still open The key, and any source text. A clear copy, draft or key sheet in his papers, the original he copied from, or Sektu’s unpublished 2017 transcription would help. Credit Brian (Sektu blog, 2017) transcribed the corpus and proposed French syllables; Matthew Brown (2021) showed his clear poems are copied; Nick Pelling (2015) noticed the initials in No. 9.

More than the usual summaries say. In 2017 Brian, who writes the Sektu blog, transcribed the whole corpus (1,188 glyphs of 425 types), decomposed the glyphs into sub-glyphs with a small grammar, and proposed that they are French syllables, the tilde marking nasalisation. That transcription was never published. An earlier version of this project’s tracker presented the glyphs’ systematic composition as a new observation; it was Sektu’s, and is credited to him here. Two further leads were public. Matthew Brown showed in 2021 that almost every clear “poem” Debosnys left is copied, mostly from Thomas Moore, which suggested the enciphered texts might be copies too. And Nick Pelling noticed in 2015 that passage No. 9 holds the clear initials H. D. D. L. M. the cipher poem chance under 10 −5 The “monographe verse” is twenty lines of rhyming couplets Lines 1–4 of the monographe verse (detail). Lines 1 and 2 end in the same curl, lines 3 and 4 in the same dotted X. Image: Brewster Memorial Library, Essex County Historical Society, Debosnys papers, the monographe verse. The last glyph of each line repeats in pairs. It is identical within 9 of the 10 couplets , and the tenth pair shares its base and differs only in where a cross is placed. Across couplet boundaries (lines 2 and 3, 4 and 5, and so on) it matches in none of 9 . Even if any two glyphs matched a fifth of the time, nine of ten would come up by chance about four times in a million. It is the flat AABB rhyme of French couplet verse, and the rhyme of the first couplet returns in the ninth, as a sound would. the unit two independent lines One glyph is one French syllable If identical final glyphs carry the rhyme, glyphs stand for sound. Which size of sound is settled by comparing the poem with 279-unit samples of real verse: unit per line types in 279 most frequent Debosnys glyphs 13.9 111 9.0% French syllables 13.5 166 3.8% English syllables 10.2 172 4.5% French words 8.6 174 4.7% French letters 37.4 26 14.7% Only syllables fit the line length, and the rhymes decide the language. In real rhyming couplets the final syllable is spelled identically 61% of the time in French verse but only 31% in Moore’s English. Nine identical endings in ten would happen with English syllables about three times in ten thousand. So the plaintext is most likely French, although nearly everything Debosnys is known to have copied was English. The text behaves like language: repeated glyph pairs occur at twice the rate of a shuffle of the same glyphs. Two details do not fit a plain syllabary. The dotted X is too frequent for a single syllable at 9%, and it appears doubled five times, perhaps one sign in two parts. the corpus one system Three passages, one script Transcribed glyph by glyph from the scans: the twenty-line poem (279 glyphs), the four cipher lines on page No. 10 (99) and the prose passage No. 9 (597), 969 glyphs of 333 types. The passages share their inventory (47 of the poem’s 111 glyph types recur in No. 9, covering 58% of the poem), and the dotted X leads both at 9.0% and 8.2%. The weak point is identity: whether two similar composites are the same sign. The transcription files record each decision, and the least legible line lies under a water stain.

Every search here was first run on a planted text (real French encoded the same way, with noise) to show that it would find a hit if one were there. None of the real searches produced one. the poem on the same page excluded The four cipher lines of No. 10 do not encode the French poem written under them The obvious crib: about 93 glyphs above a clear poem whose first eight lines have about 93 syllables, and both end in a question mark. Aligning glyphs to syllables and scoring how consistently each glyph maps, the real pairing scores 58, the same as random French verse (median 59). A planted encoding of the same poem scores 86 to 88 against a control maximum of 80. The lines are more likely the end of No. 9. French verse excluded No match in 7,821 couplet windows of French poetry Twenty-eight volumes (Racine, Corneille, Molière, Voltaire, Boileau, Chénier, Hugo, Musset, Gautier, Baudelaire, Verlaine) were cut into every 20-line window in rhyming couplets and aligned against the poem line by line. A planted encoding of one real window ranks first of 7,821 by a wide margin; the poem’s best matches form a smooth tail with no outlier. The same holds for Delille’s verse translation of the Aeneid , prompted by the lines of Virgil copied beneath the poem. what he copied excluded Not Moore, not Stoddart, not his own English copies Line-length profile and couplet structure against Moore’s complete poems, Lalla Rookh , Stoddart and Debosnys’s own clear poems: best fits at the chance level for seven thousand windows, and Moore’s couplet lines run three or four syllables short. letters, not syllables excluded The glyphs are not stacks of letters Taking each glyph’s component marks as letters in some order and searching for the key, the real glyph order scores no better than the same glyphs shuffled, in French or English.

Ciphertext-only attack needs enough text to pin the key down. For a substitution, that threshold is the unicity distance : the key’s information divided by the language’s redundancy per symbol. French verse syllables carry 7.7 bits each under a bigram model; a key for 333 glyph types, drawn from a syllable inventory of 600 to 9,000, carries 3,100 to 4,400 bits. The threshold comes out at about 800 to 2,000 glyphs , even with a perfect model and a perfect transcription. The whole surviving corpus is about 1,200. The experiment agrees. Real French verse was encoded as a clean syllabary, one glyph per syllable and no noise, and attacked with a syllable language model trained on 1.15 million syllables: glyphs glyph types text recovered guessing the commonest syllable 1,000 364 0.0% 3.2% 5,000 944 5.4% 3.3% 20,000 1,810 4.3% 2.9% At the Debosnys length the solver recovers nothing. A stronger solver would do better on far longer texts, but none can beat the information limit. If Debosnys wrote a syllabary, as the rhymes indicate, only a crib can recover the key.

His papers. The Essex County Historical Society holds the originals. A clear copy of the poem, a draft, or a key sheet among them would give the key directly. The source text. If the poem or No. 9 is copied like his clear poems, finding the original is the whole job. The search tool is built and tested; the likeliest ground not yet covered is popular French song and verse of the 1860s and 70s. Sektu’s transcription. An independent transcription of the full corpus would settle the glyph-identity decisions that weaken every test. Francesc Climent, called Çapera, was Benedict XIII’s chamberlain and treasurer and later bishop of Barcelona; he left his papers to the cathedral chapter. Among them Sebastián Puig y Puig found fourteen letters partly or wholly in cipher, deciphered them, and printed them in the appendix of Pedro de Luna, último papa de Aviñón (1920). This is one of them: Alfonso de Exea, archbishop of Seville to Climent, 23 Aug 1408 (appendix LXIV, pp. 500–503; Çapera no. 133). Puig prints the whole letter after its opening formula in italics as his decipherment. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 found no text of the letter in the repository; on 23 October Puig’s pages were fetched as images from Google Books and transcribed ( texts/exea1408_reading.md , with an English translation). It opens: “know that the Cardinal of Spain [Pedro de Frías] has played a Trebellian trick on us”: he feigned illness when the Pope left Portovenere, then went to Genoa, where the Patriarch [Simon de Cramaud] urged him in the King of France’s name to go to Paris, with the promise of the church of Rouen; the Pope has ordered his revenues seized for the Camera (translation). The originals are not digitised, and the archivist Josep Mas noted that Puig studied many of the Schism papers at home in 1920–30 and did not return them all. Puig’s print may be the only witness.

Puig never printed a key, and the only image of any of these ciphers is his facsimile of one page of Benedict XIII’s own letter of 22 June 1400. From that page the key of Benedict’s letters was rebuilt here: a plain substitution, one sign per letter. Puig writes of “la clave o claves”, the key or keys, he recovered, and nothing shows whether this letter, from another writer, used the same one. So it has its own entry. Benedict XIII’s letters are on Benedict XIII to Climent, 1399–1403 (a different or unverified cipher, with its own page); the other letters of his circle each have their own page for the same reason: Santa Cruz to Climent, 1399 , Jafet to Climent, 1400 , Comuel to Climent, December 1415 , Comuel to Climent, June 1416 .
The ciphertext. No image of the letter exists, so its cipher, its key and Puig’s reading cannot be checked. Blocker: needs the original in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona.

Where The ciphertexts are the strings copied into verify.py in the repository folder; no image of the originals was used and their source is not recorded there. The cipher Two monoalphabetic substitution alphabets, used alternately word by word. Words of even length are written backwards after substitution, and the word boundaries are dropped. How it was read David Vierra published the solution in May 2023. Here the two alphabets were applied to re-encipher his plaintexts and compared with the ciphertexts, and a word-segmenting search over the same rules recovered both texts from the ciphertexts alone. What it says No. 2 is lines 19–32 of Housman’s “Terence, this is stupid stuff”; no. 3 is the opening of Feynman’s 1953 paper on the lambda transition in helium. Still open Nothing in the solution. The re-encipherment differs from the ciphertexts in three letters of no. 3 and in a stretch of no. 2 where the encipherer broke his own rule. Credit David Vierra found the system and both plaintexts (May 2023). This page records our check of it and adds nothing to the solution.

Both ciphertexts are runs of capital letters with no spaces. Each uses only 26 distinct letters, as a substitution cipher does, and each plaintext is plain English of the period. No. 2 begins XUKEXWSLZJUAXUNKIGWFSOZRAWURORKXAOSL… and no. 3 begins WURVFXGJYTHEIZXSQXOBGSVRUDOOJXAT… . The full transcriptions are in the Full texts section below.

Vierra’s two alphabets, written as the cipher letter for plaintext A, B, C… in order (a full stop stands for a letter not fixed by the published solution): A1 = MANYREQUS.HVBCID.OLWGZX.K. A2 = JHAZTENYXMLOCUFBQVKPSGW.D. The first word of each line or sentence uses A1, the next A2, and so on. A word of even length is reversed after substitution. Word boundaries are then removed. A search that segments the ciphertext into words under those rules recovers both texts without the plaintext supplied.

No. 3 re-enciphers to the ciphertext at 228 of 231 positions. The three mismatches are one letter in “phenomenological” and a transposed pair in “principles”, slips in the encipherment or in the copy we hold. The behavior of liquid helium, especially below the lambda transition, is very curious. The most successful theoretical interpretations so far have been largely phenomenological. In this paper and one or two to follow, the problem will be studied entirely from first principles. No. 2 matches exactly for the first 118 characters and at 208 of 261 overall. The mismatching stretches decode to “England brews” (both words under A2, the documented exception) and to a line 27 whose wording differs a little from Housman’s printed text, “ale is” for “ale’s”. Why, if ’tis dancing you would be, there’s brisker pipes than poetry. Say, for what were hop-yards meant, or why was Burton built on Trent? Oh many a peer of England brews livelier liquor than the Muse, and malt does more than Milton can to justify God’s ways to man. Ale, man, ale is the stuff to drink for fellows whom it hurts to think.

The origin of the two ciphertext strings, and therefore any transcription error in them, is not recorded in the project. Three letters of no. 3 and the stretches of no. 2 named above do not re-encipher exactly; they are the encipherer’s or the copyist’s slips, not gaps in the key. Letters the solution does not need (the full stops in A1 and A2) are not fixed by these texts.

Sforza’s envoy at Milan reports an audience with Duke Filippo Maria Visconti: the state in danger, the plague, nine thousand ducats and no more money for a long while, and the Duke’s fervent wish that Sforza come at once. Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from another Guarna letter and its late clear copy and read 616 of about 852 cipher words (72.3%, the unread stretches estimated); the key is partial by our protocol, there is no fresh held-out block, and the end of the letter was already in clear on f. 156. hz b ls 7 · 6 gp qo bp · 8 q qq 4 + · che vole · bene · voria · che hz = v · b = o · ls = l · 7 = e · + = a · 4 = i Milan → Francesco Sforza · homophonic substitution with nulls, decoy words and a small code, in a letter with clear connectives · 21 May 1447 · key from adjacent plaintext, partial Nicolò Guarna to Francesco Sforza, Milan, 21 May 1447 to Francesco Sforza Go to the full text ↓ Sforza’s envoy reports an audience with the Duke of Milan on money, the plague and Sforza’s coming; the key was rebuilt from another Guarna letter and about 72% of the cipher words are read, so it is read in part. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (72% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (earlier solution) · Daniel Bourdeau (pointer to a source) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (72% of the cipher) The letter Nicolò Guarna, writing from Milan as Count Francesco Sforza’s envoy at the ducal court, to Sforza, on Sunday 21 May 1447. It is signed “Servitor N. Guarna”. The opening, the connectives and the close are in clear; most of the body, about 3,960 cipher signs over three pages, is in cipher. Where Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1584 (the Archivio Sforzesco, 1447), ff. 153r–154r, on Gallica (views 146–147). No DECODE record and no edition found. The letter is not in the catalogue; the lead for Guarna’s other letters in this volume (ff. 163–164 and others) does not list ff. 153–154. The cipher Homophonic substitution with nulls (79 distinct signs), clear decoy words written inside the cipher ( quia , adviso , mo , primum …) and a small code ( cer = Signore, mea = non, tuy = gente d’arme, tri = Re de Ragona, dn = dinari). Several signs carry more than one value in our table, which may partly reflect our own confusion of look-alike signs. How it was read Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from Guarna’s letter of 27 May 1447 (ff. 163r–163v), aligned with its 18th-century clear copy (ff. 161r–162v, 165r), and applied it to this letter, which has no copy. The tests do not validate it : both held-out measurements are partial, and there is no fresh held-out block left. What it says An audience with Duke Filippo Maria Visconti about Sforza’s coming to Lombardy: enemies in the field, troops poorly provided, the plague, nine thousand ducats and then “not another florin for a long while”. The Duke answered “more openly than the other times” and shows a fervent wish for Sforza to come quickly. Still open About 236 words are unresolved (an estimate: each unread stretch counted as its length divided by five), mostly on f. 153r and the first half of f. 153v. 72.3% is below the 95% read bar. The key is partial, and the end of the letter (f. 153v from about l. 46 to f. 154r) was already in clear on f. 156, so it is not new. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ), working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents: transcription, key, tests and reading, contributed by pull request #280. The clear text of f. 156 is the contemporary reading of the end. The training pair came from Daniel Bourdeau’s survey of the late copies in this volume.

Guarna writes to the Count from the court of Duke Filippo Maria Visconti, the last year of the Duke’s life, when Sforza, his son-in-law and condottiere, was far off in the Marche and the Duchy was short of money and men. The letter has about fifty lines on f. 153r, fifty-two on f. 153v and three on f. 154r. The salutation, many connectives and the close are in clear; the substance is in cipher, with clear decoy words scattered through it. The letter belongs to the Sforza archive volume that also holds the Duke’s own letters to Sforza and those of Barbavara and Pusterla, each in a different cipher; the Duke’s second key and the Barbavara and Pusterla letters have their own pages, and nothing here is read with them. f. 156, a 15th-century clear text, gives the end of a letter of the same day, which matches the end of this cipher. The top of f. 153r. The heading at the top names the year 1447 and Guarna. The first line is clear; from the second line clear words (as far as they can be read from the image, sempre in pensiero se potesse ) pass into runs of cipher signs. The first run decrypts with the key to remediare a questi benedetti inconve- (line 2, the opening of the block held out for the first test). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1584 f. 153r (detail), via Gallica (openapi.bnf.fr IIIF, view 146).

The signs are letter-like and geometric, written without word division. Most stand for a single letter, and several letters have more than one sign (homophones). Some signs are nulls, and a few clear words ( quia , adviso , tanto , tame , mo , cio , oto , si , ot , primum , tua , spes ) are written inside the runs and dropped when reading. A short code gives whole words: A = Papa, cer = Signore, mea = non, con = qua, tus = que, tuy = gente d’arme, ba = per, ra = perché, qt = quantunque, tri = Re de Ragona, SF = Signore de Faenza, dn = dinari. In the table as we have it, many signs list two or three values, most frequent first. That may be the cipher’s own polyphony or the contributor’s confusion of look-alike signs on a microfilm (a four-like sign and hk , a sigma and an o with a hook, t , T and z , hs and h ). A blind shape sheet on those pairs was prepared and is not yet answered, so it was not applied. The key is published as targets/guarna1447/key.tsv (CC BY 4.0).

Where the key comes from. No Guarna key was known: DECODE lists none among the keys examined, and nothing in print was found. Brice Dudout rebuilt it from the cipher of Guarna’s letter of 27 May 1447 (ff. 163r–163v), aligned with its late clear copy (ff. 161r–162v and 165r), the pair listed in the survey of late copies of this volume. The key was frozen in three stages (K, K2, K3, each fixed by SHA-256 before its test) and applied to this letter. The tests. The thresholds were fixed in advance: validated at 0.60 (words of five letters or more in Italian) or 0.85 (characters against a clear), and at least 0.30 above the best of 200 shuffled keys; partial when the gap holds without the absolute figure. test held-out block key metric score best control result 1 f. 153r ll. 1–20 (this letter) K2 Italian words of 5+ letters 0.441 0.118 partial (gap 0.323) 2 f. 164r (the training letter) against its copy f. 165r K3 characters 0.759 0.315 partial (gap 0.445) From targets/guarna1447/validation.txt . These are the contributor’s own pre-registered tests, not the project’s _validate.py . What that means. The key is partial by our protocol, twice, and not validated . Both held-out blocks are now used, so no fresh block is left to test it on. Declared slips: line 20 of the first block (clear only) was seen before the block was frozen, and the copy f. 165r was seen at low resolution while the second block was chosen, though it was not used to build the key. The end of the cipher agrees word for word with the clear text of f. 156, which the key never used, but that is not a pre-registered test.

The reading covers the cipher segments only (the clear frame of the letter is not counted): 852 words, of which 583 are certain and 33 probable, none restored and 236 unresolved. Certain and probable make 616 words, 72.3% . The unresolved count is an estimate, because a stretch that does not read cannot be cut into words: each is counted as its decoded length divided by five. By part: the held-out block 71%, the rest of f. 153r 71%, f. 153v 73%, f. 154r 91%. That is below the 95% bar, so the letter is read in part. The reader is one AI agent working on a microfilm, and no palaeographer has checked the signs. The sentences are built from stretches that construe as 15th-century Lombard Italian ( de li quali , per respecto del spaccio , senza comparatione ) with many holes, most of them on f. 153r and the early lines of f. 153v. The part where the reading is steadiest is the end, f. 153v from about line 46 to f. 154r, and that part is also the part that was already in clear on f. 156. The passage below is the end of the letter in the normalised text (a bare word is certain, {x} probable, [?n] about n unresolved words). ne {recevessimo} [?1] per le genti de Cremona restano [?1] milia li quali spero havere fra otto o diece di o non prima … ma per {dirve} quello che io credo pareme esser certo voi non haveriti piu uno fiorino per uno grande spacio se la S.V. aspecta de moverse. … vole bene voria che facesti ultimum de potentia de venire presto et Dio volese che potesti farla of which we received […] for the troops of Cremona remain […] thousand, which I hope to have within eight or ten days, not before … but to tell you what I believe, I seem certain you will not have another florin for a long while, if Your Lordship waits to move … [one who] wishes you well would want you to do your utmost to come quickly, and God grant you may do it. The danger of the state. Guarna reports that the enemies are in the countryside and that the state stands in great danger; the plague adds to it. What he wants from Sforza is not clear from the opening lines, which are mostly holes: they speak of remedying “these cursed troubles”, of how Guarna stands in the world on account of the dispatch, and of what was hoped from Sforza. Money. The main thing to remedy is to find money. Besides nine thousand ducats there is what is expected from the gabelle, and money for the troops at Cremona, to be had in eight or ten days; after that, not another florin for a long while. The Duke. He answered Guarna “more openly than he had done the other times” and shows a fervent wish for Sforza’s coming, though in effect he has no money to give. Sforza should come quickly, with all or part of his company. The gist (an audience with the Duke, money short, the Duke wanting Sforza to come) holds across the parts that read; the details of the first half are not secure.

About 236 unresolved words (estimated), mostly on f. 153r and f. 153v ll. 4–19. Blocker: illegible; the look-alike signs are not separated on the microfilm. The next step is the pending blind shape sheet and a finer re-transcription. The key is not validated (section 03), and there is no fresh held-out block . Another Guarna leaf with a complete late copy (the lead for Guarna’s letters in this volume) would serve as a new test. Not new at the end. f. 153v from about line 46 to f. 154r agrees with the 15th-century clear of f. 156, so the contribution of the reading is the rest, where no decipherment is known. Multi-valued signs. Most signs list more than one value in the key. In the reveal above the orange signs are the ones where the reading takes a value other than the first, or corrects one from the sense. One reader. An AI agent transcribed and read; no palaeographer checked the signs. Not seen. Cerioni, La diplomazia sforzesca (1970), and the printed calendars of BnF italien 1584. Four web searches (the last on 5 November 2026) found no edition of this letter; if one prints it, we will credit it.

Francesco Sforza, Milan, 21 May 1447 (BnF ital. 1584, ff. 153r-154r) Read in part (5 Nov 2026). Counted by script on the lines below (cipher segments only; the clear frame of the letter is not counted): **852 words: 583 certain, 33 probable, 0 restored, 236 unresolved** (the unresolved count is an estimate, see below), so 616 = **72.3%** certain or probable. Under 95%: read in part. Our working notes gave 862 words and 72.6%; the recount by script on this file, counting each word split at a line end once, gives the figures above. Conventions (spelling of the cipher kept; 15th-century Lombard Italian): - a bare word is **certain** (given by key K3, clear sense); - `{word}` is **probable** (one doubtful sign, or one of the sign's other values); - `<word>` would be **restored** (none here); - `[?n]` is a stretch of **about n unresolved words**: n is estimated as the length of the decoded stretch divided by 5, because a stretch that does not read cannot be cut into words. The total of 236 unresolved words is therefore an estimate. The end of the letter (f. 153v from about V47b, and f. 154r) agrees word for word with the 15th-century clear text on f. 156 of the same day ("le gente de Cremona restano … fra otto o diece di, o no prima … piu uno fiorino per uno gran spacio … ultimum de potentia de venire presto"). That part is therefore **not new**: it was in clear in the volume. A German despatch from Hamburg to the chancellor at Kassel (HStAM 4 f Dänemark Nr. 125; HCPortal 494, “partially solved”), with 26 code numbers glossed by a second hand and two short letter-cipher passages. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 9 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: partial (92% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) key matched At a glance External key matched · partial (92% of the cipher) The letter A signed despatch in German from Hamburg, dated 4/14 May 1672, to the Hessian chancellor (“Herr Canzler”) at Kassel. The writer is not identified. Where Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 4 f Dänemark Nr. 125, ff. 2–4. HCPortal record 494, “partially solved”, with no transcription attached. The cipher Names are written as three-digit code numbers (26 in the letter). Two short passages on the last page are in a letter cipher: five two-digit numbers for each letter, doubled capitals as more homophones, and signs for syllables. How it was deciphered A second hand glossed the code numbers on the leaf. The letter table of a Hessian key of 1666, filed in another Marburg collection (HCPortal key 255), reads both passages without change. What it says Danish anger at a French–Swedish treaty, a plan to bring Brandenburg into the Danish–Brunswick alliance, and Holstein “totaliter disgustirt” at the Landtag’s demands; “Gott geb das all wol ablauff”. Still open Five signs before “in Holstein” decipher as e r t a z and make no word; the 1672 key, which differs from the 1666 one in at least one cell, is not available. The gloss for code 625 is only partly legible.

The letter fills three pages. It opens “Hoch Edler Herr, Mein insonders hochgeehrter Herr Canzler” and is dated at the foot “Hamburg den 4/14 May 1672”, in both calendars. It is clear German in Kurrent script, with Latin and French words in Latin script. The writer reports on his reception at the Danish court, on ceremonial quarrels between Denmark and Brandenburg, on the mission of a Blumenthal (code 630), on a treaty between France and Sweden that left Denmark out, and on a Holstein Landtag at which the estates refused the King’s demands. This was the spring in which France opened the war on the Dutch Republic. (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.) Names are written as code numbers: 601 for the King of Denmark, 651 for the Elector of Brandenburg, 829 for Berlin, 774 for Holland, 768 for Sweden, and so on. A second hand, in black ink and Latin script, wrote the meaning over almost every number and in the margins. The same hand wrote “disgustirt und erta?in holstein” in the margin beside the first letter-cipher passage, and a few letters over the second. This is the “partial solution” HCPortal refers to. The hand is not dated: it may be the Kassel chancery’s, or a later reader’s. The top of f. 3r: code numbers 601 and 651 with the glosses “K. Dennemarck” and “Curbrandenburg”, and 625 in the margin. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 4 f Dänemark Nr. 125 f. 3r, via HCPortal record 494.

The two passages on f. 4r use a letter cipher, not the code numbers. HCPortal holds 319 cipher keys, 106 of them from the Marburg collections 4 d and 4 f. Looking through their first pages, four are of the same kind as this letter: two-digit homophones and doubled capitals. One of them, key 255 (HStAM 4 d Nr. 1234, ff. 13–16), is a Hessian key whose back sheet names Secretary Lincker and the years 1666 and 1676. Its deciphering table, key 254 on f. 12, confirms the doubled capitals. The letter table of key 255. A is 20, 30, 40, 50 or 60; the doubled capitals CC to BB stand for a to z; the bottom rows give signs for syllables such as st and tt. The note below lists the nulls. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 4 d Nr. 1234 f. 13, via HCPortal key 255. In the table, A to K take the numbers 20 to 69 in columns of ten (A 20 30 40 50 60, B 22 32…, F 21 31…), L to U take 70 to 119, and W to Z take 120 to 166. CC stands for a, DD for b, and so on to BB for z. Further signs stand for au, ch, ff, ll, st, tt and other syllables, and 1 to 19 are nulls. The table gives the second passage’s glossed letters unchanged: 63 g, 38 e, 22 b, FF d, 20 a, 75 s, 96 o, NN l, 50 a, 32 b, 110 l. The key’s word list does not fit, though: there Alliance is 311 and Denmark 184, while this letter has codes from 303 to 834. The 1672 correspondence used the same letter table with another word list, which is not on HCPortal. For the code numbers the glosses are the only source.

f. 4r: the first passage after “Totaliter”, with the margin gloss, and the second after “insidiosus hostis”, with letters written over it. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 4 f Dänemark Nr. 125 f. 4r, via HCPortal record 494. In this hand 6 looks like b and 2 like r, so “b7” is 67, “ro” is 20. The sign before 37, two tall looped b-shapes unlike the closed 6 of 26 in the same line, is the doubled capital BB. The first passage follows a report that the Holstein estates broke up “protestando” and would let it come to forced collection: Totaliter FF 67 85 33 XX st LL 113 WW · 119 74 26 · 28 83 117 20 BB · 37 104 · 634 Totaliter disgustirt und [e r t a z] in Holstein , nun sowohl als in Dänemark Adel, Bürger und Bauern nun allerorten in plaintes combiniret. “Totally disgusted and […] in Holstein, nobles, burghers and peasants are now joined in complaints everywhere, in Holstein as in Denmark.” The sign after XX is the key’s sign for st. The five signs 28 83 117 20 BB give e r t a z, which is not a word; the glosser got the same letters and wrote “erta?in”. The second passage follows a Latin sentence about an insidious enemy: insidiosus hostis 768: 55 76 tt · 63 38 22 · FF 20 75 · 20 ll · YY 96 NN · 50 32 110 au ff insidiosus hostis Sueco: Gott geb das all wol ablauff. “… the Swede, an insidious enemy: God grant that all goes well.” 768 is Sweden, as the margin note “Schweden 768” and the gloss “Sueco” say. In the 1666 table 55 is h; the glosser read g and the word is Gott, so either the 1672 table differs from the 1666 one here or 55 is a slip for 53. The last two signs are read as the key’s au and ff signs, which look like an 8 and a doubled X; as plain numbers they would be a null and u.

All 26 code numbers in the letter, with the gloss over each (H: gloss; M: gloss partly legible; I: inferred): 601 King of Denmark (four times), 834 “Rey Danae”, King of Denmark; 651 Elector of Brandenburg (three times), 653 “Cur Brandenb.”, Elector of Brandenburg; 829 Berlin (twice); 630 Blumenthal (twice); 774 Holland, 775 the States General; 576 France; 768 Sweden (twice); 634 Holstein; 447 641 “Herzog von Ploen”; 303 alliance (H). 625, twice: the margin gloss reads something like “Statthalter Ahlefeldt” (M). 447 602 in “eine estroite alliance zwischen 447 602 und 834”: the glosser wrote “Haus Braunschweig”, struck it and wrote “Kayser”. Since 447 is Herzog in the same line and the clear text above names the “Foedus Dano-Brunsvicense”, 447 602 is taken as Herzog [von] Braunschweig (I). The letter’s chief news in clear: the French–Swedish treaty, concluded without Denmark, “gibt Verdruss”, and 625 is to go to Berlin in a few weeks to bring Brandenburg into the Danish–Brunswick alliance.

The HCPortal record and its three images were fetched through the HCPortal API. The cipher parts were transcribed from full-resolution crops. The margin gloss of the first passage was tried against its signs first, with the doubled capitals as nulls and as letters; neither fitted. All 319 key records on HCPortal were then fetched, and the first pages of the 106 Marburg keys from collections 4 d and 4 f were screened in contact sheets. Key 255 was the one whose letter table gave the second passage’s glossed letters without change. A short script applies it ( decrypt.py ). The five open signs were re-cropped at three times the scan’s size and searched four ways (see below) with the project’s German language model for 1600–1670 and a corpus of period German, without a convincing word. The alliance the letter prepares was concluded at Braunschweig on 12/22 September 1672 between the Emperor, Denmark, Brandenburg, Brunswick and Hessen-Kassel. Extent: 64 cipher tokens (38 letter-cipher signs and 26 code numbers). All have a value; 59 read as sense, 92.2%. That is below the project’s 95% bar, so the extent is partial.

Passage 1, signs 28 83 117 20 BB (e r t a z) before “in Holstein”: no word. The glosser, who evidently had the 1672 key, got the same letters (“erta?in” in the margin). The 1672 table is not the 1666 one cell for cell: 55 is g in this letter but h in key 255. So either the 1672 table differs at these signs too, or the encipherer slipped; without the 1672 key or another copy of the letter, neither can be settled. The signs were re-cropped at three times the scan’s size and four searches were run: any letter at one or two places; digit look-alikes (1/7, 2/7, 3/5/8, 6/0/8, 4/9) and the key’s looped syllable signs at one or two places; the two signs not confirmed elsewhere in the letter left free; and an alignment against every word beginning er-, ver-, ir-, ex- or ent- in German printed texts of 1470–1770. The best candidates (ermatt, erstatt, erbar, ertapt) need two or more changes, and none fits the sentence well enough to adopt. Passage 2: 55 read as g (a slip for 53, M); the sign read as ll (M); the last two signs read as the au and ff signs (M). Code 625: the gloss is only partly legible (M). 602 = Braunschweig is inferred (I). The writer’s signature is not made out. The other despatches in Nr. 125 are not digitised.

The lines of figures written as superscriptions on four of Hyde’s letters to John Barwick are nulls. The 1724 editor of Barwick’s Life says so, and applying the full Hyde–Barwick key from the 1721 plate confirms it: one line decrypts to nonsense and the others use numbers outside the key. 729 · 549 · 856 · 8 · 245 · 831 729 · 549 · 856 · 21 · 245 · 831 · 99 212 · 23 · 12 · 7 · 461 · 36 Brussels · Restoration correspondence · superscriptions in figures · 1659–60 Hyde's ciphered superscriptions to Barwick from Edward Hyde Sir Edward Hyde to Dr John Barwick, Brussels, 29 Sept and 17 Oct 1659, 14 and 16 Jan 1660 · printed in Peter Barwick, Vita Johannis Barwick (1721), pp. 358, 360, 389, 396 The figures are nulls, numbers "only to puzzle the Enemy", as the 1724 editor, who had the papers, states. Applying the full key confirms it. There is no address to decipher. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not a cipher · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) closed At a glance Not a cipher The letters Four letters from Hyde in Brussels to John Barwick, the royalist agent in London, in the months before the Restoration. Where an address should be, each has a line of figures. Where Tomokiyo lists them as undeciphered, meaning no decipherment is known. They were printed from the Barwick papers in 1721 together with the Hyde–Barwick key. Why they have none The figures are nulls. The 1724 English edition says several letters “were superscribed with Numbers signifying nothing”, and cites these pages. How it was checked The full Hyde–Barwick key, transcribed here from the 1721 plate: one superscription decrypts to nonsense and the other three use numbers that do not exist in the key. What was added The item should be removed from Tomokiyo’s list as not a cipher.

Tomokiyo's page references (313, 335, 339, 441, 442 for the clear addresses; 358, 360, 389, 396 for the ciphered ones) are to the Latin Vita Johannis Barwick (London, 1721), whose appendix prints Hyde's letters to Barwick in English, with an engraved "Tabula Cryptographica" of their cipher facing p. 316. The four superscriptions, verified against the page scans (every group is followed by a full stop, so the grouping is certain): Date (Brussels) Vita 1721 Life 1724 Superscription as printed 29 September 1659 No. XVI, p. 358 No. XIII, p. 449 212. 23. 12. 7. 461. 36. / 108. 49. 498. 14. 21. 410. 17 October 1659 No. XVII, p. 360 No. XIV, p. 451 729. 549. 705. 99. 856. / 250. 245. 831. 100. 859. / 609. 858. 101. 24. 14 January 1660 No. XXIII, p. 389 No. XXI, p. 482 729. 549. 856. / 21. 245. 831. 99. 16 January 1660 No. XXVI, p. 396 No. XXIII, p. 486 729. 549. 856. 8. 245. 831. Vita Johannis Barwick (1721), p. 396: the letter of 16 January 1660 and its superscription. Image: P. Barwick, Vita Johannis Barwick (London, 1721), p. 396, via the Internet Archive. Clear superscriptions in the same series are cover names for Barwick: "For Mr. Burden", "For Mr. Brookes", "For Mr. B.", "For Mr. Burges, these"; the editor notes that "B. or any Name beginning with B. seems to have signified Barwick".

The 1721 plate gives the complete cipher: numbers 1–692 in eleven columns. Column 1 is the alphabet, three figures per letter (two for k, w, y; none for x, z); 64–69 are skipped; columns 2–11 (70–131, 132–193, 194–254, 255–317, 318–379, 380–440, 441–503, 504–566, 567–628, 629–692) each run A to Y down the rows, three rows per letter, so syllables and words are grouped by initial letter across the columns rather than in one alphabetical list. Several slots are deliberately empty. Entries relevant here: the = 370, for = 210, from = 211, Mr. = 536, Master = 475, Barwick = 572, Hyde, Lord Chancellor = 589; there is no entry for these , Sir or London .

The unabridged English Life of Dr. John Barwick (1724, tr. Hilkiah Bedford), working from the Barwick family papers, appends this note to the letter of 12 June 1659 that enclosed the cipher (pp. 408–409): But to render the Cypher more difficult to be found out, as each Letter in the Alphabet is represented by three several Numbers, except K, W, and Y only by two, and X and Z by none: So several of the Numbers have no Letter, Syllable, or Word over against them, because they stand for nothing, and were only us'd to perplex such as should attempt to read what was written hereby, without the Help of the Cypher. So several of the Letters were superscribed with Numbers signifying nothing, some with two or three Lines of them, only to puzzle the Enemy, if they should fall into their Hands, which I the rather mention here, because some Persons, for want of examining those Superscriptions, as printed in the Appendix to the Latin Life (p. 358, 360, 389, 396, and 417.) with the Cypher also published there, have wondered what was the meaning of them: and it was for the same Reason, that several of the Chancellor's Letters, besides the Number denoting his Name, were subscribed with other Numbers, that either had nothing in the Cypher to answer them, or nothing to the Purpose. As to the Superscriptions, B. or any Name beginning with B. seems to have signified Barwick. The pages he names are the four in question. The question had already been raised and answered in 1724.

Transcribed the 643 entries of the plate into a table ( targets/hyde/barwick_key.py ) and decoded all four superscriptions. Checked the shift hypothesis for the "For Mr … these" template; rejected. Searched the 1724 English edition ( lifeofjohnbarwic00barw ) for editorial matter on the cipher; found the note above.

Explore · the network The Key Web A cipher is rarely broken in isolation. A key rebuilt from one letter's margin is tried on its sibling letters. A contemporary key turns up filed under the next record number. A table published by Lasry or Tomokiyo is turned on a letter they never saw. And many keys are tried and do not fit. This page follows every key behind the site's decipherments: who made it, which letters it was used on, and where it failed. The biggest keys did the most work: made for one letter, they went on to open the rest of its series. Every key has its own link: copy it from the card.

Every link is taken from an explicit statement in the target's notes: that a named key was used on a letter, unchanged or adapted, that a key was rebuilt from that letter's own material, or that a named key was tested on it and did not fit. Links are not inferred from resemblance. A key counts as rebuilt here when this project recovered it, from the ciphertext, from glosses or from a decipherment; keys recovered by other people (Lasry, Tomokiyo, Somogyi, and outside contributors) are scholars' keys ; keys of the period are those that survive in the archives or on DECODE. A scholar's key is placed at the date of the cipher, not of its publication, which the card gives separately. Several of George Lasry's tables for the French correspondence of the 1520s and 1530s appear as one key. Letters taken straight from a contemporary decipherment, with no key rebuilt, are not shown. A key and a letter that connect to nothing else sit in the date strip under the web. The file is keys.json ; the site build checks it.

Linear A is a script with an unknown language, not a cipher, and no bilingual text exists. Tested against a random null, the Linear B sound values carry over (six word matches against 0.49 expected), and 41.8% of the corpus gives sense without the language: numbers, fractions, commodities, KU-RO totals, KI-RO deficits and three place names. Tablet HT 34 contradicts the published values of the fraction signs H and A; the proposed Semitic and Luwian relatives fit no better than Hawaiian or Yoruba. Sixty-seven rounds of pre-registered tests describe the language’s sound shape (rare e and o, standing mainly after R and T; consonant harmony), the Minoan names that survive at Knossos, and the scribes’ bookkeeping, until new tests stopped yielding results.
