Daniel Bourdeau · posted 24 September 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The texts About 1,400 Minoan inscriptions from Crete and the Aegean, c. 1800–1450 BC: accounting tablets, sealings, and offerings inscribed on stone vessels. The working corpus has 1,722 records. Where Mostly the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. Edited in GORILA (Godart and Olivier 1976–85). The digital texts used here are Robert Hogan’s lineara.xyz and the SigLA database. The script About 90 syllabic signs, the ancestor of Linear B, plus logograms for commodities, numerals and fraction signs. It writes an unknown language. It is not a cipher: nobody was hiding anything. How it was worked Linear B sound values were tested for carry-over against a random null. Every token was then given a function, all 35 totals were rechecked with fractions, and the libation formula was aligned across sites. What it says Lists of men, grain, wine, oil, olives and figs by name and place, with totals and deficits. Three places are identified: Phaistos, Sybrita and Setoija. There is also a fixed dedication formula on offering vessels. What is new Three findings, set out in section 09. Tablet HT 34 contradicts the published values of two fraction signs. The proposed Semitic and Luwian relatives match Linear A no better than Hawaiian or Yoruba do. The Linear A words that reappear in Linear B are names, all of them at Knossos. Best guess The working accounts of a regional centre: staples collected from and issued to named people and work teams, with shortfalls tracked (section 06, interpretation). Still open The language, and the newly found Knossos sceptre, which is not yet transcribed in print. The meaning of every word that is not a number, commodity, total or place name, which is 40.5% of tokens. The unidentified signs, and the fraction signs H and A.

Linear A was the script of Minoan Crete. The Mycenaean Greeks adapted it into Linear B, which Michael Ventris deciphered in 1952. That worked because Linear B turned out to write Greek, a language already known. Linear A shares most of its signs with Linear B, so its sound values can be carried over. The result reads aloud but does not translate: the language behind it has no known relative, and no text gives the same words in a known language. So this is not a cipher problem, and the project’s usual measure of a complete result (95% of the text giving sense) cannot be reached by any method. What can be done is narrower, and it can be checked: test whether the carried-over sound values are real; read everything whose meaning does not depend on the language, namely numbers, fractions, commodity pictograms and the bookkeeping terms; check the arithmetic; describe the structure of what is left. This page reports those four steps over the whole corpus, with a measure for each. Tablet HT 7a from Haghia Triada, a list of men. It reads QE-TI · VIR (heading, “men”); I-RU-JA 3; DU-JA 4; TA-NA-TI 1; DA-RE 1; TE-TU 1. The numbers and the pictogram for “man” read as sense. The five words are almost certainly personal names, readable in sound only. The photograph was matched sign by sign to the GORILA drawing of HT 7a. The painted “10.” is a museum number. Image: Archaeological Museum of Heraklion, Linear A tablet HT 7a (Haghia Triada); photograph by ShlomoKatzav, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

If the Linear B values were arbitrary labels on Linear A, Linear A words would match Linear B words only by chance. The test takes all 491 Linear A word types of three or more signs and compares them with 919 Linear B words that have Greek cognates, including place names (the NeuroDecipher list, Luo et al. 2019). It counts exact matches. The values are then shuffled among Linear A signs of similar frequency, 2,000 times, and the matches recounted. Linear A Linear B / Greek Where in Linear A PA-I-TO pa-i-to, Phaistos HT 97a, HT 120 SU-KI-RI-TA su-ki-ri-ta, Sybrita PH Wa 32 SE-TO-I-JA se-to-i-ja, Setoija PR Za 1 A-RU-RA ἄρουρα, arable land (?) HT 11a I-JA-TE i-ja-te, physician (?) PH Zb 4 DA-MA-TE da-ma-te, Demeter (?) KY Za 2 Six real matches against a random mean of 0.49; only one shuffle in 2,000 reached six (p ≈ 0.001). The values carry over. Loosening the test to words that share a stem but differ in the last sign gives 35 matches against 25.4 expected (p 0.09): nothing. Three of the six are place names on Crete, which any language would share. Only three ordinary words match in 491, so Linear A is not Greek, which is the accepted view. The consonant rows are real. A second test of the sound values needs no known word at all. Signs that Linear B puts in the same consonant row (NA, NE, NI, NU; RA, RE, RI, RO, RU) keep more similar company in Linear A words than signs from different rows (p = 0.0005), and the effect is as large as in Linear B itself. It holds with consonant harmony and word-initial vowels taken out of the comparison, and at Haghia Triada and the other sites separately. The Q, N and R rows hold together most clearly. The one row that does not is Z (ZA, ZU), which is also the least certain series in Linear B, so that is where a different Minoan value is most likely. The same method recovers a hidden sign’s vowel from context (42% against 20% by chance) but not its consonant, so it cannot yet assign values to the unread signs. A nearest-neighbour method that recovers 27% of consonants in Linear B gets only chance in Linear A: the row signal is real on average but too weak, on this corpus, to place any single sign. A lead on the vowels. In Linear B, the e- and i-signs of one row (TE and TI, KE and KI) are clearly unlike each other in context, and so are the o- and u-signs. In Linear A they lean the other way, and the difference between the scripts is marked (p = 0.003 for e/i, 0.014 for o/u). That fits a Minoan vowel system in which e and o were marginal, as the scarcity of o-signs already suggests. It is an exploratory comparison, and part of the Linear B contrast comes from Greek case endings. Later tests on fresh data found the vowels rare rather than interchangeable (see the names section). Minoan names at Knossos. The same test against the whole Linear B vocabulary uses 4,164 word types from the linearb.xyz corpus, each with its category in Chadwick and Ventris’s glossary. It finds 13 matches against 2.8 expected (p 0.0005), and they divide cleanly by kind: Names, all on Crete. Every Linear A word that matches a Linear B name is a word attested only on Crete, at Knossos. The place names are PA-I-TO, SU-KI-RI-TA and SE-TO-I-JA. The personal names are DA-I-PI-TA (Zakros), I-TA-JA (HT 28a) and KI-DA-RO (HT 47a, HT 117a). Half the Linear B names (51.3%) are Crete-only, so six of six by chance has p = 0.018. Two more Knossos words behave like names in Linear A lists. TA-NA-TI appears on four tablets, including the HT 7a list of men shown above, and PA-RA-NE on HT 115. Common words, on the mainland. The Linear B words found only on the mainland are Greek common words at Pylos, such as ma-te-re “mother” and i-ja-te “physician”. They are chance look-alikes of the kind section 07 measures. What survives of Minoan vocabulary in the Linear B record is names, and only at Knossos. The Oslo database DAMOS, queried independently, gives the same result: 12 of the 13 matches, and the same split between Knossos and the mainland. It also shows the names doing the same job in both scripts, as entries in lists of individuals. TA-NA-TI stands with 1 in the HT 7a list of men, and at Knossos it appears as “ta-na-ti, DA 1” (KN Uf 311). Likewise I-TA-JA appears as “i-ta-ja MUL 1”, one woman (KN Ap 769), and PA-RA-NE as “pa-ra-ne 1” (KN Vc 7616). One caution: SigLA reads the Phaistos sherd PH Wa 32 as SU-KI-RA-TA, not SU-KI-RI-TA, so the Sybrita match rests on the GORILA reading of one sign. Beyond exact matches. The whole stock of Knossos personal names is Minoan in shape. Compared syllable by syllable, the 637 Linear B personal names attested only at Knossos are much closer to the 358 Linear A list names than the 339 attested only at Pylos are (p = 0.0002 for all, first and last syllables). The result holds with the exactly shared names removed, and for the Linear A names of Haghia Triada, Zakros and Khania taken separately. Ordinary vocabulary shows no such difference between Knossos and Pylos, so this is a feature of the names, not of Knossian spelling. The Knossos scribes whose names are most Minoan-shaped also use the Linear B signs with no agreed value most (rho = 0.48 across 23 scribes). A second sign points the same way. Linear A uses very few o-syllables (under 3%), and inside the word Knossos names use fewer of them than Pylos names do (12% against 17%). The same holds for e: Linear A uses few e-syllables (10%), and Knossos names use fewer than Pylos names (16% against 26%, p = 0.0005), with no such gap in the ordinary vocabulary. Minoan names at Knossos carry both of Linear A’s vowel shortages, and so do Cretan place names: with the Greek ending removed, place names attested only at Knossos use e or o in 21% of syllables, against 42% at Pylos (p = 0.0005). In Linear A itself, e and o sit mostly in word endings (NE, ME and TE are word-final two times in three), as if Minoan used them mainly in suffixes. They also depend on the consonant: e and o follow Q, R, T and S far more often than P or J, and never W or Z, a dependence four times stronger than in Linear B. Taken together, the coronal consonants (T, D, N, R, S, Z) are followed by e or o in 22.5% of syllables and the others in 12.4%, even inside the word. The rule holds for e on its own, outside Haghia Triada and in list names, and it is the consonant of the same syllable that counts, not the next one. It survives dropping its strongest sign (RE), holds in words written only once and in first syllables, so it is not a matter of a few words or of endings. Consonant by consonant, though, it is narrower than “dentals”: e and o are commonest after Q (half the time), R (37%) and T (28%), then S and N, while D stays low and W and Z never take them. In practice, Minoan e and o stand mainly after R and T, where other syllables have i and u. After R and T, Linear A spreads its syllables over all five vowels. After other consonants it uses a narrower set, closer to three vowels (a, i, u). Linear B shows no such difference. Consonant by consonant, T, R, S, N and the labiovelar Q take e and o, while K, P, M, J and W avoid them. Minoan words, as Linear A spells them, were also strings of plain consonant-vowel syllables: two vowel signs never stand together, few words end in a pure vowel sign (4%, against 10% in Linear B), and QA, QE and QI start words (57–62%, against 28% in Linear B). Neighbouring syllables also tend to share a consonant (TA-TI, KU-KA), more than in Linear B, at every site and in the list names. All of this holds on both transcriptions, and the Q and final-vowel habits show up again in Knossos names. The vowel pattern replicates on SigLA’s transcription and holds at Zakros, but not at Khania, which stands apart in its signs and ligatures too. The rule holds in the religious dedications as well as the tablets. It holds at every site with enough words (Haghia Triada, Khania, Knossos, Palaikastro, Phaistos, Zakros), and on SigLA’s independent transcription as well as on lineara.xyz, as do the consonant rows. A lead that Greek scribes turned Minoan names in -u into -os (DI-DE-RU and di-de-ro) did not hold up when tested on its own: Linear A words in -u find Knossos names in -o no more often than words in -a do. Religious words end in -TE twice as often as administrative ones (A-DI-KI-TE, I-DA-MA-TE, with the mountain names Dikte and Ida). Beyond Linear A, the Pre-Greek substrate words of Greek share the profile, with fewer e and o in their stems than ordinary Greek words (p = 0.0005), and Eteocretan has little o. The Pre-Greek words do not, however, share the coronal pattern or Linear A’s consonant profile, so the parallel is in the vowel shortage only. A shortage of e and o is common among the world’s languages, though, so it describes Minoan without identifying its family. The spellings do not, however, swap e for i or o for u more than chance, so the evidence is that Minoan e and o were rare, not that they merged with i and u. How unusual the vowel rule is. The rule was set against 104 Eurasian languages (NorthEuraLex, Dellert et al. 2020), each respelled with the rules Linear B uses for Greek: consonants folded into the Linear A rows, clusters broken up, final consonants dropped. None of the 104 ties e and o to the preceding consonant as strongly as Linear A (log-odds 1.22 for T, R, S, N and Q against K, P, M, J and W). The nearest is Lak, a language of the Caucasus (0.99), and Lak passes Linear A when only R and T are counted. The result holds with every language cut to Linear A’s sample size and under a second spelling rule. So the rule is extreme but found in a natural language, and it need not be a scribal habit; Linear B’s spelling of Greek does not produce it. The comparison points to no family or region: Linear A’s nearest profiles are scattered (Lak, Estonian, Mansi, Evenki, Manchu), and nearness does not follow distance from Crete. The method is coarse: given the Linear B spelling of Greek, it ranks Modern Greek only fifth of 104. The trace goes beyond names. Knossos Linear B as a whole uses syllables at rates closer to Linear A than Pylos does. Words containing the Linear B signs with no agreed value (*18, *47, *56 and others) are about three times as common at Knossos. Linear A’s religious words, not only its names, look more like Knossos names than Pylos names, and still do with the libation-formula words taken out. Each of these survives a correction for testing 50 hypotheses together. The name result also predicts out of sample: a model that never saw a Knossos name, tested on Pylos names it was not trained on, still picks out the Knossos names as the more Minoan (AUC 0.59, p = 0.0025), and does not separate ordinary words at the two sites. This does not depend on where the Linear A words come from. A model trained only on names from sites other than Haghia Triada does as well (AUC 0.61), and so does one trained only on religious words, with no names at all (AUC 0.60). Words spelled with the signs of no agreed value are Minoan-shaped in their other syllables too. The contrast is not only with Pylos. Scored on the stem, with the ending removed, and with a model that never saw a Pylos name, Knossos names are also more Minoan than the 46 names of Thebes, Mycenae and Tiryns (AUC 0.63, p = 0.0025), and Knossos-only names more Minoan than Knossos names also found on the mainland. One limit: the earliest Knossos archive, the Room of Chariot Tablets, does not have more Minoan names than the later deposits; if anything it has fewer. Many Knossos words look like Minoan stems with Greek endings. Knossos-only words are a Linear A word plus one extra syllable more than twice as often as Pylos words (7.8% against 3.4%). Among personal names the added syllables are typical Greek endings, as in a-da-ra-ro on Linear A A-DA-RA. The Minoan signal sits in these stems, not the endings: Knossos names actually end in -o more often than Pylos names. Two cautions. The stems are ordinary Linear A words, not especially Linear A names. Against Thebes, Mycenae and Tiryns the Knossos excess is small and not significant (7.8% against 6.4%), so part of the contrast is Pylos being low.

A script ( targets/lineara/reading/build_reading.py ) gives each of the 5,339 tokens in the corpus one class, not counting dividers and damage marks. Glosses are kept to those with a stated basis: Commodity pictograms: the GORILA labels (grain, wine, oil, olives, figs, men, goats, cyperus), which rest on the same signs’ meaning in Linear B. Fraction values: Corazza et al. 2021, except the two that section 04 disputes. KU-RO: “total”, tested here. PO-TO-KU-RO: “grand total”. KI-RO: “deficit”. It heads lists that KU-RO then totals (HT 88, 94b, 117a). On HT 34 it follows a subtraction: 100 − 70 = 30. Class Tokens Share Read as sense: numbers, fractions, commodities, KU-RO / PO-TO-KU-RO / KI-RO, three place names 2,232 41.8% Read as sound, with a function only: list entries, headings, formula words, sealing marks 2,164 40.5% Unread: unidentified signs and ligatures (*301, *308…), words containing one, disputed or unvalued fractions 943 17.7% Measured on signs instead of tokens, 32.1% read as sense. HT 88 shows what a reading looks like at this level: A-DU [heading], VIR+KA [men] 20: RE-ZA 6, KI-KI-NA 7. KI-RO [deficit]: KU-PA 3 -PA 3 1, KA-JU 1, KU-PA 3 -NU 1, PA-JA-RE 1, SA-MA-RO 1, DA-TA-RE 1. KU-RO [total] 6. Sixty-six entries like these, short words each with a small number of men, are tagged as probable personal names. A word that recurs as an entry on several tablets is written by the same scribe 18% of the time, against 4% by chance, so scribes kept their own people or sections. Scribes also specialise in commodities and in transaction terms (SA-RA 2 , KA-PA, A-DU), so the Haghia Triada archive was divided by hand and subject. Each scribe also had a list style (list length, whether to add a total, the size of amounts within one commodity), and tablets with several commodities list them in a fixed order, grain first and wine last, and different scribes follow the same order. Figs have a place in it too. Linear A has no separate fig sign: it writes figs with the syllable NI, which Linear B later used as its fig logogram. NI entries take fractions like other measured goods (45%, against 6% for men), stand after grain, cyperus and oil and before wine, and appear with grain more than chance. Linear B kept these habits. Its fig logogram, the same NI sign, follows grain on all 37 Linear B tablets that record both, and takes sub-units as often as NI takes fractions in Linear A (44% against 45%). Linear B also lists grain first, puts the largest amount first and orders lists of goods largest-first. Wine last is the one Linear A habit it did not keep. The other difference is in notation: a Linear A list states its commodity sign once, at its head, and leaves it understood (38% of entries carry it). Linear B repeats the logogram on nearly every line of a list of goods (Knossos 82%, Pylos 86%, no real difference); the lower Knossos figure for lists of people comes from its women-and-children tablets, where the girls and boys lines carry their own word instead of MUL, and from two long name lists (hands 102 and 105) that state VIR once or twice for a dozen names, the Linear A way. Linear B tablets also put grain first, but beyond grain their order does not match the Linear A one. Written totals were a Haghia Triada habit: 18% of its tablets end in KU-RO, against 3% at Phaistos and Zakros and none elsewhere. The same persons recur on tablets of the same commodity. The syllables attached to commodity signs were regional: Haghia Triada and Tylissos share one set of oil ligatures (OLE+U, OLE+KI, OLE+MI), while Khania writes OLE+TA and Zakros GRA+PA. Tylissos shares Haghia Triada’s oil ligatures but none of its words, so the link was one of notation. Some unread signs are local too (*411, *409 and *311 occur only at Khania), and typical amounts of the same commodity differ by site: grain entries are large at Haghia Triada and small at Khania and Zakros, while wine entries are the reverse. Counts of men do not differ between sites, so the likelier explanation is that the sites measured grain and wine in different units. Two sets of tablets repeat whole groups of entries, HT 86 with HT 95 and ZA 4 with ZA 15: lists that were written twice. Three recurrent words get a function but no meaning: SA-RA 2 : a transaction term used only at Haghia Triada, with grain and cyperus, in 20 records. A-DU and KA-PA: heading terms. The full reading of every record ( reading/edition.txt , built by targets/lineara/reading/build_reading.py ) is not in the public repository, because the digital texts it is built from carry no licence. It is available on request. The totals. All 35 KU-RO and PO-TO-KU-RO totals were rechecked with exact fractions. For each, the entries were summed over several windows: from the start of the tablet, from the last rule, after a KI-RO heading, over both faces of the object, and by commodity. Ten balance. HT 123a’s olive total balances only when its olive entries are summed apart from the other commodities on the tablet, 31 + 31½ + 16 + 15 = 93½. The figure below replays that tablet. The rest do not, because of damage or because of slips that are long known. HT 9a is out by ¾, HT 13 by ½, HT 94a and HT 119 by 1. On HT 122 the grand total is 97, where the two faces give 31 + 65 = 96. Arithmetic restorations. Where a total is intact and the list above it is damaged, the missing amount follows: 4 on HT 11a, 4 on HT 100, 9 on HT 122a, 13 on HT 27a. Five totals cannot be reconciled in any window, and only the tablets themselves can decide those. A correction to the digital texts. They give HT 34’s KI-RO as 37, where Younger and GORILA have 30 with the 7 erased. Across tablets. The same entry words recur on different tablets far more often than chance allows. Four pairs of records share three or more names, against 0.1 expected. Three findings follow: A-KA-RU and A-DU are transaction categories. Five men (DA-ME, DI-DE-RU, KU-NI-SU, MI-NU-TE, SA-RU) receive grain on HT 86 and HT 95, split between the headings A-KA-RU and A-DU. On HT 86a they get 20 each. On HT 95b all five stand under A-DU at 10 each, exactly half. The two words are applied to the same people, so they are neither persons nor places. PA 3 marks the part delivered. HT 9 lists a wine account on its front (total 31¾) and repeats the same names on its back under PA 3 (total 24). Every shared amount on the back is equal to or smaller than the one on the front: 5¾ → 3, 10 → 8, 4 → 4, 2 → 2, 2½ → 2, 2½ → 2. HT 34 has the same shape: 100, PA 3 70, KI-RO 30. This supports Younger’s suggestion, now on two tablets. KI-RO lists count individuals. Every name in a KI-RO section (HT 88, 94b, 117a) carries exactly 1, whatever the same name carries elsewhere: KU-PA 3 -NU has 109 on HT 1, and SA-RU 20 of grain. These are functions, not translations. Across sites the picture reverses. Only 10 entry words appear at more than one site, against 33 expected by chance (p = 0.0005). Each archive has its own names. The few words that do travel are mostly administrative ones: A-DU at Haghia Triada and Tylissos, and DA-RE at Haghia Triada, Palaikastro and Khania. That suggests DA-RE, too, is a term rather than a person.

Linear A writes fractions with special signs, conventionally J, E, F, K, L2, B, D, H, A and a few rarer ones. Their values are a small cipher problem in their own right. Only one tablet fixes a value cleanly: HT 104, where 45 J + 20 J + 29 = 95, so J = ½. The largest study, Corazza, Ferrara, Montecchi, Tamburini and Valério (2021), proposes J ½, E ¼, F ⅛, H 1/16, A 1/24, B ⅕, D ⅙, K 1/10 and L2 1/20. They reached these by constraint search and optimality. Compound fractions are written largest first. Before reading that paper, this project collected every run of fraction signs within one entry of the corpus, 296 runs, and recorded the order in which pairs are written. It then scored the published values against those pairs. The older values (B = ⅓) fail on KH 9. The 2021 values fail on one firm case: HT 34, line 3 gives an amount written 2 H K . Three sources agree on that order: the GORILA drawing, the lineara.xyz text and SigLA. Written largest first, H must exceed K. The 2021 paper allows H only 1/16 or less (its 28 best solutions give 1/16 to 1/84), and K is 1/10. No value of H fixes it within that system. The other values are held at the paper’s figures, and its own rule that one value has one notation is applied. The only typologically attested values that would put H above K are ⅓, ⅖, 3/20 and 3/10, and each is already written by an attested compound (D D, B B, K L2, E L2). A second, weaker tension. Younger reads HT 34’s last lines as settling earlier items, with PU F settling the item written A. On that reading F (⅛) is at most A, but A is 1/24. The authors themselves say optimality did not fix H and A, and chose those two values on structural grounds. HT 34 is a counterexample to those two values, not an alternative system: with 29 order pairs, the evidence is too thin for one. None of the 18 works citing the 2021 paper revises the values. The team’s own later account, Corazza’s Computational methods for undeciphered scripts (2024), repeats “A = 1/24?, H = 1/16?”, still marked tentative, and does not discuss HT 34. As far as the sources reachable online show, the conflict has not been raised before. Salgarella’s 2025 book is closed access and was not checked. It is the one item left before the point can be called new with confidence. Tagging each fraction pair with its commodity does not rescue the published values either: the three exceptions fall under three different commodities, and HT 34’s is the only pair in the corpus with both H and K. New evidence is on its way. The ivory handle KN Zg 58, found at Knossos in 2024, carries six different fraction signs in a row. Its excavators say the sequence orders the values differently from every published proposal (Kanta, Nakassis, Palaima and Perna 2025), but they reserve it for the final edition. That sequence, and a good photograph of HT 34 line 3 (Heraklion Museum, HM 22), would settle the question. A two-page note setting out the HT 34 argument is drafted in targets/lineara/note_HT34/ .

Offering vessels from peak sanctuaries across Crete carry a recurring sequence of words. Across 14 inscriptions from 7 sites, the order of its slots holds in 77 of 78 pairs: A-TA-I-*301-WA-JA · [place word] · JA-SA-SA-RA-ME · U-NA-KA-NA-SI · I-PI-NA-MA · SI-RU-TE · TA-NA-…-U-TI-NU The one reversal is on IO Za 6. The variation sits in a prefix that is JA-, A- or nothing, and it moves between slots: the place word is JA-DI-KI-TU at Iouktas but A-DI-KI-TE at Palaikastro; JA-SA-SA-RA-ME alternates with A-SA-SA-RA-ME and SA-SA-RA-ME; PK Za 8 has JA-SA-U-NA-KA-NA-SI. A-DI-KI-TE is written at Palaikastro, the later centre of the cult of Diktaean Zeus. That fits the published reading “Dikte”, but it is context, not proof. The slot order and the prefix are the formula’s grammar as far as it can be seen. What the words mean is unknown: JA-SA-SA-RA-ME is usually taken for a divine name, and that is as far as the evidence goes. The measurement confirms what Davis (2014) and others describe.

Everything else on this page is measured. This section is interpretation. It sets out the most likely picture that the measured results support, and says what each part rests on. No word is translated here; what is guessed is what the entries were for. What the archive was. Most tablets come from Haghia Triada and survive because the building burned, around 1450 BC, and baked clay that was never meant to be fired. Unfired tablets were working records, kept for the current accounting period and then smoothed over or thrown away. They probably cover the last months before the fire: current business, not history. The amounts are small, from single units to a few hundred. Each site has its own names (only 10 entry words occur at two sites, against 33 expected by chance), and each measures grain and wine at its own scale. The likeliest setting is a regional centre running its own district, not one Crete-wide bureau. Goods coming in and going out. The goods are the staples of a Bronze Age Aegean economy: grain in the largest amounts, then wine, oil in several kinds marked by the syllables attached to the oil sign, olives and figs. There is also cyperus, an aromatic plant that Linear B records use for perfumed oil. Most entries pair a word, probably a person or a work-group leader, with an amount. Some are likely allocations to dependants and workers. Others are likely contributions due from local households. No word on the tablets that has been glossed marks which way the goods moved, so the direction is inferred from the few terms whose job is clear. Debts and deliveries. The clearest terms are about obligations. KU-RO is the total and KI-RO the shortfall still owed. PA 3 probably marks the part actually delivered: on HT 34, 100 was due, 70 came in and 30 is owed. KI-RO probably worked like Linear B’s o-pe-ro at Pylos, “owed, lacking”, and was used both for goods not delivered and for people who did not turn up. Every name in a KI-RO section carries exactly 1, whatever the same name carries elsewhere. That fits a list of absent individuals better than a list of small debts. Two tablets retold in plain words. These are paraphrases. The numbers and the terms KU-RO, KI-RO and PA 3 are as the tablets give them; the roles of the people are the guess. HT 88. Account A-DU: men, twenty. With RE-ZA six, with KI-KI-NA seven. Short: KU-PA 3 -PA 3 , KA-JU, KU-PA 3 -NU, PA-JA-RE, SA-MA-RO, DA-TA-RE, one each. Total short: six. Probably a labour roster: a levy of twenty men, part supplied through two team leaders, with six named men missing or still owed. HT 9. Front: wine against each name, 31¾ in all. Back, under PA 3 : the same names with the same or smaller amounts, 24 in all. Probably a collection sheet: the wine each person owed, then what each actually delivered. The kinds of account. A-DU and A-KA-RU are applied to the same five men, who receive 20 of grain each under the first on HT 86 and 10 each under A-DU on HT 95, exactly half. They are probably two kinds of allocation or obligation: a regular issue and a special one, or two instalments or seasons. SA-RA 2 , used only at Haghia Triada with grain and cyperus, is another transaction term. Earlier scholars have compared it with Akkadian šarāku , “to allocate”. The language tests in section 07 found no Semitic signal, so that comparison stays unsupported. DA-RE, which travels between sites as names do not, is probably a term too. Receipts and tags. Roundels and nodules carry a seal impression and one or two signs. The likely reading is receipts and labels: a roundel records a single transaction witnessed by the seal holder, and nodules sealed parcels or documents written on perishable material. Their signs differ by site and differ from the tablets’ own single signs, so each centre kept its own local receipting system. The offerings. The stone vessels carry what looks like a dedication, perhaps “[the dedicator] offered this at [the sanctuary] to [the deity]”, with titles or requests after it. The place slot changes with the sanctuary (Dikte, Iouktas) and the rest stays fixed, which is how a formula behaves. JA-SA-SA-RA-ME is usually taken as a divine name, and some have compared it with a Luwian phrase meaning “my lady”. The tests here give that comparison no support either. The picture as a whole. The most likely picture is a mid-sized Minoan centre running a redistribution economy for its district. It collected grain, wine and oil from local households and producers, issued goods to named people and work teams, and kept careful track of what was still owed. Its scribes split the work by section and by commodity. Its practices differed from the neighbouring centres’, and alongside the accounts the same society made formal offerings at mountain sanctuaries. When the Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos they kept much of this bookkeeping: grain first, figs after grain, largest amounts first. Where the guess is weakest. The weakest points are which way the goods moved and who the named people were: stewards, farmers, foremen or dependants. KU-PA 3 -NU is a real person who handled 109 units of something on HT 1, but whether that was a payment, a debt or a stock held is inference. A bilingual text would test these guesses, and so would a Linear A term that turns up with a known meaning in Linear B.

Minoan has been called Semitic, Luwian, Hurrian, Etruscan-like and more, usually on the strength of look-alike words: KU-RO “total” beside Semitic kull “all”, and so on. The test here asks whether a proposed relative matches Linear A better than languages that cannot be related to it. Method. Each lexicon’s words are spelled the way Linear B spells words: open syllables, final consonants dropped, l = r, voicing ignored. These rules were fixed before any result was seen, and they turn Knossos into ko-no-so and Phaistos into pa-i-to. Exact matches with the 491 Linear A word types of three or more signs are counted. Each language is also scored against its own syllables shuffled across its words. Lexicon Kind Forms Matches Ratio to own-syllable null Luwian (Melchert 1993) proposed 540 1 0.5 Hurrian (Laroche 1980) proposed 294 1 1.1 Akkadian proposed 336 3 2.1 Ugaritic proposed 288 4 3.3 Etruscan proposed 27 0 too few words Ancient Greek not proposed 28,606 27 2.3 Hawaiian, Māori, Yoruba controls 1,106 / 1,484 / 2,447 4 / 4 / 7 2.1 / 1.4 / 2.1 Real words beat the shuffled null even in unrelated languages, so what counts is whether a proposed family beats it by more than the controls do. None does: Semitic: 2.7× against the controls’ 1.7×, p = 0.22 (0.86 after correcting for four families). Luwian: below chance. Etruscan: the open lexicon is too small to test. Hurrian: tested with Laroche’s Glossaire de la langue hourrite (1980), 1 match against 0.9 expected (p = 0.6). The result holds however the lexicon’s ḫ is spelled. The individual matches look like evidence until the controls are set beside them. E-KU-RU is Akkadian eqlum “field”, and also Yoruba eguru “sandstone”. A-KA-TA is Greek akantha and Yoruba akata “panther”. For the three words whose sense the arithmetic fixes (KU-RO, KI-RO, PO-TO-KU-RO), no candidate language offers a same-spelled word of fitting meaning, while controls offer look-alikes of the wrong one (Yoruba kuro , Hawaiian kilo ). The method itself is the problem. Applied to the one case where the answer is known, Greek against Linear B, it gives 13 matches per 1,000 Greek words. Yoruba gets 22 per 1,000 against the same Linear B list. At the size of the candidate lexicons, a relationship as close as Greek to Linear B would yield under one exact match. Matched word shapes cannot identify Minoan’s relatives. They could not even identify Greek as the language of Linear B. Decipherments built on them are not evidence either way. Eteocretan, the likely descendant. Five inscriptions from Praisos and Dreros (7th–3rd century BC) record a non-Greek language in Greek letters, often thought to descend from Minoan. Its sounds are known, but most of it has no word division, so Linear A words were sought inside the text once both were spelled the Linear B way. Not one Linear A word of three or more signs occurs in it. Random word lists from Hawaiian, Māori or Yoruba of the same size produce one to three such hits. The design is barely sensitive: Linear B words turn up only two or three times in the same length of Greek. So the result weakly disfavours a close identity between Minoan and Eteocretan, and cannot test a distant one. The Pre-Greek substrate. Greek kept many words from the languages spoken before it, and Wiktionary marks about 1,600 of them. Against ordinary Greek words of the same length, these match Linear A slightly more often: 6 against 2.6, among them ákantha “thorn plant” beside A-KA-TA and kídalon “onion” beside KI-DA-RO. The excess vanishes without the one shared place name, Phaistos (p = 0.10). The Linear A words are personal names in lists, not plants or vessels. By syllable distribution, Pre-Greek is no closer to Linear A than ordinary Greek. Cretan Hieroglyphic, the earlier Cretan script. Its sign groups (Younger’s lexicon, 365 groups) were given the values CHIC assigns by sign shape. Only 20 groups can be fully read that way, and they match Linear A no more than chance (3 against 2.2). Younger’s fuller value grid does produce matches (17 against 11). But that grid was partly built by matching Hieroglyphic groups to Linear A words, so the excess proves nothing. Continuity in vocabulary between the two scripts needs the values of the signs fixed independently. Every comparison open to this project has now been run under the same rules with controls: four proposed families, the likely descendant and the known contact vocabulary. None identifies the language.

An earlier pass here collated the lineara.xyz texts with SigLA. It found more pairs of words that differ by one added sign than two randomised models predict (42 against about 23 and 26, adjusted p ≈ 0.01). Examples are PA-RA-NE / A-PA-RA-NE and DA-KU-SE-NE / DA-KU-SE-NE-TI. So Linear A words have ordered structure, affixes or compounds. No preference for suffixes over prefixes survives the test. The idea that A- marks a heading fails on ZA 10a, where TA-NA-TE and A-TA-NA-TE are both ordinary entries. These are constraints on any future decipherment, not meanings. Alice Kober found Linear B’s inflection by lining up one stem with different endings in different grammatical slots. The same test here asks whether, within a family of words sharing a stem, the ending predicts the word’s position (heading, list entry, formula, sealing). It does not, beyond chance (p = 0.20, 49 families). The initial A-/JA- leans toward headings, as in A-KA-RU, A-PA-RA-NE and A-RI-JA against the bare forms in entries, but not significantly (p = 0.07, 12 families). No family has more than nine attestations, and Kober’s method needs many more per stem than Linear A provides.

A counterexample to the published fraction values. HT 34 contradicts H = 1/16 and A = 1/24 under the system’s own rules. Nothing in the literature reachable online discusses it (section 04). A calibrated test of the language proposals. Semitic, Luwian, Hurrian and the rest do no better than Hawaiian or Yoruba, and neither Eteocretan nor the Pre-Greek substrate shows a reliable link. The positive control shows that look-alike matching cannot identify a language at this scale (section 07). Minoan names at Knossos. The Linear A words that survive into Linear B are names, significantly more than chance, and all of them Knossian, among them TA-NA-TI, KI-DA-RO, DA-I-PI-TA and I-TA-JA. Beyond these, the Knossos personal names as a whole are Minoan in shape, while the Pylos names are not (section 02). Accounting functions across tablets. A-KA-RU and A-DU are categories over the same persons. PA 3 marks a delivered part, and KI-RO lists count persons one each (section 03). Corrections to the digital texts: HT 34’s KI-RO is 30, not 37. A field in a third-party SigLA decoder was mislabelled; it holds sign position and word index, not boundary states. A word-by-word comparison of the two digital editions lists 44 disagreements for their editors ( targets/lineara/ERRATA.md ). Among them are a systematic JA/PA 3 confusion and three readings that affect results here: SU-KI-RA-TA, PA-RI-NE and DA-ZA in SigLA. Replication, now measured over the whole corpus: the Linear B carry-over (argued before by Packard, and by Steele and Meissner); KU-RO, KI-RO and PO-TO-KU-RO; the place names; the name lists; the formula order. The share of the corpus that can be read without the language (41.8% of tokens) is measured here; no earlier measure of it was found. It contains no new reading. Nothing on the language itself. No word is given a new meaning, and no language family is supported.

The meanings of the 2,164 tokens read only as sound (names, transaction terms, formula words). Blocked: the language is unidentified and no bilingual exists. 632 unidentified signs and ligatures (*301, *304, *308, QA 2 +…, MI+JA+…). They have no Linear B counterpart and no context fixes them. The fraction signs H and A, and the rare L, W, X, Y and DD. Too few attestations. Damaged entries and totals. Restorations are proposed in targets/lineara/reading/restorations.json . 631 single-sign marks on sealings. One sign per object, no syntax. Five totals that no window reconciles: HT 13, HT 25b, HT 102, HT 122b and PH(?) 31a. Only examining the tablets can say whether the scribe or the transcription erred. A fuller Etruscan test. It waits on a larger open lexicon. Salgarella, Writing in Bronze Age Crete (2025). It is closed access. A library copy would settle whether HT 34 is discussed there. The Anetaki sceptre (KN Zg 57–58), about 119 signs, the longest Linear A text. It has no published transcription yet (Kanta, forthcoming). A photograph of HT 34 line 3. Only the Heraklion Museum can supply one. Beyond these, progress needs new material: a bilingual text, or a much larger corpus.

Nine letters of the imperial agent in Rome, bound and catalogued among Alonso Sánchez’s Venice letters but in a different nomenclator, for which no published key was found. The key was recovered from adjacent plaintext: two of the letters have the clerk’s full contemporary clear version bound beside them. Four letters are complete in content and a fifth, R9649, is deciphered in full from its own clear; the other four are deciphered in part (73–80% of tokens; 76% over the five), among them a letter from Genoa of 13 September 1522 reporting Adorno’s plan to invade France through Provence. xul · ton · tu · ton·x·m · zar · x·ᶻ·4 lo · que · no · que·d·o · de · d·o·n Rome → Charles V · nomenclator of three-letter code groups with a substitution alphabet, inline with clear Spanish · Sept–Nov 1522 Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome to Charles V, 1522 to Charles V Go to the full text ↓ Real Academia de la Historia, Salazar 9/26 · DECODE R9634, R9644–R9646, R9648–R9650, R9652, R9656 · the imperial agent in Rome reporting to the Emperor on Adrian VI, in the months before the French came back into Italy Nine letters catalogued with Alonso Sánchez’s Venice letters, among which they are bound, in a different nomenclator. The key was recovered from the clerk’s contemporary clear versions bound with two of them; with it, one letter from Genoa reports a plan to invade France through Provence, eighteen months before the 1524 campaign. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 20 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (4% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (4% of the cipher) The letters Nine records of Lope Hurtado de Mendoza, the imperial agent, to Charles V, September–November 1522: eight from Rome on Adrian VI, and one (R9634) from Genoa, 13 September 1522. Where Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro 9/26 (A-26), DECODE R9634, R9644–R9646, R9648–R9650, R9652, R9656. Bound and catalogued with Alonso Sánchez’s Venice letters, but in a different key. The cipher Three-letter code groups for words and syllables, with a substitution alphabet for spelled words, inline with clear Spanish. Runs open with a mark ( Ꮒ ) often followed by null groups. How it was deciphered R9644 and R9650 carry the clerk’s full clear versions; aligning them with the cipher gave the code values. On 2 October 2026 the key was extended on R9634 itself ( ɋ = r, a plural z after codes, ducado , mar , gente , the nulls after the opener) and applied to the four letters with no usable clear. What it says Adrian VI temporising between Charles V and Francis I, his capitulation with the duke of Ferrara, the fortress of Ostia; and from Genoa, Geronimo Adorno’s plan for the Emperor and Henry VIII to invade France through Provence, la tierra mas flaca que el tiene , at 70,000 ducats a month, in March. Measured Tokens read as sense (3 October 2026): R9634 872 of 1,191 (73.2%), R9645 368 of 489 (75.3%), R9646 97 of 121 (80%), R9649 89 of 89 (100%), R9656 177 of 225 (78.7%, re-transcribed from the image); the five together 1,603 of 2,115 (76%). Under 95%, so partial. Still open About 40 code groups that occur once in R9634 and nowhere else in 21 letters, and spelled words in all four partial letters whose signs cannot be told apart at DECODE’s resolution; a word-perfect text of the ciphered leaves of R9644, R9648 and R9650.

These nine records sit in Salazar 9/26 among Alonso Sánchez's despatches from Venice, were catalogued with them, and look at first like more of the same: the same months, the same recipient, cipher mixed with clear inside the sentence, code groups of the same shape and the same three-letter build. The catalogue treated them as one target. Two tests separate them. In Sánchez's nomenclator every code group ends in one of b c d f g h l m n ; Hurtado's groups also end in p and z ( tep , tap , groups ending -z ), which Sánchez's key does not contain. And where the two keys use the same group they disagree: xul is despues in Sánchez and lo here , ho is que in Sánchez where this cipher uses ton . Same design, same chancery tradition, different key. Nor is it Juan Manuel's, the third imperial cipher of 1522 Rome: none of the values fixed here appears in Tomokiyo's 173-code table for it. That table is itself a partial recovery, so this test supports a separate key without proving it, and it is recorded that way.

Satoshi Tomokiyo's Correspondence in Cipher of Imperial Ambassadors Alonso Sanchez and Juan Manuel (1522) (Cryptiana, 6 September 2025) reconstructs two of the three ciphers in this group of volumes. It does not mention Lope Hurtado, and his records (R9634, R9644–R9646, R9648–R9650, R9652, R9656) fall outside both of the ranges it lists. A web search found no decipherment. DECODE records seven of the nine as Non-decrypted , that is, with no decipherment attached.

R9644 (ff. 237–243, 1 November 1522) holds the ciphered letter on ff. 237–239 and the clerk's own full clear version on ff. 241–242 , headed Al Rey — De Lope Hurtado, de Roma, del primero de noviembre , written out in lettered sections with A , B , C standing in the margin of both. R9650 (ff. 269–272) has the same arrangement, its clear on f. 272. R9648 (9 November, with no decipherment on DECODE) is a duplicate of R9644, so one clear version covers two records. RAH, Salazar 9/26, f. 237. The cipher runs inline with the clear; the A in the margin keys the passage to the clerk's clear version on f. 241. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro 9/26 f. 237, via DECODE R9644.

The clear at the foot of section A reads … porque esta tan escasso que nunca hombre lo fue mas ; hasta que el arçobispo venga creo que sera mejor no apretallo mucho . On the cipher page the middle clause stands in the clear, bracketing the run: six tokens for six words, with no room for misalignment: ton tab xud xul ɣm xon que nunca hombre lo fue mas and tu = no from no apretallo mucho . From there the alignment extends: zun top at da por , ᵇʒ7 and teɡ at era and para , zil ɣub zed zar at con el arçobispo de Cosenza, ɣub taf at el papa , rab at v. ma .

Three-letter code groups carry most of the text and are written as plain latin trigrams; spelled runs between them use a substitution alphabet. Three features matter for decryption, and none is described in the published account of the sibling ciphers: Homophones at code level. ta and tu both mean no , and both occur in the same line. The alphabet has them too: the single spelled word perdida writes d with two different symbols. Codes also stand for syllables. xur + zun = na + da ; ton + ℓ∞74 = que + rian ; zil + a spelled ocia = conocia ; nul + vuc +s = obligados . zun is da the whole word in da por , the second syllable of na·da , and the middle of que·da·rian . Several codes can make one word. lu + ho = porque , lul + ta = quales , ton +d+o = quedo . A code group can therefore be part of a word, a whole word, or one of several groups forming a word. A decryption that treats each group as one word goes wrong in both directions. The foot of f. 237. After the clear contento : xul ton tu ton ·d·o zar d·o·n, lo que no quedo de don [Joan]. A code completed with two alphabet symbols, then a name spelled out. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro 9/26 f. 237, via DECODE R9644.

A key fitted to its own crib can reproduce the crib and nothing else. This one was tested on other records. R9648 , which has no decipherment on DECODE, gives nine tokens for nine words with nothing left over: ʋ ton ɣub taf tu ɣof ɣuc ton + spelled venga = «y que el papa no esta en que venga» ; further down, la paz por los infieles y por la necessidad . Its spelled perdido decrypts letter by letter from six symbols fixed on the other record; the word was not searched for. R9656 is the stronger test: a despatch of 23 November with no full clear version and no duplicate (a faded clear copy on f. 335r is legible only in half of each line). Applied without a crib, the key gives el papa for ɣub taf after the clear words las cartas traxo don Correo q vino con la valante . Measured with a resolver that applies confirmed values only: 70% of tokens on R9648 f. 262, 62% on R9650 f. 270, 57% on R9645 f. 243, which has no crib of any kind. The figures do not change when the alphabet values are downgraded to probable (below), because almost all resolved tokens are code groups, the better-established half of the key. These were coverage figures for sample lines; the whole-letter readings of 2 October 2026 (sections 08 and 09) measure tokens read as sense instead.

The content of four of the nine is complete: R9644 and R9650 from their clear versions, R9648 as R9644's duplicate, and R9652 , which DECODE records as Partially decrypted though it carries no cipher at all . That leaf is written entirely in clear and signed Lope Hurtado . R9644, 1 November. Charles V had written to warn Adrian VI directly; Hurtado approves, because if the Pope will not do his duty he should at least not be able to plead that he was not warned: no se disculpe despues con dezir que v. magestad no le mando prevenir . The Pope's voluntad is good and his obras satisfy nobody; he pleads the Turks and the Emperor's need, and is tan escasso que nunca hombre lo fue mas . Hurtado presses for the papal household to be paid before the other side buys them: si no los corrompiessen dandoles . The King of France asks a safe-conduct to send an ambassador and the Pope will not have him come. R9650, November. The main news is that los franceses son determinados de venir en Italia, y enbian gran suma de dinero a Leon , brought by post from the archbishop of Bari, with Hieronymo Adorno 's intercepted letters behind it. Adrian is urged to act sin dilatar mas , and takes it tan tibiamente que no se espera de todo bien . R9652, November. A licenciado Bernardino , «gran bellaco», is in Rome; the Duke of Sessa wants him seized; the Pope will order it if the man is inside Rome, declines a night arrest when he is found lodging with his brother in the city ( aqui no seria bien ), and offers a formal suplicacion instead. It closes with las nuevas de Rodas que escrive el visorrey , the viceroy of Naples on the siege of Rhodes. Sánchez's R9653 of 20 November carries the same Rhodes news from Venice, out of Candia and the Signoria. Rome and Venice reported the siege to the Emperor in the same fortnight, in two different ciphers, now bound in the same volume.

R9634 (ff. 14–16) was transcribed on 2 October 2026 from DECODE’s three openings; DECODE attaches no decipherment or transcription to it. It is not a Rome letter. The clear close on f. 16r is dated de Genoba xiij de setiembre 1522 and signed by Lope Hurtado; DECODE has the month but neither the day nor the place. There is no clear version in the record and none in print (Bergenroth’s Calendar of State Papers, Spain ii calendars no Hurtado letter of September 1522), so the reading rests on the key alone. RAH, Salazar 9/26, f. 14r, lines 1–7 of the cipher. Line 3 ends top + seven signs, ton yaf xug : por Proentia, que es la ; line 4 opens tierra mas flaca que el tiene . The clear words in the last line are para proveer con las galeras de Genova . Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro 9/26 f. 14r, via DECODE R9634. Written four months after the imperial sack of Genoa (30 May 1522), the letter reports a plan that “sensible and honourable men” and Geronimo Adorno, the new imperial doge, put to Lope Hurtado. The Emperor and the King of England, queriendo destruir al Rey de Francia , should make war on him through Provence : que es la tierra mas flaca que el tiene, y donde el exercito de V. Mt. puede entrar seguro, una tierra fertil … [para proveer con las galeras de Genova] … donde pueden entrar bien … los de la mar y los de la tierra The French are muertos de miedo after the sack. Taking Provence and Lyon would let the allies tomarle lo otro que le queda y cercarle en Paris , which could not be done por Flandes ni por España . Asked what force it would need, Adorno said six hundred men-at-arms, light horse and soldiers, paid 70,000 ducats a month ( lxx U yob z ), if the Emperor and the King of England agreed on it; the troops already in the duchy of Milan would serve, and the Pope would be glad to see them go, por no los tener alojados en sus tierras . It must be kept secret, por que no toviesen aviso , and settled now for March : es cosa segura, de poca costa e provechosa . The clear close commends Adorno as tan buen servidor de V. Mt. Charles V and Henry VIII did invade Provence in 1524, when Bourbon and Pescara laid siege to Marseille. This is an early form of that plan, put to the Emperor from Genoa in September 1522. What the letter added to the key ( key_1522_r9634.tsv ): a new sign ɋ = r ( tierra three times); z after a code as the plural s ( xul z los , yob z ducados ), which is not the 1524 standing-alone z = n; the codes yob ducado , xep mar , xu gente , zar∂ des- ; and null groups after the run opener Ꮒ : ʃta confirmed in four letters, the others probable. The e/t confusion of the 1524 letters recurs: the closed 8 and the open-topped ϑ cannot be separated at DECODE’s resolution, so muertos , acordasen , faltasen and gastara are graded probable. Measured from the line-by-line reading ( r9634_reading.tsv ): 842 of 1,191 tokens read as sense on the first pass, 846 after a retry against the values won on R9645 (71%), and 872 (73.2%) on 3 October 2026, when codes were pooled over all 21 Hurtado letters and spelled words were matched against a Spanish lexicon with every reading of their doubtful signs ( vio , capitan , fue , vivo , tenia , ser , sostener , all probable). The key values 80% of the tokens as confirmed and 94% with probables; the gap is spelled words whose letters all have values but give no word, and about 45 code groups that occur once. A language check on the read text returns modern Spanish first.

Earlier versions of this page listed R9634, R9645, R9646, R9649 and R9656 as having no clear version. That was out of date for two of them: R9649 carries its own clerk’s clear on f. 268 , and R9656 a faded clear copy on f. 335r , legible only in the right half of each line. All four were re-read on 2 October 2026 with the extended key. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 found that R9634, R9645, R9646 and R9656, though 61–80% of their tokens have a value, have holes, open codes or paraphrase in most cipher sentences: they are decoded, not read. The same day the four were re-read on crops of the DECODE images and written out as continuous partial readings with English ( texts/R9634_reading.md and the others; label corrections in texts/<doc>_corrections.tsv : the crossed t-form is m , the 8-form stands for ϑ). R9645 f. 243r lines 1–12 gained the Ferrara capitulation ( que abia tomado assiento con el duque de Ferrara ) and R9656 f. 334v lo de [?Ostia] , but none of the four reaches the bar (clean sentence shares 0.51–0.73), and all stay decoded, not read. The summaries below are gists of the partial readings. R9649, Rome, 9 November 1522 (89 of 89 tokens, 100%). Deciphered completely, and checked word for word against f. 268. Adrian VI asks Charles to tell him to keep good guard on the fortress of Ostia, which Cardinal Santa Cruz (Carvajal, as dean of the college) claims: en la fortaleza de Ostia, y que no la de a nadie, porque no querria darsela ni tener le quexoso . The licenciado Bernardino has landed from Barcelona and is hiding at his brother’s house in Rome. The groups yω ʃta after the opener have no counterpart in the clear and are nulls. R9646, [Rome, November 1522] (97 of 121, 80%). Adrian VI’s capitulation with the duke of Ferrara is signed and a copy is coming. Charles’s request ( la decima , probable) meets papal caution: the Pope abia miedo que oviese de […] ; the archbishop advises offering money al papa para sus necesidades … que creo que por dinero … . R9645, Rome, November 1522 (368 of 489, 75.3%). Re-transcribed in the R9634 notation. The glosses at the foot of f. 243v (Bernardino’s report from London: the King of England is agreed with the Scots, who have thrown out the duke of Albany; the French boast that the English and the Emperor’s troops did nothing) confirm xu = gente and a null after the opener, and settle yib = duque . Unglossed f. 243r now reads as the terms of the Ferrara capitulation: the fief money of Pope Alexander, a hundred men-at-arms for the Church, no league save with the Pope and the Emperor, no harbouring of their enemies. R9656, Rome, 23 November 1522 (177 of 225, 78.7%). Re-transcribed from the images in the R9634 notation on 3 October 2026 (it was 131 of 214, 61%, in the older notation): the old ʒ was mostly ɣ̊ = r, and the f. 334v run now reads in full against the faded copy, que esta muy sospechoso el papa que de alla se le haya mandado lo que ha fecho ( zub = alla ). The archbishop of Bari sent the Pope no certain news of the French coming; the Pope says that if the French come it will be to their harm; he is muy sospechoso that the Emperor ordered what Don Juan Manuel has done. Six spelled words of f. 334r (ll. 6, 9, 13–16) still fail: no reading of their signs is a Spanish word.

Four letters are decoded, not read , measured as tokens with a sense-giving value: R9634 73.2%, R9645 75.3%, R9646 80%, R9656 78.7% (sections 08 and 09; R9649 is complete). What stays open in them: in R9634 about 40 code groups seen once (none recurs in the 21 Hurtado letters) ( ʃe , xer , zud , zac , ʃum , yat , zub , ʃof , xen , zer , yul …) and yel and ɣ̊e four times each, with no crib and none in print; spelled words whose letters all have values but give no word (two of them probably place names), and the force numerals other than the 600 men-at-arms and the 70,000 ducats; in R9645 tec ( ze = el from four pooled contexts, probable), ʃen and the spelled words of the unglossed lines; in R9646 two spelled words and the codes zip , zob , ʃof ; in R9656 six spelled words of f. 334r and the end of f. 334v l. 1. DECODE has no larger image than the one used, and the RAH Biblioteca Digital, which may hold better scans, sits behind a bot check that only a person in a browser can pass. Each spelled-word gap has one sign at the limit of the scan ( 8 / ϑ e/t, ∂ s/p/t, ε l/g). Graded: the codes and the alphabet signs confirmed on the clear versions are H; values taken from a single R9634 context ( yob , xep , the nulls other than ʃta ) are I; words marked probable in the reading files are M. The substitution alphabet is the limit. Nine symbols are fixed and cross-checked: ⋃ =p, 8 =e, ʒ =r, x / 6 =d, L =i, 7 =a, 4 =n, m / ᶻ =o. Beyond these, transcriptions of the spelled words contradict each other at DECODE's image resolution. One contradiction proved to be a homophone missing from the key , and the others may resolve the same way; unassigned symbols are left blank. Confidence is recorded for each value. The key file carries a confidence column; the resolver applies confirmed values only and shows probables in angle brackets. A check for pairs of codes with the same plaintext led to four retractions , kept in the file as commented RETRACTED lines, among them an early guess that zar meant Bari , when it means de . Nothing probable was used to derive anything else, so nothing downstream needed unwinding. Corrections to DECODE. R9652's status should be not enciphered ; DECODE has partially decrypted . R9634 is dated Genoa, 13 September 1522 on f. 16r; DECODE has the month only and files it with the Rome letters.

The limit is image resolution. DECODE serves these leaves at 3440×2465 for a two-page opening , about 1700 px across a folio: enough for the Latin-letter trigrams, too little to separate two similar cursive symbols. That is the cause of the alphabet limit, and further crib work does not change it. DECODE, checked with a logged-in session, has nothing better. The full-size file filesrv returns is that 3440×2465 opening; MASTER_ , MS_ , ORIG_ and .tif variants all come back as the server’s not-found placeholder, and the Image Manager answers “You do not have permission to access” to a viewer session, so its zoom view is unreachable too. The ceiling is DECODE’s stored derivative. The volume belongs to the Colección Salazar y Castro , which the Real Academia de la Historia has been digitising at its own Biblioteca Digital . If Salazar 9/26 is there, those images will be far better than DECODE’s derivative copies, and recovering the substitution alphabet becomes routine. That would give an exact text of the ciphered leaves and should allow a full decipherment of the four letters now deciphered in part, and of the faded clear copy of R9656 on f. 335r. It could not be done from here: bibliotecadigital.rah.es returns HTTP 403 to automated requests and puts a bot check in front of its search, in the same way DECODE’s image server needs a logged-in session. The search term is the old signature, Salazar y Castro, A-26 , and the leaves wanted are ff. 14–16, 237–244, 252, 260–272 and 334–335.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. R9644, Rome, 1 Nov 1522 (ff. 237-243), with its duplicate R9648 (9 Nov, ff. 260-265) Hurtado's running account of Adrian VI: the Pope's good will but unsatisfying deeds, his parsimony while he waits for the archbishop of Bari, the payment of the papal household before the other side buys it, the French King's request for a safe-conduct for an ambassador, and a leak of letters shown in copy in Castile. Read from the clerk's contemporary clear version (ff. 241-242); no full transcription of the ciphered leaves was made, only the passages aligned in NOTES.md. Transcription: NOTES.md Decryption read_r9644.md # R9644 — Lope Hurtado de Mendoza (Rome) to Charles V, 1 November 1522 RAH Salazar 9/26, ff. 237–243. DECODE R9644. Cipher on ff. 237–239; **the contemporary clear version on ff. 241–242**, headed *Al Rey — De Lope Hurtado, de Roma, del primero de noviembre*, written out in lettered sections **A**, **B**, **C** keyed to the same letters in the margin of the cipher. **R9648** (ff. 260–265, 9 Nov, DECODE *Non-decrypted*) is the duplicate of this despatch; its ciphered leaves carry the same text, so this clear reads that record too. **Read complete.** Transcribed from the image; abbreviations expanded in brackets. --- **[A]** Ha sido muy bien que v. m[agesta]d prevenga a su S[antida]d de lo que conviene a su servicio, porque aunque no haga lo que es obligado, no se disculpe despues con dezir que v. m[agesta]d no le mando prevenir, porque no supo si era mal lo que hazia. Assi mesmo fue bien escrivir largo, porque su S[antida]d tenia tanta passion que no conocia lo que don Joan le havia servido, y me tenia su persona. Y si v. m[agesta]d de alla no escriviera, pensara que don Joan y el **Cardenal de Medicis** havian ordenado [ara] lo que le havian de dezir, si aqui los hallara la carta de v. m[agesta]d. Yo he preguntado a su S[antida]d lo que le parece del duque, y me dixo que estava contento — lo que no quedo de don Joan, segun dizen todos. Es muy bien lo que v. m[agesta]d dize, que lo que hoviere de hazerse con los criados de su S[antida]d primero los sepa; pero hasta que v. m[agesta]d les de lo que fuere servido, si algo se le dixesse pensaria que era para no les dar nada, y diria que no queria que lo tomassen, y los criados quedarian descontentos, como diz que lo estan; porque como **Mossiur de la Xao** y yo le hablamos ha tanto tiempo, que ya tiene perdida la esperança. Yo tengo escrito a v. m[agesta]d la condicion del, y Mossiur de la Xao la sabe; y agora le enbio un memorial para que haga relacion a v. m[agesta]d. El **camarero Pedro** es el principal, y a este se ha de tener mas respeto que a ninguno; y es sin comparacion, y buenos los otros, si no los corrompiessen dandoles. Quando v. m[agesta]d acordare de hazerles la merced, sera bien dezir al papa … … que v. m[agesta]d les da aquello por los trabajos que tovieron en España, y porque tenga mas cuydado de servir a su S[antida]d; yo lo que v. m[agesta]d sera servido, que el papa lo haura por bien — lo que creo que no haria agora, como dicho he. Despues que el duque se fue, yo he hablado al papa lo que me ha parecido que era servicio de v. m[agesta]d. Su voluntad no puede ser mejor para lo que toca a v. m[agesta]d; las obras, ningun servidor de v. m[agesta]d la esta satisfecho. Da por descargo de lo que dexa de fazer la obligacion que tiene a procurar la paz, por ser papa, y por estar los infieles tan poderosos y su necessidad tan grande; y que v. m[agesta]d no la tiene, para que el se muestre como es obligado — que si v. al[teza] la tuviesse, no le faltaria por ninguna cosa. Y los que le tienen por frances veen si sus officios y fortalezas y servicio de su casa lo haze con franceses o castellanos. Su S[antida]d, a lo que yo pienso, espera lo que hara el arçobispo de Bari, y no gastar nada si ser pudiesse, porque esta tan escasso que nunca hombre lo fue mas. Hasta que el arçobispo venga, creo que sera mejor no apretallo mucho. **[B]** Con el arçobispo de **Cosenza** trata de algunas cosas su S[antida]d, siendo presente el otro, que sin el no hay nada; y con el, por lo de aqui, esta perdido, y creo que tarde lo sabra ganar. El arçobispo esta mal contento; dize que si no fuesse porque no le arrogerian en ninguna parte por yr de aqui, que seria ydo, porque vee en el papa algunas cosas que no le contentan; y pues el no es parte, que no quiere que digan que [aun] sera mal a su S[antida]d. Y es buen servidor de v. m[agesta]d, y le deve mandar servir. **[C]** Entendido he de **Cisterer** que es buen servidor de v. m[agesta]d, y que puede servir, que tiene la cifra; que su S[antida]d da señal de paz, y que el **Rey de Francia** pedia salvo conducto por enbiar embaxador a su S[antida]d, y que el papa no esta en que venga. Pregunte al papa que nueva tenia de Francia; dixome que el arçobispo le havia enbiado la carta de v. m[agesta]d, y que esperava sobre lo de **Inglaterra**; que desseava mucho la paz, por los infieles y por la necessidad de v. m[agesta]d, pues queda de la guerra honrrado y approvechado. Yo dixe a su S[antida]d que v. m[agesta]d siempre la queria, y el **Rey de Inglaterra**, haziendo el Rey de Francia lo justo. He scrito al arçobispo de Bari que se deve venir, pues el papa lo ha dexado a su voluntad, y que entretanto le sirva, poniendole alguna necessidad de alla. Su S[antida]d se concierte con v. m[agesta]d y **Venecia** y suyos lo antes que pueda. Yo he scrito esto conforme a lo que v. m[agesta]d me mandava. V. m[agesta]d me mande avisar si ha seydo lo bien, y lo que de aqui adelante le scriva, que yo le tengo por buen servidor de v. m[agesta]d, y pienso que no errara lo que es obligado. Tanbien halle una carta aqui, aunque es vieja, de vj de setembre: la enbio a v. m[agesta]d. Oy despacha el papa posta con la respuesta del arçobispo para el. Hable a su S[antida]d lo que v. m[agesta]d me scrivio del **principe don Enrique**. Dixo que de su abuelo no sabe nada, y que el hombre no es buelto; el engaño a su S[antida]d. Fuera mejor haverle prendido, que con su amo no puede haver buen assiento, por los inconvenientes que v. m[agesta]d dize. Assi mismo dixe a su S[antida]d de los del consejo; respondiome que del obispo no estava contento, y que las cartas que a v. m[agesta]d escrivian a Flandes le havian mostrado en Castilla el traslado; que no sabia mas, y que a todos queria bien. --- ## What it says Rome, 1 November 1522. The imperial agent's running account of Adrian VI in the months before the French came back into Italy: - **managing the Pope.** Charles V had written directly to warn him; Hurtado approves, because if Adrian will not do his duty he should at least not be able to plead ignorance. The Pope's *voluntad* is good, his *obras* satisfy nobody. - **the Pope's excuse and his parsimony.** He pleads his obligation to procure peace, the strength of the infidel, and the Emperor's need; he is *tan escasso que nunca hombre lo fue mas*, and waits to see what the archbishop of Bari will do before spending anything. - **the household.** Hurtado presses for the Pope's servants to be paid — *el camarero Pedro es el principal* — before they are bought by the other side: *si no los corrompiessen dandoles*. - **the peace track.** The Rey de Francia asks a safe-conduct to send an ambassador; the Pope will not have him come. Adrian wants peace for the sake of the Turks and the Emperor's need; Hurtado answers that the Emperor and the King of England always wanted it, *haziendo el Rey de Francia lo justo*. Su Santidad should come to terms with the Emperor and **Venecia** as soon as he can. - **prince don Enrique**, the consejo, and a leak: letters written to the Emperor in Flanders had been shown in copy in Castile. ## Status of the cipher The content is read in full from the clerk's clear. The ciphered leaves (ff. 237–239), and those of the duplicate R9648, are read in part — the aligned passages are listed in `../NOTES.md`, and the key built from them resolves about two thirds of the tokens on sight. Spanish. ## Translation **[A]** It has been very well that Your Majesty forewarns His Holiness of what is fitting for your service, because, although he may not do what he is obliged to, he may not excuse himself afterwards by saying that Your Majesty did not have him forewarned, so that he did not know whether what he was doing was wrong. Likewise it was well to write at length, because His Holiness had such passion that he did not recognise what Don Juan had served him, and [?] held his person against me. And if Your Majesty had not written from there, he would have thought that Don Juan and the **Cardinal de' Medici** had arranged [now] what they were to tell him, if Your Majesty's letter had found them here. I have asked His Holiness what he thinks of the Duke, and he told me he was content, which he was not with Don Juan, as everyone says. What Your Majesty says is very well, that whatever is to be done with His Holiness's servants he should know of first; but until Your Majesty gives them what you are pleased to, if anything were said to him he would think it was so as not to give them anything, and would say he did not want them to take it, and the servants would remain discontented, as they say they are; because, as **Monsieur de La Chaulx** and I spoke to him of it so long ago, they have already lost hope. I have written to Your Majesty of his character, and Monsieur de La Chaulx knows it; and now I send him a memorandum so that he may make a report to Your Majesty. The **chamberlain Pedro** is the principal one, and more regard is to be had for him than for any; and he is beyond comparison, and the others good, if they were not corrupted by being given [gifts]. When Your Majesty decides to grant them the favour, it will be well to tell the Pope … … that Your Majesty gives them that for the labours they had in Spain, and so that they may take more care to serve His Holiness; I [think that], as Your Majesty will be pleased, the Pope will approve it, which I believe he would not do now, as I have said. Since the Duke left, I have spoken to the Pope of what seemed to me to be Your Majesty's service. His will could not be better as regards what concerns Your Majesty; as for his deeds, no servant of Your Majesty is satisfied with them. He gives as excuse for what he leaves undone the obligation he has to procure peace, being pope, and the infidels being so powerful and his need so great; and [says] that Your Majesty has no [such need] that he should show himself as he is obliged to; for if Your Highness had it, he would not fail you for anything. And those who take him for French may see whether he fills his offices, his fortresses and the service of his house with Frenchmen or with Castilians. His Holiness, as I think, is waiting for what the Archbishop of Bari will do, and not to spend anything if it could be helped, for he is so close-fisted that never was man more so. Until the Archbishop comes, I think it will be better not to press him much. **[B]** With the Archbishop of **Cosenza** His Holiness deals on some matters, the other being present, for without him there is nothing; and with him, as regards things here, he is lost, and I think he will be slow to win him back. The Archbishop is ill content; he says that, were it not that they would not take him in anywhere for leaving here, he would be gone, because he sees in the Pope some things that do not please him; and since he has no part [in affairs], he does not want it said that he is [even] ill with His Holiness. And he is a good servant of Your Majesty, and you ought to order him to serve. **[C]** I have learned from **Cisterer** that he is a good servant of Your Majesty, and that he can serve, that he has the cipher; that His Holiness gives signs of peace, and that the **King of France** was asking for a safe-conduct to send an ambassador to His Holiness, and that the Pope is not of a mind that he should come. I asked the Pope what news he had from France; he told me that the Archbishop had sent him Your Majesty's letter, and that he was waiting concerning the matter of **England**; that he greatly desired peace, because of the infidels and because of Your Majesty's need, since you come out of the war honoured and with advantage. I told His Holiness that Your Majesty always wanted it, and the **King of England** too, the King of France doing what is just. I have written to the Archbishop of Bari that he ought to come, since the Pope has left it to his will, and that meanwhile he should serve him, putting to him some need from there. Let His Holiness come to terms with Your Majesty and **Venice** and his own as soon as he can. I have written this in accordance with what Your Majesty commanded me. May Your Majesty have me informed whether it has been well [done], and what I am to write to him from now on; for I hold him a good servant of Your Majesty, and I think he will not fail in what he is obliged to. I also found a letter here, although it is old, of the 6th of September: I send it to Your Majesty. Today the Pope is despatching a post with the answer to the Archbishop for him. I spoke to His Holiness of what Your Majesty wrote me of **Prince Don Enrique**. He said that of his grandfather he knows nothing, and that the man has not come back; he deceived His Holiness. It would have been better to have arrested him, since with his master there can be no good settlement, because of the drawbacks Your Majesty mentions. Likewise I spoke to His Holiness of those of the council; he answered me that he was not content with the bishop, and that of the letters they were writing to Your Majesty in Flanders they had shown him the copy in Castile; that he knew no more, and that he wished all of them well. Dize que antes de seys dias enbiaria aqui uno suyo, con quien avisaria largo; dize que luego embiaria a v. m[agesta]d otro. Por este respetto no enbio mi carta a v. m[agesta]d. En substancia me dize que **los franceses son determinados de venir en Italia, y enbian gran suma de dinero a Leon**, y que es menester que se entienda en la defensa, y que el papa haga lo que pudiere, pues le va mas que a nadie. Y he dicho a su S[antida]d que de **Hieronymo Adorno** me ha venido este aviso, de unas cartas que ha tomado por amor de v. m[agesta]d; y por lo que deve, no se ponga en esto — que por servicio de Dios y remedio de la yglesia y de su estado deve pensar lo que ha de hazer sin dilatar mas, porque despues no havra tiempo. Esto le dixe antes que viesse lo del arçobispo. Scrivieme que no pensasse que otra avisaria; tomalo tan tibiamente que no se espera de todo bien. En todo me ha dicho que lo miraria, y que despues me hablaria. Trabajare de saber lo que el arçobispo scrive, y vere la respuesta de su S[antida]d; y luego avisare a v. m[agesta]d, que agora no puede ser, porque el duque me ha scrito que oy partira la posta y que no la detenga. Yo le he avisado desto, y a **don Joan Manuel** y al **visorey de Napoles**. Creo que el duque scrivira a v. m[agesta]d su parecer y lo que piensa hazer. Yo he scrito al arçobispo conforme a lo que v. m[agesta]d me ha mandado, y me dize en su venida que queria hazer la [paz] de conveniente el papa, si los franceses vienen; y el papa dissimula de no fazerse parte, sino tener alla su mundo. Vea v. m[agesta]d si sera mejor que vaya otro que es el arçobispo, si alla esta; siempre avisaria. Si aqui viene, tengo por cierto que ha de tener lugar cabe el papa mejor que los otros, despues de enthenar, y apretaran a su S[antida]d … --- ## What it says Rome, November 1522, in the weeks before the French re-entry into Italy. Hurtado reports: - **the French are resolved to come into Italy and are sending a great sum of money to Lyon** — the intelligence came by post from the archbishop of Bari; - **Hieronymo Adorno has intercepted letters** and passed the warning on, "por amor de v. magestad"; - the Pope is urged to act *sin dilatar mas* for the sake of the Church and his own state, and answers **tibiamente** — lukewarmly, promising only to think about it; - the Duke [of Sessa] is despatching the post the same day, so a fuller report must wait; - **don Joan Manuel** at Rome and the **visorey de Napoles** have been told; - and the Pope *dissimula de no fazerse parte* — will not declare himself. The lukewarm Pope is Adrian VI, six months into a pontificate spent trying not to choose between Charles V and Francis I. Hurtado's *tomalo tan tibiamente que no se espera de todo bien* is a serving ambassador's verdict on that policy, three weeks before the French came down. ## Status of the cipher The letter's *content* is read in full, from the clerk's clear.
