Spanish. ## Translation Yesterday a post came from the Archbishop of Bari; he writes to me from the [23rd] to the [1st] of this month. He says that within six days he would send one of his men here, by whom he would give full news; he says he would then send another to Your Majesty. For this reason I do not send my letter to Your Majesty. In substance he tells me that **the French are resolved to come into Italy, and are sending a great sum of money to Lyon**, and that it is necessary to see to the defence, and that the Pope should do what he can, since more is at stake for him than for anyone. And I have told His Holiness that this warning has come to me from **Hieronymo Adorno**, from some letters he has taken out of love for Your Majesty; and, for what he owes, let him not set himself against this; for the service of God and the remedy of the Church and of his state he ought to consider what he has to do without further delay, because afterwards there will be no time. This I told him before he saw the Archbishop's [letter]. He writes to me not to think that another would give warning; he takes it so lukewarmly that not every good is to be hoped for. In all he has told me that he would look into it, and would speak to me afterwards. I shall work to learn what the Archbishop writes, and shall see His Holiness's answer; and I shall then inform Your Majesty, for now it cannot be, because the Duke has written to me that the post leaves today and that I should not hold it back. I have informed him of this, and **Don Juan Manuel** and the **Viceroy of Naples**. I believe the Duke will write to Your Majesty his opinion and what he thinks of doing. I have written to the Archbishop in accordance with what Your Majesty has commanded me, and he tells me, on his coming, that he wanted to make the [peace] fitting [for] the Pope, if the French come; and the Pope dissimulates so as not to make himself a party, but to keep his world there. Let Your Majesty see whether it will be better that another should go than the Archbishop, if he is there; he would always give warning. If he comes here, I hold it certain that he must have a place near the Pope better than the others, after [?…], and they will press His Holiness … R9652, Rome, Nov 1522 (ff. 295-296), wholly in clear A letter entirely in clear: the licenciado Bernardino, a 'gran bellaco', has turned up in Rome and Adrian VI declines a night arrest in the city; the viceroy of Naples' news of the siege of Rhodes is forwarded in copy. Hurtado and the Duke [of Sessa] want him arrested; the Pope will order it if the man is inside Rome but leaves it to the Duke if he is outside, and when the Duke finds he is in the city, lodging with his brother, and asks for a night arrest, Adrian VI declines — *aqui no seria bien* — and offers a formal *suplicacion* instead. Rome and Venice were reporting the same disaster to the Emperor in the same fortnight, in two different ciphers, bound now in the same volume. ## Status Content read in full; no cipher to break on this leaf. Spanish. ## Translation I wrote to Your Majesty on the [x] of this month how the **licentiate Bernardino** had come here. Then I went to the Duke, and spoke to His Holiness, and he told me he would order justice to be done on him, because he was a great scoundrel. The Duke came back here at once; he begged His Holiness to be pleased to let him have him arrested. The Pope answered him that, if he was inside Rome, he would order it to be done, and if he was outside, that he should do as seemed good to him. The Duke has learned that he is in the city, in his brother's house; he has sent to beg His Holiness to be pleased that he may have him arrested there one night. The Pope has answered me that here it would not be well, but that we should put in a petition that His Holiness order justice to be done. Let Your Majesty write to the Duke what is to be done in this; and it would be well to send an information of his guilt, so as to proceed against him here as far as possible, to get him out of the Pope['s hands], so that Your Majesty may order justice to be done. And it seems to me that I ought to inform Your Majesty, so that you may send orders for what may be for your service. At this hour I am writing the Pope's answer to the Duke, so that he may see what ought to be done. I have informed His Holiness of **the news of Rhodes** which the Viceroy writes; I send Your Majesty with the present the copy of the [Viceroy's] letter and of the news. R9634, Genoa, 13 Sept 1522 (ff. 14-16) decoded, not read Four months after the imperial sack of Genoa, Hurtado reports a plan put to him by Geronimo Adorno: the Emperor and the King of England should make war on the King of France through Provence, his weakest land, with six hundred men-at-arms, light horse and soldiers at 70,000 ducats a month, settled now for March; an early form of the 1524 Provence invasion. A mechanical decode with holes in most sentences: shown so that the transcription and the key can be checked and improved, not as a reading. DECODE R9634 (3 openings, `img/IMG_R9634_I45360_P1-3.jpg`), first worked 2026-10-02. Status: **read in part, 71% of cipher tokens read as sense (measured)**. - **f. 14r** (P1 right): *S. C. C. Mt*, clear opening (the sack of Genoa, Lope's illness), then cipher from l. 14. - **f. 14v, f. 15r** (P2): cipher with clear words between the runs, 24 + 25 lines. - **f. 15v** (P3 left): 13 cipher lines, then clear (*pareceme que era razon de escrevir a V. Mt. esto que aqui he oydo, especial siendo de tan buen servidor de V. Mt. como es Geronimo Adorno ...*). - **f. 16r** (P3 right): clear only — Cesarino's illness, don Juan Manuel in Rome; dated *de Genoba xiij de setiembre 1522*, autograph signature. DECODE has the month (9) but not the day or the place. - **No clear version** of the cipher in the record, and none in print: Bergenroth CSP Spain ii calendars no Hurtado letter of Sept 1522 (searched 2026-09-21, NOTES "Escalation"). The reading below rests on the key alone. Files: transcription `r9634_cipher.txt` (one line per manuscript line, 1191 cipher tokens), line-by-line reading with unread counts `r9634_reading.tsv`, values specific to this hand `key_1522_r9634.tsv`, decoder `python decode.py --letter r9634` (confirmed / probable coverage, unvalued tokens). ## What the letter says Written from Genoa four months after the imperial sack of the city (30 May 1522), it reports a plan that "honourable and sensible men" and Geronimo Adorno (the new imperial doge) put to Lope Hurtado: the Emperor and the King of England, *queriendo destruir al Rey de Francia*, should make war on him through **Provence**, > que es la tierra mas flaca que el tiene, y donde el exercito de V. Mt. puede entrar seguro, una tierra fertil > ... [para proveer con las galeras de Genova] ... donde pueden entrar bien ... los de la mar y los de la tierra The French are *muertos de miedo* after the sack. Taking Provence and Lyon (*y Leon y parte del ...*) would cost the King of France the rest; *tomarle lo otro que le queda y cercarle en Paris* — something not to be done *por Flandes ni por España*. Lope asked Adorno what force would be needed: **six hundred men-at-arms, [...] light horse and [x thousand] soldiers, and for their pay 70,000 ducats a month** (*lxx U yob z*), if the Emperor and the King of England agreed on it; the [lansquenets and Italians] in the duchy of Milan, *el exercito de [...] soldados y mil hombres darmas*, would serve. Adorno added that the Pope would be glad to see the troops go on *por no los tener alojados en sus tierras*, that the light horse should be paid and given their arrears, *con que pagar su sueldo y sobrados dineros*; that it must be kept secret *por que no toviesen aviso*, and settled now for **the month of March**; *es cosa segura, de poca costa e provechosa*; the King of France would only garrison the fortresses, and with the great armies that the Emperor and the King of England keep at excessive cost the whole could be paid for. The clear close commends Adorno as *tan buen servidor de V. Mt.* This is an early form of the Provence invasion that Charles V and Henry VIII did launch in 1524 (Bourbon and Pescara before Marseille), here proposed from Genoa in September 1522. ## Coverage (measured) Token counts: `decode.py --letter r9634` counts 1191 tokens (it keeps the five `·` marks and a few punctuation tokens); `python docs/_check_profile.py --measure r9634_tokens.txt` counts 1174 symbols. Majesty, Since I wrote to Your Majesty from here, illness has not left me until now, when I am well, and I leave tomorrow, God willing, for Rome, where His Holiness is. What I have been told from there I do not write to Your Majesty, because I take it for certain that Don Juan Manuel will send a post informing Your Majesty of the affairs of His Holiness and of your service. Sire, as I have been ill, many kinds of people have come to see me, men of war and others, and the people here, though they are not, know everything in the world, because they go about in it from birth; and some have told me, sensible and honourable men, *that because […] are so […] of Your Majesty and of the King of England, wishing to destroy the King of France, […] […] the war through [?Provence], which is the weakest land he has, and where Your Majesty's army […] can enter safely, a fertile land […] the […] by the […]* to supply with the galleys of Genoa *and of Your Majesty, and where […] those of the [?sea] and those of the land can well enter […] who never [?saw] […], they are [?dead] with fear* of the sack of Genoa and of the other things Your Majesty's men have done; *[…] of war that […] that the […] everyone* and that they will put themselves in pledges for it, if *[…] that by […] Your Majesty put an army, not […] and Lyon and part of the […] most of […] which will be to take from the King of France the […] things that […] and destroy himself; because from these parts* it can be said, *for […] the […] and the […] of Your Majesty with what* they took from him they maintained themselves to grow great, *and to take from him the rest that remains to him […] [?besiege him] in Paris*; and that what would be done *by […] with […] ducats […] will not be done through Flanders or through Spain with two* millions, *because the […] are* provided with the artillery and supplies needed, *and here […] the people are border people* who have seen war and are fit to fight; *here no […] man who has […]*. Some say they will now enter with Your Majesty's men *into France, that if […] not […] the* Prospero and the Marquis *would not have had enough for […] […] what* they wanted *[…] the […] had […] them*. Having seen what they told me, it seemed to me, once I was well, that it was right to share it with Geronimo Adorno, who is a wise and sensible man and a servant of Your Majesty, in my opinion as much as I have seen; I told him what I have told Your Majesty here, and asked what he thought; he told me not to take it *for […] those who had said this*, for he swore to God *that if the Great [?Captain] [?were] [?alive] he would not […] Italy for war*; and that since Your Majesty *was […] the men […] and the King of England to destroy the King of France*, and they had the means for it, *they would have the […] with […] of the world* if they failed *to take from him what was in their hand.* I asked him *what force would be needed*; he told me *six hundred men-at-arms and […] light [?horse] and […] soldiers*; and that for their pay *70,000 ducats a month would be needed, and that […] for need of the Emperor and the King of England to [?agree] with […] and […] of […] in the […]* in the duchy of Milan *[…] army of […] soldiers and a thousand men-at-arms so that […] […] that […] nor […] should not cross* at present, where the men could be had; he told me that Your Majesty *had the men-at-arms*, because the […] *guard of […] and the Pope's and […]* could come if Your Majesty wrote it to him, and that His Holiness would be glad *that they came, so as not to have them quartered* in his lands; *and the men that […] would go forward;* the light horse that *were [?lacking], that […] there would be* lansquenets and Italians, *could be [?raised] so that […] those who […] should pay*, adding to them their arrears, *and that he would put the […] […] that […] of […] months they would have the means to pay their wages* and money to spare. *But that if this were [?to be], it had to be […] so that they should have no warning, for […] […]*; After the post left, His Holiness told me *that he had reached a settlement with the Duke of Ferrara, and three conditions of the capitulation […]:* the money *of the fief that Pope Alexander [?remitted] to him at the [?marriage] of his [?daughter]; the Duke* to be bound to serve the Church with a hundred men-at-arms for half a year when it needs them; *and that he may not confederate with [?any] [?prince] or [?lordship] except with His Holiness and with Your Majesty; that he may not harbour in his state disservants […] nor of Your Majesty.* His Holiness [?reminded] us of the other conditions; he says they are to bring them tomorrow signed *by the said Duke*, and he will send the copy to Your Majesty. His Holiness gives him no more than what he now holds. He has told me *that he will [?not do] […] to Your Majesty; that […] what they [?wish], but that the [?camp] does not [?come]; that he cannot [?do]* what he would like, *and [?they come] […] that the […] of the Duke of […]* comes upon […]. *And […] and that the Duke, with […] men dismissed*, the captain and some men-at-arms, and that Your Majesty's men *[?treat] their […] badly* in their quarters; and although some come upon *and […]* with plenty of men, they think it is done by the servants *of Your Majesty […] him […] of […], because he [?will do] what Your Majesty asks.* I have informed the Duke of Sessa, *and made [?great] […] […] to the Pope; and I have told His Holiness not to think that a servant of Your Majesty would have* such daring. *His Holiness is [?very] […] that all of the Duke of […].* It seemed to me that Your Majesty should be told, because this is the second news that has come to the Pope today, and the first I made known to the Duke; I believe he will have written to Your Majesty, so that you may send orders as best serves you. Likewise Bernardino de [?Aviño] has written from London of the [date] of last month; *he says that the King of England had come to terms with the Scots and that they had thrown out the Duke of Albany*, and that he was waiting for the King, who had gone on a pilgrimage, and that on his return the Cardinal had told him he would dispatch him. By the reckoning made here, Bernardino will be late. The Pope has been much pleased with the agreement with Scotland, which has been a knife for the French. Here they comfort themselves much *by saying that the English and Your Majesty's men did nothing*, and that they left *discontented*. El arçobispo de Bari no escrevio al papa nueva *de la venida de los franceses* ni a nadie sino a mi; a lo que he podido entender, todo era remitirse al suyo que ha de embiar. Venido el criado del arçobispo, luego avisare a V. Mt. *de lo que [?truxiere].* *Y como [?assi] se [?tomaran].* Despues que escrevi a V. Mt., dizen que Roma esta muy mejor, de que el papa esta muy contento. [?A Gaspar] Mollete catalan aya dado el papa las galeras; ha viij dias que murio. El duque le ha suplicado que las de a [?Alcayca] o Figueroa; el papa me respondio que V. Mt. no conoce a estos, que por importunidad las quiere para ellos. Sera bien que V. Mt. scriva a Su Sd. que las de a uno dellos; yo creo que hasta el verano no las proveera. Hame mandado que torne a escrevir a V. Mt. sobre *lo de [?Ostia]*, y Su Sd. me ha dicho que escriva a V. Mt. largo. Lo de don Juan mande V. Mt. satisfazer, *que esta muy sospechoso el papa que de alla se le haya mandado lo que ha fecho.* Guarde Nuestro Señor y acreciente la muy real persona y estado de V. Mt. Translation R9656_en.md # R9656 — Lope Hurtado to Charles V, Rome, 22 November 1522 — English Translation of `R9656_reading.md`, with the same holes. Passages in cipher in the original are in *italics*. S. C. Majesty, The Archbishop of Bari did not write the Pope news *of the coming of the French*, nor to anyone but me; as far as I have been able to understand, everything was referred to the man of his whom he is to send. The letters were brought by a courier who came with the [?valante]; *the Pope does not [?want] […] the coming of the French.* I have asked *[?His Holiness] in […] if they come […] what the Pope will do*, so that I could write his answer to Your Majesty; he has told me that in everything he can reach of the Pope's will he will not fail Your Majesty, nor will the Secretary in what he can, and that Your Majesty should have no doubt of it. *[…] has told me* that he has heard the Pope say that if the French come it will be to their harm. His Beatitude cannot fail Your Majesty; what the Pope answered the Duke in this matter Your Majesty will see by his letter. Nothing *[?moves] the Pope; they are […] […] for peace; he does not [?believe] that he has […] of the […] to lose […] the state, if not of no [?more] than money, which is the thing in the world that most […] [30].* His Holiness says that he is Your Majesty's. When the Archbishop's servant has come, I shall at once inform Your Majesty *of what he [?brings]*. *And how [?so] they [?will take] it.* Since I wrote to Your Majesty, they say that Rome is much better, at which the Pope is very content. The Pope [has given] the galleys to [?Gaspar] Mollete, a Catalan; he died eight days ago. The Duke has begged him to give them to [?Alcayca] or Figueroa; the Pope answered me that Your Majesty does not know these men, and that they want them for themselves by importunity. It would be well for Your Majesty to write to His Holiness to give them to one of them; I believe he will not fill them before the summer. He has ordered me to write again to Your Majesty *about the matter of [?Ostia]*, and His Holiness has told me to write to Your Majesty at length. As to Don Juan, let Your Majesty give satisfaction, *for the Pope is very suspicious that he was ordered from over there to do what he has done.* May Our Lord keep and increase Your Majesty's most royal person and estate. From Rome, 22 November 1522. Key: key_codes.tsv , key_1522_r9634.tsv , key_1522_from1524.tsv , key_1522_from1524_B.tsv

Thirty-five cipher enclosures of the papal nuncio and legate in France in one key (DECODE R18–R58 and R17). The key is the one Meister printed in 1906 as no. 40, which George Lasry identified from his statistical recovery of part of it; because the figures run together in units of one to three digits, the decryption is under-determined and was resolved with a language model of 16th-century Italian. All thirty-five decrypted end to end: the Estates of Blois, the murder of the Guises, Henri III’s march on Paris. Where Vatican, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 22 (items 22/1 to 22/37). DECODE holds them transcribed digit by digit, listed as partially decrypted with no plaintext posted. The cipher A homophonic substitution with two or three digits per letter, cluster and word codes, a dotted three-digit nomenclator and nulls. The figures run on without separators, so a sheet can be divided into units in many ways. How it was read With George Lasry’s partial key of 2020 and the full key Aloys Meister printed in 1906, which Lasry identified as the same. A search over the divisions, scored by a 16th-century Italian language model, gives continuous Italian. What it says The fight to publish the Council of Trent in France, the Estates of Blois, and the Duke of Guise “amazato a colpi di pugnale” on 23 December 1588, then Henri III’s march on Paris in June 1589. Still open Two sheets of spring 1589 are in a second, syllabic key Lasry recovered only in part. A few dotted codes outside Meister’s list and single-letter slips remain.

Francia 22 is the volume of Morosini’s originals and ciphers from 25 July 1588 to 20 September 1589 (ff. 10–583). DECODE holds 36 of its cipher enclosures, items 22/1 to 22/37 (22/29 has no record; R23–R26 and R50, inside the same run of record numbers, are other material). Most are marked dup.to , the duplicate sent by a second courier; the clear covering letters that go with them are partly transcribed on DECODE as well. Two of them, R53 and R54 (items 22/32–33), are in a second key and have their own page ; the other thirty-four are in the key below. A thirty-fifth despatch in the same key sits in another volume. DECODE R17 (Francia 18/3, ff. 233r–235v) is filed with the despatches of the bishop of Bergamo and the archbishop of Nazareth of 1585–86, with an incomplete key note (“ASV F22”) that points to Meister no. 40 and a “decryption” that is the error trace of a Java program. The decoder below reads it on all five pages, so it is a despatch of Morosini’s nunciature, from 1587 (it moved to this page from the Francia 18 page on 14 October 2026). The key is Meister no. 40 ( Die Geheimschrift im Dienste der päpstlichen Kurie , pp. 393–394), issued to Morosini on 8 June 1587. Each letter has two or three homophones: a 21 212 2, e 35 153 5, i 17 171 7, n 10 01 0, o 91 191 9, r 00 13 1, s 54 45 4, t 51 15 6, u 37 173 3, and so on. There are about twenty codes for clusters (cr 22, pr 33, st 47, str 49) and twenty for words (che 56, per 64, non 61 71, quando 99). A three-digit nomenclator is marked with a dot on the middle figure: 111 the Pope, 113 the King of France (“S. M.tà Christ.ma”), 116 the Queen Mother, 129 Duca di, 131 Cardinale di, 133 Arcivescovo, 227 Heretici, 232 “il già Re di Navarra”. An 8 with any following figure is a null. Francia 22 f. 308r, the head of the despatch of 23 December 1588 (docket “dup.to di 23 Decembre”), whose opening lines report the murder of the Duke of Guise. The despatch of 23 December 1588 (R43) begins, in the reading of 22 October 2026: […] questa matina di […] il duca di Guisa nela camera del Re è stato per ordine di S. M.tà amazato a colpi di pugnale, et la sua morte è seguita a questo modo. […] mandato a chiamare il duca di Guisa, che si truouaua nel Consiglio di Stato, uenuto et entrato subito nela camera fu preso da due a trauerso et da altri aterato con molte pugnalate, et dopo hauere indarno fata grandisima difesa con le mani et con i denti, senza però mai hauere potuto caciare mano ala spada. […] Morto lui, et posti prigioni il cardinale di Guisa, che si truouaua pure in Consiglio, il duca di Nemurs, il duca d’Elbeuf, il principe di Ianuile, l’arciuescouo Lione, il preuosto di mercanti di Parigi et il presidente Nogli, et mesa guardia al cardinale di Borbone, il Re andò a ritrouare la Regina Madre (This morning the Duke of Guise was killed with daggers in His Majesty’s chamber on His Majesty’s order. Called from the council of state, he came in and was seized, and, after a great defence with his hands and teeth, without ever getting his hand to his sword, died of many dagger blows. The Cardinal de Guise, Nemours, Elbeuf, Joinville, the Archbishop of Lyon, the prévôt des marchands of Paris and the président Nogli were arrested, and the Cardinal de Bourbon put under guard.) The duplicate of the next day (R44) adds that the Cardinal de Guise “questa matina solam[ente] è rimasto priuo di uita”. The legate, because a cardinal had been killed, leaves the answer to the Pope.

DECODE’s transcriptions give the figures one by one, marking a dotted figure X Y^. Z . Dotted groups were taken as nomenclator codes. The rest of each page is a single string of digits, and each position can open a code of one, two or three figures. The decoder ( targets/morosini1588/decrypt.py ) keeps, at every position, the best-scoring decryption for each four-letter context. It scores the letters it emits with the repository’s shared Italian 5-gram model ( lang/ , it-cinquecento , built from Renaissance letters and nunciature reports, without spaces). It charges a fixed cost for a null (8 and any figure) and a larger one for a figure it cannot place. A page of 1,500 figures runs in about a second. The Spanish enclosure (R35, a copy of Philip II’s letter to the Queen Mother) comes out in readable Spanish although the model is Italian. R17 went through the same decoder unchanged, from DECODE’s transcription D1611 (volunteer TimB, 2015). The re-reading of 22–23 October 2026. The character decode above follows the gist but does not build sentences. A word-level decoder with a model of transcription slips ( research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py ) split each page into words; every break was then re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures and, where a figure was in doubt, on crops of the DECODE images (55 corrections from the images). Each reading was aligned word by word with its figures, and every word the figures do not fully carry is bracketed. What had garbled the decode: spurious nomenclator dots in DECODE’s transcriptions (250 is “Bles” in letters), real codes with the dot on the wrong figure or none, the clerk’s -mente abbreviation (m and the null 8), numbers in plain figures between nulls, and page order (R30, R31, R43, R45, R47). No new code value came out of it. Tempesti’s Vita di Sisto V (1754), which paraphrases many of these letters, was used for names and sense only, never as a source of words. The readings are texts/<R>_reading.md , with English in _en.md and the corrections and logs beside them.

Nomenclator: 113 is “Il Re di Francia, S. M.tà Christ.ma” in Meister and is rendered “S. M.tà” throughout (H). 165 and 166, printed “quelli” and “questi”, serve for every form of quello and questo (H), and 161 likewise for quanto (C). Dotted groups not in Meister’s table (162, 191, 250, 516, 617, 712, 716, 770 and a few others): the re-reading of 22 October 2026 showed them to be spurious dots on ordinary letter groups, or real codes with the dot on the wrong figure. No new code value. About 540 short holes in 33,000 words of reading: openings and closings, and groups of one to eight figures that no word parse fits. On 23 October 2026 every hole of R49, R51 and R55 was checked on the images, with sample lines of R27, R35, R39, R40 and R57; many are encipherer’s slips transcribed as written, and on R40 (f. 293r ll. 15 and 21) two are stretches the encipherer crossed through, which DECODE gives as ordinary figures. The other records are still to be cropped (listed in each texts/<R>_reread_log.md ). R35 loses a stretch to a hole in the paper (f. 202v l. 8) and its last line to damage. With these holes, R32 reads at 93.8% of its words, R33 at 94.8% and R35 at 92.5% (measured 24 October 2026): each builds coherent sentences, but under the 95% a complete reading needs. Letter-level slips in the first decode (“euisone” for Soissons) are corrected in the readings; the raw decode stays in decrypt_raw.txt . Proper names are graded C (Soissons, Nevers, Poigny); Tempesti’s paraphrase confirms several. Rome’s own decipherments of these despatches are in Segreteria di Stato, Francia 27 (Hübner, Sixte-Quint , 1870, cites them as “déchiffré à Rome, 9 janvier 1589”), not imaged online. Missing leaves: R46 between ff. 382v and 383r, R47 after f. 385v; R17 f. 233v and the last leaf of R22 are not imaged. R17: five groups open (519, 911, 556, 722, 561, most likely transcription slips), and the date within 1587 is not fixed. Item 22/29 is not on DECODE and was not seen. The clear covering letters were not edited here.

Morosini to Montalto, [Paris], 10 August 1588 (duplicate): the Council of Trent and the Gallican liberties (Francia 22/1, ff. 32r–35r) Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1686 (TimB, Jan 2016) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by `research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R18_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures and, where a figure itself was in doubt, on the DECODE images (crops; `R18_corrections.tsv`). The heading in clear on 32r reads "dup.a di 10 d'Agosto"; the letter is written from Paris ("hora che mi ritrouo in Parigi"). The "cleartext" images attached on DECODE (ff. 30–31 and an address leaf) are the covering letter in clear, not a decipherment. No interlinear glosses on the cipher pages. Rome's decipherments of Morosini's letters (Segr. Stato Francia 27) are not imaged. Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 129 duca, 132 principe, 133 arciuescouo, 135 uescouo, 141 clero, 151 Francia, 154 Spagna, 161 quanto, 165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 173 Inghilterra, 213 ambasciatore, 226 catolici, 227 heretici). The encipherer abbreviates with m + 8 (-mente) and "bo. mem." with 8. Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [162] a dotted code not in the key. ## Reading [f. 32r] […] circa la publicatione del concilio di Trento io non ho mancato né manco di fare tuti quei più eficaci ofici et [?oporsi] a fine che sia fata senza alcuna limitatione o conditione, ma in efeto trouo grandisima resistenza in tuti, che non uogliono sentire a modo alcuno parlare contro a questa loro pretensa libertà dela chiesa galicana. Et dicono che anche in Spagna, nel regno d'Aragone, per non pregiudicare a i loro priuilegi hano uoluto acetarlo; che in quello che concerne dogmi di fede loro la acetarano senza alcuna ecetione o conditione, ma quanto ala riforma, et è cosa manifesta che non si può dare regola uniuersale et uniforme che serua a tuti i regni, hauendo ognuno li suoi particolari costumi, da' quali con tropo dificoltà si potriano leuare; et che essendo questo molto bene conosciuto da la santa sede apostolica, nel tempo che era qui nuntio mons. il uescouo di Rimini di bo[na] me[moria] si era uenuto ad alcuni temperamenti per acomodare il tuto con sodisfatione di N. S., ma che non si era potuto far tanto che bastase. Questi propositi sono tenuti uniuersalm[ente] da tute le parti, et anco da quelli che a mia instanza hano posto nele loro dimande questo articolo dela publicatione del concilio; ma non mancano anco di quelli che parlano [f. 32v] più libera et impertinentem[ente], a' quali, se bene non manco di rispondere come conuiene, temo però che se si douese pasare a ofici più uiolenti di quelli che per sino a qui si sono fati, facilm[ente] si ueneria a rotura, la quale penso io che sia bene fugire più che si può, non uedendo che da quella ci posi riuscire se non perdita a cotesta santa sede. Tutauia, se io hauesi mala opinione, quando ne sarò auuertito da V. S. Ill.ma non lasarò di sequire precisem[ente] tuto quello che mi ha racomandato. Hora che mi ritrouo in Parigi non laso con questi dela Sorbona, come ho anco fato con quelli del consiglio del Re prima che io partisi da Sciartres, [di] dimostrare con quelle ragioni che mi sono soministrate dal Signor Dio [162] sono obligati di coadiuuare una così utile et santa opera, et che molto bene conueniua che se pure di Francia tiene il titolo di christianisimo si contentase anco di riceuere nel suo regno eso concilio liberam[ente], come si è fato neli altri regni et prouincie di christiani catolici, et che era già male hauere tardato tanto con sì graue scandalo di christiani et con prouocarsi l'ira di Dio, anzi che douria esere S. M.tà quella che hauese [?dato] l'esempio a gli altri; ma in efeto ritrouo in tuti grandisima dificoltà et renitentia. L'ultima uolta che io par[f. 33r]lai con S. M.tà in questo proposito, oltre quello ch'ho già scrito con altre mie, le disi che, uolendo lei stabilire le cose sue, bisognaua che si mostrase più ardente degli altri nele cose che concernono l'honore di Dio et l'esaltatione dela religione catolica; che ela uedeua che l'honore dela publicatione del concilio di Trento saria atribuito a quelli dela lega, perché loro l'haueuano nei articoli dimandata, ma che in mano dela M.tà S. era leuare a loro questo auantagio et aquistarlo per sé, con uolere che quello che hano esi dimandato con conditione et restritione sia liberam[ente] et senza conditione publicato et acetato. Et dicendomi lei come uoleuo che ela contrauenise a quello che si era già acordato, per tornare un'altra uolta al'armi, le risposi che questo non saria contrauenire, ma più tosto coadiuare; et che almeno, quando gli altri si dolesero et uolesero l'esecutione secondo la forma del acordo, che la S. M.tà guadagnaria nel'opinione di N. S. et di tuta la christianità, quello che con la dilatione in publicarlo ueniua ad hauere per […] sopra gli altri, la colpa del impedimento. Mi rispose che con questo ueniuano anco loro a guadagnare più il fauore nel regno, poiché uniuersalm[ente] ognuno uole la conseruatione de li priuilegi et [f. 33v] libertà dela chiesa galicana, a' quali, quando lei si mostrase contraria, si renderia odiosa uniuersalm[ente] a tuti. Io disi che nele cose d[i] Dio non bisognaua caminare con rispeti mondani o altri interesi, ma che almeno doueua S. M.tà dare conto di tuto ciò a N. S. et rimetere nela […] N. S. la risolutione, asicurandola che in quello che si potese ritrouaria magiore pronteza in N. S. di compiacerla et mostrarsi benigna et fauoreuole a questo regno di quello che ela stesa poteua desiderare, con molte altre parole in questa sostanza, ale quali S. M.tà non mi rispose altro se non che quelli che dimandauano hora la publicatione del concilio erano aponto quelli che più degli altri se le erano oposti, et specialm[ente] l'arciuescouo di Lione, che lei lo haueua sempre desiderato, promettendosi che in quelle cose che portasero pregiudicio al'autorità sua che N. S. ui hauria rimediato. Io disi che la S. M.tà poteua da N. S. aspetare ogni paterna dimostratione, ma che non ci era nel concilio alcuna cosa che, come a uero re et giusto principe, portase alcuna lesione o nocumento, se uoleua che le cose del suo regno pasasero con giustitia et con disciplina nel clero; che S. M.tà si fa[f. 34r]cese dire da questi che la disuadono dala publicatione quali siano i ponti che trouano loro contrari ala sua autorità, perché mi persuadeuo che ela stesa, considerati che li habia, conoscerà la poca ragione c'hano di meterle in capo questi pensieri. Non lasarò di continouare neli medesmi ofici, ma con poca speranza di migliore risolutione, non bastando parole a persuadere il contrario, et il uenire a rimedi più potenti potria facilm[ente] condurci a qualche rotura, nela quale, sì come con grande facilità si può incorrere, così si può temere che con molta dificoltà si potria senza magiore dano rimediarui. Onde forsi saria più oportuno procurare di guadagnare questo ponto, che il concilio fose publicato nel modo c'hano già acordato, et che li ponti dele dificoltà siano rimesi a N. S., dandole magior speranza di sodisfatione, poiché non si uegono disposti di rinontiare a le gratie et priuilegi che pretendono hauere di longa mano dala sede apostolica, per dimandarne de' nuoui. V. S. Ill.ma considerarà tuto questo et sarà contenta d'auisarmi quello che douerò fare, perché io non mancarò di ubidire a quanto mi sarà comandato. L[f. 34v]e cose del regno nel'aparenza caminano asai bene, perché il Re mostra di uoler dare ogni sodisfatione a mons. di Guisa, et sua Ecel. procede con grandisima humiltà et riuerenza con S. M.tà; ma con tuto ciò si può temere asai di qualche nuouo acidente, perché il re è risolutisimo di tenire i Stati Generali del regno, sperando con questo, oltre molti altri particolari per seruitio suo, di ridure anco mons. di Guisa et quelli del suo partito ala restitutione dele piaze che tengono; et da altra parte il duca teme asai questi stati, et fa quanto può sotomano per disuadere il re da tenerli, ouero di metere tempo in mezo per hauere comodità di fare le sue pratiche, perché siano deputati ai stati persone di sua sodisfatione. Ma non può già fare tanto segretam[ente] questo che il re non conosca chiaram[ente] che egli non li uorebe, da che nasce in S. M.tà magiore desiderio di tenerli et di acelerare la radunanza, pensando che quello che a loro non piace deba riuscire a magior suo uantagio; da che asai manifestam[ente] si conosce che gli animi sono tutauia disuniti et pieni di sospeti. Si conosce anco che l'intentione del re saria, quando egli non fose per hauer prole, di stabilire la sucesione dela corona [f. 35r] in quelli che sono del suo sangue, a' quali per ragione del regno apertiene di sucedere; il che non può in modo alcuno piacere a gli altri, et se bene non ardiscono scuoprire questo loro afeto, tutauia soto altri pretesti non lasano d'impedire, [quanto] posono, questi disegni del re. Io non manco di fare tuto quello che è in me per mostrare così a S. M.tà come ali altri che il ritornare di nuouo a rotura saria la totale rouina di questo regno, et hora con l'uno et hora con l'altro uado leuando dele sospecioni, et procurando con l'autorità di N. S. di esortarli a la uera unione fra loro, per potere atendere tanto meglio ala stirpatione deli heretici. L'ambasciatore di Spagna ha fato gran querela meco che in alcuni porti di questo regno l'armata d'Inghilterra habia hauti rinfrescamenti, ma questi lo negano apertam[ente]; né sino a qui ho potuto hauer ne sicura relatione. Quando io ne sia certo, non mancarò di dolermene con S. M.tà et far quello uficio che in simil caso conuiene. Translation R18_en.md # R18 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Paris], 10 August 1588, duplicate: the Council of Trent and the Gallican liberties) Translation of `R18_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 32r] […] concerning the publication of the Council of Trent, [I] have not failed and do not fail to do all the most effective offices, and [to oppose (?)], so that it be done without any limitation or condition; but in fact I find very great resistance in everyone, for they will not in any way hear anything said against this pretended liberty of the Gallican church. And they say that in Spain too, in the kingdom of Aragon, they chose to accept it so as not to prejudice their privileges; that in what concerns dogmas of faith they will accept it without any exception or condition, but as to the reform — and it is a plain thing that no universal and uniform rule can be given that suits all kingdoms, each having its own particular customs, from which they could be drawn away only with too great difficulty — and that this being very well known to the Holy Apostolic See, at the time when Monsignor the Bishop of Rimini, of good memory, was nuncio here, some arrangements had been reached to settle the whole to the satisfaction of Our Lord, but that it had not been possible to do enough. These views are held universally on all sides, even by those who at my instance have put this article on the publication of the council among their demands; but there is no lack of those who speak [f. 32v] more freely and impertinently, to whom, although I do not fail to answer as is fitting, I fear that if one had to go on to more violent offices than those made so far, it would easily come to a rupture, which I think it is well to avoid as much as one can, since I do not see that anything could come of it but loss to that Holy See. Nevertheless, if I had a wrong opinion, when I am advised of it by Your Most Illustrious Lordship I shall not fail to follow exactly all that you have recommended to me. Now that I am in Paris I do not fail to [show] to these men of the Sorbonne — as I also did with those of the King's council before I left Chartres — with the reasons furnished to me by the Lord God, that [162] are bound to assist so useful and holy a work; and that it was very fitting that, if [the King] of France holds the title of Most Christian, he should be content also to receive the said council in his kingdom freely, as has been done in the other kingdoms and provinces of Catholic Christians; and that it was already wrong to have delayed so long, with such grave scandal to Christians and provoking the wrath of God; nay, that His Majesty ought to be the one who had [given] the example to the others. But in fact I find very great difficulty and reluctance in everyone. The last time I spoke [f. 33r] with His Majesty on this matter, besides what I have already written in other letters, I told him that, wishing to establish his affairs, he needed to show himself more ardent than the others in the things that concern the honour of God and the exaltation of the Catholic religion; that he saw that the honour of the publication of the Council of Trent would be attributed to those of the League, because they had asked for it in their articles, but that it was in His Majesty's hands to take this advantage from them and gain it for himself, by willing that what they had asked for with condition and restriction be published and accepted freely and without condition. And when he asked me how I wanted him to go against what had already been agreed, so as to return once more to arms, I answered that this would not be going against it but rather helping it; and that at least, when the others complained and wanted execution according to the form of the agreement, His Majesty would gain, in the opinion of Our Lord and of all Christendom, what by delaying its publication he was coming to have [lay] on the others — the blame for the impediment. He answered that with this they too were gaining more favour in the kingdom, since everyone universally wants the preservation of the privileges and [f. 33v] liberty of the Gallican church, to which, were he to show himself contrary, he would make himself universally hateful to all. I said that in the things of God one must not proceed with worldly regards or other interests, but that His Majesty at least ought to give an account of all this to Our Lord and leave the decision to […] Our Lord, assuring him that in whatever could be done he would find greater readiness in Our Lord to please him and to show himself kind and favourable to this kingdom than he himself could desire, with many other words to this effect. To these His Majesty answered me nothing except that those who were now asking for the publication of the council were precisely those who more than the others had opposed it, and especially the Archbishop of Lyon; that he had always desired it, trusting that in the things that might prejudice his authority Our Lord would have provided a remedy. I said that His Majesty could expect every fatherly demonstration from Our Lord, but that there was nothing in the council that would bring any harm or damage to him as a true king and just prince, if he wanted the affairs of his kingdom to proceed with justice and with discipline in the clergy; that His Majesty should have those who dissuade him [f. 34r] from the publication tell him which are the points they find contrary to his authority, because I was persuaded that he himself, once he has considered them, will see how little reason they have to put these thoughts into his head. I shall not fail to continue the same offices, but with little hope of a better decision, since words are not enough to persuade the contrary, and coming to stronger remedies could easily lead us to some rupture, into which, as one can fall with great ease, so one may fear that it could be remedied only with much difficulty and without greater harm. So perhaps it would be more opportune to try to gain this point, that the council be published in the manner they have already agreed, and that the points of difficulty be referred to Our Lord, giving them greater hope of satisfaction, since they do not seem disposed to renounce the graces and privileges they claim to have had long since from the Apostolic See in order to ask for new ones. Your Most Illustrious Lordship will consider all this and be pleased to advise me what I must do, for I shall not fail to obey whatever I am commanded. The [f. 34v] affairs of the kingdom outwardly go quite well, for the King shows that he wants to give every satisfaction to Monsieur de Guise, and His Excellency proceeds with very great humility and reverence towards His Majesty; but with all that one may well fear some new accident, for the King is most resolved to hold the Estates General of the kingdom, hoping by this, besides many other particulars for his service, to bring Monsieur de Guise and those of his party to restore the places they hold; and on the other side the Duke greatly fears these Estates, and does all he can underhand to dissuade the King from holding them, or else to gain time so as to have the means to carry on his dealings, so that persons to his liking are deputed to the Estates. But he cannot do this so secretly that the King does not see clearly that he would not want them; from which there grows in His Majesty a greater desire to hold them and to hasten the assembly, thinking that what they dislike must turn out to his greater advantage. From which it is quite plainly seen that minds are still divided and full of suspicions. It is also seen that the King's intention would be, should he have no offspring, to settle the succession of the crown [f. 35r] on those who are of his blood, to whom by right of the kingdom it belongs to succeed; which cannot in any way please the others, and although they do not dare to reveal this feeling of theirs, nevertheless under other pretexts they do not fail to hinder these designs of the King [as much as] they can. I do not fail to do all that is in me to show both His Majesty and the others that returning again to a rupture would be the total ruin of this kingdom, and now with the one and now with the other I go about removing suspicions, and trying with the authority of Our Lord to exhort them to true union among themselves, so as to be able to attend all the better to the extirpation of the heretics. The Spanish ambassador has complained loudly to me that in some ports of this kingdom the English fleet has received supplies, but these people deny it openly; and so far I have not been able to get a sure report of it. When I am certain of it I shall not fail to complain of it to His Majesty and do the office that is fitting in such a case. M.tà come a quelli dela Sorbona et altri che si douese publicare il concilio di Trento senza altra conditione. Il giorno medesmo che io parti di Parigi per uenirmene a ritrouare S. M.tà, li deputati del clero di tuto il regno, che per altri negotii si ritrouano in quella città, comparuero al parlamento per oponersi a la publicatione di eso concilio, dicendo che era contrario in molte cose ala libertà dela chiesa galicana; il che ha meso nuoua dificoltà in questo negotio. Però domenica, nel'audientia che [?si] da S. M.tà, feci nuoua instanza per la publicatione, et le disi che l'opositione che faceuano i deputati del clero non la doueua ritardare, ma più tosto ecitare dauantagio a uolere che sia publicato, perché da ciò conosceua quanto era magiore il bisogno che ci era di riforma, poi che loro non la uoleuano. S. M.tà mi rispose che lei sempre haueua desiderato non solo la publicatione ma anco l'intiera esecutione d'eso concilio, ma che era persuasa che ci fosero molt[e] cose che portariano notabilisimo pregiuditio ala sua autorità; et che se un re [f. 71v] ouero un abate, per piciolo che fose, meritaua laude et era obligato di fare ogni cosa per conseruare le sue giurisditioni, molto più lo doueua fare un grande re come lui, perché, hauendo piaciuto al sig. Dio di meterlo in quello stato, meritaria gran biasimo se si l[a]sase leuare la autorità et quei priuilegi che per molti centenara d'ani haueua goduti questa corona. Io disi a S. M.tà che molte uolte le haueuo deto, et io pensauo certo, che nel concilio non ci fose alcuna cosa che le portase pregiuditio, perché, quanto al'autorità sua, non uedeuo io che cosa l'importase che i preti et i monaci fosero più tosto giudicati dai suoi uescoui o abati, come uole ogni ragione, che dali parlamenti, che non sono loro giudici competenti; [?manco] uedeuo che interese potese hauere S. M.tà che la nominatione a certi benefici fose più tosto concesa a certi parlamenti che quello a che di ragione s'aspeta, poi che tanto sono franzesi gli uni come gli altri, et così bene S. M.tà prouede a i suoi uescouati et abatie come faceua di consiglieri di esi parlamenti; che io la pregauo a farsi dare in [f. 72r] nota quei ponti che loro dicono pregiudicare a la sua autorità, et che me li facese uedere, perché mi asicurauo di poterla chiarire che era male informata; et che, se pure ci fose qualche cosa, che si rimetese a la benignità di N. S., perché teneuo per certo che nele cose honeste hauria da la S.tà di N. S. riceuta ogni sorte di sodisfatione; che non era bene consigliare questo punto con quei del parlamento, perché sono interesati, metendo le conto che tuto il giorno uadino al loro tribunale li canonici a litigare con i loro uescoui et li monaci con li loro abati, perché da questo cauano il loro profito. Mi dise S. M.tà che in efeto ela non sapeua quali fosero questi punti, et che se li faria dare, uolendo in ogni modo eserne bene informata. Io non lasai di replicare, facendo quel più uiuo et eficace oficio che io sapeuo per farla presto risoluere et non uolere continouare più longam. nel mal conceto che si era posta in tuta la christianità con la dilatione a publicare eso concilio. Mi dise che questo era sempre stato il suo desiderio, ma che non doueua lasare di conseruare li suoi [f. 72v] priuilegi. Le disi che, se erano priuilegi, bisognaua che da pontefici le siano stati concesi, et che, non esendo meno pontefice N. S. di quelli che si fosero i suoi precesori, poteua, come quelli per il seruitio di Dio haueuano giudicato a proposito di concederle qualche priuilegio per alhora, così al presente per [?il] medesmo rispeto riuocarli; […] esendo tanto Re di Francia come sono stati i suoi pasati, per il seruitio del suo regno poteua mutare o riuocare una lege che da quelli altri fose stata fata. Che non mi rispose S. M.tà alcuna cosa. Io non lasarò di continouare nei medesmi oficii et con S. M.tà et con tuti gli altri; ma a [16] che io uego, et per quello che uado subodorando, sarà questo punto rimeso a la [?asenblea] de i Stati Generali, li doue si correrà gran pericolo di magiore contraditione, poiché quasi tuti i preti inferiori, per l'interese de i capitoli, che non uogliono esere sotoposti ai uescoui, farano ogni opera perché il concilio non sia publicato. Io non mancarò di fare tuto quello che sarà in me, con quella magiore diligenza che mi sarà posibile; et si [f. 73r] da V. S. Ill.ma mi sarà dato qualche auuertimento, non mancarò di ubidire, et gliene restarò con infinito obligo. Dopo scrita, esendomi ritrouato con il sig. cardinale di Uandomo, mi dimandò sua sig. Il[l].ma s[e] haueuo haute le facoltà dela legatione; et dicendole di sì, mi dise che bisognaua farle uerificare dal parlamento. Io le risposi che questo non mi pareua necesario né conueniente, perché il parlamento non haueua da metere mano ne le gratie di N. S. Mi replicò che questo era costume inueterato in questo regno, et che così haueuano fato tuti gli altri legati che sono uenuti in Francia, che saria cosa imposibile il uoler fare hora in contrario, et questo non era diminutione del'autorità di N. S. ma piutosto confirmatione, perché senza la aprobatione del parlamento io non sarei ubidito da alcuno et bisognaria di continouo contendere; doue che, quando il parlamento ha uerificate [?le] facoltà, se alcuno [?uolese] calcitrare, il medesmo parlamento lo fa obedire. [16] medesmo mi è stato deto anco da altri. Con tuto ciò io non farò altro [f. 73v] sino a tanto che non habia risposta di quello che ho scrito a V. S. Ill.ma in questo proposito. Il medesimo cardinale mi parlò molto a longo sopra l'asolutione de suoi frateli, per la quale inuia a posta il latore dele presenti a N. S., se bene spera che anco prima del suo arriuo a Roma haurà la S.tà di N. S., per l'instanza che le sarà stata fata dal ambassadore di S. M.tà, mandato qui ordine per l'asolutione, mostrando di marauigliarsi che i[n] quele mie facoltà non habia autorità di poterlo fare, come non ho; et credo che saria bene che l'hauesi pure. Io mi rimeto al prudentisimo giudicio di N. S. Questo cardinale, insieme con li suoi frateli, uniti con il duca di Monpensier, […] pare che uadino adunando da tute le parti i fautori et dipendenti loro per farli uenire ai Stati; et si dice c'haurano seco più di 500 gentilomini, perché, hauendosi da tratare dela sucesione ala corona, uogliono asicurarsi che non li ha fato alcuno pregiuditio. Et già si dice che il marsciale d'Umon, che fa profesione di dipendere [f. 74r] da questa parte, habi deto che questi signori sarano ai Stati così forti che, quando uolesero dechiarare alcuna cosa contro di loro, che si fariano con l'armi ragione da loro medesmi. D'altra parte il duca di Guisa, uedendo le prouisioni che questi fano, ha scrito ancora lui a tuti i suoi per non esere manco forte di loro; onde si teme che non uenga a sucedere qualche scandalo, et che in cambio di prouedere ai bisogni del regno non si uenga ad una sanguinosa bataglia fra catolici. Per questo io non manco di fare ogni buono oficio da tute le parti, et con le loro Maestà ho procurato che si deba fare un ordine che tuti quei principi che uorano uenire ai Stati non posino condure con sé […] magiore compagnia di quello che sono soliti di hauere quando uengono in corte; et penso che così sarà ordinato, hauendolo le loro Maestà trouato bono. Si ua [?anco] procurando di metere […] questo […] disegno, anco di parentarli insieme, che saria con dare per moglie al conte di Suissone [f. 74v] la figliuola del duca di Guisa. Translation R19_en.md # R19 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Chartres, 24 August 1588, duplicate: the Council of Trent and the Estates) Translation of `R19_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 71r] […] Our Lord […] that I was working, at Paris and here, to persuade both His Majesty and those of the Sorbonne and others that the Council of Trent should be published without any other condition. The very day I left Paris to come and find His Majesty, the deputies of the clergy of the whole kingdom, who are in that city on other business, appeared before the Parlement to oppose the publication of the said Council, saying that it was contrary in many things to the liberty of the Gallican Church; which has put a new difficulty into this business. But on Sunday, at the audience that [is given] by His Majesty, I pressed again for the publication, and told him that the opposition the deputies of the clergy were making ought not to delay it, but rather spur him on the more to want it published, because from this he could see how much greater was the need for reform, since they did not want it. His Majesty answered that he had always wanted not only the publication but also the full execution of the said Council, but that he was persuaded there were many things in it that would bring most notable prejudice to his authority; and that if a [king?] [f. 71v] or an abbot, however small, deserved praise and was bound to do everything to preserve his jurisdictions, much more ought a great king like himself to do so, because, it having pleased the Lord God to put him in that state, he would deserve great blame if he let himself be stripped of the authority and those privileges that this crown had enjoyed for many hundreds of years. I told His Majesty that I had said to him many times, and I held it certain, that there was nothing in the Council that would prejudice him, because, as to his authority, I did not see what it mattered to him that priests and monks should be judged by their own bishops or abbots, as all reason wants, rather than by the Parlements, who are not their competent judges; [still less] did I see what interest His Majesty could have in the nomination to certain benefices being granted to certain Parlements rather than to that to which it belongs by right, since the one and the other are equally French, and His Majesty provides to his bishoprics and abbeys just as well [as] he did with councillors of those Parlements; that I begged him to have [f. 72r] a list made of the points they say prejudice his authority, and to let me see them, because I was sure I could show him that he was misinformed; and that, if there were something after all, he should leave it to the kindness of Our Lord, because I held it certain that in honest matters he would receive every sort of satisfaction from His Holiness; that it was not good to take counsel on this point with those of the Parlement, because they are interested parties, reckoning that every day canons come to their tribunal to litigate with their bishops and monks with their abbots, since from this they draw their profit. His Majesty told me that in fact he did not know what those points were, and that he would have them given to him, wanting by all means to be well informed of them. I did not fail to reply, doing the liveliest and most effective office I knew to make him resolve quickly and not wish to continue any longer in the bad opinion he had brought upon himself throughout Christendom by the delay in publishing the Council. He told me this had always been his wish, but that he must not fail to preserve his [f. 72v] privileges. I told him that, if they were privileges, they must have been granted to him by the pontiffs, and that, Our Lord being no less pontiff than those, whoever they were, who were his predecessors, he could, as they had judged it fitting for the service of God to grant him some privilege at that time, so now for [the] same consideration revoke them; […] being as much King of France as his forebears were, for the service of his kingdom he could change or revoke a law that those others had made. To which His Majesty answered me nothing. I shall not fail to continue the same offices both with His Majesty and with all the others; but from [what] I see, and from what I am scenting out, this point will be referred to the [assembly] of the Estates General, where there will be great danger of greater opposition, since almost all the lower clergy, through the interest of the chapters, who do not want to be subject to the bishops, will do everything so that the Council is not published. I shall not fail to do everything in my power, with the greatest diligence possible; and if [f. 73r] Your Most Illustrious Lordship gives me any instruction, I shall not fail to obey, and shall remain infinitely obliged for it. After writing, being with the Cardinal of Vendôme, His Most Illustrious Lordship asked [me whether] I had received the faculties of the legation; and when I told him yes, he told me they had to be registered by the Parlement. I answered that this did not seem to me necessary or fitting, because the Parlement had no business laying hands on the graces of Our Lord. He replied that this was an inveterate custom in this kingdom, that all the other legates who have come to France had done so, that it would be impossible to want to do otherwise now, and that this was no diminution of Our Lord's authority but rather a confirmation, because without the approval of the Parlement I would be obeyed by no one and would have to contend continually; whereas, when the Parlement has registered the faculties, if anyone [should want] to kick against them, the Parlement itself makes him obey. [This] same thing has been told me by others as well. All the same I shall do nothing else [f. 73v] until I have an answer to what I have written to Your Most Illustrious Lordship on this matter. The same Cardinal spoke to me at great length about the absolution of his brothers, for which he is sending the bearer of these presents expressly to Our Lord, although he hopes that even before his arrival in Rome His Holiness, at the instance made to him by His Majesty's ambassador, will have sent an order here for the absolution, showing surprise that in my faculties I should have no authority to do it, as I have not; and I think it would be well that I had it. I leave it to the most prudent judgement of Our Lord. This Cardinal, together with his brothers, united with the Duke of Montpensier, […] it seems are gathering from every part their supporters and dependants to bring them to the Estates; and it is said they will have more than 500 gentlemen with them, because, since the succession to the crown is to be treated, they want to make sure that no prejudice is done them. And it is already said that the Maréchal d'Aumont, who professes to depend on [f. 74r] this side, has said that these lords will be so strong at the Estates that, if they wanted to declare anything against them, they would do themselves justice by arms. On the other side the Duke of Guise, seeing the provisions these are making, has written to all his people as well, so as not to be less strong than they; so that it is feared some scandal may arise, and that instead of providing for the needs of the kingdom it may come to a bloody battle among Catholics. For this I do not fail to do every good office on all sides, and with Their Majesties I have worked for an order that all the princes who wish to come to the Estates may not bring with them […] larger company than they are used to have when they come to court; and I think it will be so ordered, Their Majesties having found it good. They are [also] trying to put […] this […] design, also of allying them by marriage, which would be by giving the Count of Soissons as wife [f. 74v] the daughter of the Duke of Guise. […] what is done, Your Most Illustrious Lordship will be informed of it. […] R20, Francia 22/3, 9 Sept [1588] The King gave the Count of Soissons letters clearing him of his service with Navarre and the Huguenots. Paris citizens and the prévôt protested to the Parlement. Cardinal de Vendôme and the Princess of Condé were furious. M.tà fare il medesmo per il Nauarro, o metere loro in pericolo di cadere soto il dominio tiranico deli heretici, con molte altre considerationi in questo proposito. Il gentilomo [f. 89r] di mons. di Guisa comprobò quello che io diceuo, ma con tuto ciò dise che non sapeua che sicurtà si potese hauere che tutauia intrinsicam. il sodeto conte non fauorisce il Nauarro. A che io disi che gran sicurtà saria quella se lui medemo andarà a fargli la guerra. In questo mentre che io stauo ragionando con questo, soprauene il sig. cardinale di Uandomo, il quale mi dimandò se haueuo hauto alcuna risposta intorno a l'asolutione dei suoi frateli, mostrando che gli premese […] la tardanza, douendosi dare principio ali Stati. Io disi che non portaua il tempo che fose potuta uenire esa risposta, et che quanto prima io l'hauesi non mancarei di farlo intendere a S. S. Il[l].ma; ma che bene mi dispiaceua che, mentre che si staua aspetando l'ordine di N. S., si andase cauando lettere patenti del Re, che non si doueua fare se non dopo otenuta l'asolutione da N. S. Mi dise il sig. cardinale che quello che si era fato non era per altro che per auanzare tempo, del quale ne hano estremo bisogno; et hauendo suo fratelo spedito un gentilhuomo a [112], [?da] la Santità del quale aspetauano benignisima risposta, mentre che questa ueniua haueuano [f. 89v] proc[u]rate queste lettere perché fosero pronte subito che suo fratelo si fose riconciliato con santa chiesa, dela quale uoleua esere obedientisimo et deuotisimo figliolo et seruitore; et che lui non pensaua già che si douesero se non alhora presentare al parlamento, et che ciò si era fato senza suo consenso; et io uedeuo che, dipoi che gli haueuo deto che non era bene che il conte uenise in corte prima che si hauese risposta da N. M.tà da quei dela città che erano andati in numero di milia al parlamento, parlò con molta pasione, dicendo che questo era stato un grande ardire et che intacaua tropo la dignità del Re, et che meteua la S. Page order 88r–90r, then 87r–v (a second sheet). ## Translation [f. 88r] […] here last Sunday, in the company of a gentleman of Monsieur de Guise, sent by His Excellency, […] to find me, an échevin of the city of Paris; and after some offices of compliment made to me in the name of the city, he told me that the prévôt des marchands and the others who are in the government had thought it necessary that I be informed of what had happened in Paris in the days before, so that I might take up their protection with His Majesty. He said that, having learned that His Majesty had granted the Count of Soissons letters patent by which he [cleared] him of all the guilt he had incurred by having been with the King of Navarre and with the Huguenots, and that these letters had been presented to the Parlement for [it] to approve or register them, as they say here, many pious and Catholic men of that city had gone to the said Parlement to oppose this registration, and had presented a request of the tenor that Your Most Illustrious Lordship will see from the translated copy I am sending you. He said that here the Cardinal of Vendôme and the Princess of Condé had made such an uproar with Their Majesties that they wanted all the citizens of Paris for dead men, and therefore he begged me to be willing [f. 88v] to defend them and protect their cause, since they had moved for nothing else than zeal for the Catholic religion, fearing that, if this discharge of the Count of Soissons passed without opposition, His Majesty might one day do the same for Navarre, or put them in danger of falling under the tyrannical rule of the heretics; with many other considerations on this subject. I did not fail to answer [as] was fitting, assuring them first of my affection and good will towards that most Christian and most devout city, and praising the zeal they have for the preservation of the Catholic religion, exhorting them […] to keep the peace that had been newly concluded, by which all must subscribe to the Union; and the said Count of Soissons having […] subscribed and sworn like the others to make war on the heretics, and having always been a Catholic, having also lately sent a gentleman to [the] Queen Mother [to] obtain from Our Lord absolution for his error, it seemed to me a great gain to have drawn him over to us and separated him from the heretics, and that he should now want to be one of those who go to make war on them. The gentleman [f. 89r] of Monsieur de Guise confirmed what I said, but all the same said he did not know what security there could be that the said Count does not still inwardly favour Navarre. To which I said that it would be a great security if he himself went to make war on him. While I was talking with him, the Cardinal of Vendôme came in, who asked me whether I had had any answer about the absolution of his brothers, showing that the delay weighed on him […], since the Estates were about to open. I said that time did not allow that answer to have come yet, and that as soon as I had it I would not fail to let His Most Illustrious Lordship know; but that it displeased me greatly that, while Our Lord's order was being awaited, letters patent of the King were being drawn out, which ought not to have been done until after the absolution had been obtained from Our Lord. The Cardinal told me that what had been done was for no other purpose than to gain time, of which they are in extreme need; and his brother having sent a gentleman to [112], from whose Holiness they expected a most benign answer, while that was coming they had [f. 89v] obtained these letters so that they would be ready as soon as his brother was reconciled with Holy Church, of which he wished to be a most obedient and devout son and servant; and that he did not think they were to be presented to the Parlement before then, and that this had been done without his consent; and I could see that, since I had told him it was not good for the Count to come to court before there was an answer from Our Lord, he had not let him come, though there were many who urged him to the contrary, his interest being handled here too coarsely, […]. And speaking of the opposition made to His Majesty's letters by those of the city who had gone a thousand strong to the Parlement, he spoke with great passion, saying that this had been a great boldness, that it touched the King's dignity too much, and that it put His Majesty under the necessity of resenting it, with other similar words. I told him that the fault was theirs, because they ought first to have awaited the judgement of Our Lord, which would have stopped everyone's mouth [f. 90r] at court; and the Count of Soissons would have come to Blois in these days: I did a strong office with Their Majesties that they should not allow it unless the absolution came from Rome first, as they promised me to do. […] [f. 87r] […] that I urged His Most Illustrious Lordship, adapting himself to the necessity of the present times, not to make a noise about this affair, because he was making himself more hateful to the chief city of the kingdom, and would again be trying to set the King at odds with that people, who would easily return to their usual tumults without there being any means to prevent them. The Cardinal showed that it was very hard for him to have to bear this affront, and although he said he valued my advice highly, it did not seem to me that he was altogether calmed; so, so as not to let some other trouble arise, [I asked for] the audience of Their Majesties. With His Majesty I complained greatly that, while grace for the Count of Soissons was awaited from Our Lord, he should have granted those letters. The King answered me that he meant the letters not to serve until after the absolution had been given to the Count, which he thought Our Lord would not refuse him, and that after it these were needed to free the said Count from the temporal penalties he had incurred under his [edicts]; that he was much grieved by what had [f. 87v] happened in Paris, because in such a matter it [?was not for] the people to oppose his will, and therefore a remedy was needed, so that this did not become an example. I told His Majesty that, [if] the presentation of his letters had been put off until after the Count had obtained absolution from Our Lord, this trouble would not have happened; and that the best remedy that could be found was to do nothing more until an answer came from Rome on the matter of that Count. And His Majesty showing that he would do it willingly, were he not [afraid] of displeasing the Cardinal of Vendôme, I told him that I begged him to have more care for his own service than for pleasing others. His Majesty told me that this was right, but begged me to speak of it myself with the said Cardinal. I said I had done so, but that His Majesty should also, as in matters of the honour of the Church and in his service, he would not depend on the will of others but govern himself by reason alone. His Majesty answered that this was as it should be, and that he would speak of it with the Queen his mother; and because it was publicly said […] R21, Francia 22/4, n.d. [Sept 1588] The King dismissed his secretaries of state and the chancellor all at once, leaving the court anxious. Mons. de Nevers(?) and the Queen Mother were displeased not to have been consulted. Morosini warned the King that new men would be inexperienced and the old ones could side with his enemies. Dopo questo ragionamento entrò S. Translation R21_en.md # R21 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 10 September 1588: the King dismisses his ministers) Translation of `R21_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 94r] […] Our Lord: the resolution taken by His Majesty to remove at one and the same time all his secretaries of state, the Chancellor and Monsieur de Bellièvre, with some other officers, has thrown the whole court into great suspicion and talk; and as His Majesty has given no reason that moved him to so sudden a change, everyone reasons according to his own sense, and few are those who praise this deed, with which Monsieur de Guise shows himself little satisfied, since it seems to him that His Majesty's not having communicated anything to him on this matter is a clear sign that he has little confidence in him. The same happens with the Queen Mother, with whom, they say, His Majesty no more wanted to take counsel in this case; and she shows, at least in appearance, that she resents it greatly, because most of these men had been brought into their offices by her in the time of the minority of the Kings her sons. All the same I am assured that, on leaving Chartres, the King communicated this plan of his to Her Majesty, a plan that [had] its origin in his mind from the time he left Paris because of the revolt of this [f. 94v] city, as he then thought he had found in these men little secrecy, not to say loyalty. All the rest of the court also shows displeasure, and many have begun to fear that the same may happen to them as has happened to these, because the change happened the same day. And I went to the audience of His Majesty I took the occasion to ask him whether what I had heard of this change was true. He answered that it was most true. And I told him that, although all that His Majesty did ought to be counselled with great prudence and settled with mature deliberation, I, with the affection I bore to his service and to the universal good of the whole kingdom, wished to say that this resolution was of the greatest importance, since His Majesty was depriving himself at one stroke of all those who understand the true state of his affairs, to bring new men into the government; and even were they the best in the world, they would still have to learn at his cost the way to serve him well, and only with difficulty and after a long time could they reach the perfection that these others, by their [f. 95r] own worth, being most excellent men and with long experience, had already acquired; and that it seemed to me that, these men having full knowledge of his every secret thought and knowing where every weakness of this kingdom lies, they could do him great harm if, ruled by indignation, they let themselves be persuaded to join His Majesty's enemies; adding various other reasons that then came to my mind, which it would be too long to relate in full. His Majesty answered that he did not think these men were of so bad a condition as to turn against him; they were all rich and would be glad to enjoy in peace the many goods they had acquired in his service; and he wanted to learn from Our Lord, who made himself obeyed and feared by everyone — as he said he had just been reading a letter from his ambassador resident with Our Lord, in which, by order of Our Lord, he wrote to him that he too should make himself obeyed and feared by his ministers and his subjects; that he was now 37 years old, and wanted from now on to attend unweariedly [f. 95v] to the government of his kingdom, and to see whether, governing in his own way, he could bring things to a better state than he had done with the counsel of these men; of whom he said that, had he not removed them now, it would easily have happened that the assembly of the Estates itself would have asked for them to be removed from the council, because they had been the instruments of putting forward many [courses] that have caused great harm in the kingdom and the worst dissatisfaction among the people. I praised His Majesty's wish to make use of the […] fatherly counsels of Our Lord, assuring him that, if he did so, it would put his affairs in a [state] […] better than they are; but that I did not see Our Lord advising him, in a time of such need as this, to deprive himself at a single blow of all the ministers who know his secrets, and that this was a dangerous act and would give the whole world much to talk about; that if he would have it so, he should at least try, since he did not show that he had any fault against them worthy of punishment, to keep them in his [f. 96r] devotion, so that they do not take another side, as Monsieur du Ferrier did, who, not being esteemed by him, became chancellor of the present King of Navarre. His Majesty told me that he was quite disposed to do this, and that in effect he would hold them under his protection against anyone who wanted to offend [them], but that he no longer wanted to use [them], being resolved to have people who serve him in his way, and not like these, who served him in theirs. After this conversation His Majesty went on to thank me for the good offices I had done with Monsieur d'Épernon and with the abbé del Bene to keep him in his devotion, and told me that he had sent his physician back to the said Épernon to see whether he could bring him to give up Boulogne and Metz, [for] he would then be content to leave him all the rest of the governments he holds; but from what I hear on the other side, it seems to me that he shows himself most resolved not to do it, and it is much feared that he may join Montmorency and Navarre. Although His Majesty does not believe it, thinking that he, so as not to lose the 400 [f. 96v] thousand scudi he finds he has on the salt farm, will not abandon his side. I do not fail to do what I can, both with the said Épernon and with the King and the Duke of Guise, to see that this man is kept on the side of the Catholics, judging that this is of the greatest importance because of the large forces in his hands; and he quite often gives me firm assurance of it in his letters, showing the greatest desire that Our Lord should remain well satisfied of his actions, for which reason he still says he wants to send a man to Our Lord.
