Ill.ma di 19 del pasato […] non ocore dire, che quanto ala publicatione del concilio di Trento io non ho mai tralasciato di fare ogni eficacisimo oficio perché sia liberam[ente] et senza alcuna conditione publicato, come anco con diuerse mie lettere ne ho dato conto a V. S. Ill.ma; et già ho hauto promesa da tuti tre li Stati, se bene separatam[ente] l'uno dal altro, che tuti insieme lo dimandarano nei loro capito[li] a S. M.tà. Non lasarò di continouare, seruendomi di quelle persuasioni che sono esprese nela deta cifra. Quanto a presentare le facoltà dela legatione al parlamento, scrisi già a V. S. Ill.ma con mie di 12 del pasato di hauerle presentate […], così consigliato da persone molto principali et deuotisimi di N. S. et di cotesta Santa Sede. S. M.tà tutauia le tiene apreso di sé, non hau[en]do hauto tempo di uederle et considerarle; io non mancarò di fare quanto oficio che […] mi comete. Ma è da sapere che se le […] facoltà non sono uerificate dal parlamento, che tuti gli ati che io facesi sariano [f. 132v] senza anima […], esendo il parlam[ento] quello che ha da farli esequire et ubidire, come anco sucede di tuti li editi et ordini che fa il Re medesmo; che se non sono uerificati dal parlamento non uengono ubiditi, portando così la forma del gouerno di questo regno. Quanto ala asolutione dei principi di Uandomo, hauendo ueduto quello che V. S. Ill.ma mi scriue fuori di cifra con più sue, che deba in ogni modo [?aspetare] altro ordine prima che uenire ad esa asolut[i]one, et considerato poi quello che si contiene in esa cifra, io non ho saputo pigliare partito; perché se bene mi dice di mandarmi la facoltà et il modo di asoluerli, et che io, secondo che mi parerà bene, la esequisca o la ritardi, come giudicarò esere bene del regno, con tuto che pensasi di potere dar hora in uigore di questo ordine la asolutione, non ho però creduto poter alterare il modo che la mi manda; del quale non si uolendo a modo alcuno contentare il conte di Suisone, dicendo che non si deue acusare [f. 133r] di pecato che non ha pure pensato, non che comeso, ho risoluto di diferire, se bene con grandisimo risentimento così del conte sodeto come di tuti i suoi et del Re medesmo; ma, amando io più tosto di ubidire precisem[ente] ali ordini di N. S. che di sodisfare ad altri, ho creduto non potere pasare più oltre la loro querela. […] che, hauendole io fato intendere […], come V. S. Ill.ma mi scrise con le sue di 22 d'agosto, et io con mie di 2 del pasato auisai V. S. Ill.ma di hauere comonicato questo […] le loro Maiestà et con li ilustrisimi di Borbone et di Uandomo, sopra di che haueuano tratato meco dela forma del[a] asolutione, et fato condesendere il sodeto conte a contentarsi di abiurare nela forma che uedrà V. S. Ill.ma per la copia che le mando, nela quale è narrato la uerità del fato et posta la sostanza di quello; et a me è parso che più importase leuando quelle parole [f. 133v] che ofendeuano questi signori. Et il giorno medesmo che mi capitorono le lettere di V. S. Ill.ma io doueuo dargli la asolutione, esendosi ordinato che, giungendo il conte in breue […] andase altroue, uenise a smontare ala casa dela mia habitatione, doue con le debite circonstanze si saria fato l'uficio. Però, esendosi partito di casa sua et condoto a due leghe uicino a qui, g[l]i pareua di riceuere grande afronto se io non [l']asolueuo. Io mi sono scusato con dire […] di non potere fare dauantagio di quello che mi [?uiene] comandato, et [che] N. S. ama il sig. conte di Suisone et gli darà in ogni modo la sodeta asolutione, ma che, hauendo sua Ecel. mandato un gentilomo a N. S. per questo efeto, […] mandarà quello ordine che le parerà a proposito. Il che inteso, dai sig. cardinali di Borbone et di Uandomo uenero subito a ritrouarmi, facendomi grande instanza a uolerli compiacere del[a] asolutione; et io, dapoi hauere ueduto che non si [f. 134r] contentauano dela forma mandata da V. S. Ill.ma, risposi a le loro sig. ilustris. in conformità di quello haueuo deto prima; onde si risolsero di andare a ritrouare il Re, con il quale hano fato gagliardisimo oficio perché S. M.tà spedisca […] in diligenza a Roma per questo rispeto. Et hora mi uengono a dire che il corriere partirà fra due hore; però io scriuo la presente in molta freta, ma non uoglio lasar di dirle che qui mostrano di sapere che questa mutatione [?procede] per mali ofici che siano stati fati con N. S. ad instanza del sig. cardinale di Sans, dal ilustris. Alesandrino, et si lamentano di [?me], che io li habi esortati a mandare un huomo espreso a N. S., poi che molti uescoui in Francia haueuano autorità di asoluerli senza andare a Roma. Io, per quello che conosco et sono informato, truouo che il conte di Suisone non ha più di 20 anni, et che quando fu dato al sig. cardinale di Borbone non haueua più di 4 anni, et dapoi è stato educato da sua Sig. ilustris. et uisuto sempre catolico, et hora si mostra [f. 134v] afetionatis. ala religione catolica; et temo che il metere dificoltà nel'asolutione non posi giouare né ala religione catolica né al regno, perché questo al sicuro renderà più dificile il ritorno del Nauarro al'obedienza dela Sede apostolica, et sarà causa di rinouare l'odio fra questo Re et quelli di Guisa, poi che tengono per certo che tuto il male uenga da loro, se bene al presente, per ofici fati anco da me, si mostrano insieme asai bene disposti. Pare anco che il Re di ciò se ne risenti molto, et che uoglia diferire sino al ritorno di questo […] il dare principio ali Stati; ma [?con] me S. M.tà non ne ha ancora parlato, non hauendo potuto andare a ritrouarla per hauermi fato male a un piede, che non mi permete di poter caminare. Spero fra uno o duo giorni poter uscire, il che desidero somam[ente] per certificarmi se è uero che quello ambasciatore del Re di Dania, che fuori di cifra scriuo esere uenuto a questa corte, uenga per persuadere S. M.tà di unirsi con il suo Re a difesa dela Regina d'Inghilterra, per fare in [f. 135r] tal caso quello oficio che sarà conueniente per [h]onore del sig. Dio et seruitio di N. S. Mi sono molto marauigliato che mons. uicelegato di Auignone si dolga, come V. S. Ill.ma mi scriue nela sodeta cifra, che, hauendomi lui scrito più uolte per cose importanti al suo gouerno, io non gli habi risposto; il che quando fose uero, con gran [r]agione V. S. Ill.ma potria dire che questo non piace a N. S. Ma la deue restare sicura che io non ho hauto dal sodeto mons. […] che tre lettere sole di qualche negotio, ale quali tute non solo ho risposto con lettere, ma anco con tuti quelli efeti che posino uenire da me, come benisimo lo ha il Fiorauanti, secretario suo, che da molti mesi in qua se ne sta in corte tratando negoti del uicelegato senza comonicare meco se non quello che li torna a comodo. Il medesmo poso dire al'ultimo capo dela sodeta cifra, doue mi dice che il duca di Epernone et la Ualeta suo fratelo si dolgono di esere abandonati da cotesta Santa Sede, et che N. S. si marauiglia che io per questi signori [f. 135v] non habi fato l'uficio conueniente, come mi è stato scrito per lettere famigliari, per breui et per instrutioni; et mi consolo che V. S. Ill.ma nela terza lettera sua dela medesima data di 19 de[l] pasato, fuori di cifra, mi scriue che l'oficio fato da […] p[e]l duca di Guisa per beneficio di Epernone et del fratelo, et le lettere scrite loro, siano piaciute a N. S., et uole che si camini inanzi in questo negotio. Però prego V. S. Ill.ma di asicurare N. S. che io non lasarò mai di ubidire con ogni pronteza ali o[r]dini di N. S., né temo che haurà mai causa di tenermi per negligente, esendo tropo grand[i] gli oblighi miei di inuigilare sempre al suo seruitio, come farò con il fauore del sig. Dio tuto il tempo dela mia uita. […] saprà che, oltre quello che di tempo in tempo ho scrito di hauere fato in questo proposito, ho anco operato dauantagio asai, et per non stancare V. S. Ill.ma con tropo longa scritura ho lasato di scriuere; ma in efeto pare a me che loro non douriano ricusare il partito che S. Translation R22_en.md # R22 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 7 October 1588: the Council of Trent, the faculties, Soissons' absolution, Avignon, Épernon) Translation of `R22_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 132r] This […] to the sheet of cipher that came in Your Most Illustrious Lordship's letters of the 19th of last month […] there is no need to say, that as to the publication of the Council of Trent I have never failed to do every most effective office so that it be published freely and without any condition, as I have also reported to Your Most Illustrious Lordship in several of my letters; and I have already had the promise of all three Estates, though separately from one another, that all together they will ask for it in their articles (cahiers) to His Majesty. I shall not fail to continue, using those persuasions that are set out in the said cipher. As to presenting the faculties of the legation to the Parlement, I already wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship with mine of the 12th of last month that I had presented them […], so advised by persons of the first rank and most devoted to Our Lord and to that Holy See. His Majesty nevertheless keeps them by him, not having had time to see and consider them; I shall not fail to do whatever office […] commits to me. But it must be known that if the […] faculties are not verified (registered) by the Parlement, all the acts I made would be [f. 132v] without life […], since the Parlement is what has to have them executed and obeyed, as also happens with all the edicts and ordinances the King himself makes: if they are not verified by the Parlement they are not obeyed, such being the form of government of this kingdom. As to the absolution of the princes of Vendôme: having seen what Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes me outside the cipher in several letters, that I must in any case [wait for] further orders before coming to that absolution, and having then considered what the cipher contains, I have not known what course to take; for though you tell me that you are sending me the faculty and the manner of absolving them, and that I, as I think fit, may carry it out or delay it as I judge good for the kingdom, and although I thought I could now give the absolution by virtue of this order, I did not think I could alter the form that you send me. Since the Count of Soissons would in no way accept it, saying that he should not be accused [f. 133r] of a sin he had not even thought of, let alone committed, I resolved to defer it, though with the greatest resentment both of the said Count and of all his people and of the King himself; but, loving rather to obey precisely the orders of Our Lord than to satisfy others, I believed I could not go further with their complaint. […] that, having made known to them […], as Your Most Illustrious Lordship wrote me with yours of 22 August, and I with mine of the 2nd of last month informed Your Most Illustrious Lordship that I had communicated this […] to Their Majesties and to the Most Illustrious (Cardinals) of Bourbon and of Vendôme, on which they had treated with me of the form of the absolution, and made the said Count condescend to be content to abjure in the form Your Most Illustrious Lordship will see in the copy I send you, in which the truth of the fact is told and the substance of it set down; and it seemed to me that it mattered more to remove those words [f. 133v] that offended these lords. And on the very day your letters reached me I was to give him the absolution, it having been arranged that the Count, arriving shortly […] go elsewhere, should alight at the house of my lodging, where the office would have been done with the due circumstances. But having left his house and come within two leagues of here, it seemed to him he was receiving a great affront if I did not absolve him. I excused myself by saying […] that I could do no more than I am [ordered], and that Our Lord [loves] the Count of Soissons and will in any case give him the said absolution, but that, His Excellency having sent a gentleman to Our Lord for this purpose, […] will send whatever order he sees fit. This being heard, the Cardinals of Bourbon and of Vendôme came at once to find me, pressing me hard to oblige them with the absolution; and I, after seeing that they were not [f. 134r] content with the form sent by Your Most Illustrious Lordship, answered their Most Illustrious Lordships in conformity with what I had said before; whereupon they resolved to go to the King, with whom they have made a most vigorous office that His Majesty should send […] post-haste to Rome on this account. And now they come to tell me that the courier leaves within two hours; so I write this in great haste, but I will not omit to tell you that here they show they know that this change [proceeds] from bad offices done with Our Lord at the instance of the Cardinal of Sens, by the Most Illustrious Alessandrino, and they complain of [me], that I exhorted them to send a man express to Our Lord, since many bishops in France had authority to absolve them without going to Rome. I, from what I know and am informed, find that the Count of Soissons is not more than 20 years old, and that when he was given to the Cardinal of Bourbon he was not more than 4, and since then he has been brought up by His Most Illustrious Lordship and has always lived a Catholic, and now he shows himself [f. 134v] most attached to the Catholic religion; and I fear that making difficulties over the absolution can help neither the Catholic religion nor the kingdom, because it will certainly make harder the return of Navarre to the obedience of the Apostolic See, and will be cause of renewing the hatred between this King and those of Guise, since they hold for certain that all the evil comes from them, though at present, through offices done by me too, they show themselves quite well disposed together. It seems too that the King resented it much, and wants to put off the opening of the Estates until the return of this […]; but [with] me His Majesty has not yet spoken of it, as I have not been able to go and find him, having hurt a foot, which does not let me walk. I hope in one or two days to be able to go out, which I greatly desire, to make certain whether it is true that the ambassador of the King of Denmark, who I write outside the cipher has come to this court, comes to persuade His Majesty to unite with his King in defence of the Queen of England, so as to do in [f. 135r] that case the office that befits the honour of the Lord God and the service of Our Lord. I have been much surprised that Monsignor the vice-legate of Avignon complains, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes me in the said cipher, that, though he wrote to me several times on matters important to his government, I have not answered him; which, were it true, Your Most Illustrious Lordship could with great reason say that this does not please Our Lord. But you may rest assured that I have had from the said Monsignor […] only three letters on some business, to all of which I have not only answered by letter but also with all the effects that could come from me, as Fioravanti his secretary knows very well, who for many months now has stayed at court handling the vice-legate's business without communicating with me anything but what suits him. The same I can say on the last head of the said cipher, where you tell me that the Duke of Épernon and La Valette his brother complain of being abandoned by that Holy See, and that Our Lord wonders that I have not done [f. 135v] the proper office for these lords, as I have been written by familiar letters, by briefs and by instructions; and I take comfort that Your Most Illustrious Lordship, in your third letter of the same date of the 19th of last month, outside the cipher, writes me that the office done by […] with the Duke of Guise for the benefit of Épernon and his brother, and the letters written to them, have pleased Our Lord, and that he wills that this business go forward. I therefore pray Your Most Illustrious Lordship to assure Our Lord that I shall never fail to obey with all promptness the orders of Our Lord, nor do I fear that he will ever have cause to hold me negligent, my obligations being too great not to watch always over his service, as I shall do with the favour of the Lord God all the time of my life. […] will know that, besides what I have written from time to time of having done in this matter, I have also worked a great deal more, and so as not to tire Your Most Illustrious Lordship with too long a letter I have left off writing it; but in effect it seems to me that they ought not to refuse the arrangement His Majesty proposes to them, as I have written to the Duke of Épernon, which is to leave the government of Provence [and] that of the […] R27, Francia 22/6, n.d. (fragment) On governments for Épernon (Saintonge, Angoulême, Cognac) and on Boulogne. Épernon's side refuses to give anything back and is said to deal with the Queen of England and Navarre. Morosini hopes for peace between Guise and the others, though with little confidence. Transcription DOC_R27_D1691_1691.txt #CATALOG NAME: Segr. And nevertheless they show themselves most resolved not to restore anything; on the contrary, from what His Majesty has told me, they are in very [close] dealings with the Queen of England, with the former King of Navarre, with Casimir and with Montmorency, of which the said Majesty assures me he has most certain proofs, so that […] without great suspicion of them; besides which, if he were content to leave them everything, he would put himself on bad terms with these others. I certainly do not fail, nor shall I fail as far as lies in me, to promote every good, but I have little hope of being able to make peace between the Duke of Guise and these others, because it does not suit Guise to have their friendship, since being their enemy has been the chief cause of winning him the affection and the following of the people; just as, on the contrary, the King's having [f. 137v] chosen to support and favour [them] has been the cause of his ruin and of all the evils that have followed […]. R28, Francia 22/7, [early] Oct [1588] (duplicate) While walking in the palace garden with the King, the Queen Mother and the Cardinals of Bourbon and Vendôme, Morosini learned that the King would send Signor Girolamo Gondi to Rome about pulling Marshal Montmorency away from the Huguenots. Morosini urged the King to win Guise over with money, since Guise is heavily in debt; Guise refused the grant offered. Vendôme reports that Cardinal Joyeuse worked against the Count of Soissons in Rome. M.tà, come soglio fare spese uolte, doue esendo sopra uenuta la Regina Madre, mi posi a pasegiare et ragionar seco; ma soprauenendo poco dopo S. M.tà, acompagnato da li sig.[ri] cardinali di Borbone e di Uandomo, [?di] Gondi et molta nobiltà, io mi ritirai con li sodeti sig.[ri] cardinali, lasando che il Re parlase con la regina sua madre. Ma subito mi chiamarono, et mi presero in mezo fra loro dui, et pasegiando di quel modo incominciò il Re a dirmi che io più uolte, anco per nome di N. S., l'haueuo esortato a uedere di ritirare a sé il marsciale di Momoransi, et che lui in ciò conosceua la buona uolontà di N. S. uerso di lui, et però era risoluto di mandarle un gentilomo, che dise che saria il sig. Hieronimo Gondi, per apresentare a N. S. tuto quello ch'ella pensa di uoler fare a beneficio però [?et] di [?sodi]sfatione di eso Momoransi, a fine di [ri]tirarlo da l'amicitia del già re di Nauarra et altri heretici et ridurlo al suo seruitio; et perché conoscendo N. S. [f. 142v] non solo ragioneuoli ma anco importanti tute le sicurtà che pensa di dare al sodeto Momoransi, [?…] posi ela con l'autorità sua interponersi per condure a buon fine questo negotio, che desiderauano d'intendere il mio parere; ma che sopra tuto […] uenise secretisimo, perché quando si risapese non [?mancariano] molti che procurariano disturbare questa riconciliatione. Io le disi che, quanto ala secreteza, io non ne parlarei con alcuno; ma che 'l dire l'opinione mia sopra questo particolare mi pare superfluo, poiché molte uolte et con uiue ragioni haueuo esortata S. M.tà a fare ogni opera per ritirare dal'amicitia de li ugonotti quel signore, et che io teneuo per certo che N. S., che non ha altro fine che il bene uniuersale dela christianità et l'unione de' catolici ala distrutione del'heresie, non potria hauere nuoua che gli fose più cara che intendere in questo fato la buona uolontà di S. M.tà, et che io credeuo che non lasaria d'interponere de l'autorità sua per ridurla a quel fine che si desidera, lodando [f. 143r] asai la persona che S. M.tà pensa di mandare a Roma, perché è ueram[ente] molto degna per qualsiuoglia carica, et molto diuota et benemerita di cotesta Santa Sede, hauendo in ogni tempo seruito [?con] tuto il cuore tuti li legati, nuntii et altri che sono mandati dala Sede Apostolica a questa corte. Dapoi entrati a parlare di mons. di Guisa, feci eficacisimo oficio per persuadere S. M.tà di pigliar seco confidenza et leuargli ogni ocasione di sospetione che ela non habi[a] qualche mal animo uerso di lui, perché altram[ente] io pre[ue]deuo ritornare le cose in pesimi termini; et le considerai che se mons. di Guisa, senza fare altro male, una matina si partise di corte con quelli dela sua fatione, che moto saria di nuouo in tuto questo regno, et che lei non si [?stimaria] sicura in Bles, et che partendo non si poteua asicurare di ritirarsi in alcun luogo doue fose riceuta uolontieri, non temino più mons. di Guisa che S. M.tà, ma temano più loro stesi che gli altri; et sano molto [f. 143v] bene et in tempo di guerra quando si conuiene hauere apreso soldati et guardie, che [?tanto] male riceuono da gli uni come da gli altri. Mi dise S. M.tà che quello che le diceuo era uerisimo, et che quanto a lei cercaua di dare ogni sodisfatione a mons. di Guisa, et di asicurarlo per ogni uia dela sua buona uolontà, et che non sapria fare d'auantagio, che uole ricordarsi qualche cosa che lo faria […]. Disi che S. M.tà non haueua bisogno di mio ricordo, ma che tutauia non lasarei di dirle che per opinione mia crederei che due cose giouasero asai per asicurare il sodeto di Guisa dela buona uolontà dela S. M.tà: la prima era che S. M.tà hauese in efeto nel suo cuore questa buona uolontà, et l'altra che procurase di mostrarla anco con gli efeti; che mons. di Guisa era carico di debiti et tutauia continouaua a spendere più che non ha d'entrata, et che S. M.tà, che era liberalisima con gli altri, usase anco con lui di questa liberalità, perché io mi persuadeuo che li danari sariano benisimo impiegati, et si [?…]riano [f. 144r] certo il sodeto di Guisa dela buona uolontà di S. M.tà, così rimediando al suo bisogno, non gli permeteriano di pensare ad altri modi per prouedere ale su[e] necesità. Il Re mi ringratiò molto di questo ricordo, et mi dise che lo uoleua fare in ogni modo, ma che gli doleua di non hauere al presente comodità di poterlo fare con efeti, poiché non poteua esere in magior streteza di danari di quello che al presente si ritroua; ma che egli […] daria de le intentione che se ne saria potuto asicurare. Et io dopo ho inteso che S. M.tà il medesmo giorno gli mandò per mons. d'O a dire che gli uoleua asignare sopra l'entrate del ano futuro un donatiu[o] di 200 milia scudi, […] non l'ha uoluto acetare, dicendo che hora la S. M.tà haueua tropo bisogno di danari, et però si riseruaua di acetare di simili fauori quando le cose fosero in migliore termine. Con tuto ciò pare che dapoi habia […] tratato con S. M.tà molto più apertam[ente] et con molta [f. 144v] sodisfatione di ambe le parti. Ma l'inimico del'humana natura uole che così apreso S. M.tà come apreso il duca di Guisa ci siano persone che ad altro non atendono che a nodrire le difidentie et [?seminare] discordie. Translation R28_en.md # R28 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [8 October 1588]: the garden talk with Henri III on Montmorency and Guise) Translation of `R28_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 142r] […] before I made myself […], I found myself one morning walking in an avenue of this garden of His Majesty, as I often do, where the Queen Mother having come upon me, I started to walk and talk with her; but His Majesty coming up shortly after, accompanied by the Cardinals of Bourbon and Vendôme, [?by] Gondi and much nobility, I withdrew with the said cardinals, leaving the King to talk with the Queen his mother. But they called me at once and took me between the two of them, and walking in that way the King began to tell me that I had several times, also in the name of His Holiness, urged him to try to draw Marshal Montmorency to himself, and that in this he recognised the good will of His Holiness towards him; and therefore he had resolved to send him a gentleman — he said it would be Signor Girolamo Gondi — to set before His Holiness everything he intends to do for the benefit [and] [?satis]faction of the said Montmorency, in order to [with]draw him from the friendship of the former King of Navarre and the other heretics and bring him into his service; and because, His Holiness recognising [f. 142v] not only as reasonable but also as important all the securities he intends to give the said Montmorency, [?…] she might with her authority interpose herself to bring this business to a good end, he wished to hear my opinion; but that above all […] it should remain most secret, because if it became known [?there would not be lacking] many who would try to disturb this reconciliation. I told him that, as to secrecy, I would not speak of it to anyone; but that to give my opinion on this particular seemed superfluous to me, since many times and with lively reasons I had urged His Majesty to do everything to draw that lord away from the friendship of the Huguenots, and that I held it for certain that His Holiness, who has no other aim than the universal good of Christendom and the union of the Catholics for the destruction of heresy, could have no news dearer to him than to learn His Majesty's good will in this matter, and that I believed he would not fail to interpose his authority to bring it to the desired end; praising [f. 143r] highly the person whom His Majesty intends to send to Rome, because he is truly most worthy of any office, and very devoted to and deserving of that Holy See, having at all times served [?with] all his heart all the legates, nuncios and others sent by the Apostolic See to this court. Then, having come to speak of Monsieur de Guise, I made a most earnest representation to persuade His Majesty to take him into his confidence and remove from him every cause of suspicion that she [His Majesty] might bear him some ill will, because otherwise I foresaw matters returning to the worst condition; and I put it to him that if Monsieur de Guise, without doing any other harm, left the court one morning with those of his faction, there would be a rising again throughout this kingdom, and that she [His Majesty] would not [?consider herself] safe in Blois, and that, leaving, she could not be sure of withdrawing to any place where she would be willingly received; [?they do not] fear Monsieur de Guise more than His Majesty, but fear more for themselves than for the others; and they know very [f. 143v] well, and in time of war, when one must have soldiers and guards about, that they suffer [?as much] harm from the one side as from the other. His Majesty told me that what I said was very true, and that for her part she was trying to give every satisfaction to Monsieur de Guise and to assure him in every way of her good will, and that she could do no more, that she wanted to be reminded of anything that would make him […]. I said that His Majesty had no need of my reminder, but that I would nevertheless not fail to tell her that in my opinion two things would greatly help to assure the said Guise of His Majesty's good will: the first was that His Majesty should truly have this good will in his heart, and the other that he should take care to show it also by deeds; that Monsieur de Guise was loaded with debts and yet went on spending more than his income, and that His Majesty, who was most liberal with others, should use this liberality with him too, because I was persuaded that the money would be very well spent, and [it would assure] [f. 144r] the said Guise of His Majesty's good will; and so, remedying his need, they would not allow him to think of other ways of providing for his necessities. The King thanked me much for this advice, and told me that he wanted to do it by all means, but that he was sorry not to have at present the means to do it in deeds, since he could not be in greater straits for money than he presently is; but that he […] would give him such intentions as he could be assured of. And I have since learned that His Majesty on the same day sent Monsieur d'O to tell him that he wished to assign him, on next year's revenues, a gift of 200,000 scudi; […] he would not accept it, saying that His Majesty now had too much need of money, and therefore he reserved himself to accept such favours when matters were in a better condition. All the same, it seems that since then he has […] dealt with His Majesty much more openly and with much [f. 144v] satisfaction on both sides. But the enemy of human nature wills that, both about His Majesty and about the Duke of Guise, there are persons who attend to nothing else than feeding mistrust and [?sowing] discord. I do not fail on every side to do all I can to bring about […] the good [?understanding], [from which] one can hope for the quiet of this kingdom and the rooting out of heresy; and to this end I would think it very much to the purpose that His Holiness should be content to grant the absolution to the Count of Soissons in the form in which he has already been content to do it, deferring however to the singular prudence of His Holiness and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship. Now I am told by the Lord Cardinal Gondi that the most illustrious [Cardinal] of Vendôme has told him he has heard that the Lord Cardinal of Joyeuse, and not the one of Sens, was the author of the bad offices done with His Holiness against the Count of Soissons his brother, and that in the consistory, at His Holiness's chair, they had spoken against the Lord Cardinals Alessandrino and Santi [f. 145r] Quattro, but that the same Joyeuse had been in His Holiness's rooms to do the same; which will serve as a notice to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. Translation R29_en.md # R29 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Blois], 10 October 1588: the Tuscan marriage, Saluzzo, Soissons, Denmark) Translation of `R29_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 152r] […] yesterday evening a courier arrived here on his way back from Florence, sent by the Queen Mother for the conclusion of the Grand Duke's marriage with this Princess of Lorraine. He reports that Signor Orazio Rucellai will be [here] within four days to complete this business, the Grand Duke wishing the bride to be at Marseille by the end of [November], where the Queen Mother herself intends to accompany her. This courier says he was held for four days in Savoy, that Lord Duke not having been willing to let him pass, so that he should not carry news of the enterprise carried out by His Highness, who, the said courier says, has made himself master of all the strongholds of the marquisate of Saluzzo. At this news everyone here is left astonished, and the Duke of Guise has sent to tell me that he sees very well that this event will be the ruin of the Catholic religion: […] in order to be able to make war on the Duke of Savoy they will try to make peace with the former King of Navarre and with the heretics, since one cannot at the same time make war on the one [f. 152v] and on the other. And although he promises me to hold firm, with all his friends, so that no other religion is permitted in the kingdom, […] and that before this event happened he was sure that the Estates would all have demanded the total destruction of the others, whereas now he feared that necessity might lead them to some other resolution. This most important and dangerous event, which could cause very great mischief, has made me add this too to the long despatch of yesterday, the courier not having left yet, as I wish Your Most Illustrious Lordship to be pleased to give me orders on what I am to do if it came to asking for this universal peace, with permission of a religion other than the Catholic, in order to attend to the recovery of the said marquisate, as is greatly to be feared; which would truly be the total ruin of this kingdom and of religion. To remedy the discontents of the King and of this Lord of Bourbon at the refusal [f. 153r] of absolution for the Count of Soissons, and believing it to be in Our Lord's service to soften them, and also to remove the occasions of greater [disturbances], I have tried, through the Cardinal de Gondi, to persuade them to be content to make the abjuration in the manner and form Your Most Illustrious Lordship sent me; and this is why the courier is being held, to see whether they can be brought to this. I have not yet had their resolution on what they intend to do. Just now I am told that here they greatly praise the good offices done by Our Lord's nuncio resident in Turin on this occasion of the taking of the said […] strongholds by that Duke. The Cardinal de Gondi has assured me that the ambassador of Denmark has treated nothing else here than the restitution of certain merchandise taken from his King's subjects by French ships, and that it is not true that he spoke for the Queen of England or on any other particular matter. I have [heard] the same by another way: he has not spoken more [f. 153v] than once with the King, and few […] words; and he is now pressing [with] great diligence for his despatch, which His Majesty has [ordered] to be made […]. R30, Francia 22/9, 3 Oct [1588], Blois Morosini took on the job of reconciling the Duke of Guise and Mons. de Nevers, who have been at odds since they married sisters; with the King's approval, both promised to follow his advice. He pressed Guise and the Cardinal of Guise on publishing the council. The clergy is split: the lower deputies want Gallican liberty reserved. Transcription DOC_R30_D1694_1694.txt #CATALOG NAME: Segr. Però mi parue di fare con S. E. ogni eficace oficio per meterla d'acordo con il sodeto duca di Guisa, conoscendo che il continouare loro in mala inteligenza insieme era causa che così l'uno come l'altro non lascia di fare di mali ofici con il Re, a graue pregiudicio dela quiete et conseruatione dela […]; et dopo molte ragioni et persuasioni, seruendomi anco dela autorità di […] N. S., con dire che questa unione saria gratisima a N. S., lo ridusi a termini che, dopo una longa narratiua di ofese che diceua di hauere riceute dal sodeto di Guisa, finalmente si contentò di prometermi di fare in ciò tuto quello che io giudicasi conueniente. Però, a fine di procedere in questo negotio con quella circonspetione che conuiene et non dare alcuna sospetione a S. M.tà, andai li giorni […] pasati [f. 162r] a ritrouarla, et le considerai il dano che ela riceueua da questa disunione, che è grandisimo per ogni rispeto, ma principalm[ente] perché, per nuocersi l'uno et l'altro, ueniuano anco il più dele uolte a nuocere a le cose del suo seruitio, oltre ala confusione che nasceua nel animo di S. M.tà per le difidentie et sospeti che erano seminati fra lei et gli altri; et mi ofersi d'interpormi fra loro per riconciliarli insieme, se la lo trouaua buono, […] disi che non haueuo uoluto ponere mano se prima non sapeuo la mente di S. M.tà, con tuto che hauesi dal duca di Niuers la parola che si contentaua di fare tuto quello che io hauesi giudicato conueniente. Mostrò il Re di hauere gratisimo questo oficio, confesando che saria di gran bene ale cose sue se questi si quietasero insieme, et mi pregò di parlarne con mons. di Guisa et uedere di ridurlo a questa compositione, come feci il giorno seguente, e[s]endo S. E. uenuta a uedermi; la quale, se bene uolese […] darmi conto di tute le mali sodisfationi che le haueua date mons. di Niuers, incominciando per sino dal tempo che si maritò nela [f. 161v] sorela dela sua moglie, tutauia in fine dise che, con tuto che io [?fidase] molto nela parola che io diceuo esermi stata data dal sodeto duca di Niuers, et ela ancora mi prometeua di fare tuto quello che a me parese conueniente. Hora si atenderà a formare i capitoli del acordo con il consenso et uolontà del Re, per uedere di dar fine a così buona et salutare riconciliatione, nela quale non mancarano molte dificoltà. Piacia al sig. Dio di fauorirmi con la sua santis. gratia, che io, per quello sarà in me, non lasarò di afaticarmi con tuto lo spirito; et di quello seguirà ne darò auiso a V. S. Ill.ma. Feci anco con mons. di Guisa eficacisimo uficio per la publicatione del concilio di Trento, dicendoli apertam[ente] che io sapeuo che fra il sig. cardinale suo fratelo et lui haueuano tanta parte et autorità neli Stati che, quando unitam[ente] non dimandasero la publicatione di eso concilio, […] saria de loro: non hauriano procurato da uero. Mi promise il sig. duca […] di fare ogni suo potere, et tuto quel più che io gli hauesi ricordato. Simile oficio ho fato con il sig. cardinale di Guisa [f. 161r] suo fratelo et con tuti quelli che mi uengono a parlare; ma ho inteso che, esendo stato proposto l'altra matina fra il clero questo punto, si era scoperta fra di loro una grandisima diuisione, esendo che, da li uescoui in fuori, tuti gli altri deputati inferiori, non ricusando la publicatione del concilio, uogliono che prima si uega quello che pregiudica ala libertà dela chiesa galicana, et che questo sii in ogni modo ecetuato. Non ho mancato anco di parlare a S. M.tà, esortandola a publicare esa di sua spontanea uolontà il sodeto concilio senza aspetare di esere ricercata dai Stati; et se pretenderà qualche gratia, che già sapeua quello che io per nome di N. S. le haueuo promeso, che in tute le cose honeste saria compiaciuta; et mi ha promeso di così fare. Io non mancarò di continouare li ofici con quella magiore instanza che mi sarà posibile, et di quanto seguirà ne ragua[g]liarò V. S. Ill.ma. Ho [?inteso] hora che una dele cose che si propone fra lo stato eclesiastico si […] che da N. S. non si posino concedere alienationi di beni eclesiastici in questo regno senza il consenso del clero; et io non ho mancato, né mancarò, [f. 160r] di fare ogni oficio perché non si uenga a tratare questo punto, con dire che non aspeta a loro di metere mano nela potestà di N. S., et che era anco superfluo il tratarne, perché io credeuo certo che N. S., né con il consenso né senza, permeterà più uendita di beni dela chiesa, poi che pur tropo se ne erano uenduti con molto dispiacere di N. Translation R30_en.md # R30 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 3 October 1588: reconciling Nevers and Guise, the Council of Trent, the clergy) Translation of `R30_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 162v] And the other […] from the conversations I have had with Monsieur de Nevers I have discovered quite plainly an ill feeling that His Excellency (Nevers) has towards Monsieur de Guise; of which, though I had some notice of it before, I did not believe it had come to the point of being able to bring the harm to the quiet of this kingdom that I have since recognised. So it seemed right to me to do every effective office with His Excellency to bring him to agreement with the said Duke of Guise, knowing that their continuing on bad terms together was the reason why both the one and the other did not [cease] to do ill offices with the King, to the grave prejudice of the quiet and preservation of the […]; and after many reasons and persuasions, using also the authority of […] Our Lord, saying that this union would be most welcome to Our Lord, I brought him to the point that, after a long account of the offences he said he had received from the said Guise, he at last agreed to promise me to do in this all that I should judge proper. So, in order to proceed in this business with the circumspection it requires and to give no suspicion to His Majesty, I went some days ago [f. 162r] to find His Majesty, and put to him the harm he was suffering from this disunion, which is very great in every respect, but principally because, in harming each other, the one and the other came most often to harm the affairs of his service as well, besides the confusion that arose in His Majesty's mind from the distrust and suspicions sown between him and the others; and I offered to interpose myself between them to reconcile them, if His Majesty thought it good; […] I said that I had not wished to put my hand to it unless I first knew His Majesty's mind, although I had the Duke of Nevers' word that he would do all I should judge proper. The King showed that he found this office most welcome, admitting that it would be of great benefit to his affairs if they made peace together, and he asked me to speak of it to Monsieur de Guise and see whether I could bring him to this settlement, as I did the next day, His Excellency (Guise) having come to see me; who, though he wished […] to give me an account of all the grievances Monsieur de Nevers had given him, beginning from the time he married the [f. 161v] sister of his (Guise's) wife, nevertheless said in the end that, although I [trusted] much in the word that I said had been given me by the said Duke of Nevers, he too promised me to do all that I should think proper. Now they will set about drawing up the articles of the agreement with the King's consent and will, to see whether so good and salutary a reconciliation can be completed, in which there will be no lack of difficulties. May it please the Lord God to favour me with His most holy grace, for I, as far as lies in me, shall not fail to labour at it with all my spirit; and of what follows I shall inform Your Most Illustrious Lordship. I also made a most effective office with Monsieur de Guise for the publication of the Council of Trent, telling him openly that I knew that the Cardinal his brother and he had so much part and authority in the Estates that, if they did not jointly ask for the publication of the Council, […] would be theirs: they would not have worked for it in earnest. The Duke […] promised me to do all in his power, and everything more that I should remind him of. I have done a similar office with the Cardinal of Guise [f. 161r] his brother and with all who come to speak to me; but I have heard that, this point having been proposed among the clergy the other morning, a very great division had appeared among them, since, apart from the bishops, all the other lower deputies, while not refusing the publication of the Council, want it first seen what prejudices the liberty of the Gallican church, and that this be excepted in any case. I have also not failed to speak to His Majesty, urging him to publish the said Council of his own free will without waiting to be asked by the Estates; and if he should claim some favour, he already knew what I had promised him in Our Lord's name, that in all honest things he would be gratified; and he has promised me to do so. I shall not fail to continue the offices with the greatest insistence I can, and of all that follows I shall inform Your Most Illustrious Lordship. Quanto a mons. d'Epernone et la Ualeta suo fratelo, non [?io] ho mancato di fare ogni buono oficio; ma non hauendo loro uoluto acetare i partiti che li erano fati da S. M.tà [de], come [?lei] con altre mie ne diedi conto a V. S. Et per questo rispeto S. Translation R31_en.md # R31 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 23 October 1588: Gondi to Rome, Épernon and Provence, the fundamental law, Martinengo) Translation of `R31_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 173r] […] in the last audience I had with the King I did with His Majesty the office that Your Most Illustrious Lordship charges me with in your letters of the 29th of last month, on the memorial presented to Our Lord by order of the Most Serene [Duke] of Savoy about drawing Monsieur de Montmorency away from the union with the Huguenots. I found His Majesty very well disposed, going on to tell me that for this purpose he wanted to send Signor Girolamo Gondi to Rome, so that Our Lord might be well informed of his intention and know the generous terms he meant to offer him to draw him into his service. But he did not think it good advice to send him a gentleman with the confirmation of his government free and the means to maintain the garrisons unless he first promises to separate himself from the Huguenots; and it seems to me that His Majesty [has] remained somewhat in suspense on learning that this was a proposal of the Duke of Savoy, with whom he is greatly irritated, the events of the marquisate of Saluzzo pressing on his very heart, as they also press on all these princes, lords and peoples; so that there is great reason to fear that, unless a remedy is found, some mischief [may] easily [f. 173v] follow, to the grave prejudice of the Catholic religion. His Majesty told me in this connection that he was greatly satisfied with the words Our Lord had spoken to his ambassador, and that he hoped for every fatherly demonstration from Our Lord. As to Monsieur d'Épernon and La Valette his brother, [I] have not failed to do every good office; but since they would not accept the terms offered them by His Majesty [de], as I reported to Your Most Illustrious Lordship in other letters, I fear that matters are now reduced to a worse state, and that the King could hardly give [him] now what he had offered them before. Nevertheless Monsieur de Mases, sent by the said Épernon, is still staying here, and is in some hope of a settlement; but I hope little from it, because affairs in Provence keep getting worse. On this account His Majesty is sending Monsieur de Sainte-Marie back into that province with orders both to La Valette and to Monsieur de Vins that they lay down their arms and live in peace, until, once better informed of those matters than he is, he can [f. 174r] take whatever course is most suitable for the quiet of that government. But I seem to have discovered that His Majesty's intention would be to put another governor there, being very ill satisfied with La Valette, not only for the troubles in Provence but also because he thinks him to blame for the loss of the marquisate of Saluzzo, which was his government. I have again commended the states of Avignon to the King and to Monsieur de Guise, and I am given very good words, but I do not see that they have the means to give much help, the Duke of Mayenne not having forces enough to do it. I have also reminded the Cardinal de Bourbon of the same, considering the […] he has not only as a Christian and a cardinal but also as legate of this […]; he shows himself most desirous of being able to do every service. I have not failed and shall not fail to work that no novelty be made in the Estates to the prejudice of the Catholic faith, for which Your Most Illustrious Lordship will see that much has been done, since by a fundamental and irrevocable law of the kingdom it has been established [f. 174v] always to maintain the sole Catholic, Apostolic and Roman religion, without ever being able to make peace with heretics; which, having been embraced with the consent of the Estates General, who represent the whole kingdom, is a thing for which to praise the Lord God, since it followed with the applause of all the people and the incredible satisfaction of everyone. I have done with His Majesty the office about the faculties of the legation that Your Most Illustrious Lordship committed to me in the previous dispatch; but in fact, unless they are verified by the Parlement, they will not be obeyed anywhere, even if the King commanded it. And I am told that the Keeper of the Seals, who still has them in his hands, lets it be understood that the Parlement will never consent to my having authority to visit and reform as the bull contains, saying that this is directly against the liberty of the Gallican church. To me not a word [has been said] of this. By letters of the Cardinal Santa Severina I am advised of Our Lord's wish that a Count Ulisse Martinengo, a heretic, should be seized, [f. 172r] [who came] to Lyon to deal with the Huguenots, and then sent to Avignon into Our Lord's power. Having taken this up with His Majesty, he at once, with great readiness and desire to please Our Lord, had Monsieur de Mandelot, governor of Lyon, written to that he should use every diligence to find this man, and when found keep him in good custody, sending word here that he has been detained, so that order [may] be given to have him taken safely to Avignon. The Cardinal of Guise has told me he has heard that Our Lord was recalling the vice-legate of [191 = Avignon?], and therefore begged me to do an office that Our Lord be pleased to give him that charge, as had been asked on other occasions by the Cardinal de Bourbon, affirming that he would do such work for the security of that state that Our Lord would be well content. I answered him that I did not know that Our Lord had any thought of recalling the present vice-legate, but that I would not fail to advise Your Most Illustrious Lordship of all he told me, as I do [with] this letter, [which] I believe will be carried as far as Florence by a courier whom Signor Orazio Rucellai is sending [f. 172v] with the articles of the marriage contract between [the] Grand Duke of Tuscany and the Princess of Lorraine. […] some little difference having arisen from the diversity of the customs of [141] and those of France in the case of restitution and increase of the dowry, the said Rucellai has not been able to conclude without new orders from His Highness on this point, in which I believe there [will] be no difficulty. Morosini protests over Cardinal Lenoncourt's indult and over church revenues in the Cambrai truce, and the Queen Mother answers him. The DECODE "cleartext" image (f. 180) is the covering letter in clear, Blois 24 October 1588 ("Il resto sarà nell'incluso foglio"), not a decipherment; 182r carries a clear docket "Del S. Card. Morosini, li 24 ottobre 1588". Two cipher sheets: 181r–v (one letter, its start probably lost with an earlier sheet) and 182r–183v (a second, the last page breaking off mid-sentence). Tempesti, *Vita di Sisto V* (1754) II, book VII §§ XIX–XXIV, tells the Saluzzo affair from Morosini's letters (Poigny sent to the Duke of Savoy to demand the marquisate, offering repayment of his costs and the government to the Duke of Nemours, "della medesima casa"); used for names and sense only. Quello che duole ai buoni è di uedere che questi acidenti sarano la rouina dela religione catolica in questo regno, et forse anco in altri, che il sig. Dio non lo uoglia. Translation R32_en.md # R32 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 24 October 1588: Saluzzo, Provence, the Cambrai canon, the bull of the *confidenze*) Translation of `R32_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 181r] In the Assembly, to see how his authority [may] now give [to] this business the good end that is desired; and so […] His Majesty promised me. He has been warned (that the Duke of Savoy, not content [?] with what he has done in the marquisate of Saluzzo) [that he] also has other secret […] in Provence, and especially [in] the cities of Marseille and Arles; for […] in that direction, and he holds it certain that as soon as the Estates are over His Majesty will go to Lyon […] importune […] by the whole world to [resent it] against the one [who has helped]; and the Duke of Guise has said publicly that if the King will not do it, he will do it in any case by himself alone. What grieves good men is to see that these events will be the ruin of the Catholic religion in this kingdom, and perhaps in others too, which the Lord God forbid. Today Monsieur de Poigny is to leave to make representations to the said Duke, that he restore the marquisate, offering to repay him whatever he has spent on this enterprise, and [f. 181v] to give him satisfaction and assurance that he need not fear that in future the marquisate might fall into the hands of a governor not in his confidence, they offer [962] […] to give it to Monsieur de Nemours, who is of his house and a descendant […], [of which] he had no cause to be discontented. […] Monsieur de Poigny came to see me and take leave of me, asking me to write to Monsignor [of Fano], nuncio of Our Lord, that he would help […]. [I have written] without going into any other particular than to tell him about this gentleman and commend him to his courtesy. […] [f. 182r] […] the Cardinal de Lenoncourt has told me that he has given Our Lord a detailed account of the obstacles put in his way so that he cannot use the indult granted him by Our Lord; which spares me the occasion of repeating the same to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. I will only tell you that I have not failed to show His Majesty the greatest resentment I could, as was fitting for the dignity of Our Lord and of that Holy See; and nevertheless […] I [have gathered] that His Majesty was much displeased to hear that the Parlement of Rennes had gone so far, not only […] in the bull […] to forbid the said cardinal its execution against His Majesty's express order, that I should have [the] memorial given to her. [He will see] to provide in the best way possible, and tomorrow I shall draw up the said memorial with the advice of the said cardinal and have it presented to the archbishop; nor shall I fail to do all in my power to have the Parlement's arrêt revoked and annulled; and with the bishops of that province I shall also do what is fitting to move them from the opposition they make to Our Lord's orders, although I have gathered from some that regard for the person [f. 182v] of the said cardinal, who is little liked by many of them, more than the will to oppose the authority of Our Lord, makes them […] contest the indult; to whom I have said plainly that this increases their fault, since they oppose out of their own passion and knowing they do wrong. A canon of Cambrai has arrived here, sent by that archbishop to see that in the truce now being negotiated again between that Majesty and the Duke of Parma for the said city of Cambrai it be expressly declared that from now on the archbishop and other clergy […] enjoy freely their revenues and temporal goods. [I] have already spoken of it with the […] and with [162], showing them that they ought to make no difficulty, because it has never been heard that the […] Most Christian and Catholic [kings], on taking a city, made themselves masters of the revenues of the [741]. They answered me that they would speak of it together and then let me know their intention. I did not fail to reply that the matter was so clear that it needed no counsel, and that I did not know how their confessors could absolve them of this sin of wanting church property to be enjoyed [f. 183r] by soldiers. The Queen Mother told me that she did not want it, but that the affairs of this kingdom are at present in such a state that every governor wants to act in his own way, and that Monsieur de Balagny, who holds the government of that city, said many things on this subject; so she feared that even if the King did what I asked, the said Balagny would not obey, […] that Their Majesties should do on their side what they ought, to show the world their justice and piety […] remedy that Balagny should obey. With all that I could get no other decision; I shall not fail to press [the dispatch], and of what follows I shall give notice to [161]. Today I went back to [speak] with His Majesty about Monsieur d'Épernon and La Valette, and His Majesty told me that it is most [true …], and that they be removed from Provence, because otherwise that province was ruined, and there was no way to hope that those peoples would ever be content to obey La Valette, having declared themselves too much against him; and that in exchange he meant to leave him the [f. 183v] government of Metz, and that Monsieur de […] should be put in Boulogne, to leave free to Monsieur d'Épernon the government of Angoulême, [Saintonge] and Cognac. I told His Majesty that I feared those lords would not be content with this, and that to preserve themselves they might take some bad decision; but he replied that for now nothing else could be done, and that he hoped they would be content. I presented to His Majesty the bull of the *confidenze*, letting him know that Our Lord, by special grace and for […] souls of this kingdom, had reformed it and brought it to such terms that no one could any longer reasonably oppose it; and therefore I begged him to have it published and inviolably observed. His Majesty showed that he [valued it] and said that it had come very much in time, that he would have it examined and then speak to me. I have also again reminded His Majesty of the publication of the Council of Trent, which he has promised me, and tomorrow he will deal with it in any case, especially since it is to be discussed in the Estates tomorrow as well. I have pressed the Cardinal of Bourbon that he too be present […] R33, Francia 22/12, n.d. [Oct-Nov 1588] read in part The King referred the council to the clergy's congregation. There the chapters, bishops and others quarrelled over exemptions, and they finally asked for publication with four reservations (royal authority, Gallican liberty, chapter exemptions, particular privileges). Morosini argued that it must be published without conditions. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (95% here); the holes are marked in the reading. S. di dar[mi] intorno ala publicatione del concilio di Trento, che S. M.tà senza più dilatione uenise al'esecutione di quello che haueua promeso nei capitoli del acordo ultim[a]m[ente] fato a Parigi con questi signori di Guisa, di che il sodeto concilio sia riceuto […] liberam[ente], come si è fato neli altri regni et prouincie di christiani, […] parue ala S. M.tà di chiamare a sé alcuni prelati et altri dotori che si ritrouano qui ragunati per li stati, a' quali fece intendere l'instanza che io faceuo per la publicatione di eso concilio et […] et [?d]esiderio che ela hauea non solo di dar sodisfatione a N. S., ma anco di fare questo bene al suo regno, che grandem[ente] haueua bisogno di una buona riforma; che però uedesero d'esere insieme per truouare modo di fare questa publicatione senza diminuire dela sua autorità. Li prelati presero tempo di comonicare questo negotio nela loro congregatione del clero, doue esendo stato proposto, non ostante gli ufici che io prima haueuo fati a parte et le promese che mi erano state fate, ci furono molti contrasti et molta diuisione; perché, se bene tuti in uniuersale lodauano la publicatione del concilio, nondimeno [f. 189v] ognuno, discendendo a considerare il suo particolare interese, truouaua dele dificoltà grandi et insoportabili. Et prima li capitoli diceuano di non uole[r] [?per]dere i loro priuilegi di esere [?esenti] da i loro uescoui; et perché questi sono in numero di più di otanta et li uescoui non sono più che uenti, [et] per uedere di aquetarli molti di esi uescoui s'ofersero di dimandare unita[mente] con i capitoli a N. S. che li conseruase le loro esentioni. Altri non la uogliono intendere, dicendo che era cosa impertinente che 'l uescouo non potese coregere i uitii et gli abusi de i suoi canon[i]ci, et che [?…]inouando [questo] disordine non si poteua aspetare fruto alcuno da eso concilio. Altri si grauauano per la pluralità et incompatibilità de' benefici che [?posedono]; altri per questa loro pretensa libertà […] dela chiesa galicana, che uogliono per pontiglio d'honore et per hauere questa superiorità [?fra] tute [l']altre nationi christiane [?mantenere] ostinatam[ente]. Onde, dopo longhe dispute et dopo hauere ridoto la nobiltà et il terzo stato nela loro uolontà, ritornarono dal Re et disero a S. M.tà che tuti insieme la ringratiauano di uole[r] publicare il concilio, ma perché ci uoria [f. 190r] il tempo almeno di [?dui anni] per dichiarare gli interesi del regno, la pregauano di publicarlo con riserua di quatro sole ecetioni: la prima, di riseruare l'autorità sua; la seconda, la libertà dela chiesa galicana; la terza, le esentioni dei capitoli; et l'ultima, i particolari priuilegi che diuersi haueuano otenuto per godere più benefici insieme. Di che esendo io informato, dopo hauermi grauem[ente] doluto di così esorbitante risposta priuatam[ente] con diuersi di tuti li stati, andai al'audientia da S. M.tà et feci seco quello oficio più […] che io potei per persuaderla a mantenere la sua promesa, et non uolere ascoltare quei che, in[st]igati dal demonio, la uoleuano diuertire da questa santa et necesaria publicatione, et che in ogni modo si doueua fare senza alcuna ecetione: perché mai più si era udito nela chiesa di Dio che un concilio generale, ligitimam[ente] con[gregato] et finito, fose riceuto con conditioni et ecetioni; che [l]oro non poteuano negare et il concilio di Trento non fose generale et ligitimam[ente] congregato, poiché ci erano i loro prelati in bonisimo numero, et specialm[ente] il sig. cardinale di Lorena di bo[na] mem[oria], et li medesmi [f. 190v] ambasciatori di [?S. M.tà], che tuti insieme l'haueuano sotoscrito [?et] aprouato; che però considerasero se quello che con il consenso et parere di un gran numero di dotisimi et pii padri di tute le nationi dela christianità et con l'asistenza delo spirito santo si era risoluto et confirmato dala santa sede apostolica douese hora esere limitato et coreto da chi non ha autorità alcuna; che questa era cosa tropo indecente, et che dispia[c]eria asai a N. S., pregando[la] a considerar che, se ela tiene il titolo di christianis[si]mo, non [d]ourebe hauere tardato tanto a publicarlo con scandalo di tuto il resto dela christianità, ma che a lei conu[e]niua di hauere dato l'esempio agli altri, et che io temeuo che questo ritardare hauese prouocato l'ira di Dio sopra questo regno. Mi rispose il Re che egli desideraua quanto me che il [?concilio] [fose] publicato et oseruato; ma che […] considerasi che la chiesa galicana haueua sempre da molti centinara d'ani in qua, per i meriti de i seruitii fati ala chiesa catolica, goduto dei priuilegi et dele esentioni che non sono concesi ad altri [f. 191r] stati né imperi, et che non era honesto che si perdesero, poiché i Re suoi predecesori, che sono sempre stati non solo catolici ma anco santi, haueuano uoluto sempre conseruarli, et che per questo non furono mai stimati manco catolici et pii di qualsiuog[l]ia altro re dela christianità. Io disi a S. M.tà che io non truouauo nel simbolo degli apostoli altro che una sola chiesa, et però bisognaua che la chiesa galicana fose una con la romana, altrimenti che ci sariano più chiese, contra quello che faciamo profesione di credere, et contra quello [che] S. M.tà medesma et nel'edito d'unione et nel suo rag[i]onam[ento] fato ali stati haueua più uolte protestato et promeso di non uolere nel suo regno altr[a] religione che quella che insegna la chiesa catolica [?apost.] romana, ala quale deue ricorrere se desidera qualche gratia o priuilegio, perché come madre pia non mancarà riseruare et concedere di nuouo priuilegi et gratie ala [?Francia]; che però si deue publicare il concilio senza altra conditione, nel modo medesmo che ha fato tuto il resto dela christianità, et poi di mandare a N. S. quelle riserue che desidera, perché io mi asicurauo che in tute le cose honeste saria sodisfata da N. S. In che feci tuta quella più gagliarda [f. 191v] et eficace instanza che potei, poiché nei ricordi di N. S. si dice che senza questa conditione non si uenga ad alcun acordo. S. M.tà mi dise che [?non] poteua sprezare l'autorità sua, né meno [?contra] il consenso di tuti li stati del suo regno fare una risolutione che potria causare qualche grande inconueniente con rouina et destrutione dele cose sue; che però mi pregaua di hauere un poco di pacientia, perché fra dui o tre giorni mi hauria fato chiamare, et dal suo guardasigilo fato[mi] intendere ala sua presenza tuto quello che ella hauese potuto fare, et che desideraua grandem[ente] di potermi dare sodisfatione, così per rispeto di N. S. come anco per mio particolare contento. Io disi a la maestà sua che non pretendeuo altro contento che l'honore del sig. Dio et il beneficio di questo regno; con che mi partii, et dopo non ho lasato di tratare il medesmo con tuti quelli che ho stimato poter giouare a questo negotio. [?Ma] da qualch'uno mi è stato deto che io mi riscaldauo tropo, et che N. S. non la pigliaua di questo modo, perché haueua comandato al ambasciatore di Francia residente costà, quando da principio fu dimandato neli capitoli proposti da quei dela lega la [f. 192r] publicatione del concilio, che scriuese al suo Re che di ciò non si metese in pena, perché ela non intendea di uolere che per forza si [p]ublicase il concilio, ma di buona uolontà dela S. M.tà; che però io non doueuo fare più di quello che uoleua N. S. Io risposi che io sapeuo molto bene quali fosero li miei ordini, et che però se il Re credese che questo fose motiuo mio, che ne poteua [scr]iuere a N. S., perché quando io hauesi trapasato le mie comisioni haurei riceuto quella riprensione che meritauo. Questo è quello che sin qui si è fato, da che V. S. Ill.ma potrà uedere che sarà cosa molto dificile, et forse imposibile, di potere guadagnare questo punto che il concilio sia riceuto senza alcuna conditione, poiché né il Re né li stati lo uogliono sentire, et quelli che più lo douriano procurare, che sono quelli del clero, metono loro [?più] dificoltà de gli altri. Però prego V. S. Ill.ma farmi gratia di comandarmi distintam[ente] et risolutam[ente] quello che io dourò fare, senza rimetere alcuna cosa al mio giudicio, perché confeso che non saprei che partito pigliare, parendomi ragioneuole molto che il concilio sia publicato et liberam[ente] riceuto, et d'altra parte molto pericoloso quando continouasero nel primo proposito procedere a qualche […] [f. 192v] […] generale congregatione de li stati di tuto il regno. Però andarò continouando nei medesimi ofici, procurando con modi destr[i] di guadagnare più che […] in questo punto, et […] si potrà spontare, m'andrò tratenendo sino a tanto che posi hauere lume da V. S. Ill.ma di quello [che] dourò [f]are per sodisfare compitam[ente] a […] uolontà et desiderio di N. S. Translation R33_en.md # R33 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [Oct–Nov 1588]: the clergy and the publication of the Council of Trent) Translation of `R33_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 189r] […] His Holiness, since I have continually pressed, according to the orders His Holiness was pleased to give [me] about the publication of the Council of Trent, that His Majesty should without further delay carry out what he had promised in the articles of the agreement lately made at Paris with these lords of Guise — namely that the said Council be received […] freely, as has been done in the other kingdoms and provinces of Christians — […] His Majesty decided to call to him some prelates and other doctors who are here assembled for the Estates, to whom he made known the pressure I was applying for the publication of the said Council, and […] and the [d]esire she [His Majesty] had not only to give satisfaction to His Holiness but also to do this good to his kingdom, which greatly needed a good reform; therefore they should meet together to find a way to make this publication without diminishing his authority. The prelates took time to communicate this business to their congregation of the clergy, where, when it was proposed — notwithstanding the offices I had first made in private and the promises made to me — there were many disputes and much division; because, although all in general praised the publication of the Council, nevertheless [f. 189v] each one, coming down to consider his own particular interest, found great and unbearable difficulties. First, the chapters said they did not want to lose their privileges of being [exempt] from their bishops; and because these are more than eighty in number and the bishops no more than twenty, [and] to try to appease them, many of those bishops offered to ask His Holiness, jointly with the chapters, to preserve their exemptions. Others will not hear of it, saying it was an impertinent thing that the bishop could not correct the vices and abuses of his canons, and that, [this] disorder [continuing], no fruit at all could be expected from the said Council. Others complained of the plurality and incompatibility of the benefices they [hold]; others, for this pretended liberty […] of the Gallican Church, which they want, as a point of honour and to have this superiority [among] all [the] other Christian nations, to [maintain] obstinately. So, after long disputes and after bringing the nobility and the Third Estate round to their will, they went back to the King and told His Majesty that all together they thanked him for being willing to publish the Council, but since it would take [f. 190r] at least [two years] to set out the interests of the kingdom, they begged him to publish it with the reservation of only four exceptions: first, to reserve his authority; second, the liberty of the Gallican Church; third, the exemptions of the chapters; and last, the particular privileges that various persons had obtained to hold several benefices together. Being informed of this, after complaining gravely and privately to several of all the Estates about so exorbitant an answer, I went to an audience with His Majesty and made with him the most […] representation I could to persuade him to keep his promise and not listen to those who, [in]stigated by the devil, wanted to divert him from this holy and necessary publication, and that in any case it must be done without any exception: because it had never been heard in the Church of God that a general Council, legitimately [assembled] and concluded, was received with conditions and exceptions; and they could not deny that the Council of Trent was general and legitimately assembled (literally "could not deny, and the Council of Trent not be general", the period's double negative), since their own prelates were there in very good number, and especially the Lord Cardinal of Lorraine of good memory, and the very [f. 190v] ambassadors of [His Majesty], who all together had signed and approved it; and therefore they should consider whether what had been resolved, with the consent and opinion of a great number of most learned and pious fathers of all the nations of Christendom and with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, and confirmed by the Holy Apostolic See, should now be limited and corrected by those who have no authority at all; that this was a thing too indecent, and would greatly displease His Holiness; begging [him] to consider that, since he holds the title of Most Christian, he should not have delayed so long in publishing it, to the scandal of all the rest of Christendom, but that it would have become him to have given the example to the others, and that I feared this delay had provoked the wrath of God upon this kingdom. The King answered that he desired as much as I did that the [?Council] [be] published and observed; but that […] it should be considered that the Gallican Church had for many hundreds of years, for the merits of the services done to the Catholic Church, enjoyed privileges and exemptions not granted to other [f. 191r] states or empires, and that it was not right that they should be lost, since the Kings his predecessors, who have always been not only Catholic but even saints, had always chosen to preserve them, and that for this they were never thought less Catholic and pious than any other king of Christendom. I told His Majesty that I found in the Apostles' Creed only one Church, and therefore the Gallican Church had to be one with the Roman, otherwise there would be several churches, against what we profess to believe, and against what His Majesty himself, both in the Edict of Union and in his speech to the Estates, had many times protested and promised: to want no other religion in his kingdom than the one taught by the Catholic [apostolic] Roman Church, to which he must have recourse if he wants some grace or privilege, because as a loving mother she will not fail to reserve and grant anew privileges and graces to [France]; and therefore the Council must be published without any other condition, in the same way as all the rest of Christendom has done, and then he should send to His Holiness the reservations he wants, because I was sure that in all honest things he would be satisfied by His Holiness. In this I made the most vigorous [f. 191v] and effective pressure I could, since in His Holiness's instructions it is said that without this condition no agreement is to be reached. His Majesty told me that he [could not] disregard his authority, nor [against] the consent of all the Estates of his kingdom make a resolution that could cause some great trouble, with ruin and destruction of his affairs; and so he begged me to have a little patience, because within two or three days he would have me called and have his Keeper of the Seals tell me, in his presence, all that he could do, and that he greatly wished to be able to give me satisfaction, both out of respect for His Holiness and for my own particular contentment. I told His Majesty that I claimed no other contentment than the honour of the Lord God and the good of this kingdom; with which I left, and since then I have not failed to deal with the same with all those I thought could help this business. [But] I have been told by someone that I was getting too heated, and that His Holiness did not take it this way, because he had ordered the ambassador of France resident there, when at the beginning the publication of the Council was asked for in the articles proposed by those of the League, [f. 192r] to write to his King not to worry about it, because he did not intend the Council to be published by force, but by His Majesty's good will; and that I therefore ought not to do more than His Holiness wanted. I answered that I knew very well what my orders were, and that if the King believed this was my own motive he could write about it to His Holiness, because if I had exceeded my commission I would have received the reprimand I deserved. This is what has been done so far, from which Your Most Illustrious Lordship can see that it will be very difficult, and perhaps impossible, to win this point, that the Council be received without any condition, since neither the King nor the Estates will hear of it, and those who ought most to work for it, namely those of the clergy, make [more] difficulty than the others. Therefore I beg Your Most Illustrious Lordship to do me the favour of ordering me distinctly and decisively what I am to do, without leaving anything to my judgment, because I confess I would not know what course to take, it seeming to me very reasonable that the Council be published and freely received, and on the other hand very dangerous if they persisted in their first intention to proceed to some […] [f. 192v] […] general congregation of the Estates of the whole kingdom. So I shall go on with the same offices, trying by skilful means to gain more than […] on this point, and […] can be carried, I shall temporise until I can have light from Your Most Illustrious Lordship on [what] I am to do to satisfy fully […] the will and desire of His Holiness.
