Come si tiene anco per certo che mons. di Epernone et la Ualeta suo fratelo siano molto ale strete per unirsi con mons. di Guisa, il che causaria magiore sospeto nel animo del Re. Io non manco di fare tuti quelli ofici che io poso per leuare le difidentie et per introdure una buona et sincera unione, ala quale seruiria asai se il negotio dela amicitia di Spagna, che ho deta di [?sopra], sortirà quel bono efeto che si aspeta […] N. S. […] questo […] [f. 199r] […] l'ambasciatore di Spagna fu auanti hieri al'audientia da questa Maiestà et ala Regina Madre. Dise che, hauendogliela più uolte fata molta instanza di adoprarsi per introdure una buona inteligenza et unione fra il suo et questo Re, et considerando che ela, esendo madre de l'uno et del altro et già carica d'anni, non proponeria cosa simile quando non uenise dal cuore et con sincerità d'animo, si era moso a scriuerne al suo Re et rapresentargli molte uiue ragioni, per le quali non solo doueua dare d'orechio a questa proposta, ma anco desiderare grandem[ente] di condurla a fine […]; in [?risposta] haueua hauto che il Re di Spagna lodaua estremam[ente] la [?buona] intentione di esa Regina et la pregaua di condure inanzi questa pratica, oferendosi lui di non scordarsi prima tute le male sodisfationi che sino a qui gli erano state date; et per comprobatione di questo ha dato copia ala sodeta Regina dela medesma lettera che gli scriue il suo Re, la quale io ho ueduta et leta, et ne mando copia con questa in lingua […]. Pare a me che si camini in modo che molto facilm[ente] potria sucedere questa amicitia. L'ambasciatore, con tuto che fose meco asai longam[ente] prima che andase al'audientia, et che io molte uolte [f. 199v] habia tratato seco di questa unione, come ho scrito già a V. S. Ill.ma, non me ne ha però [?fato] il secretario moto alcuno; anzi pare che non uoglia usare il mezo d'altri, che a me leuarà la fatica et il trauaglio. Con tuto ciò spero di douere sapere di tempo in tempo tuto quello che si tratarà, et ne darò auiso a V. S. Ill.ma. Quello che fuori dela lettera è, che per parte di Spagna si desidera la restitutione di Cambrai, et in quello cambio procurare con i [?resti] […] armata, che dice esere capitata in Spagna, et con qualche aiuto che di qui si potrà hauere di gente, di metere la Rocela in mano del Re; il che spera che si posi molto [pr]esto et facile fare. Di più, che si aiuti Spagna nele cose di Fiandra con modi asai facili ala Francia et senza spesa; et per conuerso, che ela aiutarà S. M.tà per caciare tuti li heretici di Francia et farlo ubidire da' suoi uasali, dicendo […] che quando S. M.tà haurà pensiero d'ampliare i termini del suo regno, che la aiutarà ad impadronirsi per sino […], et al incontro […] ela si[a] aiutata nel'impresa d'Inghilterra. In conclusione parmi che sino a qui non ci sia cosa di pregiudicio ad alcun principe catolico, anzi di molto auantagio dela santa Sede apostolica, et che si posi sperare buona [f. 200r] risolutione di questo importantisimo negotio. Sarà bene che sia tenuto secretisimo, per quei rispeti che posono esere considerati dala singolare prudentia di V. S. Ill.ma, nel quale non uoglio però restare di dirle che il uedere che, esendo stato introdoto da N. S. questo negotio et procurato qui da me con grandisimo afeto, sia […] hora tratato senza alcuna participatione di N. S. né mia, mi genera qualche sospeto, che mi farà andare più auertito per poterne auisare V. S. Ill.ma. Con tuto ciò, in quello che io potrò, senza però mescolarmi più intrinsicam[ente] di quello che sarò ricercato, non mancarò di coadiuare la buona conclusione del negotio, credendo che habia ad esere di seruitio dela religione catolica et grande instromento per l'istirpatione del heresie. Il sodeto ambasciatore di Spagna ha ragionato meco dele cose del marchesato di Saluzo, biasimando asai il sig. duca di Sauoia di hauere fato questo moto, asicurandomi che né il suo Re né alcuno de' suoi ministri non ne sono stati né consentienti né partecipi. Il medesmo parmi che habia deto ale loro Maie[f. 200v]stà, che tutauia sentono uiuam[ente] questo fato et solecitano la partita del sig. Hieronimo Gondi, che potria esere per lunedì prosimo, il quale uenirà diritam[ente] a Roma per fare oficio con N. S., non solo le cose di Saluzo ma anco per la riconciliatione di Momoransi et per il grado di cardinale per l'arciuescouo di Lione, […] del qual sig. Gondi ho già scrito a V. S. Ill.ma quanto meriti la buona gratia di N. S. et di V. S. Ill.ma, perché in ogni tempo si è dimostrato deuotisimo di cotesta santa Sede et dela particolare casa di V. S. Ill.ma; et io deuo pregarla per seruitio di santa Chiesa ad acarezarlo et mostrarle di sapere la sua buona uolontà et i continoui seruici che ha sempre fato et fa a' ministri di N. S., a fine che tanto più si confermi nel auenire di fare il medesmo. Le cose di qui, con tuto che uadino continuando nela pace et unione fra S. M.tà et il duca di Guisa, nondimeno nasce speso nuoui ocasioni per intorbidare, come hora, che hauendo S. Translation R34_en.md # R34 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Blois, November 1588]: Mendoza's offer of a Franco-Spanish union; Saluzzo; Gondi; Orléans) Translation of `R34_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 198r] […] their […], [and] by His Majesty it was felt with very great displeasure, as he knows very well the cause of this move. It is also held for certain that Monsieur d'Épernon and La Valette his brother are in close dealings to unite with Monsieur de Guise, which would cause greater suspicion in the King's mind. I do not fail to do all the offices I can to remove mistrust and to bring in a good and sincere union, which would be much helped if the business of friendship with Spain, of which I spoke [above], has the good effect that is expected […] Our Lord […] this […] [f. 199r] […] the ambassador of Spain was at audience the day before yesterday with His Majesty and with the Queen Mother. She said that, he having many times pressed her to work to bring about good understanding and union between his King and this one, and considering that she, being mother of the one and of the other and already laden with years, would not propose such a thing unless it came from the heart and in sincerity of mind, he had been moved to write of it to his King and to put before him many strong reasons why he should not only lend an ear to this proposal but also greatly desire to bring it to an end […]; in [answer] he had had that the King of Spain praised highly the [good] intention of the said Queen and begged her to carry this negotiation forward, offering for his part not to remember first all the ill satisfactions that had been given him until now; and in proof of this he has given the said Queen a copy of the very letter his King writes to him, which I have seen and read, and I send a copy of it with this in […] language. It seems to me that things are going in such a way that this friendship could very easily come about. The ambassador, although he was with me quite a long time before he went to the audience, and although I have often [f. 199v] treated with him of this union, as I have already written to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, has [made] me no sign of it at all; rather it seems he does not want to use anyone else's mediation, which will spare me the effort and the trouble. Even so I hope to learn from time to time all that will be treated, and I shall send word of it to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. What there is beyond the letter is that on Spain's part the restitution of Cambrai is desired, and in exchange to try, with the [remains] […] armada, which he says has reached Spain, and with some help of men that can be had from here, to put La Rochelle into the King's hands, which he hopes can be done very [soon] and easily. Further, that Spain be helped in the affairs of Flanders by means very easy for France and without expense; and conversely, that she will help His Majesty to drive all the heretics out of France and make him obeyed by his vassals, saying […] that when His Majesty thinks of enlarging the bounds of his kingdom she will help him to make himself master even of […], and in return […] she be helped in the enterprise of England. In conclusion it seems to me that so far there is nothing prejudicial to any Catholic prince, but rather much to the advantage of the Holy Apostolic See, and that a good [f. 200r] resolution of this most important business can be hoped for. It will be well to keep it most secret, for the reasons that the singular prudence of Your Most Illustrious Lordship can consider; in which I will not fail to tell you that to see that, this business having been introduced by Our Lord and pursued here by me with very great zeal, it is […] now treated without any participation of Our Lord or of me, gives me some suspicion, which will make me more watchful so as to be able to inform Your Most Illustrious Lordship. Even so, as far as I can, without however mixing in more intimately than I am asked, I shall not fail to assist the good conclusion of the business, believing it will serve the Catholic religion and be a great instrument for the extirpation of heresy. The said ambassador of Spain has spoken with me about the affairs of the marquisate of Saluzzo, much blaming the Duke of Savoy for having made this move, and assuring me that neither his King nor any of his ministers consented to it or had a part in it. The same, it seems to me, he told Their Majesties, [f. 200v] who still feel this deed keenly and are pressing the departure of Signor Girolamo Gondi, which could be next Monday. He will come straight to Rome to do office with Our Lord, not only about the affairs of Saluzzo but also for the reconciliation of Montmorency and for the rank of cardinal for the Archbishop of Lyon […]. Of this Signor Gondi I have already written to Your Most Illustrious Lordship how much he deserves the good grace of Our Lord and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship, since he has always shown himself most devoted to that Holy See and to Your Most Illustrious Lordship's own house; and I must beg you, for the service of Holy Church, to make much of him and to show him that you know his good will and the continual services he has always done and does to Our Lord's ministers, so that he may be the more confirmed in doing the same in future. Things here, although they go on continuing in peace and union between His Majesty and the Duke of Guise, nonetheless new occasions for trouble often arise, as now: His Majesty having drawn the governor of Orléans to his side, these others have stirred up the people and had ambassadors of the city come to demand that the citadel be put into the hands […] R35, Francia 22/14, n.d. read in part Copy, in Spanish, of a memorandum ("scritura") the Spanish ambassador gave the Queen Mother: Philip II answers her wish to see the two crowns in close friendship and good understanding, praises it as worthy of the mother of two kings, and urges union against the heretics. Not a letter of Philip II (the Italian heading in cipher says so). Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (92% here); the holes are marked in the reading. Translation R35_en.md # R35 — English (copy of a memorandum given to the Queen Mother by the Spanish ambassador; Spanish, with an Italian heading) Translation of `R35_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 202r] […] Copy of a paper given to the Queen Mother by the ambassador […] of the King of Spain resident at the court of France; the said paper is in the Spanish language. […] What I said to Her Most Christian Majesty the Queen Mother on behalf of the King my lord, in answer to what [she?] ordered to be written to him, from hers, concerning the desire to see these two crowns in a very close friendship and good understanding, is as [follows]: the King my lord cannot fail to praise and esteem highly the desire of [Her] Most Christian Majesty, exhorting the two crowns to greater union and friendship, a thing well worthy of one who is mother of the two Kings; and that, besides the past proofs, in which by deeds were seen the assistance and aid that the King my lord gave to this crown, and the love and plainness with which he did it, this now […] more disposed to draw closer than ever, [inasmuch as] he knows better that, these two powers together, no one is enough to provoke them, and that they can settle public and private affairs to the great service of God and their own entire security. [f. 202v] But, to speak with the plainness that the troubled state of Christendom's affairs demands, it would not be fitting that these talks should end in fine words and in [private] ends, which make no lasting union nor sure [correspondence], but that, seeing that the vigour of human forces depends on the power of God, and that if […] enemies the heretics […] the two crowns, and have taken the pretext and colour of religion to […], they settle their discords in their erring opinions, their own malice […] in the outward designs, and that it is not the private business of each of the two provinces in which it is spreading but common and general to all Christendom, […] to this fire, if it come to […] or be, since one already touches with the hand that, when for the honour of God, which is the greatest obligation and must be the principal aim, [they] did not move for […], the interest of each one ought to [set aside] for […] very earnestly [f. 203r] to this, in which so much is at stake for both; and the King my lord offers to Their Most Christian Majesties that, if what is said to him to go forward on this footing, dismissing all distrust and removing its cause, and both taking as their target the service and glory of God and that of the Catholic cause and the obedience of the Roman church, on which depend the entire obedience and security of their states together, and if the two Kings answer in deed to the name and [attributes] by which they are styled, and […] inherited, then in that case, the King my lord forgetting [other] […] that he could remember, […] wishes to set it aside; His Most Christian Majesty will find him so good a friend and brother, and so ready to draw close and become one and the same thing with him, as […] Our Lord […] R36, Francia 22/15, 10 Nov [1588] (duplicate) A fever kept Morosini indoors. The Savoy ambassador reported the Poigny talks to the Queen Mother: the Duke will not return the Saluzzo places, and claims to have acted by the Pope's order (Carmagnola). Ill.ma c'haueuo pensiero di fare qualche oficio oltre quello che prima haueuo fato con le loro Maestà per le cose di Saluzo; ma quella sera medesima mi soprauene una gran febre, la quale, ancorché sia riuscita una efimera, mi ha nondimeno leuata la comodità di poter sino a questa hora uscire di casa. Et in questo mentre è capitato […] l'ambasciatore del sig. duca di Sauoia, con auiso di quello che mons. di Pugni haueua tratato con quella Alt[ezza] et di certo acordo fato per le cose di [?Rouen]; per il che, hauendo il sodeto ambasciatore dimandata audientia ale loro Maestà, non hauendo potuta otenere dal Re per altre sue ocupationi, è stato hogi dala Regina Madre, ala quale ha dato conto di tuto quello che è pasato fra il duca suo et il sodeto mons. di Pugni: che [?la] conclusione era che sua Alte[zza] non poteua lasare di non leuare di mano dei dipendenti dela Ualeta quello che restaua del marchesato di Saluzo, non uolendo hauere per uicini quelli che già si era dechiarato inimico, et che non poteua manco per molti suoi rispeti restituire a eso Pugni quelle piaze, dicendo che, per hauere egli due frateli heretici, non se ne poteua fidare; di che è [f. 249v] [?rimasta] malisimo sodisfata esa Regina. L'ambasciatore sodeto, partito da[l]a Regina Madre, è uenuto da me et m'ha portata una lettera di sua Alt[ezza], dela quale le mando in questa copia a V. S. Ill.ma, et in conformità di quello che ha riferto a la Regina ha anco dato conto a me del medesmo. Onde può ben pensare V. S. Ill.ma in che pensieri m'habia posto questo […] di sua Alt[ezza], poiché mi dice che tuto quello che ha fato è di ordine di N. S.; et lei ha benisimo quanto m'ha scrito in questo proposito, hauendomi mandata copia dela lettera scritale da sua Alt[ezza] sopra la presa di Carmagnola, dala quale chiaram[ente] si arguisce il contrario; et però io ho sempre gagliardam[ente] sostenuto che in ciò N. S. non haueua parte alcuna, tocando con mano che nisuna cosa può esere di magiore pregiuditio in questo regno a cotesta santa sede che 'l lasare imprimere nei popoli […] che di ordine di N. S., come questi andauano diseminando, il duca di Sauoia […] haueua fata quella impresa, perché era un rendere odiosisimo N. S. non solo a S. M.tà ma anco a tuta la […], hauendo tuti tre i Stati, come con altre mie ho scrito a V. S. Ill.ma, ecitato il Re et oferto gli grandisimi aiuti per [f. 250r] uendicarsi contra eso duca, nominandolo ingrato, pergiuro et fautore di heretici. Onde pare a me più che necesario l'andare sganando ognuno et asicurare S. M.tà che N. S., come padre comune, procurarà sempre la pace et unione fra principi catolici, né sarà mai consentiente che l'uno leui lo stato a l'altro, anzi che con tuta la sua autorità procurarà che ognuno si contenti del suo; […] termini […] qui mi sono gouernato, et continouarò nel'auenire, se altro in contrario non mi comandarà V. S. Ill.ma; ala quale non uoglio lasare di dire che se bene io non mancarò di fare ogni oficio perché non si uenga al'armi, temo di potere fare poco fruto, uedendo gli animi arabiati […] da tute le parti, et il Re asai risoluto, hauendomi deto di uolere più presto perdere tuto quello che ha al mondo et la uita stesa che soportare questa ingiuria. So anco che S. M.tà è solecitata da alcuni […], et che molti […] stimano che la salute del proprio regno sarebe il fare la guerra con forestieri; gli altri […] altro non bramano, poiché questa saria la loro intiera salute. Onde, se al sig. Dio non piace di amorzare questo [f. 250v] fuoco, io temo che ne posano sucedere dani importantisimi ala christianità, con detrimento irreparabile dela religione catolica. Ho uoluto dire tuto ciò a V. S. Ill.ma, pregandola a darmi lume del modo con che parerà a N. S. che io mi habia a gouernare; agiongendole che il sodeto ambasciatore di Sauoia mi ha deto che, se bene crede che il sig. duca suo si contentarà che il gouerno del marchesato sia dato a mons. di Nemurs, nondimeno [?uorrà] altre conditioni, et del luogotenente, et altre simili, che non harano mai acetate. Translation R36_en.md # R36 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 10 November 1588, duplicate: Poigny's mission fails) Translation of `R36_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 249r] […] with my last letters I wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship that I intended to make some further representation, beyond what I had already made to Their Majesties, about the affairs of Saluzzo; but that very evening a high fever came upon me, which, although it turned out to be an ephemeral one, has nevertheless taken from me the means of leaving the house until this hour. Meanwhile the ambassador of the Duke of Savoy has arrived […], with news of what Monsieur de Poigny had negotiated with His Highness and of a certain accord made about the affairs of [Rouen?]; whereupon the said ambassador, having asked audience of Their Majesties and not having been able to obtain it from the King because of his other occupations, went today to the Queen Mother, to whom he gave an account of all that passed between his Duke and the said Monsieur de Poigny: [the] conclusion was that His Highness could not refrain from taking out of the hands of La Valette's dependants what remained of the marquisate of Saluzzo, not wishing to have as neighbours men who had already declared themselves his enemies, and that for many reasons of his own he could not restore those places to Poigny either, saying that since Poigny has two heretic brothers he could not trust him; with which the Queen [f. 249v] was very ill satisfied. The said ambassador, after leaving the Queen Mother, came to me and brought me a letter of His Highness, of which I send a copy herewith to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, and in conformity with what he reported to the Queen he also gave me an account of the same. So Your Lordship can well imagine into what thoughts this […] of His Highness has put me, since he tells me that all he has done is by order of Our Lord; and you have very well what you wrote to me on this subject, having sent me a copy of the letter His Highness wrote to you on the taking of Carmagnola, from which the contrary is clearly inferred; and so I have always vigorously maintained that Our Lord had no part in it, seeing plainly that nothing could be more prejudicial in this kingdom to that Holy See than to let it be impressed on the people […] that the Duke of Savoy had made that enterprise by Our Lord's order, as these men were spreading abroad, since that made Our Lord most odious not only to His Majesty but to the whole […], all three Estates (as I wrote to Your Lordship in other letters) having stirred up the King and offered him very great aid to [f. 250r] avenge himself on the said Duke, calling him ingrate, perjurer and abettor of heretics. So it seems to me more than necessary to go on undeceiving everyone and to assure His Majesty that Our Lord, as common father, will always procure peace and union among Catholic princes, and will never consent that one take another's state, but rather will procure with all his authority that each be content with his own; […] terms […] I have governed myself so far, and will continue in future, unless Your Most Illustrious Lordship commands me otherwise; to whom I will not fail to say that although I shall not fail to do every office so that it does not come to arms, I fear I can do little good, seeing minds enraged […] on all sides, and the King very resolute, having told me he would sooner lose all he has in the world and his very life than endure this injury. I also know that His Majesty is being urged by some […], and that many […] think the salvation of the kingdom would be to make war on foreigners; the others […] want nothing else, since that would be their complete salvation. So, if the Lord God does not please to put out this [f. 250v] fire, I fear that very grave harm may follow for Christendom, with irreparable detriment to the Catholic religion. I wanted to tell Your Lordship all this, begging you to give me light on the way in which it will please Our Lord that I govern myself; adding that the said ambassador of Savoy told me that, although he believes his Duke will be content that the government of the marquisate be given to Monsieur de Nemours, he will nevertheless [want] other conditions, about the lieutenant and other such things, which they will never accept. […] R37, Francia 22/16, 21 Nov [1588] (duplicate) Morosini urged the King and Queen Mother to settle Saluzzo peacefully. The Savoy ambassador had offered to restore the places if they were given to a Catholic knight, with Nemours as governor. Guise advised force instead, sending Mayenne into Bresse. M.tà si contentase di meterle in mano di caualiere catolico et del quale Sua Al[tezza] non hauese a temere di mala uicinanza; che, se la S. M.tà continouaua ne la resolutione presa di dare quello gouerno a mons. di Nemurs, che è così streto parente del duca di Sauoia et del quale non si può dubitare che non sia catolico, mi pareua che si douese lasare intendere, perché il sodeto ambasciatore haueua deto a me che teniua per certo che di lui Sua Al[tezza] si saria contentata, con che si meteria fine a questo fastidio, si […] negotio senza spargimento di sangue fra catolici. La Regina Madre fu la prima a rispondere, et dise al Re che in efeto l'ambasciatore haueua deto il medesmo anco a lei, et che le pareua buono il mio consiglio; et uoltandosi [f. 256v] uerso di me dise che il duca di Guisa consigliaua il contrario, dicendo che non ci era la riputatione del Re a tratare, come per uia di compositione, di farsi restituire il suo; che bisognaua atendere ad ingrosare le forze al duca di Umena et stare a uedere la risposta che darà il duca di Sauoia a mons. di Pugni, per farsi poi da sé steso la ragione, mostrando che con grandisima facilità si poteua in pochi giorni leuare a quello duca la Bresa et la Sauoia. Il Re, dopo esere stato un poco pensoso, dise che stimaua da cardinale il mio parere, che lo uoleua esequire, perché quando poi il duca di Sauoia non uorrà rimetere quelle piaze, sarà tanto più conosciuta la sua mala uolontà. Io le disi che non bastaua nominare il gouernatore, perché non si poteua obligarlo a [?…] in Piemonte, ma che era necesario che la S. M.tà nominase anco il luogotenente che si doueua tratenire nel marchesato, del quale eso duca faria forsi più caso che del gouernatore; et che perciò la S. M.tà sciegliese un gentilhuomo dabene catolico et del quale così esa come S[ua] Alt[ezza] potesero confidarsi, perché di questa maniera giustificaria così bene le sue ationi che non ci saria più che dire in contrario. Lodarono le loro maestà anco questa proposta, dicendo che [?ui] [f. 257r] pensariano, poiché sino a quest'hora non l'haueuano fato; et mi partii con risolutione che hogi si spediria un corriere a mons. di Pugni con queste particolari sopra questo negotio. Oltre quello che ho scrito li giorni pasati a V. S. Ill.ma, mi ocore dirle che qui si [è] deto che l'ambasciatore del Re di Spagna residente a questa corte si è doluto con quello di Sauoia perché habia deto che il Re suo padrone aiutaria in questa atione il duca suo; et però il sig. cardinale Gondi m'ha rifer[i]to che, ragionando seco l'ambasciatore di Sauoia, gli dise che al suo padrone non mancariano aiuti se bene non hauese quelli del Re di Spagna; l'ambasciatore del quale publicam[ente] biasima questa atione di Saluzo, asicurando ognuno che non è stato di consenso del suo Re, né meno d'alcuno dei suoi ministri in Italia. Il che mi fa tanto più credere che non sia bene il permetere che si dica questa esere seguito di ordine di N. S., perché in efeto renderia a tuta la Francia odiosa la persona di N. S.; né si può sperare per qualsiuoglia sorte di ofici di rimouere S. M.tà et tuto il regno insieme dala ferma risolutione di fare la guerra al sodeto sig. duca se non restituise il marchesato, come V. S. Ill.ma haurà più chiaram[ente] inteso dal sig. Hieronimo Gondi, che partì di qui a li 17 del presente, non si hauendo potuto spedire prima. Il che seruirà [f. 257v] per hora di risposta anco a quel capo dela sua cifra uenuta con le lettere del ultimo del pasato, doue trata dele cose di Saluzo, ala quale, per breuità di tempo, incalciandomi la partita del ordinario, non poso più particolarm[ente] rispondere; ma con la prima ocasione non lasciarò di farlo in quelle parti che ne haurano bisogno. Translation R37_en.md # R37 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [21 November 1588]: Saluzzo, the King and the Duke of Guise) Translation of `R37_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 256r] […] yesterday morning, finding myself with Their Majesties, […] I made the representation I had planned about the affairs of Saluzzo, urging them to proceed in this business with moderation and not let themselves be carried away by passion; and that it seemed to me a way would easily be found to settle everything, if what I had heard from the ambassador of the Lord Duke of Savoy was true: that the day before he had clearly told the Queen Mother that his master would promptly have restored all the places he held of the marquisate of Saluzzo, if His Majesty were content to put them in the hands of a Catholic knight from whom His Highness need not fear bad neighbourliness; that, if His Majesty held to the resolution taken to give that government to Monsieur de Nemours, who is so close a relative of the Duke of Savoy and of whose Catholicism there can be no doubt, it seemed to me he should let this be known, because the said ambassador had told me he held it for certain that His Highness would be content with him, which would put an end to this trouble, […] the business without shedding of blood among Catholics. The Queen Mother was the first to answer, and told the King that in fact the ambassador had said the same to her too, and that my advice seemed good to her; and turning [f. 256v] towards me she said that the Duke of Guise advised the contrary, saying that it was not for the King's reputation to negotiate, as if by way of a settlement, to have his own restored to him; that they must attend to strengthening the forces of the Duke of Mayenne and wait to see the answer the Duke of Savoy will give Monsieur de Poigny, so as afterwards to do himself justice, showing that with the greatest ease Bresse and Savoy could be taken from that duke in a few days. The King, after being thoughtful for a while, said that he valued my opinion as a cardinal's, and that he wanted to follow it, because when the Duke of Savoy then refuses to give back those places, his ill will will be all the better known. I told him that it was not enough to name the governor, because he could not be obliged to [?…] in Piedmont, but that His Majesty must also name the lieutenant who was to be kept in the marquisate, of whom the said duke would perhaps take more account than of the governor; and that therefore His Majesty should choose a worthy Catholic gentleman whom both he and His Highness could trust, because in this way he would justify his actions so well that nothing more could be said against them. Their Majesties praised this proposal too, saying that they [would] [f. 257r] think about it, since until now they had not done so; and I left with the resolution that a courier would be sent today to Monsieur de Poigny with these particulars on this business. Besides what I wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship in the past days, I have to tell you that it is said here that the ambassador of the King of Spain resident at this court has complained to the Savoy ambassador because he said that the King his master would help his duke in this action; and so the Lord Cardinal Gondi has reported to me that the Savoy ambassador, talking with him, told him that his master would not lack help even if he did not have that of the King of Spain; whose ambassador publicly blames this action over Saluzzo, assuring everyone that it was not done with the consent of his King, nor of any of his ministers in Italy. This makes me all the more believe that it is not good to allow it to be said that this was done by order of His Holiness, because in effect it would make the person of His Holiness hateful to all France; nor can one hope, by any sort of offices, to move His Majesty and the whole kingdom together from the firm resolution to make war on the said lord duke if he does not restore the marquisate, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship will have heard more clearly from Signor Girolamo Gondi, who left here on the 17th of this month, it not having been possible to send him off earlier. This will [f. 257v] serve for now as an answer also to that section of your cipher, which came with the letters of the last of last month, where you deal with the affairs of Saluzzo; to which, for shortness of time, the departure of the ordinary post pressing me, I cannot answer more in detail; but at the first opportunity I shall not fail to do so in those parts that need it. […] R38, Francia 22/17, n.d. [late Nov-Dec 1588] The Savoy ambassador complained that Mayenne was ordered into Bresse. Morosini urged the King not to start a war before trying every other way, and to fight the heretics first. The King said he gave Mayenne no such order, but called the Duke of Savoy ungrateful. M.tà asai lo[n]gam[ente], et perché il giorno inanzi l'ambasciatore del sig. duca di Sauoia m'haueua de[t]to d'esere auertito per cosa certa che S. M.tà haueua spedito al duca d'Umena che con le sue forze entrase nela Bresa et […] a' dani del suo padrone, di che mi dise hauer[…] auisato in diligenza S. Alteza, parue a me di fare ogni eficace oficio con S. M.tà, esortandola a non uolere principiare una guerra se prima non hauese tenta[t]o ogn'altra uia per ricuperare il suo, ricordandole che quelli che la persuadeuano a muouere l'armi non procurauano altro che di tenerla sempre ocupata, perché non posa mai farsi ubidire nel suo regno; et però saria molto meglio che la S. M.tà procurase prima l'istirpatione deli heretici, perché quando atenderà a questo N. S. a sue spese le farà poi restituire il marchesato di Saluzo, esendo credibile che'l duca di Sauoia habia prese quelle piaze con intentione di leuarle a la corona di Francia, con la quale sa di non potere contendere, ma a fine che non rientrase […] a' dani suoi et d'Italia; et che per ciò la S. M.tà non doueua pigliare alteratione, anzi più presto, come suo parente et seruitore, [?] ualersi di lui, et che N. S. operarà che lo seruir[à] bene; et uolendo sicureza, che N. S. si sforzarà con l'armi spirituali et temporali di asicurarla. Mi rispose S. M.tà che non haueua dato ordine alcuno al duca d'Umena, perché queste erano [f. 282v] inuentioni del ambasciatore [di] Sauoia, che staua aspetando la risposta che le sarà fata sopra la proposta di metere al gouerno del marchesato mons. di Nemurs; il che quando il duca di Sauoia non uogli acetare, farà chiaram[ente] conoscere a tuti la sua mala uolontà; che di fare la guerra a gl'Ugonotti et procurare di caciargli totalm[ente] dal suo regno ela n'era più che risoluta, ma che di contentarsi di lasciare i suoi stati in mano d'altri non credeua che alcuno la douese consigliare, et che sapeua certo che se N. S. fose nel suo loco non lo comportaria mai; che a lei non mancaua [?] né al suo regno [?] di farsi la ragione, quando pure la necesità lo sforzarà a pigliar l'armi, et che la giustitia [è] dal canto suo, perché N. S., per il loco che tiene, non potrà mancare di fauorire la sua causa. In che si distese asai, mostrando qualche dispiacere, se bene con modestisime parole, che N. S. non solo non facese quello risentimento che parea a la S. M.tà che conueniria contra il sodeto duca, ma che più presto se gli mostri fauoreuole, dicendo che, se il duca di Sauoia ha così buono zelo contra gl'Ugonotti come [?] uol dare ad intendere, che deuria caciarli prima de' suoi stati, et che nondimeno li comporta […], perché in Italia molte liberam[ente] et publicam[ente] predicano et [e]sercitano il Caluinisimo. [f. 283r] Io non lasciai di rispondere ala S. M.tà in conformità di quello mi comete V. S. Ill.ma nela sua cifra di […] del pasato, pregandola, dopo molte parole, a non uoler credere che N. S. mai [?] più il duca di Sauoia che lei, [et] io poteuo asicurarla che la mente di N. S. non potria esere migliore di quello che è uerso S. M.tà et tuto questo regno, ma che come [p]adre comune et uicario di Christo, hauendo ri[g]uardo al ben uniuersale, esortaua S. M.tà a fare più tosto la guerra a gl'heretici che a li catolici, et che il medesmo oficio doueua esere certa che N. S. facese anco con il duca di Sauoia. Ma per cosa che io dicesi mostrò di non restare sodisfata, parendole quasi che io hauese deto tropo. Con tuto ciò mi comunicò l'uficio […] che il Re di Spagna haueua fato seco in questo proposito, del quale io ne fui anco auertito dal medesmo ambasciatore, et paso in questa sostanza: che se bene le ationi pasate del Re di Spagna, et particolarm[ente] la [c]ontinoua uigilanza che ela haueua sempre hauta di mantenere la buona amicitia con S. M.tà et di conseruare la pace in Italia, poteuano esere certi inditii che le cose sucese nel marchesato di Saluzo non fosero seguite né con consiglio né con saputa sua, nondimeno ela anco in parola di principe afermaua di non hauerne [?hauta] parte [f. 283v] alcuna; anzi, subito intesa la nuoua, haueua spedito un suo consigliere a[l] sodeto sig. duca di Sauoia per […] da lui […] la causa che lo haueua moso a questo efeto, con intentione, quando non uolese caminare per la [?uia] dela r[a]gione, di persuader[lo] ad abraciarla; et che dela risposta che daria Sua Alteza ne daria conto a S. M.tà, oferendosi d'interporre l'autorità sua per ridure il suo genero nele cose dela ragione. Che ha risposto S. M.tà, et si asicuraua che fose uero tuto quello che l'ambasciatore per nome del suo Re gli diceua, et che lo ringratiaua asai, agiungendo che gli sarano carisimi tuti quelli ofici che sarano fati [?con] il duca di Sauoia perché si risolua di restituirgli il suo, desiderand[o] molto che questo più tosto habia da seguire per uia di pace, [con]seruando l'amore, che di esere astreto di procurarlo d'altra maniera. La qual risposta ha mandata S. M.tà al sodeto ambasciatore per [un] suo secretario di stato per […] di qua, uilagio discosto tre leghe da qui, doue alogiano gli ambasciatori, et si sta aspetando se [?] uorrà replicare altro. In questa audienza feci […] quello che V. S. Ill.ma mi scriue intorno ala legatione d'Auignone per il sig. cardinale di Guisa, il quale uene poi [f. 284r] a ritrouarmi a casa et mi dimandò i particolari dele lettere di V. S. Ill.ma in questo proposito; al quale disi quello che mi parue necesario, et specialm[ente] che bisognaua giurare di mantenere quella legatione secondo l'obligo conuenuto con la santità di Pio quarto; et per questo rispeto mi ha deto sua signoria Il[l].ma che faria scriuere al Re, facendo lei ancora il medesmo, spedendo poi un corriere [?steso] per dare a N. S. tuta […] [?sodisfatione] che desideraua in questa parte. Ho fato ogni instanza a S. M.tà perché sia riuocata la sentenza data dal parlamento di Renes contra l'indulto del sig. cardinale Lenoncort, et che posi sua signoria Ill.ma esercitare il carico impostogli da N. S.; la quale mi ha promeso di ricordarlo al guarda sigilo, per uedere se era uenuta la risposta di eso parlamento, al quale si era scrito che douese rendere le ragioni che l'haueua moso a fare quella sentenza. Et io non mancarò di fare et solecitare quello più che potrò in seruitio di sua signoria Ill.ma, la quale da alcuni giorni in qua si è partita di corte et ritirata [a] casa sua, dicendosi che l'habi fato per mala sodisfatione, uedendosi odiata da mons. di Guisa [f. 284v] et manco fauorita dal[a] M.tà di quello che prima soleua esere. Hora ho inteso che S. M.tà è stato longam[ente] in consiglio sopra le cose del marchesato di Saluzo, et che in efeto sono a torno a fare prouisioni per la guerra, quando pure il duca di Sauoia continoui nela risolutione di uolere tenire quelle piaze. [Blois, late November – December 1588], duplicate: Savoy, Saluzzo and Mayenne; Lenoncourt; the Avignon legation) Translation of `R38_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 282r] […] I was with His Majesty at great length the day before yesterday; and because the day before the ambassador of the Duke of Savoy had told me he had been informed as a certain thing that His Majesty had sent word to the Duke of Mayenne to enter Bresse with his forces and […] to the harm of his master, of which he said he had informed His Highness in haste, it seemed to me right to do every effective office with His Majesty, urging him not to begin a war before he had tried every other way to recover what was his, reminding him that those who were persuading him to take up arms sought nothing else than to keep him always occupied, so that he could never make himself obeyed in his kingdom; and that it would therefore be much better for His Majesty to work first for the extirpation of the heretics, because when he attends to this, Our Lord will at his own expense have the marquisate of Saluzzo restored to him — it being credible that the Duke of Savoy took those places with the intention of taking them from the crown of France, with which he knows he cannot contend, but so that [they] should not come back […] to his own harm and Italy's; and that therefore His Majesty ought not to take offence, but rather, as his kinsman and servant, [to] make use of him, and that Our Lord would see to it that he serves him well; and, wanting security, that Our Lord would strive with spiritual and temporal arms to assure it to him. His Majesty answered me that he had given no order to the Duke of Mayenne, for these were [f. 282v] inventions of the ambassador of Savoy, who was waiting for the answer to be given him on the proposal to put Monsieur de Nemours in the government of the marquisate; which, if the Duke of Savoy would not accept it, would make his ill will plain to all; that he was more than resolved to make war on the Huguenots and to drive them entirely out of his kingdom, but that he did not believe anyone would advise him to be content to leave his states in other men's hands, and that he knew for certain that if Our Lord were in his place he would never tolerate it; that he and his kingdom did not lack [the means] to obtain justice, should necessity force him to take up arms, and that justice was on his side, because Our Lord, by the place he holds, could not fail to favour his cause. On this he spoke at length, showing some displeasure, though in very moderate words, that Our Lord not only did not show the resentment that His Majesty thought fitting against the said Duke, but rather showed himself favourable to him; saying that if the Duke of Savoy had such good zeal against the Huguenots as he [would] have it believed, he ought first to drive them out of his own states, and that he nevertheless tolerates them […], for in Italy many freely and publicly preach and practise Calvinism. [f. 283r] I did not fail to answer His Majesty in conformity with what Your Most Illustrious Lordship charges me in your cipher of […] of last month, begging him, after many words, not to believe that Our Lord ever [?] the Duke of Savoy more than him; [and] I could assure him that Our Lord's mind could not be better than it is towards His Majesty and this whole kingdom, but that as common father and Vicar of Christ, having regard to the universal good, he urged His Majesty to make war on the heretics rather than on the Catholics, and that he should be certain that Our Lord was doing the same office with the Duke of Savoy too. But whatever I said, he showed himself not satisfied, as if he thought I had said too much. Nevertheless he told me of the office […] that the King of Spain had made with him on this matter, of which I was also informed by the same ambassador, and it ran in this substance: that although the past actions of the King of Spain, and in particular the constant vigilance he had always had to maintain good friendship with His Majesty and to preserve peace in Italy, could be sure signs that what happened in the marquisate of Saluzzo had not been done with his counsel or knowledge, he nevertheless affirmed on the word of a prince that he had [?had] no part [f. 283v] in it; on the contrary, as soon as he heard the news he had sent one of his counsellors to the said Duke of Savoy to [learn] from him […] the cause that had moved him to this act, with the intention, should he not be willing to proceed by the [?way] of reason, of persuading him to embrace it; and that he would give His Majesty an account of the answer His Highness would give, offering to interpose his authority to bring his son-in-law to reason. To which His Majesty answered that he was assured that all the ambassador told him in his King's name was true, and that he thanked him very much, adding that all the offices done [with] the Duke of Savoy to make him resolve to restore what was his would be most dear to him, as he much wished that this should come about rather by way of peace, preserving love, than that he should be forced to obtain it otherwise. His Majesty sent this answer to the said ambassador by [one of] his secretaries of state, to […], a village three leagues from here, where the ambassadors are lodged, and it is awaited whether he will reply anything further. In this audience I made […] what Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes to me about the legation of Avignon for the Cardinal of Guise, who then came [f. 284r] to see me at home and asked me the particulars of Your Most Illustrious Lordship's letters on this matter; I told him what seemed necessary to me, and especially that he would have to swear to maintain that legation according to the obligation agreed with His Holiness Pius IV; and on this account His Most Illustrious Lordship told me that he would have the King write, doing the same himself, and then send a courier [?] to give Our Lord all the […] [?satisfaction] he desired in this respect. I have pressed His Majesty in every way that the sentence given by the Parlement of Rennes against the indult of the Cardinal de Lenoncourt be revoked, and that His Most Illustrious Lordship may exercise the charge laid on him by Our Lord; he has promised me to remind the Keeper of the Seals of it, to see whether the answer of the said Parlement had come, which had been written to give the reasons that moved it to give that sentence. And I shall not fail to do and press it as much as I can in the service of His Most Illustrious Lordship, who for some days has left the court and withdrawn to his house, it being said that he did so out of dissatisfaction, seeing himself hated by Monsieur de Guise [f. 284v] and less favoured by His Majesty than he used to be. Now I have heard that His Majesty was a long time in council on the affairs of the marquisate of Saluzzo, and that in fact they are about making provision for war, should the Duke of Savoy persist in his resolve to keep those places. And Monsieur de Guise has told me that war will be made on Savoy; the King would have to make […] a truce with the Huguenots of Dauphiné, so as not to have enemies at his back and in front. And although I answered His [Excellency] that this should in no way be done […], that he saw no remedy […] Our Lord […]. R39, Francia 22/18, 8 Dec [1588] (duplicate) A courier from Turin came from Poigny. In the council, Guise insisted on war with Savoy even if Saluzzo were restored; the others would forgive the Duke if he gave the places back. Munitions and artillery are to be sent to Lyon. He also told me that, the council having discussed what was to be done in case the King of Spain chose to move in favour of the Duke of Savoy, the said Monsieur de Guise had maintained that that Majesty would not do it, [f. 289v] his own interest not allowing it; and that if he did declare himself, he would show His Majesty the very easy way to make him lose all the Low Countries within a few months, it being in his power to cut off the victuals and the supplies of men and money needed to hold those parts. I cannot know whether all these things are really true [that] are being said to frighten the Duke of Savoy, but I must not fail to report them to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, being things of such great importance and consequence; you will then weigh them as your singular prudence sees fit. As for me, I see quite manifest signs of war, and the preparations seem to me to go forward vigorously; yet it may be that my great wish that things should pass without arms makes me fear more than I should. News came here yesterday from Mâcon that the Duke of Savoy had had a good number of pieces of artillery brought from Montmélian to Bourg-en-Bresse, and that on the borders of [Savoy] and Bresse there were about eight thousand foot; whereupon His Majesty assembled his council, and, considering that His Highness must be making these preparations with some new design, after [long] discussion it was resolved to send at once to raise 15,000 Swiss [and] 8,000 Landsknechts with [Frech], and 1,500 reiter horse, and that all of them, with the greatest speed possible, join the other troops that are with the Duke of Mayenne; and orders have already been given to find the money for this need, which will not be much, since there is someone who offers to raise the cavalry without [?or with little] money; as the Duke of Guise has also offered His Majesty that Colonel Pfyffer will raise the Swiss for ten thousand scudi, and Monsieur de Bassompierre the Landsknechts [Frech]; and besides, the Estates say that tomorrow they will find 500,000 scudi, and the […] and the treasurers offer to give one million three hundred thousand scudi, [f. 293v] if the Estates will assure them that they will be repaid this and their other credits within four or five years. So it is clearly seen that this business cannot end without arms, to my very great grief, seeing the great disorder that must […] come of it — which God forbid. This morning I went to the Capuchin fathers in the hope of finding the King there, to renew with him (although he already holds me suspect in this business) my efforts to turn him from thoughts of war; but His Majesty did not come. […] I did find […] told her what I judged fitting for the general peace; but I have very well perceived that His Majesty has not been willing to open himself to me as he used to. I shall try to speak again with the King and do all in my power to bring him to the end Our Lord shows he desires; but I fear my counsels will be of little profit. Now it seems that with this resolution of the […] His Majesty has drawn very close to the Duke of Guise, and on this account it is believed that he has dismissed Monsieur de Cenagli, head of his finances, and the physician Miron, his [f. 294r] brother, for being little liked by the said Guise, although before they were among His Majesty's most intimate and trusted men. It is said too that he will do the same with Monsieur d'O and some others who have always shown themselves opposed to the said Monsieur de Guise. Of what follows I shall not fail to keep you informed. […] R41, Francia 22/20, n.d. [Blois, Dec 1588] The Duke of Savoy has seized the Marquisate of Saluzzo and offers to give it back once the Dauphiné is free of Huguenots, with his wife or a son as a hostage. The Duke of Guise tells Morosini he must press the King to recover Saluzzo by force, or else retire from court; the Savoyard ambassador has been refused. Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread. ## Reading [f. 298r] […] per lettere del sig. Hieronimo Gondi scrite a S. M.tà d[i] Siuiglia […] si è inteso che il sig. duca di Sauoia non hauea acetato il partito di metere mons. di Nemurs, suo cugino, nel marchesato di Saluzo; ma che sua Alt[ezza], persistendo di [?uolere] tenire quelle piaze in sua mano sino a tanto che il Delfinato fose libero da[gli] Ugonotti, oferiua per sicurtà di restituirle a quel tempo di mandare la moglie in Francia et di dare per hostagio un suo figliuolo; dele quali proposte sono rimasti qui malisimo sodisfati, et si atende ale prouisioni dela guerra, se bene non con quello uigore che da principio si uedeua, rispeto ale mali sodisfationi che tutauia si nutriscono fra S. M.tà et monsig. di Guisa, che impediscono asai ogn'altra risolutione; con tuto che in questo particolare sono molto d'acordo, anzi mons. di Guisa si mostra anco più ardente di S. M.tà, sapendo di guadagnare per questo magiore gratia apreso la nobiltà et popoli di Francia, che non posono aquietarsi di uedere che il duca di Sauoia habia uoluto atacare la guerra con questo regno. Et pure hieri matina, esendo stato longam[ente] meco eso mons. di Guisa, mi dise che per modo alcuno egli non può per honor suo lasare di far ogni sforzo per uendicare l'ingiuria che la Francia ha riceuta dal sig. duca di Sauoia, il quale [f. 298v] che di già incominciaua a riconoscere di hauere fata mala risolutione a rompersi con questa corona, poiché tuti i suoi popoli dela Bresa et dela Sauoia si oferiuano di aprire le porte dele tere a S. M.tà sempre che ui mandarà le sue forze; et che l'ambasciatore di quella Alteza l'haueua fato più uolte ricercare di audientia, et che gli hauea risposto che se uoleua tratare dela restitutione del marchesato lo ascoltaria, ma che d'altra maniera non haueua che fare seco; et con tuto ciò il sodeto ambasciatore haueua deto a madama di Nemurs sua madre che il duca suo sig. si contentarà di restituire tuto se sua Ecelenza gli uol prometere che, uenendo a morte il Re senza figlioli, lo farà ritornare in poseso di quello marchesato; et che lui non gli ha uoluto dare orechie. Io non lasai di considerargli il dano grande che riceueriano i catolici di Francia con questa guerra, et l'auantagio degli Ugonotti, con quello di più che mi parue a proposito; ma egli mi rispose che tuta questa era colpa del sig. duca di Sauoia, che soto pretesto di perseguitare gli heretici ueniua a fauorir[li], et che era una propositione masima nela profesione dela guerra et buono gouerno di un regno di mantenere sempre le frontiere, perché, conseruate quelle, era poi facile di rime- [f. 299r] -diare a que' disordini che sucedono nel corpo del regno; et che per conseruare lo suo stato et l'honore l'huomo si mete ad ogni sorte di pericolo; con molte altre parole in questa sostanza, ale quali, se bene io non mancai di rispondere, seruendomi di quelle ragioni che sono adote da V. S. Ill.ma nela sua cifra di oto del pasato et di molte altre ancora, tutauia egli stete sempre fermo di non potere per honor suo mancare di consigliare il Re a fare ogni potere per ricuperare quello che con tanta indignità sua et di questo regno l'era stato tolto, et che quando S. M.tà non lo uolese fare, che egli pigliaria licenza per ritirarsi in casa sua, per non esere partecipe dela uergogna che riceueria quando comportase questo afronto. Et dale sue parole parmi che uolese dire di eser stato lui autore di fare che il Re mandase al'ambasciatore di Sauoia il pasaporto di potersene ritornare, come V. S. Ill.ma intenderà fuori di cifra, et di fare richiamare anco monsig. di Pugni, al quale hieri fu spedito un gentilhuomo in diligenza con ordine che quanto prima se ne deba ritornare in Francia. Hieri giunse qui il sig. Alfonso Corso, mandato da monsig. di Umena per far saper al Re che il sig. duca di Sauoia fra pochi giorni si douea ritrouare a Ciamberi, et che hauria seco buon numero di gente da guerra; che [f. 299v] però desideraua di sapere da S. M.tà come uoleua che egli si gouernase, hauendo il nimico tanto uicino, et ricercando magior numero di caualeria di quello che hora si ritroua seco, non hauendo più che 500 cauali et intorno a 4000 fanti. [?Però] dicono che sino a tanto che siino fate le genti che ho già scrito esere destinate per quella guerra, che se gli mandarano altri 500 cauali et quel magior numero de fanti che si potrà, solecitando poi pel resto le già date speditioni. Li Stati caminano ala conclusione, et per quello che mi ha deto mons. di Guisa, auanti [?uenti] giorni potriano hauere finito; però prima che si uenga ala conclusione sua Ecelenza, che conosce il suo uantagio per il gran potere che ha con esi Stati, uorria con l'autorità loro uedere di necesitare il Re a fare un consiglio secreto per tratare tute le cose del regno, nel quale non ci fose alcuno contrario al suo partito; circa che non so quello [che] potrà fare, non esendo posibile che S. M.tà di buona uoglia sia per consentirui, et l'usare uiolenza, come hano fato in diuerse altre cose che ho già scrite a V. S. Ill.ma, potria esere pericoloso di fare rompere. Translation R41_en.md # R41 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [8?] December 1588, duplicate: Savoy refuses the Nemours solution; Guise urges war) Translation of `R41_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 298r] […] from letters of Signor Girolamo Gondi written to His Majesty from Seville […] it is learned that the Duke of Savoy had not accepted the proposal to put Monsieur de Nemours, his cousin, into the marquisate of Saluzzo; but that His Highness, persisting in [?wanting] to keep those places in his hand until the Dauphiné should be free of the Huguenots, offered, as security for restoring them at that time, to send his wife into France and to give one of his sons as hostage. With these proposals they are very ill satisfied here, and preparations for war go on, though not with the vigour seen at the start, because of the ill feeling that still persists between His Majesty and Monsieur de Guise, which greatly hinders every other decision; although on this particular they are very much agreed, and Monsieur de Guise even shows himself more ardent than His Majesty, knowing that he gains by it greater favour with the nobility and peoples of France, who cannot rest at seeing that the Duke of Savoy has chosen to start a war with this kingdom. And indeed yesterday morning, having been with me a long time, the said Monsieur de Guise told me that on no account could he, for his honour, refrain from making every effort to avenge the injury France has received from the Duke of Savoy, who [f. 298v] was already beginning to recognise that he had taken a bad decision in breaking with this crown, since all his peoples of Bresse and Savoy offered to open the gates of their towns to His Majesty whenever he sends his forces there; and that the ambassador of that Highness had several times asked him for an audience, and he had answered that if he wished to treat of the restitution of the marquisate he would listen to him, but otherwise he had nothing to do with him; and for all that the said ambassador had told Madame de Nemours, his mother, that the Duke his master would be content to restore everything if His Excellency would promise him that, should the King die without children, he would put him back in possession of the marquisate; and that he would not give him a hearing. I did not fail to put before him the great harm the Catholics of France would suffer from this war, and the advantage to the Huguenots, with whatever else seemed to me to the point; but he answered that all this was the fault of the Duke of Savoy, who under pretext of pursuing heretics was coming to favour [them], and that it was a maxim in the profession of war and of the good government of a kingdom always to hold the frontiers, because, these being kept, it was then easy to remedy [f. 299r] the disorders that occur in the body of the kingdom; and that to preserve his state and his honour a man exposes himself to every kind of danger; with many other words to this effect. Although I did not fail to answer, using the arguments Your Most Illustrious Lordship gives in your cipher of the 8th of last month and many others besides, he remained firm that for his honour he could not fail to advise the King to do all in his power to recover what had been taken from him with such indignity to him and to this kingdom, and that if His Majesty would not do it he would take leave to retire to his house, so as not to share in the shame the King would incur if he put up with this affront. And from his words it seems to me he meant to say that he had been the author of having the King send the Savoy ambassador his passport to return home, as Your Lordship will learn outside the cipher, and of having Monsieur de Poigny recalled too; to whom yesterday a gentleman was sent post-haste with orders that he return to France as soon as possible. Yesterday Signor Alfonso Corso arrived here, sent by Monsieur de Mayenne to let the King know that the Duke of Savoy was to be at Chambéry within a few days, and would have with him a good number of soldiers; that [f. 299v] he therefore wished to know from His Majesty how he wanted him to act, having the enemy so near, and asking for a larger number of cavalry than he now has, since he has no more than 500 horse and about 4,000 foot. [However] they say that until the troops I have already written are destined for that war are raised, another 500 horse and as many more foot as possible will be sent him, the dispatches already given being pressed for the rest. The Estates are moving to their conclusion, and from what Monsieur de Guise has told me they might be finished within [twenty] days; but before it comes to the conclusion His Excellency, who knows his advantage from the great power he has with these Estates, would like to use their authority to force the King to set up a secret council to treat all the affairs of the kingdom, in which there would be no one opposed to his party. What he will be able to do about this I [do not know], since it is not possible that His Majesty will consent to it willingly, and to use violence, as they have done in various other matters I have already written to Your Lordship, could be dangerous and bring about a break. And so I do not fail to do every kind of office so that union and peace may be kept […] R42, Francia 22/21, n.d. [Blois, Dec 1588] Morosini tells the King at the Capuchins that the Pope is displeased the Council of Trent has not been published; the King answers through Gondi. Guise complains that the King does not trust him, and Morosini urges the King to satisfy Guise. He also reports on the papal bull against procurers of abortion and says the Queen Mother has a fever. Translation R42_en.md # R42 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 19 November 1588: the King, the Council of Trent, Guise and the sick Queen Mother) Translation of `R42_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 303r] […] in answer to the cipher […] in Your Most Illustrious Lordship's letters of the 7th [of last month] […] that, being with His Majesty this morning at the Capuchins, I told him of the displeasure Our Lord [feels] that in the publication of the Council of Trent His Majesty has not yet taken the resolution that befitted a most Christian king, and one who in his actions shows himself so zealous for the honour of the Lord God and of the Catholic religion, as […] His Majesty; begging him with much affection not to wish any longer to […] this due and holy resolution, without lending his ears any more to those who, under […] pretexts of worldly interests, want to deprive him of what belongs to heaven; assuring him that Our Lord, as a pious and most kind father, will not fail to grant him most abundant graces in all that he can [grant with] his authority and the [good] of this kingdom; and I made use of the imprecations contained in your cipher, in case His Majesty, forgetting his obligation to the Lord God, did not come to the publication of the Council. The King answered that it grieved him that his good will was not recognised, for [Our Lord] could be assured that, if His Holiness could see his heart as blessed God sees it, he would have no cause to remain dissatisfied with him; that he would await [f. 303v] the answer of [266], and on this matter he had ordered Signor Girolamo Gondi to treat with Our Lord, and then he would give me his decision. And because Monsieur de Guise had complained to me in the days before that His Majesty did not confide in him, and was very slow in carrying out what was resolved in council, showing that he was thinking of withdrawing, I began to speak with His Majesty about the affairs of the kingdom, [and] urged him to find a way to satisfy the said Monsieur de Guise by making use of him and giving him occasion to exercise the power he has given him, otherwise I feared he could hardly be calmed and contented. His Majesty showed that he valued my advice, and asked me what way I thought he should take to content him. I told him he was too wise not to find for himself the way to satisfy him, but that for my part I believed that what I had told him many other times was the only means of doing well: to make his heart sincere, not to lend his ears to those who bring him evil reports of him, and, knowing that he is poor and laden with debts, to give him some means to maintain himself, keeping him […] always [f. 304r] employed in some business suited to his inclination and profession. The King said he found this good, and that I should speak of it with the Queen Mother, who […] knew that, although she was not [yet] wholly free of her illness, she would nonetheless see me willingly. I also did an office with His Majesty for the Archbishop of Arles, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship instructs me, and for the publication of Our Lord's bull against […] by the Archbishop […] first. His Majesty answered that I should speak of it with the Archbishop Gondi, […] other, that the bull was most holy and that he will have it published. Then, having left His Majesty, I went to the Queen Mother, who, although she had the chill of the fever, wanted by all means to see me and to discuss with me the particulars I had treated with the King, and showed herself very pleased with the office I had done with His Majesty. She said that I should come to see her as soon as possible, and that she […] would speak with me. I, to tell the truth about the state of the said Queen, am not […] content, because her chest is still very, very full of catarrh, with a most troublesome cough, and the fever, which comes to her every [f. 304v] day, besides her being much weakened by the illness, [and] with seventy years on her back, which makes everyone fear […] the others, these lords of Guise, who let it be understood that, if she came to die, they would no longer trust themselves to stay at court, fearing that the King, persuaded by their enemies, might attempt something against the person of Monsieur de Guise. May the Lord God in his mercy […] to what is for his greater glory and the service of Christendom. […] R43, Francia 22/22, Blois, 23 Dec [1588] Guise is killed with daggers in the King's chamber on the King's order, after warnings that he meant harm to the King. The Cardinal of Guise, the Prince de Joinville, the Dukes of Nemours and Elbeuf, the Archbishop of Lyon, the prévôt des marchands and a Paris president are arrested, and the Cardinal de Bourbon is put under guard. The Queen Mother is left speechless, the city is locked down, Morosini seeks an audience in vain, and the Cardinal of Guise is feared dead too. S., 216 avisi, 143 guerra). Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread. ## Reading [f. 308r] […] questa matina di […] il duca di Guisa nela camera del Re è stato per ordine di S. M.tà amazato a colpi di pugnale, et la sua morte è seguita a questo modo. Essendo da più parti auuertito S. M.tà de la mala intentione che il sodeto di Guisa haueua contra la sua persona, et essendo arriuato qui, come V. S. Ill.ma haurà inteso con l'ultime mie, il sig. Alfonso Corso, mandato dal duca di Umena per le cause scrite, et con auisi che S. M.tà si douesse hauere buona custodia de mons. di Guisa suo fratelo, che machinaua contra la sua persona, et che lui medemo saria uenuto a Bles quando hauesse creduto di poterui arriuare a tempo per diuertirlo da suoi pensieri; et hauendo hieri [?medesimamente] eso duca di Guisa deto a S. M.tà che se non fosero in piedi li Stati Generali di sua mano hauria amazati molti che le stauano atorno et faceuano sempre catiui ofici contra di lui, agiongendo molte altre parole minatorie, per le quali il Re in fine, senza comunicare questo pensiero con persona uiuente, propose nel animo suo di leuarlo di uita; et hieri sera diede uoce di uscire questa matina ala cacia, et fece intendere ad alcuni, i quali fin hora non si nominano, che fosero ale cinque hore de la matina al gabineto, come esequirono; et entrati da S. M.tà, aperse loro l'animo suo, et hauendoli trouati prontisimi a esequirlo, li fece [f. 308v] fermare in camera et mandato a chiamare il duca di Guisa, che si truouaua nel Consiglio di Stato, uenuto et entrato subito nela camera fu preso da due a trauerso et da altri aterato con molte pugnalate, et dopo hauere indarno fata grandisima difesa con le mani et con i denti, senza però mai hauere potuto caciare mano ala spada. Mentre si esequiua il fato, S. M.tà stete ritirata in gabineto col sig. Alfonso Corso solo, che tene seco per sua guardia. Morto lui, et posti prigioni il cardinale di Guisa, che si truouaua pure in Consiglio, il duca di Nemurs, il duca d'Elbeuf, il principe di Ianuile, l'arciuescouo Lione, il preuosto di mercanti di Parigi et il presidente Nogli, et mesa guardia al cardinale di Borbone, il Re andò a ritrouare la Regina Madre et le dise le cause per le quali era stato necesitato a preuenire i disegni del duca per liberar se da pericolo et il regno di tiranide. La Regina Madre restò atonita et non puote rispondere parola. Fin che [?fu] esequito tutto questo, le guardie stetero in arme, et furono prese tute le porte et […] principali dela terra, nela quale si […] et non è seguito alcuno mouimento. Subito che fui auuertito da miei di casa, che da le fenestre uidero serare le porte del castelo et metersi in arme le guardie, procurai di intendere [f. 309r] la causa, et fu deto che il Re uolea far pigliare uno che nela camera di S. M.tà haueua posto mano ad un pugnale; né si puote mai intendere il uero sino a tanto che il sig. cardinale di Gondi per nome di S. M.tà uene a darmi la nuoua del suceso et dele cause che l'haueuano necesitata a fare quella esecutione, così per quello che si è deto di sopra, inteso per uia del duca di Umena, o per altro scrito da quello d'Umala, suo cugino germano. Io non ho saputo che rispondere, essendo restato mezo morto di questo auiso; et pure le disi che io piangeuo la disgratia di quello principe et pregauo Dio che ciò non fose a magiore dano et ruina di questo regno. Procurai di hauere audientia, ma non [è] stato posibile, scusandosi S. M.tà con li molti impedimenti che haueua. Non lasarò di continouare a dimandarla per fare almeno quello oficio che deuo per quelli che restano uiui, et per quello che mi dice il sig. cardinale di Gondi si può tenire per certo che non moriranno. S. M.tà fu poi ala mesa et mangiò in publico senza mostrare alteratione alcuna in [?uiso], et il cardinale di Uandomo le diede la saluieta ale mani. È stato mandato un bando che tuti i padroni del[e] case debano hogi dare in nota i nomi di tuti quelli che alogiano; et S. M.tà ha dopo fato intendere ali duchi di Nemurs et d'Elbeuf [f. 309v] che debano stare alegri, che non sarano ofesi. È stato medesima[mente] […] mandato soto pena dela uita che nisuno deba partire di Bles senza licenza in scrito. Con tuto ciò molti seruitori et amici del duca di [Guisa] hanno sgombrato. Mi uiene afermato che Sua Ecelenza fu auisata hieri da più bande che si guardase dal Re, ma […] che lui non si potese persuadere che S. M.tà fose per fare tale risolutione, o perché fose giunta la sua hora. […] ho deto […]. […] mi uiene afermato che il sig. cardinale di Guisa sia ancora lui morto, il che però non poso sapere di certo, se bene lo temo asai, sapendo le mali sodisfationi che il Re haueua di sua signoria Il[l].ma per le parole che liberam[ente] diceua contra la sua persona, et perché sapeua che lei era quella che spingeua i Stati contra di lui. Sono anco auertito che S. M.tà ha spedito al duca di Niuers pregandolo instantem[ente] di atendere più che mai ala guerra contra il Nauarro, essendo molto risoluta di uolere continouare con ogni suo potere per sraticare le heresie dal suo regno, [a]ciò il mondo non creda che l'ha più tosto per conpiacere al duca di Guisa che per sua propria inc[l]inatione, sino a [f. 307r] [?hora], l'hauese fata. Ha ancora S. M.tà spedito il sig. Alfonso Corso a Lione con patenti di suo logotenente generale di quelle forze che sono con il duca di Umena, et scriue a sua Ece[lenza] che [?mosa] principalm[ente] dal aduertimento che lei gli haueua mandato per il sodeto sig. Alfonso Corso, conforme a molti altri che da diuerse parti hauea hauti del medesmo tenore, si era risoluto a far quella esecutione contra il duca di Guisa, che ela intenderia, dela quale credeua che […] biasimar[la]; […] era condota a questo non per odio che porta ala sua casa, ma per pura necesità di saluare la sua uita et quietare il suo regno; et però in ogni ocasione le faria conoscere nel suo particolare il desiderio che ha di giouarle et di gratificarla; ma che per adeso la esortaua di ritirarsi al suo gouerno et consignare le forze destinate per l'impresa del Delfinato al sodeto sig. Alfonso, perché quando […] la uedrà pigliare questo fato di quella maniera che deue, non lasarà di honorare la sua persona con gratie magiori. Io mi truouo così tribolato et confuso, et aspetarò con ardentisimo desiderio risposta […] con questo ordine che piacerà [f. 307v] a N. S. di darmi; et a V. S. Translation R43_en.md # R43 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 23 December 1588: the killing of the Duke of Guise) Translation of `R43_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 308r] […] this morning […] the Duke of Guise was killed in the King's chamber, by order of His Majesty, with dagger blows, and his death came about in this way. His Majesty had been warned from several quarters of the evil intention that the said Guise had against his person; and Signor Alfonso Corso having arrived here, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship will have heard by my last letters, sent by the Duke of Mayenne for the reasons written, with warnings that His Majesty should keep good guard against Monsieur de Guise his brother, who was plotting against his person, and that he himself would have come to Blois had he thought he could arrive in time to turn him from his designs; and the said Duke of Guise having told His Majesty yesterday [likewise] that, were the Estates General not sitting, he would with his own hand have killed many of those who stood around him and always did him bad offices, adding many other threatening words — for these reasons the King at last, without communicating this thought to any living person, resolved in his mind to take his life. Yesterday evening he gave out that he would go hunting this morning, and he let some men know (who are not named so far) that they should be in the cabinet at five in the morning, as they did; and when they had come to His Majesty he opened his mind to them, and having found them most ready to carry it out, he had them [f. 308v] stay in the chamber and sent to call the Duke of Guise, who was in the Council of State. He came, and as soon as he entered the chamber he was seized by two men from the side and thrown down by others with many dagger blows, after making a great defence in vain with his hands and his teeth, without ever being able to put his hand to his sword. While the deed was being done His Majesty stayed withdrawn in the cabinet with Signor Alfonso Corso alone, whom he keeps with him as his guard. Guise dead, and the Cardinal of Guise (who was also in the Council), the Duke of Nemours, the Duke of Elbeuf, the Prince of Joinville, the Archbishop of Lyon, the prévôt des marchands of Paris and the president de Neuilly made prisoners, and a guard set on the Cardinal of Bourbon, the King went to find the Queen Mother and told her the reasons why he had been forced to forestall the Duke's designs, to free himself from danger and the kingdom from tyranny. The Queen Mother remained astonished and could not answer a word. Until all this had been done the guards stood under arms, and all the gates and principal […] of the town were taken, in which […] and no disturbance has followed. As soon as I was told by my household, who from the windows had seen the castle gates being shut and the guards taking up arms, I tried to learn [f. 309r] the reason, and was told that the King wanted to have a man arrested who had put his hand to a dagger in His Majesty's chamber; nor could the truth be learned until the Cardinal de Gondi, in His Majesty's name, came to give me the news of what had happened and the reasons that had forced him to that execution, both what has been said above, learned through the Duke of Mayenne, and other things written by that d'Aumale, his first cousin. I did not know what to answer, being left half dead by this news; and yet I told him that I wept for the misfortune of that prince and prayed God that it might not be to the greater harm and ruin of this kingdom. I tried to have an audience, but it has not been possible, His Majesty excusing himself with the many business he had. I will not cease to go on asking for it, to perform at least the office I owe for those who remain alive; and from what the Cardinal de Gondi tells me, it can be held for certain that they will not die. His Majesty then went to mass and dined in public without showing any change [in his face?], and the Cardinal de Vendôme gave him the napkin for his hands. A proclamation has been issued that all the masters of houses must today give in the names of all those lodging with them; and His Majesty has since let the Dukes of Nemours and Elbeuf know [f. 309v] that they should be of good cheer, for they will not be harmed. It has [likewise] been […] ordered, on pain of death, that no one may leave Blois without a written licence. For all that, many servants and friends of the Duke of [Guise] have cleared out. I am assured that His Excellency was warned yesterday from several quarters to beware of the King, but […] that he could not persuade himself that His Majesty would take such a resolution — or else his hour had come. […] I have said […]. […] I am assured that the Cardinal of Guise too is dead, which however I cannot know for certain, though I much fear it, knowing the King's great displeasure with His Most Illustrious Lordship for the words he spoke freely against his person, and because he knew that it was he who pushed the Estates against him. I am also told that His Majesty has sent to the Duke of Nevers, begging him urgently to attend more than ever to the war against Navarre, being quite resolved to continue with all his power to root out heresy from his kingdom, so that the world should not believe that he has made it rather to please the Duke of Guise than from his own inclination [f. 307r] [up to now]. His Majesty has also sent Signor Alfonso Corso to Lyon with letters patent as his lieutenant general of the forces that are with the Duke of Mayenne, and writes to His Excellency that, [moved] chiefly by the warning that he had sent him through the said Signor Alfonso Corso, in agreement with many others of the same tenor he had had from several quarters, he had resolved to carry out that execution against the Duke of Guise, which he would understand, and which he believed […] blame; […] he had been driven to it not by hatred of his house but by pure necessity of saving his life and quieting his kingdom; and therefore on every occasion he would show him, in his own person, his wish to help and gratify him; but for the present he urged him to withdraw to his government and hand over the forces intended for the Dauphiné enterprise to the said Signor Alfonso, because when […] he sees him take this deed in the way he should, he will not fail to honour his person with greater favours. I find myself so troubled and confused, and I shall await with most ardent desire an answer […] with the order that it will please [f. 307v] Our Lord to give me; and I kiss Your Most Illustrious Lordship's hands again […].
