Ill.ma che oltre la morte del sig. duca di Guisa che […] si diceua che era morto ancora il sig. cardinale suo fratelo, et non fu uero alhora, ma questa matina solam[ente] è rimasto priuo di uita: alcuni dicono di fero come il fratelo, altri con una fune strangolato, che per ancora non si intende il uero. Mi uiene deto che il Re si sii risoluto di farlo morire hauendo scoperto che egli disegnaua di fugire, et che per questo efeto si uedeua qualche soleuatione di gente. Di questa morte io sono rimasto molto più confuso che di quella del sig. duca di Guisa, esendo persona eclesiastica et cardinale, né so come gouernarmi, temendo di erare in tuti modi. Ma dopo hauere maturam[ente] considerato tuto quello che può sucedere, ho risoluto, poiché da ciò non segue alcun pregiudicio ala santità di N. S. né a cotesta santa sede, et può sempre usare la sua autorità, di uolere più tosto andare destregiando con rimostrare al Re il suo erore et contenerlo nela debita ubidientia ala santa sede apostolica, che esere io l'autore di qualche scandalosa risolutione, dela quale, per quello che io uego, si può asai temere quando si hauese da tratare con termini più rigorosi; et in cosa di tanta importanza et consequenza ho stimato più conueniente di lasare il giuditio ala soma prudentia [f. 313v] di N. S., che uolere deliberare da me. Però la suplico con ogni humiltà a farmi quanto prima sapere la risoluta uolontà di N. S. Dimani io andarò dal Re, hauendomi hogi mandato S. M.tà un biglieto scrito di sua mano, la tradutione del quale sarà con questa. Il sig. cardinale di Borbone sta tutauia guardato dale guardie del Re, se bene nel leto con febre et un [f]luso di sangue, che, agionta la mala contenteza et il timore che ha, potria facilmente fargli perdere la uita, come […] bene, dicono che sarà mandato in prigione insieme con il principe di Ianuile nel castelo d'Amboisa, come anco l'arciuescouo [di] Lione, in qualche altro loco sicuro. Hogi hano esaminato il secretario di mons. di Guisa, hauendogli prima promesa la uita se diceua il uero di quello che gli sarà dimandato; et fra molte altre cose ha deto che pochi giorni prima N. S. hauea scrito al sodeto duca una lettera di tre faciate di carta tuta di propria mano in fauore del sig. duca di Sauoia per le cose del marchesato di Saluzo. Et mi uiene deto che S. M.tà lo raconto ala Regina Madre, dicendole che questi non erano ofici da padre comune, et che se N. S. uolese procedere seco di questa maniera, che lui ancora faria dal suo canto quello che le conueniua, non uolendo [f. 314r] […]: "Monsignore legato, hora io sono il Re, et ho preso tal risolutione di non uolere più soferire ingiurie né mali tratamenti, che io continouarò, a dano di chi si uoglia, la mia generosa risolutione, con l'esempio del nostro santo padre N. S.", esendomi bene ricordato dela forma del parlare che tiene continouam[ente], che bisogna farsi obedire et castigare quelli che ci ofendono. Translation R44_en.md # R44 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Blois], 24 December 1588, duplicate: the death of the Cardinal of Guise) Translation of `R44_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 313r] When [I] wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship yesterday evening that, besides the death of the Duke of Guise, […] it was said that his brother the Cardinal was dead too, it was not true then; but only this morning has he been deprived of life: some say by the sword like his brother, others strangled with a rope, for the truth is not yet known. I am told that the King resolved to have him die having discovered that he was planning to flee, and that for this purpose some rising of people was to be seen. By this death I have been much more confounded than by that of the Duke of Guise, he being an ecclesiastical person and a cardinal, and I do not know how to conduct myself, fearing to err in every way. But after maturely considering all that may happen, I have resolved — since no prejudice follows from it to His Holiness or to that Holy See, and he can always use his authority — to choose rather to proceed with dexterity, showing the King his error and keeping him in due obedience to the Holy Apostolic See, than to be myself the author of some scandalous decision, of which, from what I see, there is much to fear if one had to deal in harsher terms; and in a matter of such importance and consequence I have thought it more fitting to leave the judgement to the supreme wisdom [f. 313v] of Our Lord than to wish to decide it myself. I therefore beg you with all humility to let me know as soon as possible Our Lord's settled will. Tomorrow I shall go to the King, His Majesty having today sent me a note written in his own hand, the translation of which will come with this letter. The Cardinal de Bourbon is still guarded by the King's guards, although in bed with fever and a flux of blood, which, added to his discontent and the fear he is in, could easily cost him his life; as […], they say he will be sent to prison together with the Prince of Joinville in the castle of Amboise, as will the Archbishop of Lyon, to some other safe place. Today they examined Monsieur de Guise's secretary, having first promised him his life if he told the truth about what he would be asked; and among many other things he said that a few days before, Our Lord had written to the said Duke a letter of three sides of paper, all in his own hand, in favour of the Duke of Savoy over the affairs of the marquisate of Saluzzo. And I am told that His Majesty related this to the Queen Mother, telling her that these were not the offices of a common father, and that if Our Lord chose to proceed with him in this manner, he too for his part would do what suited him, not wishing [f. 314r] […]: "Monsignor Legate, now I am King, and I have taken such a resolution not to suffer any more insults or ill treatment, that I shall carry on my generous resolution, to the harm of whoever it may be, with the example of our Holy Father, Our Lord" — for I well remember the form of words he constantly uses, that one must make oneself obeyed and punish those who offend us. Since I have reached the end, [I] shall see tomorrow whether […] God […]. [f. 315r, a separate leaf] […] fail to tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship that His Majesty, this event having turned out so entirely to his satisfaction — since without the least movement or disturbance of the people he has got the upper hand over these enemies of his, who were reckoned invincible by all the world — has gained such confidence from it that, were he pressed, he could very easily show resentment […] heretics […]. R45, Francia 22/24, n.d. [Blois, Jan 1589, after Catherine de' Medici's death] Morosini defends his conduct. The Archbishop of Lyon refuses lay examiners because he is primate of France. The Estates' article excluding Navarre carries a clause reserving the Bourbon succession. M.tà non uoleua esequire quello che già haueua promeso, cioè di dechiarare il Nauarro per heretico et incapace ala sucesione di questo regno, anzi di più che si ritrouaua qui un huomo mandato da lui per tratare con la S. M.tà qualche acordo; il che, agiunto al hauere lei richiamato l'esercito che faceua la guerra agli heretici per seruirsene contra quelli di Orliens, pareua a me che ueniua a dare gran campo a quelli che mostrano di tenere la S. M.tà per poco catolica di comprobare con questi argomenti molto bene la loro opinione; che però la pregauo a considerare molto bene quello che conueniua a [?un] Re christianisimo et che faceua profesione di uero catolico, ricordandosi quanto è grande l'obligo che ela ha al sig. Dio, che l'ha fata nascere così gran Re, et quanto ela deue procurare di placare l'ira di sua diuina Maestà, che deue esere contra di lei grauem[ente] irritata per le cose pasate; che uolese considerare la mala sodisfatione che daria a tuti i catolici del suo regno et di tuta la christianità quando lasciase di fare la dechiaratione che ha promesa contra eso [f. 360r] Nauarro, perché faria sicuram[ente] credere il suo fine esere di uolere che egli dopo lei hauese a sucedere in questo regno, cosa aborita da tuti i buoni, et che la S. M.tà più d'ogn'altro douria aborire per il proprio interese; poiché, esendo eso Nauarro non solo heretico et inimico di Dio, ma che pretende anco di peruenire ala sucesione di questa corona, non potrà mai la S. M.tà asicurarsi che egli, per potere più presto peruenire a tanta grandeza, non habia ad insidiare la sua persona; et che quando non sia dechiarato inhabile et incapace ala sucesione haurà molto più seguito che non hauria quando tuti sapesero che egli non potrà mai esere Re di Francia; et che di tratare acordo seco senza il consenso di N. S. se ne guardase molto bene, perché quando lei uenise a questo io mi sarei subito partito di Francia, et che mi perdonase se lo facesi senza andarmi a licentiare da lei; che la pregauo a considerare molto bene le cose sue, guardandosi di non metere N. S. in necesità di fare ogni seuera dimostratione contra di lei, come io teneuo per certo che faria quando uedese la S. M.tà, dopo le cose sucese, fare anco qualche altro impiastro con li heretici. Mi rispose S. M.tà asai quietam[ente], se bene parue a me che si turbase in facia, et mi dise che quello [?mi] [f. 360v] haueua deto di uolere più che mai proseguire la guerra contra gli heretici me lo tornaua a confirmare, et che speraua che gli efeti comprobariano asai compitam[ente] questa sua ferma risolutione; et che il chiamare hora mons. di Niuers con quelle genti non ripugnaua ala sua parola, perché questa era una necesità presente, ala quale d'altro modo non si poteua per adeso rimediare, et che speraua di potere così presto spedirsi da questo bisogno che si saria stato in tempo ancora di fare contra li heretici quello che hauea deto; che era uero che non uoleua fare quella dechiaratione contra il Re di Nauarra, perché nel'edito dela pacificatione era già dechiarato che nisuno heretico potese sucedere a questa corona, il che bastaua asai per escludere eso Nauarro senza uenire a più espresa dechiaratione contra la sua particolare persona, perché questo saria meterlo in disperatione di non poter mai più farsi catolico, contra quello che io di ordine di N. S. le haueuo deto, che bisognaua fare ogni opera per ridurlo al'obedientia di santa chiesa, come ela credeua che ognuno douese desiderare; ma che egli hauese mandato huomo qui per tratar seco acordo, questo era falsisimo, et che quando fose me lo diria certo, se non come [f. 358r] a legato, almeno come a suo amico; et che mi poteuo asicurare che non farà mai acordo che prima non sia egli acordato con santa chiesa. Io replicai a S. M.tà che quanto a me haurei desiderato che ela per altra uia, senza richiamare mons. di Niuers, hauese proueduto a suoi bisogni; et che quanto al Nauarro mi pareua che douese esere così certa che mai egli posi esere buon catolico, che per questo rispeto non douria restare di fare quella dechiaratione che ha promesa a tuti i suoi Stati et a tuto il mondo, leuando lui totalm[ente] dala speranza et tuti i catolici dal timore che posi mai [pe]ruenire a questa corona; et che pareua a me che per ragione politica ancora S. M.tà lo doueua in ogni modo fare, per leuargli il seguito et per asicurare la sua propria uita, contra la quale più animosam[ente] [?conspirarà], [?sperando] di poter esere Re, che quando sarà certo di non potere esere. Mi dise S. M.tà: "Uoglio parlarui chiaro in confidentia, sapendo che lo tenirete apreso di uoi, perché è cosa di grandisima importanza, come ue ne prego. Sapiate che dopo la morte di questo di Guisa il cardinale di Uandomo et suoi frateli si credono già di esere Re di Francia, et però hano operato che nel capitolo proposto da i Stati di escludere il Re di Nauarra [f. 358v] ui si è agiunta una clausula importantisima, la quale è che, se bene quello è dichiarato inhabile, si dice riseruando nondimeno il dirito dela sucesione a quelli dela casa di Borbone. Hor sapiate che, se a loro apertiene di sucedere a questa corona, io non uoglio leuarli le loro ragioni; ma non uoglio meno aprouare […] che restino confirmate nei Stati generali del regno, aciò non posino con questa sicureza dela sucesione insidiare ala mia uita." Risposi a S. M.tà che se questa clausula le dispiaceua, che douria farla leuare et publicare il resto. Mi rispose che questo non si potria far senza rumore et senza pericolo di soleuare anco questi contra di lei, doue che, leuando insieme tuto il capitolo, non haueuano di che dolersi, parendo che questo fose più tosto in loro fauore che altrim[ente]; ma che haueua risoluto per altra uia di proseguire contra eso Re di Nauarra, perché il giorno seguente uolea incorporare tuti i suoi beni ala corona come di ribele et heretico, che tanto ualerà quanto anco publicarlo per quella altra uia. Al che replicai che, purché la S. M.tà facese la dichiaratione con il consenso dei Stati che egli resti escluso in tuto di poter mai suce- [f. 361r] -dere ala corona come heretico et incapace, che non diceuo io che lo douese fare più per una che per un'altra uia. Con che si terminò questo ragionamento, che fu asai più longo che qui non si dice per scansare il tedio a V. S. Ill.ma. Entrai poi a parlare di nuouo a S. M.tà sopra la publicatione del concilio, et l'esplicai quello apunto che si contiene nela cifra di V. S. Ill.ma di [?5] del pasato, mostrandole la giusta indignatione di N. S. anco contra di me per le conditioni che intendeua la S. M.tà di agiungere nela publicatione di eso concilio; che però io la pregauo et esortauo a pensarui meglio et consigliarsi con persone inteligenti et timorose del sig. Dio, perché non trouaria alcuno catolico che aprobase che i concili[i] generali confirmati dala santa sede apostolica posino esere in questo modo mutilati da qualsiuoglia Re o principe per grande che sia; et che quando la S. M.tà continouase nela prima risolutione daria grande ocasione a quelli che non l'amano di comprobare con questo argomento che ela non habia quello zelo ala religione catolica che conuiene ad un Re christianis[imo], et che per un'ombra falsa d'interese dela sua autorità ueniria a perdere la più bela ocasione che se le posi presentare di mostrare ala Santità di N. S. et al mondo tuto come falsam[ente] uenga la S. M.tà [f. 361v] imputata nele cose dela religione; doue facendo in contrario non solo doueua temere la giusta ira di Dio, ma anco l'indignatione di N. S. et la mala opinione di tuto il christianesmo; che io, nel dispiacere che sentirò dele auersità che per questo le posono sucedere, haurò nela propria conscienza questo refrigerio di sapere almeno di non hauere mancato in uoce molte uolte et in scrito ancora di ricordarle quello che per debito di conscienza et per utilità dele cose sue è tenuta di fare in questo proposito. Et dopo le mandai un memoriale del medesmo tenore, che lo facese legere nel suo consiglio, insieme con una scritura fata ad instanza del uescouo di [?Eureus] et sotoscrita da molti uescoui et altri dei Stati generali, che dicono che il concilio si deue publicare senza alcuna conditione. Mi rispose S. M.tà che non mancaria di considerare sopra quello che io le diceuo; ma che le pareua che dele conditioni "saluis iuribus regis et regni" io me ne douesi contentare. Disi a la S. M.tà che lei douea publicare il concilio come stà et giace, senza altra conditione, come hano fato tuti gli altri Re et principi catolici, che non manco di lei uogliono conseruare la loro autorità; et se pretende alcuna riserua, che acetando il concilio ne ri- [f. 357r] -cercase N. S., che, come molte uolte per nome dela [Santità di] N. S. le haueuo deto, saria in tute le cose honeste compiaciuta. La S. M.tà non mi rispose altro, et io mi licentiai. Ho uoluto dire questo tuto a V. S. Ill.ma perché la resti informata di tuto quello che pasa, se bene io non so se haurò fato bene o male, considerando quello che la mi scriue nela sodeta sua cifra, doue mi dice che non […] mi laso dare la burla, o che mi sodisfo di discorsi. Quanto ala burla, [?non] mi tengo per tanto soficiente che non mi posi esere data; ma quanto a discorsi, pare a me di non far altro nele mie ma che rapresentare a V. S. Ill.ma il uero di tuto quello che pasa; et se in ciò io non sodisfo al suo desiderio, può esere certa che molto me ne duole et ne sento estremo dispiacere; ma la suplico a credere che io non saprei fare meglio, et che non ho magiore desiderio che di seruire bene, né penso ad altro il giorno et la note. Ma se non sucedono le cose come ela uorria, so che per la molta sua prudenza conosce che in mano mia non è di potere far fare al Re di Francia quello che egli non uole. Si uano formando i procesi contra questi sig. di Guisa, et l'altra matina mandarono dui consiglieri per esaminare l'arciuescouo [di] Lione; ma egli dise che, esendo arciuescouo et primato di Francia, non poteua esere esaminato da laici; et io ancora feci intendere a S. Translation R45_en.md # R45 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [mid-]January 1589: audience with Henry III on Navarre, Nevers, the Council of Trent) Translation of `R45_reading.md` (pages in the cipher's catchword order); holes as there. ## Translation [f. 359r] […] although I wished, before returning to audience with the King, to wait for some word from Your Most Illustrious Lordship to learn Our Lord's mind after the unhappy event of the deaths of the Cardinal and the Duke of Guise (may they be in glory), nevertheless, having heard that a man sent by the King of Navarre was here to negotiate some accord with His Majesty, and having also learned beforehand that he would not come to the declaration already settled against Navarre, as all the Estates of the kingdom demand, so as not to fail on my side to do all I can to prevent anything prejudicial to the Catholic religion, I thought I should not fail to seek audience of His Majesty. He granted it me today, and I was with him a long time. After making the office of condolence fitting for the death of the Queen Mother (may she be in heaven), I told His Majesty that the last time I spoke with him he had earnestly begged me to write to Our Lord assuring him that he was more than ever resolved to make every effort to drive heresy out of this kingdom, meaning to proceed with all rigour against the heretics, to confiscate and sell all their goods and use the money to pursue the war against them; that I had not failed [f. 359v] to write this to Your Lordship so that you could report it to Our Lord; but that I feared I must now write the very opposite, since I heard that His Majesty would not carry out what he had promised, namely to declare Navarre a heretic and incapable of the succession to this kingdom, and moreover that a man sent by him was here to negotiate an accord with His Majesty; which, added to his having recalled the army that was making war on the heretics in order to use it against the people of Orléans, seemed to me to give great scope to those who show they hold His Majesty to be a poor Catholic to prove their opinion very well by these arguments. Therefore I begged him to consider carefully what befitted [a] Most Christian King who professed to be a true Catholic, remembering how great is his obligation to the Lord God, who had him born so great a king, and how much he must seek to appease the wrath of His Divine Majesty, which must be gravely provoked against him by past events; to consider the ill satisfaction he would give all the Catholics of his kingdom and of all Christendom if he failed to make the declaration he has promised against the said [f. 360r] Navarre, for it would surely make people believe that his aim was that Navarre should succeed him in this kingdom — a thing abhorred by all good men, and which His Majesty more than anyone ought to abhor in his own interest; since, Navarre being not only a heretic and enemy of God but also claiming the succession to this crown, His Majesty could never be safe from his plotting against his person to reach such greatness sooner; and that unless he were declared unfit and incapable of the succession he would have a much larger following than if everyone knew he could never be King of France; and that he should take great care not to negotiate an accord with him without Our Lord's consent, because if he came to that I would leave France at once, and he must forgive me if I did it without coming to take leave of him. I begged him to consider his affairs carefully, taking care not to put Our Lord under the necessity of making every severe demonstration against him, as I held it certain he would if he saw His Majesty, after what had happened, make some other patched-up arrangement with the heretics. His Majesty answered me quite calmly, though it seemed to me his face was troubled, and told me that what he [f. 360v] had said about wanting more than ever to pursue the war against the heretics he confirmed again, and hoped the effects would prove this firm resolve of his quite fully; that recalling Monsieur de Nevers with those troops now was not contrary to his word, because this was a present necessity which could not be remedied otherwise for now, and he hoped to be done with this need so soon that there would still be time to do against the heretics what he had said; that it was true he would not make that declaration against the King of Navarre, because in the Edict of Pacification it was already declared that no heretic could succeed to this crown, which was quite enough to exclude Navarre without a more express declaration against his particular person, since that would drive him to despair of ever becoming a Catholic — contrary to what I, by Our Lord's order, had told him, that every effort must be made to bring him back to the obedience of Holy Church, as he believed everyone ought to wish; but that Navarre had sent a man here to negotiate an accord was utterly false, and that if it were so he would certainly tell me, if not as [f. 358r] legate, at least as his friend; and that I could be sure he would never make an accord before Navarre was reconciled with Holy Church. I replied to His Majesty that for my part I would have wished him to provide for his needs some other way, without recalling Monsieur de Nevers; and that as to Navarre, it seemed to me he should be so certain Navarre could never be a good Catholic that he ought not on that account to refrain from making the declaration he had promised to all his Estates and to the whole world, taking away from Navarre all hope, and from all Catholics the fear, that he might ever come to this crown; and that it seemed to me that for reasons of policy too His Majesty ought by all means to do it, to take away his following and to secure his own life, against which Navarre would [conspire] more boldly, [hoping] he might be King, than when he is sure he cannot be. His Majesty said to me: "I want to speak plainly to you in confidence, knowing you will keep it to yourself, for it is a matter of very great importance, as I beg you. Know that after the death of this Guise the Cardinal of Vendôme and his brothers already believe themselves Kings of France, and so they have contrived that in the article proposed by the Estates to exclude the King of Navarre [f. 358v] a most important clause has been added, which is that, although he is declared unfit, the right of succession is nevertheless reserved to those of the House of Bourbon. Now know that if the succession to this crown belongs to them, I do not want to take their rights from them; but neither do I want to approve […] that they be confirmed in the Estates General of the kingdom, so that with this security of the succession they cannot plot against my life." I answered His Majesty that if this clause displeased him he should have it removed and publish the rest. He answered that this could not be done without uproar and without danger of raising these men too against him, whereas by removing the whole article together they had nothing to complain of, since this seemed rather in their favour than otherwise; but that he had resolved to proceed against the King of Navarre by another way, since the next day he meant to annex all his goods to the crown as a rebel and heretic, which would be worth as much as publishing it by that other way. To which I replied that provided His Majesty made the declaration, with the consent of the Estates, that he remain wholly excluded from ever succeeding [f. 361r] to the crown as a heretic and incapable, I did not say it must be done by one way rather than another. With this the conversation ended; it was much longer than is told here, to spare Your Lordship tedium. I then spoke again to His Majesty about the publication of the Council, and set out to him exactly what is contained in Your Lordship's cipher of the [5th?] of last month, showing him Our Lord's just indignation, against me as well, at the conditions His Majesty meant to add to the publication of the Council; and so I begged and exhorted him to think it over and take counsel with intelligent and God-fearing persons, for he would find no Catholic who would approve that general councils confirmed by the Holy Apostolic See could be mutilated in this way by any king or prince however great; and that if His Majesty persisted in his first resolution he would give great occasion to those who do not love him to prove by this argument that he has not the zeal for the Catholic religion befitting a Most Christian King, and that for a false shadow of interest in his authority he would lose the finest occasion that could be offered him to show His Holiness and the whole world how falsely His Majesty [f. 361v] is accused in matters of religion; whereas by doing the contrary he would have to fear not only the just wrath of God but also Our Lord's indignation and the ill opinion of all Christendom; and that in the grief I shall feel at the adversities that may befall him for this, I shall have in my own conscience this comfort, at least to know I did not fail, by word many times and in writing too, to remind him of what he is bound to do in this matter by duty of conscience and for the good of his affairs. Afterwards I sent him a memorial to the same effect, that he might have it read in his council, together with a paper drawn up at the instance of the Bishop of [Évreux?] and signed by many bishops and others of the Estates General, who say the Council must be published without any condition. His Majesty answered that he would not fail to consider what I told him; but that it seemed to him I ought to be content with the conditions *saluis iuribus regis et regni*. I told His Majesty that he ought to publish the Council as it stands, without other condition, as all the other Catholic kings and princes have done, who no less than he wish to preserve their authority; and if he claims some reservation, that in accepting the Council he should ask it [f. 357r] of Our Lord, who, as I had told him many times in His Holiness's name, would oblige him in all honest things. His Majesty answered nothing more, and I took my leave. I have wished to tell all this to Your Lordship so that you may remain informed of everything that happens, though I do not know whether I shall have done well or ill, considering what you write me in your said cipher, where you tell me that I […] let myself be fooled, or that I content myself with talk. As to being fooled, I do not hold myself so able that it could not happen to me; but as to talk, it seems to me I do nothing in my letters but represent to Your Lordship the truth of all that happens; and if in this I do not satisfy your wish, you may be sure it grieves me much and I feel extreme displeasure; but I beg you to believe that I could not do better, and that I have no greater wish than to serve well, nor think of anything else day and night. But if things do not turn out as you would wish, I know that in your great prudence you understand that it is not in my hand to make the King of France do what he will not. The trials against these Guise lords are being prepared, and the other morning they sent two councillors to examine the Archbishop of Lyon; but he said that, being archbishop and primate of France, he could not be examined by laymen; and I too let His Majesty know that he should refrain from it, as he has done […]. R46, Francia 22/25, Blois, 24 Jan 1589 (dup.) The Pope rejects the clause "saluis iuribus regis et regni", and Morosini works on the King's confessor and the Keeper of the Seals, who promise to argue his case. Saluzzo is set aside for now. At length Morosini complains of the Pope's displeasure and the false reports reaching Rome, and he begs leave to come to Rome to justify himself. Io poi, per scarico dela mia conscienza, se bene mi scriue V. S. Ill.ma che non me ne pigli altro fastidio, credendo nondimeno che il desiderio suo fose di uedere bene terminato questo negotio per gloria di Dio et beneficio di questo regno, non ho mancato con l'abate di Sanlis, confesore di S. M.tà a casa il guarda sigilo insieme con il suo confesore, che per nome suo mi disero che, hauendo S. Se poi riesce dela legatione mia quello fruto che aspetaua N. S., la suplico a considerare se il mancamento uiene da me o da […], né uoglia per l'amore di Dio atribuire a me le colpe che non sono mie et darmi la pena de' pecati altrui. A me non duole meno questo che a N. S.; ma consideri lei se mai mi ha comandata cosa che io prontam[ente] non l'habia esequita, et se mai per rispeto di chi si sia io habia lasciato di seruire fedelm[ente] a N. S., procurando sempre con tuti li spiriti et con ogni uiueza la conseruatione dela riputatione et dignità sua, sperando di potere con questi mezi farmi degno dela sua buona gratia et di conseruare quel poca di riputatione che con le fatiche di molti ani ho procurato d'aquistarmi, la quale io confeso di stimare più che la propria uita. Però, uedendomi senza alcuna mia colpa, col fare il meglio ch'ho saputo, a questo mal termine del'uno et del'altro, conuengo uiuere scons[f. 383v]olatisimo sino a tanto che piacia a N. S. che io uenga a la presenza sua per giustificare le ationi mie; […] prego con ogni afeto V. S. Ill.ma di adoprarsi per farmi otenire questa licenza, perché non solo farà gratia a me, ma anco seruitio a cotesta santa Sede, esendo che, se io sino a qui ho fato poco fruto mentre che il Re [?et] il regno pensauano che io hauesi credito et qualche autorità apreso N. S., hora che sono persuasi del contrario conuenir[à] a esere molto meno, né faranno alcuna stima di me, poiché tuta quella che si faceua tuta nasceua per il reflesso dela buona gratia di N. S. […] Et per dire il uero io non saprei come più sapere seruire, uedendo che con il fare meglio che ho saputo ho nondimeno disgustato tanto N. S., che mostra anco di restare mal sodisfata di quello che con ogni fedeltà scriuo dele cose che peruengono a mia notitia; onde nel auenire, sempre che mi uenirà ocasione di scriuere qualche cosa o di Saluzo o d'altro, conuenirà et scriuen[f. 384r]do et tacendo temer sempre di far dispiacere a N. S. Suplico V. S. Ill.ma a discusarmi se l'ho fastidita con questa longa diceria, considerando che a ciò mi ha spinto l'estremo dispiacere che io sento di uedere in tanto pericolo quello che sopra tute le cose del mondo stimo, che è la buona gratia di N. S., insieme con il mio honore. Racomando dunque a V. S. Ill.ma l'un[o] et l'altro con ogni afeto, per sostenere una creatura sua che non mancarà mai di adoprarsi in suo seruitio, pregandola a credere che io non mi sono moso a scriuerle per uolere hauer ragione alcuna con N. S., perché da lei non desidero altro che quello solo che le piace, ma perché sia informata dela uerità et posi sincerare l'animo dela Santità di N. Translation R46_en.md # R46 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Blois, 24 January 1589]: the Council of Trent; the Pope's displeasure) Translation of `R46_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 381r] […] with my last letters I had no time to answer Your Most Illustrious Lordship's ciphers of the 24th of last month. Now I tell you that, having understood what you write me about the Council of Trent, I at once let the King know that Our Lord not only does not accept the clause "saving the rights of the King and of the kingdom", but curses it; and so I urged His Majesty, who had resolved that day to publish this in the Estates, not to do it except freely and without any condition, because doing otherwise he would offend God, with whom one does not make bargains, and would give dissatisfaction to Our Lord and to all Christendom; reminding him that the words of general councils are words of God, for the Fathers say "it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us", [and] repeating to him in substance what I had told him and written many other times, to Your Most Illustrious Lordship with my last letters. On this His Majesty, having considered again, left off publishing this point in the Estates, but said that, as for the publication of the said council, he wanted it in any case to be published and accepted, and was letting them know so, that they should hold it as such; but that, since certain difficulties about reservations [f. 381v] put forward by those Estates were not yet well resolved, he wanted to give them still riper consideration, and would resolve them together with the other articles, which for shortness of time had not yet been settled. I then, to discharge my conscience — although Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes me not to trouble myself further about it, believing nonetheless that your wish was to see this business well concluded for the glory of God and the good of this kingdom — have not failed to do every effective office with the Abbé of Senlis, His Majesty's confessor, with the Keeper of the Seals and with all those others who have authority with him, urging them to persuade him to publish it without any condition; and it seems to me that I have in any case had some result, for yesterday His Majesty sent the Keeper of the Seals to my house together with his confessor, who told me in his name that His Majesty, having considered the memorials I had sent him on this matter, would much have wished to find a way of satisfying me without displeasing his whole kingdom, [and] that he begged […] [f. 382r] occasion for Our Lord to work, with his authority, to make him obeyed by his vassals in so just and reasonable a matter. They showed themselves well persuaded of what I told them, and left promising to tell the King that my reasons were excellent and that His Majesty ought to do so. They are now awaiting his resolution, and I shall send word of it to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. As for the affairs of Saluzzo, I have nothing more for now, since these latest events keep His Majesty busy with other thoughts that press him more at present. And as to my never having acknowledged receipt of the copy of the letter of His Most Serene Highness of Savoy [written] to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, which you sent me with yours of the third of October, I think your many occupations have not let you notice that in my very ciphers of the 1[8th?] of November, to which you answer with this same cipher, it is mentioned, besides what I acknowledged in mine of the 23rd of October in answer to yours of the third of the same month. What grieves me extremely is to see in this cipher of yours, as also in some of the [f. 382v] preceding ones, that Our Lord shows himself ill satisfied with me, without my being able to imagine the cause; and it presses me much more that this rumour has already reached the ears of the King and of this court, certain vexatious particulars having been written to His Majesty […] so far not only from the truth but even from the possible that I remain more than certain that neither Your Most Illustrious Lordship nor still less Our Lord, who is full of such prudence and of such rare and exquisite judgement, could have given [them] any kind of credence. And although my actions of many years can clear me before the whole world of such impostures, nevertheless I shall receive it as a singular grace from Our Lord if it please him to grant me to come as soon as possible to his most holy feet to justify all my actions; for, with the favour of the Lord God, I hope he will see quite clearly that I have served him with as much fidelity, sincerity and devotion as could be wished in any other minister, who, although he could have served with greater […] [f. 383r] […] greater authority and dominion than over me. If then the fruit Our Lord expected from my legation does not […] come, I beg you to consider whether the fault comes from me or from […], and not, for the love of God, to lay on me faults that are not mine and give me the penalty of others' sins. This grieves me no less than Our Lord; but let you consider whether he has ever commanded me anything that I did not promptly carry out, and whether for regard of anyone at all I have ever failed to serve Our Lord faithfully, always working with all my spirit and all my vigour for the preservation of his reputation and dignity, hoping by these means to make myself worthy of his good grace and to keep the little reputation that I have tried to win with the labours of many years, which I confess I value more than my own life. Therefore, seeing myself, through no fault of mine and while doing the best I knew, in this bad state with the one and with the other, I must live most disconsolate [f. 383v] until it please Our Lord that I come into his presence to justify my actions; […] I beg Your Most Illustrious Lordship with all my heart to work to obtain this leave for me, since you will do not only a favour to me but a service to that Holy See: for if until now I have done little good while the King [and] the kingdom thought I had credit and some authority with Our Lord, now that they are persuaded of the contrary it will have to be much less, and they will take no account of me, since all the esteem there was came wholly from the reflection of Our Lord's good grace […] And to tell the truth I would not know how to serve any better, seeing that, doing the best I knew, I have nevertheless so displeased Our Lord that he even shows himself ill satisfied with what I write in all fidelity of the things that come to my knowledge; so that in future, whenever I have occasion to write anything, about Saluzzo or anything else, I shall have, both in writing and in keeping [f. 384r] silent, always to fear displeasing Our Lord. I beg Your Most Illustrious Lordship to excuse me if I have wearied you with this long discourse, considering that I was driven to it by the extreme distress I feel at seeing in such danger what I value above everything in the world, which is the good grace of Our Lord, together with my honour. I commend, then, to Your Most Illustrious Lordship the one and the other with all my heart, in order to sustain a creature of yours who will never fail to work in your service, begging you to believe that I have not been moved to write to you in order to be in the right against Our Lord — for from him I desire nothing but what pleases him — but so that you may be informed of the truth and may set His Holiness's mind at rest, should he be informed otherwise by persons of little conscience […] R47, Francia 22/26, n.d. [Blois, Jan 1589] Morosini continues his defence and denies ever dealing with the English ambassador. He explains why the Council could not be forced through the parlements and the Estates. He had suggested that the King publish it at once and then send a personage to Rome to ask for his privileges. Transcription DOC_R47_D1712_1712.txt #CATALOG NAME: Segr. The order of the two leaves (386r–v before 385r–v) is the reading's, not certain. ## Translation [f. 386r] […] to consider that in these turbulent times one had to proceed with many regards, fearing that, even if he had chosen to order the Parlement to publish the said council without any reservation, they would not have obeyed him, because, as I knew, all three orders of the Estates General were asking for some reservation. Therefore, he having said several times that Our Lord did not mean by this to remove his privileges or the prerogatives of the kingdom, and asking me whether I thought it good that His Majesty should send a personage to Rome to show Our Lord the heads in which his authority is touched, begging him to be pleased to reserve them, because once this was done he would then publish the council without any other condition or reservation — I told him that, to do well and gain favour with Our Lord, he must now, without further delay, publish the council in the same manner in which it has been published in all the [rest] of Christendom, and then send the personage to Rome to ask [f. 386v] Our Lord for the graces and privileges he desired, promising him in Our Lord's name, in accordance with the orders sent me by Your Most Illustrious Lordship, that in all honest and reasonable things he would be satisfied. They told me they feared this was perhaps impossible to do in that way, because neither the people nor the parlements would accept it. I answered them that neither the people nor the parlements are called to the celebration of councils, but only the prelates, to whom [it belonged] to teach the others doctrine no less than morals; and that when this was confirmed by the Holy Apostolic See the people had no other consideration to make than to observe the orders and constitutions laid down, because what we see in our faith is good and true in so far as it is commanded and taught us by the Church; and that therefore His Majesty ought not on this account to fail to publish the said council, because, [if] the people would not obey him in this, he at least would have done his part in what he is bound and obliged to do, and to give [f. 385r] to the King […]. And he certainly could not [do it] with more prudence than I, nor with greater ardour nor greater fidelity, since I have never had any other aim than the honour of the Lord God and the good service of Our Lord and of that Holy See. And although I know that someone shows himself dissatisfied with me because I have had more regard for my duty than for their wishes, I nevertheless count it to my greater honour, since this happened because I, without regard for others, always chose to serve my master well, whose dignity is more at stake in the [treatment] given to me in his presence and in my own. Nor has this dissatisfaction of others ever been able to turn me from continuing always in the same purpose of serving my prince well, because, besides the deadly obligations I have to him, for which I shall always spend my own life, he is also the Vicar of Christ, which can suffice for every Christian to make him walk in his service with the same fidelity and truth that he would with the Lord himself, who sees the inmost depths [f. 385v] of our hearts. Therefore, when Our Lord finds in me — I do not say the enormous and execrable failing of having had dealings with the ambassador of England, whom I neither know nor ever, to my knowledge, have seen, as I am advised and as is written to the King himself to have been said to Our Lord — but any other least failing that I may have committed through malice in his service, I beg him to have no pity or mercy on me, but to punish me with the [harshest] and severest punishments that can be given to the most wicked man in the world. [But] I, if I am not mistaken, would believe that neither with Your Most Illustrious Lordship nor with Our Lord ought anyone to have had more trust than I, since there is no one more obliged to him; besides which I believe that, by the grace of the Lord God, I have been known by all who have had dealings with me to be utterly removed from the vice of ingratitude; and when Your Most Illustrious Lordship chooses to test my fidelity and gratitude, you will find that you have no one in this world on whom you can have more […] R48, Francia 22/27, Blois, 30 & 31 Jan 1589 Morosini again asks for his leave. The Parisians have put themselves under Mayenne's protection, and the King is leaving for Amboise with his prisoners. Morosini protests about moving the Cardinal de Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon. of Paris; his audience with the King on the removal of the prisoners to Amboise (Francia 22/27, ff. 399r–402v) Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1713 (KaJo, Jan 2016) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by `research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R48_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures (`R48_corrections.tsv`). Two sheets, as the transcriber noted: 399r–400v (an answer to Montalto's cipher "del 7 del presente", with the news from Paris, Mayenne, the King's departure for Amboise and the Maréchal de Retz's leave for the baths of Lucca) and 401r–402v (Morosini's audience with the King on the morning the Cardinal of Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon were to be taken to Amboise; the King's promise to have the Council of Trent published by letters patent). Neither is dated in cipher; both belong to January 1589, after the killing of the Guises and the arrest of the Cardinal of Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon. Tempesti, *Vita di Sisto V* (1754) II, book IX (scratch OCR ll. 4907–4943), paraphrases the audience of 401r–401v closely ("Prego Vostra Maestà di ricordarsi del grave delitto commesso nella persona del Cardinal di Guisa … non si suol perdonare né anco a' figliuoli … tenerle tutte unite …"); it was used to recognise sense only, never as a source of words. The DECODE "cleartext" images are despatches in clear, not a decipherment. Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [word] supplied. ## Reading [f. 399r] […] hauendo io di già con l'ultime mie scrito a soficienza a V. S. Ill.ma sopra de' miei particolari, et intendendo di non disputare con chi uoglio riuerire, [?obedire] et seruire, basterà hora dirle per risposta dela sua cifra del 7 del presente che in tanta mia aflitione et mestitia sento pure anco qualche scintila di refrigerio, uedendo che N. S. tiene memoria di quei comandamenti che piacque a la Santità di N. S. di darmi quando mi impose il carico di questa nuntiatura, ali quali et a tuto quello che fin hora mi è stato imposto ho di hauere esatisimam[ente] obedito, sicome si può uedere dale lettere che di mano in mano ho scrite et dale risposte che ne ho riceute, le quali sole posono più d'ogn'altra cosa bastare per fare la pieno conoscere le ationi mie, le quali, se ben sono deboli, tutauia sono piene di soma sincerità et fedeltà uerso il seruitio di N. S. Et se bene non poso negare che le male sodisfationi che ela dimostra hauere di me et le punture che mi da continouam[ente] non mi penetrino nel intimo del cuore, riceuerei nondimeno anco l'istesa morte per grandisimo premio, quando con esa si potese rimediare et sodisfare a quello che desidera la Santità di N. S., nel piisimo animo di [f. 399v] cui non poso però persuadermi che non sia restata qualche scintila di beneuolenza uerso una sua humilisima et deuotisima creatura, che per qualsiuoglia acidente non lasarà mai di riconoscere gl'immortali oblighi che le tiene, né cesarà di pregare, come del continouo fa, il sig. Dio per la sua intiera felicità et prosperità. Intorno a che non agiongerò altro, senon che con infinito desiderio sto aspetando quella licenza che con le precedenti mie suplic[he]uolm[ente] le ho dimandata, per potere presentialm[ente] uenire a rendere conto di tute le ationi mie fate in questa nuntiatura et legatione. Le cose pasano qui per S. M.tà poco prosperam[ente], esendosi inteso che quei di Parigi, dopo hauere hauta promesa dal sig. duca di Umena di pigliare la protetione loro et da acetare la carica dela guerra contra S. M.tà, si sono ridoti a quelle dimostrationi che V. S. Ill.ma haurà inteso fuori di cifra; et quel colonelo che haueua data intentione a S. M.tà di ridure quella cità al'obedientia sua, come già le ho scrito con altre mie, ha fato sapere che, ritornato a Parigi, ha ritrouati in modo mutati gli humori che non è più in man sua di esequire quello che haueua promeso; onde si crede che [f. 400r] […]rauo di fare con il Re questo oficio, così per sodisfare a questo, come anco per ricordare a la M.tà S. quello che giudico necesario per uedere se fose posibile di truouare qualche modo da quietare questo regno. Ma S. M.tà è andata diferendo et protrahendo con uarie scuse l'audienza, la quale […] non ho però dimandata con instanza se non da tre giorni in qua. In questo punto mi è uenuto a dire il sig. marsciale di Res che dimani il Re partirà di qui per Ambuosa, et che si crede che condurà seco questi signori che tiene prigioni, perché siano guardati in quel castelo, et che il giorno seguente se ne ritornarà qui. A me non ha S. M.tà fato sin qui intendere alcuna cosa, ma mi uiene deto che, non sapendo la Regina regnante questa risolutione di S. M.tà se non per le uoci che andauano per la corte, fece chiamare il gran priore et lo mandò a dimandare al Re se era uero che la M.tà S. uolese partire, et quello che ela doueua fare; in risposta di che le mandò a dire che uoleua andare a metere insieme le sue forze, ma che ela non si haueua a mouere, che pensaua di tornare presto. Mi ha anco deto il sodeto sig. marsciale che pensa di partire dimani per Italia, hauendo hauto licenza da S. M.tà di andare a' bagni a Luca [f. 400v] per medicarsi di alcune sue indispositioni; che uolea il Re che egli portase lettere al sig. duca di Sauoia perché si contentase di far consignare in man sua le piaze del marchesato di Saluzo; ma che lui […] le haueua uolute, dicendo però che, quando il sodeto sig. duca se ne contentase et così parese buono a N. S., che egli per seruitio comune lo facese, […] non ricusaria di entrarui, con risolutione però di fare in modo che né il Re né il sig. duca hauesero ca[u]sa di lamentarsi di lui […] [f. 401r] […] hauendo questa matina molto per tempo inteso che si mandaua il sig. cardinale di Borbone in Ambuosa, temendo di qualche altro inconueniente, senza dimandare altra audientia me n'andai subito a S. M.tà, et entrato nela sua camera, stando ela uestendosi nel gabineto, le feci dire che io desiderauo di parlarle prima che si partise; et fatomi entrare, le disi che, hauendole dimandata più uolte audienza senza hauerla potuto otenire, et intendendo che si mandaua nel castelo d'Ambuosa il sig. cardinale di Borbone con l'arciuescouo di Lione, et che lei medesma si partiua di qui, per sodisfare al mio debito non haueuo potuto lasare di usare questa sicurtà di andare là [a] parlare senza hauere hauta asignatione di audienza, per dirle che la pregauo di ricordarsi il graue eceso che ela haueua comeso nela persona del sig. cardinale di Guisa, che sia in gloria; di che, oltre l'ofesa del sig. Dio, era anco restata malisimo sodisfata N. S.; et che io, come ministro suo, quando ela continouase ad agiungere disordine a disordine, haurei conuenuto fare l'oficio mio, che pareua a me, poiché ela diceua di custodire questi non per farli alcun male ma solo per sicureza sua, che si potria contenta[f. 401v]re che continouasero a stare qui nel medesmo modo che erano stati per il pasato, al meno sino a tanto che uenise qualche [?ordine] da N. S. Mi rispose il Re che egli credeua, hauendo fata giustitia di quelli che uoleuano leuargli l'honore et la uita, di non hauere fato alcuno pecato, et che si sa bene che in questi simili casi non si suole perdonare anco a i propri figliuoli; che già mi haueua deto, et che hora a me lo replicaua, che né il sig. [?cardinale] di Borbone né l'arciuescouo di Lione hauriano male alcuno, ma che uoleua che non potesero anche esi fare male a lei; che già io doueuo hauere inteso che mons. di Umena s'auicinaua a queste parti, et che però ela non poteua fermarsi qui, bisognandole montare a caualo et acostarsi con le sue forze a Orliens per tenirle tute unite per potere resistere a i disegni de' suoi inimici; che però era necesario che ela si asicurase di quei prigioni, perché era certificata che in Parigi non desiderauano alcuna cosa più che la libertà del sodeto cardinale per crearlo subito Re di Francia; et che ben sapeua che N. S. medesma non lo consigliaria di fare […] per impedire che, mentre uiuerà, non ci [?sia] [?in] Francia altro Re, […] come era risolutisima di uoler fare [f. 402r] anco che fose con perdita dela uita; et si prometeua che N. S. non trouaria male che, per asicurarsi la uita, il stato et l'honore suo, ela per qualche tempo tratenise il sodeto cardinale in un belisimo castelo, doue haurà comodità di chiesa, di giardino, di buon stanze et tuti quei seruitori che uorrà hauere seco. Io disi che il mondo uedeua le esecutioni fate da S. M.tà, ma che sino a qui non s'intendeua le ragioni che aciò l'hauesero mosa. Mi dise che per il uescouo di Umans haueua mandato a darne conto a N. S., et che anco qui si publicaria una dichiaratione di tuto, dolendosi in estremo che le ationi sue fosero sempre interpretate in mal senso, et specialm[ente] da' predicatori, che erano sola causa di soleuare i popoli. Io sogiunsi che, se S. M.tà hauese publicato il concilio, hauria fermata la boca a tuti questi predicatori; sopra di che, entrata di nouo nel solite dispute, dopo molte altercationi restò in questa risolutione, di far hora spedire fra lettere patente a tuti i uescoui, facendoli sapere che lei acetaua il sodeto concilio di Trento, [?et] che loro lo facesero publicare et oseruare ognuno nela [f. 402v] sua diocesi senza agiongerli conditione alcuna o riserua; et che per il uescouo di Umans faria rapresentare a N. S. quei capi che ela desidera che dala Santità di N. S. li siano riseruati, come io per nome di N. S. le haueuo promeso. Et in mia presenza, chiamato il guarda sigilo et il primo secretario di stato, comise al'uno et al'altro che si formase questa lettera, et che a me desero una copia di esa, la quale, se mi sarà mandata, inuiarò con le prime mie a V. S. Ill.ma; et procurarò che ela si […] in buona forma et senza alcuna conditione, come mi ha promeso S. M.tà. Translation R48_en.md # R48 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Blois, January 1589]: his defence; news of Paris; the audience on the prisoners' removal to Amboise) Translation of `R48_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 399r] […] having already written enough to Your Most Illustrious Lordship about my own affairs with my last letters, and meaning not to dispute with one whom I wish to revere, [obey] and serve, it will suffice now to tell you in answer to your cipher of the 7th of this month that in so much affliction and sadness I still feel some spark of relief, seeing that Our Lord remembers the commands His Holiness was pleased to give me when he laid on me the charge of this nunciature, which, and everything that has been laid on me until now, I have obeyed most exactly, as can be seen from the letters I have written from time to time and from the answers I have received, which alone can serve better than anything else to make my actions fully known; and these, though they be weak, are nevertheless full of the utmost sincerity and fidelity towards Our Lord's service. And although I cannot deny that the dissatisfaction he shows with me and the stings he continually gives me pierce me to the depths of my heart, I would nevertheless receive death itself as a very great reward if by it what His Holiness desires could be remedied and satisfied, in whose most pious mind [f. 399v] I cannot however persuade myself that there does not remain some spark of goodwill towards a most humble and devoted creature of his, who for any accident whatever will never fail to acknowledge the undying obligations he owes him, nor will cease to pray, as he continually does, to the Lord God for his entire happiness and prosperity. On which I shall add nothing more, except that I await with infinite longing the leave I have humbly asked for with my preceding letters, so as to be able to come in person to give account of all my actions in this nunciature and legation. Things here are going poorly for His Majesty, for it has been learned that those of Paris, after obtaining a promise from the Duke of Mayenne to take their protection and to accept the command of the war against His Majesty, have come to the demonstrations Your Most Illustrious Lordship will have learned outside the cipher; and that colonel who had given His Majesty to understand that he would bring that city back to obedience, as I wrote with other letters, has let it be known that on returning to Paris he found the humours so changed that it is no longer in his power to do what he had promised; so it is believed that [f. 400r] […] to do this office with the King, both to satisfy this and also to remind His Majesty of what I judge necessary to see whether some way could be found to quiet this kingdom. But His Majesty has gone on deferring and putting off the audience with various excuses — which […] I have not however asked for with insistence except in the last three days. At this moment the Maréchal de Retz has come to tell me that tomorrow the King will leave here for Amboise, and it is believed that he will take with him these lords he holds prisoner, so that they may be guarded in that castle, and that the following day he will come back here. To me His Majesty has not so far let anything be known; but I am told that the reigning Queen, not knowing of this resolution of His Majesty except from the rumours going round the court, had the Grand Prior called and sent him to ask the King whether it was true that His Majesty meant to leave, and what she was to do; to which he sent word that he wished to go and gather his forces, but that she was not to move, as he meant to return soon. The said Maréchal has also told me that he intends to leave tomorrow for Italy, having had leave from His Majesty to go to the baths at Lucca [f. 400v] to treat some indispositions of his; that the King wanted him to carry letters to the Duke of Savoy so that he would agree to have the strongholds of the marquisate of Saluzzo handed over into his hands; but that he […] had wanted them, saying however that if the said Duke agreed and Our Lord thought it good that he should do it for the common service, […] he would not refuse to enter them, resolved however to act so that neither the King nor the Duke should have cause to complain of him […] [f. 401r] […] having learned very early this morning that the Cardinal of Bourbon was being sent to Amboise, and fearing some further mishap, without asking another audience I went at once to His Majesty, and having entered his chamber, while he was dressing in his cabinet I had him told that I wished to speak to him before he left. And when I had been let in, I told him that, having asked audience several times without being able to obtain it, and learning that the Cardinal of Bourbon was being sent to the castle of Amboise with the Archbishop of Lyon and that he himself was leaving here, I had not been able, to discharge my duty, to refrain from taking the liberty of going there to speak without having been granted an audience, in order to tell him that I begged him to remember the grave excess he had committed in the person of the Cardinal of Guise, God rest him; with which, besides the offence to the Lord God, Our Lord had also been most ill satisfied; and that I, as his minister, should he go on adding disorder to disorder, would have had to do my office; that it seemed to me, since he said he was keeping these men not to do them any harm but only for his own safety, that he could be content [f. 401v] that they should go on staying here in the same way as they had been until now, at least until some [order] came from Our Lord. The King answered me that he believed, having done justice on those who wanted to take away his honour and his life, that he had committed no sin, and that it is well known that in such cases one does not pardon even one's own children; that he had already told me, and now repeated to me, that neither the [Cardinal] of Bourbon nor the Archbishop of Lyon would come to any harm, but that he wanted them not to be able to do harm to him either; that I must already have heard that Monsieur de Mayenne was approaching these parts, and so he could not stay here, having to mount his horse and draw near to Orléans with his forces, to keep them all together so as to be able to resist the designs of his enemies; that it was therefore necessary for him to make sure of those prisoners, since he was certain that in Paris they wanted nothing more than the freedom of the said Cardinal in order to make him King of France at once; and that he knew well that Our Lord himself would not advise him to do […] to prevent there being, while he lived, any other King in France, […] as he was most resolved to do, [f. 402r] even at the loss of his life; and he trusted that Our Lord would not take it ill that, to secure his life, his state and his honour, he should for some time keep the said Cardinal in a most beautiful castle, where he will have the use of a chapel, a garden, good rooms and all the servants he wishes to have with him. I said that the world saw the executions carried out by His Majesty, but that so far the reasons that had moved him were not understood. He told me that he had sent through the Bishop of Le Mans to give an account of it to Our Lord, and that a declaration of the whole would also be published here, complaining bitterly that his actions were always interpreted in a bad sense, and especially by the preachers, who were the sole cause of stirring up the people. I added that if His Majesty had published the Council he would have shut the mouths of all these preachers; on which, entering again into the usual disputes, after many altercations he settled on this resolution: to have letters patent sent out now to all the bishops, letting them know that he accepted the said Council of Trent, [and] that they should have it published and observed each in his [f. 402v] diocese without adding any condition or reservation; and that through the Bishop of Le Mans he would put before Our Lord the heads he wishes His Holiness to reserve to him, as I had promised him in Our Lord's name. And in my presence, having called the Keeper of the Seals and the first Secretary of State, he ordered the one and the other to draw up this letter and to give me a copy of it, which, if it is sent to me, I shall forward with my next to Your Most Illustrious Lordship; and I shall see that it […] in good form and without any condition, as His Majesty has promised me. I did not fail to remind him to have it approved by the Parlement as well; but he answered me that there was no Parlement now, since he had taken away its authority […] R49, Francia 22/28, n.d. Translation R51_en.md # R51 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Tours, 27 March 1589: news of the war, Navarre's conquests, the abbé del Bene under guard) Translation of `R51_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 466r] […] yesterday evening a gentleman arrived here, sent by the Count of Soissons to the King with news that the day before, near Umans [Le Mans?], he had routed two companies of horse of Monsieur de Sagonne and Monsieur de Falandre, captains of the Duke of Mayenne, who had escaped alone into […], Monsieur de Falandre having been wounded in the [loins?] and in the [head] by such great sword-thrusts that it was feared he would die; and that the said Count had likewise captured the baggage of five companies, and hoped soon to send His Majesty some further news. His Majesty, hearing of this event while at supper, said to those who stood around the table: "And yet I must, against my will, rejoice at the ruin of my own subjects, nay at my own". They say that those of Orléans have forbidden their preachers to speak ill of the King from the pulpit, and sent out a proclamation to all the others not to name him except as King, and likewise ordered that the revenues be paid to His Majesty's treasurers, and they [?keep] the new orders of the city's magistrates. They also write that those of Amiens had driven out of the [f. 466v] city the Duke of Aumale for the insolences and extortions he committed; and that the Duke of Longueville, coming out of Saint-Quentin, had routed two ensigns of Walloons who were coming into the pay of the lords of the League. The Duke of Mayenne is still in Paris, from which, it is thought, he will not leave until the feast days are over; and having had nine pieces of artillery brought to Étampes, which, as I know, were not yet mounted on the wheels being made at Orléans, where he would have taken three more pieces; but that he had great difficulty in gathering pioneers, and that in sum His Excellency did not have so great a number of men as had first been published, since they do not reach 10,000 foot and 1,400 horse; so that here the King seems to begin to breathe again, especially hearing that the nobility is preparing in force to come and join him. All the same His Majesty greatly desires peace, foreseeing on the one hand the great ruin this war is bound to bring with it, and on the other the gains that the King of Navarre is making at this juncture, having in very few days, as I wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, made himself master of Niort, of Loudun, [f. 467r] of Lilibasar (L'Île-Bouchard), of Le Blanc [in] Berry, of Argenton and of Montmorillon, with an infinite number of villages. Guards have been posted in the house of the abbé del Bene by His Majesty's order, as he is suspected of passing information not only to those of the League, from whom he has always shown himself most estranged, but also to Navarre; and if he is convicted it could go badly for him, although many believe he will soon clear himself. […] R52, Francia 22/31, Tours, 6 April 1589 The castellan of Angers refuses the League's bribe, and Marshal d'Aumont secures the castle for the King, who writes him a letter in his own hand. The count is sent to Brittany against the Duke of Mercoeur; Alfonso Corso is in Auvergne; Épernon's command is disputed; Mayenne is still in Paris. The King keeps Holy Week and Easter devotions and touches for the scrofula. Et hogi si è deto che il colonelo San Polo sia arriuato a Gian con alcune genti, et che haueua lasciati a Fontanableo 4 regimenti di fanteria che lo seguiuano; onde molti sono entrati in opinione che mons. d'Umena potese hauere qualche pensiero d'asediare Sansera, luogo celebre per quello longo et duro asedio che patirono gli Ugonotti nel'altre guerre, prima che mons. di Montegni, che si truoua dentro per il Re con 300 fanti et con una compagnia di cauali, habia magiore comodità di fortificarsi. Ma aspetando io d'hora in hora un huomo di Parigi, sperarò di potere forse scriuere a V. S. Ill.ma qualche altro particolare d'eso mons. d'Umena prima che io spedisca questo piego. Il Nauarro, che non perde tempo et che fa mercantie de [f. 474v] trauagli d'altri, dopo hauere mostrato d'andare uerso Saumur, s'è uoltato […] Monlione, che fu ultimam[ente] preso et presidiato dal sig. duca di Niuers, et ha seco 4000 fanti et 600 cauali; pure si spera che, esendo dentro La Uardino, suo capitalisimo nimico et capitano di molto ualore, gli mostrarà intrepidam[ente] la fronte et renderà uani tuti i suoi disegni. L'abate dal Bene, che fu sequastrato in casa per i sospeti che io scrisi a V. S. Ill.ma con l'ultime mie, è stato permeso […] tuti questi dì santi et feste di Pascha d'andare a le chiese in compagnia di due huomini soli deputati dal gran Preuosto, et si crede che presto sarà liberato del tuto. L'arciuescouo di Tours, che sta nel paese d'Angiu per esere infermo et già [?otuagenario], ma prelato di gran dotrina, ha mandato fuori il preceto che la uedrà qui ocluso, il quale potria dare da dire asai a molti predicatori del regno, che già cominciano per altro ancora a contradirsi l'uno l'altro, senza alcun guadagno dela nostra fede catolica et con molto scandolo di tuti i buoni. A Parigi, in casa di quel Molano, thesoriero del Esparmi, sono stati trouati fin hora 300 milia scudi, et altri 60 milia ne deuono esere secondo un suo memoriale; onde questi danari che sono stati rubati a S. Translation R52_en.md # R52 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Tours, 6 April 1589: Angers, the war in the provinces, Épernon, Mayenne, Holy Week) Translation of `R52_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 473r] […] which; the castellan of Angers having noticed that those of the town, through the work of Monsieur de Brissac, were about to join the other confederate towns and were waiting only for the arrival of Monsieur de Bois-Dauphin to carry out their design (he was approaching the town with 100 horse and 1,200 arquebusiers), he at once wrote to Marshal d'Aumont that, to forestall and break this plot, he should with all possible speed come that way with his troops, the castellan meanwhile pretending not to be wholly averse to the offer they had then made him of […] thousand écus and of the confirmation for life of that charge, […] that he should hold the castle at their devotion — the castle that is reputed the strongest in France. Whereupon the marshal, who was […] of [Le Mans], on the news of such an important event set off at once without losing time, reached the castle, and through it entered the town at the very hour when the townsmen were beginning to entrench and rampart the houses nearest the fortress, and when Monsieur de Bois-Dauphin was already very close with his troops; at the marshal's sudden entry the townsmen were left so dismayed and overcome with fear that without further movement they showed themselves ready to obey and serve the King. The King was told of this event by a gentleman sent express, who arrived here on Easter day; His Majesty showed infinite joy at it and greatly praised the loyalty and generosity of mind of the castellan, who had stood firm against the blows of […] thousand écus, and at once wrote him a most affectionate letter in his own hand. This town is most important not only as a curb on all Brittany but also for the revenues drawn from it, which come to more than 200,000 écus a year; and so His Majesty has at once sent Monsieur d'O there to get money, and according to some will also have their arms taken from them, […] they cannot raise their horns again against [f. 473v] him. He has also sent the Count of Soissons, who was here for the feast, into Brittany, [joined] with the Duke of Montpensier, who as they say has more than 400 horse together, nearly all of them noblemen, [who] can fight the Duke of Mercœur; the latter, despite the offices made with him by the Queen his sister, has declared for the League, at which the Queen feels infinite grief for love of her husband. While His Majesty was going to mass on Tuesday, he was presented with the cornet of a company of Monsieur de Mayenne's men, which had been routed in a village near Chartres by a band of 60 of His Majesty's horse, who fell on the others at night while they were sound asleep. Those of Abbeville too have cut to pieces two companies of League arquebusiers for the outrages they were committing in their territory. It is also said, though so far without confirmation, that those of Amiens have driven out Balagny, as one who wanted to arrogate too much authority to himself, and set at liberty the mother, the wife and the brother of the Duke of Longueville, into whose hands they wanted to put back the whole government of that province. His Majesty has already written twice to the Duke of Nevers to go into Champagne and make war in that province, to divert and divide the League's forces all the more; but His Excellency has not yet accepted the charge, showing that he wants more troops than Monsieur de Dinteville now has, which as they say are about three thousand foot and 150 horse. On Thursday a courier reached the King with news that Signor Alfonso Corso had appeared in Auvergne with 4,000 foot and 300 mounted arquebusiers, part of whom would come to His Majesty and the other part would go to the relief of Burgundy, where he has been appointed by the King as his lieutenant and head of that [f. 474r] nobility, which, because none of them would obey another, had very insistently asked for a captain of valour and experience. The Duke of Épernon, as is said and publicly affirmed, has together 400 lances, 600 mounted arquebusiers and 3,000 foot, and waits for nothing from His Majesty to come and serve but his order and command. It is true he lets it be understood that he wants to exercise his charge of colonel-general of the infantry, since otherwise he cannot serve with honour, and so far His Majesty has not been willing to agree to it; and this is all I can tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship about the particulars of the war on the King's side. The Duke of Mayenne has for many days, as I have written several times, been due to take the field with his army; but His Excellency is still in Paris, waiting perhaps for his troops scattered through the kingdom to come together and for the foreign aid to be near, so as then to resolve on and undertake whatever enterprise he judges most fitting; some hold that he will go towards Beaugency and Blois, others that he will come straight this way. And today it was said that Colonel Saint-Paul has arrived at Gien with some troops, and that he had left at Fontainebleau 4 regiments of infantry following him; so many have come to think that Monsieur de Mayenne might have some idea of besieging Sancerre — a place famous for the long and hard siege the Huguenots suffered there in the earlier wars — before Monsieur de Montigny, who is inside for the King with 300 foot and a company of horse, has more opportunity to fortify himself. But as I expect from hour to hour a man from Paris, I hope perhaps to be able to write Your Most Illustrious Lordship some further particular of the said Monsieur de Mayenne before I send off this packet. Navarre, who loses no time and trades on [f. 474v] other people's troubles, after making a show of going towards Saumur, has turned […] Monlione (Mauléon?), which was lately taken and garrisoned by the Duke of Nevers, and has with him 4,000 foot and 600 horse; yet it is hoped that, Lavardin being inside, his bitterest enemy and a captain of great valour, he will show him a fearless face and make all his designs vain. The Abbé del Bene, who was confined to his house on the suspicions I wrote of to Your Most Illustrious Lordship in my last, has been allowed […] all these holy days and feasts of Easter to go to church in the company of only two men appointed by the Grand Provost, and it is believed he will soon be wholly freed. The Archbishop of Tours, who lives in Anjou as he is sick and already [an octogenarian], but a prelate of great learning, has issued the ordinance you will see enclosed here, which could give much to say to many preachers of the kingdom, who are already beginning on other grounds too to contradict one another, without any gain for our Catholic faith and with much scandal to all good men. In Paris, in the house of Molan, treasurer of the Épargne, 300,000 écus have been found so far, and another 60,000 should be there according to a memorandum of his; so this money stolen from His Majesty could keep the war going for them for some time. The Cardinal of Lenoncourt says that the Parisians have sold all his furniture and conferred two of his abbeys, because he is at court. These three days of Holy Week His Majesty attended the offices at San Francesco di Paola, at Saint-Martin and at the Franciscans, and took communion on Thursday, Saturday and Easter day, having washed the feet of the poor as usual in a great hall richly adorned, and touched for the scrofula, with other offices of piety; which will serve as the end of this […] R55, Francia 22/34, Moulins, 11 June 1589 A gentleman of the Grand Duchess of Tuscany reports that the Comte de Soissons (?) was captured in bed by the Duke of Mercoeur, and that a League count was killed by a gunpowder explosion. The King is marching on Paris, where Mayenne is and the city is barricaded, with 4,000 horse and 17,000 foot; Swiss and Casimir's cavalry are coming, and Épernon has taken Montereau. Morosini also passes on, with doubts, a rumour of a plot to kill the King. Transcription DOC_R55_D1719_1719.txt #CATALOG NAME: Segr. Mi ha deto che 'l Re mostraua grandisimo cuore, hauendo molto speso auisi dei felici sucesi dele sue genti contra quelli dela lega, et che non uoleua più sentire a parlare di pace, dicendo che S. M.tà ha in esere quatro milia cauali et dieci sete milia fanti, oltre che li Suizeri che di nuouo uengono in suo socorso erano uicini a San Gian di Lona, come anco il Casimiro, che con buon numero di caualeria era presto d'intrare in Francia; hauendo ancora questo dì il duca d'Epernone preso Montereo Faultiona, luogo molto forte. On the other side he tells of the death of the Count of [?Santignan], who was of the League: inspecting some barrels of powder at night with a light in his hand, a spark fell and set the powder alight, and he was burnt. […] that the rout at Chartres of some companies of horse of the Duke of Mayenne. He says that the King was to be at Beaugency tomorrow, and that his resolution was to go towards Paris, where the Duke of Mayenne already was, since that city is in great confusion, having already barricaded [f. 516v] all the narrow streets, and the people being in great fear and at odds among themselves. He told me that the King showed very great courage, having had very often news of the happy successes of his troops against those of the League, and that he would no longer hear talk of peace, saying that His Majesty has on foot four thousand horse and seventeen thousand foot, besides the Swiss who are newly coming to his help and were near Saint-Jean-de-Losne, as also Casimir, who with a good number of cavalry was ready to enter France; and the Duke of Épernon having taken this very day Montereau-Fault-Yonne, a very strong place. It is also said that one Georges de Voi[?], a Norman, had been taken, who had resolved to kill the King. I wanted to tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship this much, although I do not hold it all for true, since the news comes from the court, where news is always shaped to the advantage of [its] side.
