Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [x] supplied. ## Reading [f. 522r] […] in questa mia conualescenza nisuna cosa mi poteua afligere […] più che l'intendere per la lettera di V. S. Ill.ma di 29 del pasato, come in conformità m'haueua deto il mio secretario, senza però sapere alcun particolare, che mi fose stato scrito longam[ente] per ordine di N. S.; perché, non mi esendo capitate le lettere, né meno sapendo doue fare capo per hauerle, da questa segue che non solo io, con mia infinita molestia et forse con diseruitio di N. S., non posa sapere quello che mi era comandato, ma che ancora deba ragioneuolm[ente] dubitare di qualche stratagema et fraude, però [?colto] fine di che desiderase di torbidarmi quella gratia che con tanta ansietà ho procurato sempre di meritarmi dala benignità di N. S. Onde io uiuo sconsolatisimo, et non mi potrò mai dare pace finché non habia da V. S. Ill.ma quello lume di questo fato che è necesario per ubidire et seruire; del quale io la suplico con quello più humile et riuerente afeto che si posa desiderare cosa di questo mondo. Io pensauo di ritirarmi a Lione per metermi in sicuro, poi che, quando sarà publicato qui quello monitorio che di costà scriuono esere di già stato afiso in San Pietro, et che s'intenderà la partita di corte del sig. cardinale di Gioiosa et del ambasciatore di Francia, si potrà temere che a me non sia fato qualche afronto, et forsi non senza pericolo dela uita. Però, hauendo inuiato a Lione per sapere se io poteuo sicuram[ente] andare et fermarmi sino ad altro ordine di V. S. Ill.ma, prima cortesem[ente] mi fecero sapere che m'hauriano ueduto uolontieri, ma dapoi mi hano scrita una lettera con la quale mi dicono che, per leuare ogni ocasione di mala sodisfatione a quei popoli, mi pregauano di contentarmi di non stare più che tre soli giorni in Lione. Onde mi ritrouo in termine così infelice che non ho più doue poterne andare né stare; et se N. S. non si muoue a pietà con liberarmi da queste miserie, io corerò manifesto pericolo di riceuere qualche importantisimo dano con poca dignità di cotesta Santa Sede; il [f. 522v] che ho uoluto dire a V. S. Ill.ma, non perché io tema la morte, ma perché ela intenda lo stato in che mi ritrouo; et se è in piacere di N. S. che io cora questo pericolo, ecomi pronto a soportare ogni martirio. Sino a questo giorno qui non s'intende che il sodeto monitorio sia stato publicato in alcuna di quelle cità che sono nominate; né però è da marauigliarsi, se bene sono già pasate tre setimane, che il comendatore di Dio [?si] è partito da Lione per andare a Parigi, ma le strade sono così rote da soldati che non si può più a modo alcuno andare atorno. Qui si è deto che il Re era andato a Charteres, et che haueua perdonato a quella cità con molta amoreuoleza la sua ribelione, et che tute le cose di S. M.tà caminauano molto prosperam[ente]; […] dicono che i Suizeri doueuano ali 15 del presente esere a Langres, come uedrà V. S. Ill.ma dala copia di un capitolo di lettera scrita a mons. dela Guicha. Per queste nuoue, o uere o false che siano, questi popoli si sono posti in gran timore; et però, se bene prima pareua che la magiore parte inclinase a la lega, et che il gouernatore medesmo presidente auese di già segnata l'unione, hano però mutato tuti pensiero, et con la uenuta di mons. dela Guicha hano fato un solene giuramento di fedeltà al Re, dela forma che uedrà V. S. Ill.ma dala copia che sarà con questa, et scaciati tuti quelli dela lega; se bene li più afetionati et che si mostrauano più apasionati degli altri sono stati li primi a giurare di uolere morire soto l'obedientia di S. M.tà, per il quale rispeto si renderà anco manco sicuro il mio stare in questo loco. Dicono che mons. d'Umena era andato ad un castelo di un thesoriere di S. M.tà, lontano oto in dieci leghe da Parigi, nominato la Granche le [?Roe], stimato asai forte, et che l'haueua preso con speranza di ritrouarui quantità di danari, ma che per sino [f. 523r] a quella hora non haueuano ritrouato cosa alcuna. Si speraua che a questa hora l'arciuescouo Lione forse liberato con quelli danari che altre uolte ho scrito a V. S. Ill.ma, ma pare che mons. d'Epernone impedisca la liberatione. Hogi si è deto che il sig. Alfonso Corso haueua pasato il Rodano uerso Mirabelo con due milia fanti et alquanti cauali per andarsi a congiungersi con i Suizeri che uengono per il Re. Queste nuoue non mi asicuro che siano tute uere; ma io non poso scriuere a V. S. Ill.ma se non quello che intendo, et anco parcam[ente], perché se io scriuesi tuto quello che qui si dice, sarei sicuro di dirle molto più falsità che uerità. Translation R56_en.md # R56 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Moulins, mid-June 1589: the monitory, Lyon closed to him, Lyon turns royalist) Translation of `R56_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 522r] […] in this my convalescence nothing could afflict me […] more than to learn from Your Most Illustrious Lordship's letter of the 29th of last month, as my secretary had told me to the same effect, though without knowing any particular, that I had been written to at length by order of Our Lord; for, the letters not having reached me, nor knowing where to turn to get them, it follows that not only can I not know, to my infinite distress and perhaps to the disservice of Our Lord, what I was commanded, but that I must also reasonably suspect some stratagem and fraud, with [the] aim of whoever wished to disturb for me that favour which I have always so anxiously sought to deserve from Our Lord's kindness. So I live most disconsolate, and shall never be able to give myself peace until I have from Your Most Illustrious Lordship that light on this matter which is needed to obey and serve; for which I beg you with the most humble and reverent affection that can be wished for anything in this world. I was thinking of withdrawing to Lyon to put myself in safety, since, when the monitory is published here which they write from there has already been posted at St Peter's, and when the departure from court of the Cardinal of Joyeuse and of the ambassador of France is known, it may be feared that some affront will be done to me, and perhaps not without danger to my life. But having sent to Lyon to learn whether I could safely go and stay there until further orders from Your Most Illustrious Lordship, they first courteously let me know that they would have seen me willingly, but afterwards they wrote me a letter in which they say that, to remove every cause of ill feeling among those people, they begged me to be content not to stay more than three days in Lyon. So I find myself in so unhappy a plight that I no longer have anywhere to go or stay; and if Our Lord is not moved to pity by freeing me from these miseries, I shall run manifest danger of suffering some very serious harm, with little dignity for that Holy See; which [f. 522v] I wanted to tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship, not because I fear death, but so that you understand the state I am in; and if it pleases Our Lord that I run this danger, here I am, ready to bear any martyrdom. To this day it is not heard here that the said monitory has been published in any of the cities named; nor is that to be wondered at, though three weeks have already passed, for the commander of Dio[u?] has left Lyon to go to Paris, but the roads are so broken up by soldiers that one can no longer go about in any way. Here it is said that the King had gone to Chartres and had pardoned that city its rebellion with much kindness, and that all His Majesty's affairs were going very prosperously; […] they say that the Swiss were to be at Langres on the 15th of this month, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship will see from the copy of a paragraph of a letter written to Monsieur de La Guiche. At this news, true or false, these people have fallen into great fear; and so, although before it seemed that the greater part inclined to the League, and that the governor-president himself had already signed the Union, they have all changed their mind, and on the arrival of Monsieur de La Guiche they have taken a solemn oath of loyalty to the King, in the form Your Most Illustrious Lordship will see from the copy that will be with this, and driven out all those of the League; though the most attached, who showed themselves more passionate than the others, were the first to swear they would die in obedience to His Majesty — for which reason my staying in this place will become even less safe. They say that Monsieur de Mayenne had gone to a castle of a treasurer of His Majesty, eight or ten leagues from Paris, called La Grange-le-[Roy?], reckoned quite strong, and that he had taken it in the hope of finding a quantity of money there, but that up [f. 523r] to that hour they had found nothing. It was hoped that by now the Archbishop of Lyon [would be] freed with the money I have written of to Your Most Illustrious Lordship at other times, but it seems that Monsieur d'Épernon is hindering the release. Today it was said that Signor Alfonso Corso had crossed the Rhône towards Mirabel with two thousand foot and some horse, to go and join the Swiss who are coming for the King. I am not sure that all this news is true; but I can write to Your Most Illustrious Lordship only what I hear, and sparingly at that, because if I wrote all that is said here I am sure I would tell you much more falsehood than truth. […] R57, Francia 22/36, n.d. (enclosures dated "dix di giugno" [1589], Moulins) This record holds copies of papers sent to M. de la Guiche. The first says the King's Swiss army (about 12,000 Swiss and 2,000 lansquenets, some 17–18,000 men with 12 guns) is marching, paid with money lent by Strasbourg. The second is the oath of the inhabitants of Moulins to live and die Catholic and loyal to "Henri, by the grace of God King of France and Poland". DECODE's transcription D1721 (KaJo, Jan 2016) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by `research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R57_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures and, for the numbers, on the image (`R57_corrections.tsv`). The sheet carries Italian translations ("tradutione") of two French pieces: (1) a letter to M. de la Guiche, grand master of the artillery, signed "Regnault", on the Swiss army (dated "questo dì x di giugno 1589"), and (2) the oath of loyalty to Henri III taken by the town of Moulins (16 June 1589). Numbers are written in plain figures between null 8s (1500, 6000, 1589). Not in Tempesti. Spelling as the figures give it (the clerk's Italian of French names: Monbeliard, Langres, Digion, Authun, Dezize, Strasburg, Sanci, Cheseron = Chazeron); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 146 danari, 151 Francia, 152 franzesi, 165/166 quello/questo, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 221 lettere, 226 catolica). Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread. ## Reading [f. 524r] Que V. S. Ill.ma […] tradutione dela lettera scrita a mons. dela Guicha. Mio [s]ignore, quando io cercauo un huomo [?espreso] per inuiarui, io ho trouato questo portatore mesagiero di Molins, che mi ha promeso di uenirui a uedere et darui la presente, per la quale io ui farò intendere il felice suceso del mio uiagio fin qui, gratia di Dio, con buonisime nouele, che io spero, mediante la gratia di Dio, portare al Re migliori di quello che egli si aspetaua. La sua armata di suizeri [?…] a quatro leghe da Monbeliard [?…] hora che […] lasciati […] sarano a Langres […] di questo mese ala più longa; si sono al numero di tredici milia suizeri, due milia lanzquinech et 1500 raitri; il resto sono franzesi; posono esere in tuto diecisette in diecioto milia huomini, et con […] dodici pezi d'artigliaria. Questo è un strano caso del credito di S. M.tà et dele grandi oferte che gli hano fate d'huomini et di danari: la cità di Strasburg h[a] sola presta[to] […] milia scudi, de' quali mons. di Sanci ha pagato [?6000] raitri et dodici milia suizeri che seguirano questa armata sei setimane. Io ho trouato il sig. Cesare [?a] Semur et nela [?…], [col] quale ho deto ciò che gli bisogna che facia in pasando per la contea, perché […] si fa forte dela lega, [che] corre grande fortuna. Io gli ho dato un pasaporto et gli ho insegnato ciò [f. 524v] che bisogna che facia. I diti suizeri uengono a Langres, et di là io credo che e' si pasarano a [?le] porte di Digion, et di là a Authun, di Dezize. Questo dì [?x] di giugno 1589. Uostro più che humilisimo et obedientisimo seruitore, Regnault. […] tradutione del giuramento fato da quelli dela cità di Molins al dì d'hogi 16 giugno 1589, ala presenza di mons. dela Guicha, consigliere del Re nel suo consiglio priuato di stato, gran mastro dela artigliaria di Francia et luogotenente [?generale] per S. M.tà nela sua armata di stranieri di suizeri. I consoli et escheuini, manenti et habitanti dela uila et [fa]uborghi di Molins nel Borbonese, congregati nel castelo di Molins, hano unanimem[ente] fato et prestato il giuramento di fedeltà al Re nostro sire Henrico terzo, per la gratia di Dio Re di Francia et di Polonia, et nele mani di mons. di Cheseron, logotenente generale per S. M.tà nel [?gouernamento] del deto paese, et promeso sopra la loro fede, uita et honore, et nela loro lealtà et conscienza, di uiuere et morire nela religione catolica apost[olica] et romana, soto l'obidienza di S. M.tà, et di non partirsene in alcuna maniera, né intraprendere o fauorire, in che modo si sia, gli inimici del suo stato et persona, et di restare suoi fedeli [f. 525r] sogeti et humilisimi seruitori, [et] di esa et difenderla uerso et contra tuti, come esendo loro re legitimo et sourano, et ubidire ali comandamenti che li sarano fati tanto da mons. di Cheseron che altri luogotenenti generali di S. M.tà per seruitio di quello; et per questo efeto hano rinuntiato et si sono partiti da tute le promese et asociationi che potesero hauere fate in contrario, se alcune ce ne ha. In testimonio di che quelli sodeti habitanti che sanno segnare hano segnato, et per lo risguardo di coloro che non sanno segnare hano dati li loro nomi, che sono stati trascriti dal notaio dela signoria di Borbones[e], nel fine dele presenti. Translation R57_en.md # R57 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Moulins, June 1589]: two French papers sent to M. de la Guiche, in Italian translation) Translation of `R57_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 524r] [For] Your Most Illustrious Lordship […] translation of the letter written to Monsieur de la Guiche. My lord, while I was looking for an express messenger to send you, I found this bearer, a messenger from Moulins, who promised me to come and see you and give you the present letter, by which I shall let you know the happy outcome of my journey so far, thanks be to God, with very good news, which I hope, by the grace of God, to bring to the King, better than he expected. His army of Swiss [?…] four leagues from Montbéliard […] now that […] left […] will be at Langres […] this month at the latest; they number thirteen thousand Swiss, two thousand landsknechts and 1,500 reiters; the rest are French; in all they may be seventeen to eighteen thousand men, with […] twelve pieces of artillery. It is a strange thing, the credit of His Majesty and the great offers of men and money made to him: the city of Strasbourg alone [has] lent […] thousand scudi, out of which Monsieur de Sancy has paid [?6,000] reiters and twelve thousand Swiss who will follow this army for six weeks. I found Signor Cesare [?at] Semur and in the […], to whom I said what he must do in passing through the county, because […] is holding out for the League, [which] runs a great risk. I gave him a passport and showed him what [f. 524v] he must do. The said Swiss are coming to Langres, and from there I believe they will pass by [?the] gates of Dijon, and from there to Autun, [and] Decize. This [?10th] day of June 1589. Your more than most humble and most obedient servant, Regnault. […] translation of the oath taken by those of the town of Moulins on this day, 16 June 1589, in the presence of Monsieur de la Guiche, councillor of the King in his privy council of state, grand master of the artillery of France and lieutenant [?general] for His Majesty in his army of foreigners, of Swiss. The consuls and échevins, residents and inhabitants of the town and [fau]bourgs of Moulins in the Bourbonnais, assembled in the castle of Moulins, have unanimously made and taken the oath of fidelity to the King our sire Henri the Third, by the grace of God King of France and of Poland, and in the hands of Monsieur de Chazeron, lieutenant general for His Majesty in the [government] of the said country, and have promised on their faith, life and honour, and on their loyalty and conscience, to live and die in the Catholic, apostolic and Roman religion, under the obedience of His Majesty, and not to depart from it in any way, nor to undertake or favour, in any way whatever, the enemies of his state and person, and to remain his faithful [f. 525r] subjects and most humble servants, [and] to [?…] it and defend it towards and against all, he being their legitimate and sovereign king, and to obey the commands that shall be given them, whether by Monsieur de Chazeron or other lieutenants general of His Majesty, for his service; and to this effect they have renounced and withdrawn from all promises and associations they may have made to the contrary, if there are any. In witness whereof those of the said inhabitants who can sign have signed, and as regards those who cannot sign, they have given their names, which have been transcribed by the notary of the lordship of Bourbonnais at the end of these presents. […] R58, Francia 22/37, Moulins, 5 July 1589 (dup.) The King has taken Jargeau ("Giorgio") and its Loire bridge, hanged a captain and pardoned the governor. Other Loire towns have surrendered, and the King is heading for Paris, where four faubourgs are said to favour him. Mayenne has taken Montereau and Nemours is raising money at Lyon for the League's Swiss. Transcription DOC_R58_D1722_1722.txt #CATALOG NAME: Segr. Si è inteso che il Re habia preso Giorgio, hauendo quei di dentro aspetato il canone prima che uolersi rendere; et perché il logo è debolisimo, se bene d'importanza per hauere un ponte di pietra sul fiume dela Loira et per esere quatro sole leghe lontano da Orliens, dicono che S. M.tà non habia uoluto acetar loro alcuna conditione, ma liberam[ente] a sua discretione; con tuto ciò l'ha preseruato dal saco, non senza molta dificoltà et mala sodisfatione de' soldati, che, non esendo pagati, sperauano almeno di guadagnare qual[che] cosa in quella ocasione. Entrata [?…] S. M.tà con i principali caualieri che sono seco, ha fato impicare un capitano che fu incolpato d'esere stato quello che haueua persuasi i popoli a non si rendere, et di farli abrusciare un borgo di fuori per leuare la comodità da alogiamenti al esercito, oltre che questo capitano poco tempo prima haueua tochi danari per fare gente in seruitio del Re, et nondimeno, da poi riceuti, si era uoltato in fauore dela lega. Haueua anco S. M.tà condanato nela medesma pena il gouernatore di quella tera; ma, condoto al logo del suplicio, hauendo diuersi signori intercesso per lui con dire che era bon soldato et che nel auenire hauria seruito a S. M.tà, […] il perdonò; ma però si tiene tutauia prigione. Ha anco S. M.tà fato carcerare alcuni de' principali dela tera per hauere danari. S'intende che quello di Gian, tera dieci leghe discosta da Giorgio, doue è un altro ponte di pietra sopra il fiume dela Loira, ueduto che il Re s'apresaua a quella uolta, haueuano inuiato a dimandare socorso al sig. duca di Umena; ma non l'hauendo hauto, senza aspetare l'esercito haueano inuiato a rendersi a S. M.tà, come fano quasi tute l'altre tere di quei contorni, che non si posono [f. 533v] longam[ente] tenire, la quale li haueua amoreuolm[ente] riceuti. Nel medesmo tempo dicono che il Nauarro haueua con inganno preso Pluuiers, et oue si era incaminata S. M.tà, che hora si ritroua padrona di tuti i ponti che sono sopra la Loira, da Orliens et Nantes in poi; et dicono che sia risoluta d'andare diritam[ente] uerso Parigi. Per doue dicesi che sono anco incaminati li suoi suizeri, che di nuouo uengono incontro, ai quali haueua S. M.tà inuiato il duca di Longauila in iscambio di mons. dela Guiscia, che era prima stato destinato a questa carica et partito ancora con buona compagnia; ma due giorni dopo hebe lettere del Re con le quali gli comandaua di ritornarsene in queste parti del Borbonese, dicendo che presto gli inuiar[i]a gente per fare la guerra in Ouernia contra quelli dela lega. Si dice da altra parte che il duca di Umena haueua ripreso Montereo et anco castelo […], et che s'incaminaua per andare a combatere li suizeri del Re prima che si posino unire con S. M.tà, et che mons. di Nemours usaua ogni diligenza a Lione per hauere danari per dare ai suizeri che uengono in seruitio dela lega, ne li quali dicono esere giunti a Ciamberi in numero di undici milia, tuta buona gente, la quale non uole pasare oltre se non le uengono dati danari; ma che subito [?hauuti] s'incaminarano per la Borgogna ala coda de gl'altri suizeri heretici per combaterli. Gli afetionati del Re dicono che S. M.tà ha, senza li suizeri et raitri, 30 milia persone in esere, et che il sig. duca di Umena ha pochisima gente; et gli afetionati dela lega dicono che egli ha più di 25 milia persone, et che il Re non ne ha sei milia, et che i suizeri heretici, che gli altri dicono che […] molto inanzi, non hano ancora trouata uia per entrare in Francia. Onde io non saprei che afermare a V. S. Ill.ma, se bene io [f. 534r] ho parlato con uno del duca di Niuers, che mi dice hauere lui medesmo lasato i sodeti suizeri a Langres già molti giorni; ma egli ancora potria dire il falso. In questo punto è uenuto a uedermi mons. di Forges, che partì mercordì pasato da Pluuiers, [?doue] dice che il medesmo giorno era anco partito il Re per Etampes, hauendo hauto auisi dal Nauarro che i borghi di quella tera erano tuti per S. M.tà, et che già haueuano anco guadagnata la fosa et piantata l'artigliaria, intanto che sperauano molto presto di hauere la tera. Dice anco che quatro de i borghi di Parigi, cioè san Marceo, san Uitor, san Iaches et san Germano, haueuano fato sapere a S. M.tà che teniuano per lei, et che, uolendo andare a quella uolta, che loro l'hauriano molto alegram[ente] riceuuta; et che per questo rispeto, subito che sarà terminata l'impresa di Etampes, senza aspetare più longam[ente] i stranieri, il Re col suo esercito s'incaminarà a quella uolta, intendendosi che il duca di Umena era a Meos un poco amalato. Referisce ancora che il conte di Soisone, che era prigione nel castelo di Nantes, si era saluato con metersi in una cesta, nela quale soleuano portargli il mangiare in castelo: cosa asai dificile da credere. Non ho uoluto lasare di dire a V. S. Ill.ma quello che questo mons. mi ha referto, se bene io gli presto poca fede, esendo molto partiale seruitore del Re. [?Adeso] certo che uiene dala corte, hauendomi [p]ortate lettere del sig. Galeazo Fregoso, et dele nuoue si rimete a quello che intenderò da eso mons., non mi è parso douer lasare di darne conto a V. S. Ill.ma, che le meterà in quella consideratione che parerà ala singolar sua prudenza. Translation R58_en.md # R58 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Moulins, 5 July 1589: Jargeau taken, the King's march on Paris) Translation of `R58_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 533r] […] this […] of things here, I shall not fail to tell you what is heard, although one can learn the truth only with great difficulty, since everyone speaks according to his own feeling. It is heard that the King has taken Jargeau, those inside having waited for the cannon before being willing to surrender; and because the place is very weak, though important for having a stone bridge over the river Loire and for being only four leagues from Orléans, they say His Majesty would accept no conditions from them, only [surrender] freely at his discretion; nevertheless he saved it from the sack, not without much difficulty and the displeasure of the soldiers, who, not being paid, hoped at least to gain something on that occasion. [Having entered] […] with the principal knights who are with him, His Majesty has had a captain hanged who was accused of having persuaded the people not to surrender, and had a suburb outside burned, to take away the convenience of quarters from the army; besides, this captain had shortly before received money to raise men in the King's service, and nevertheless, after receiving it, had turned to the League's side. His Majesty had also condemned the governor of that town to the same penalty; but when he had been brought to the place of execution, and several lords had interceded for him, saying he was a good soldier and would in future serve His Majesty, […] pardoned him; but he is still kept prisoner. His Majesty has also had some of the principal men of the town jailed to get money. It is heard that those of Gien, a town ten leagues from Jargeau, where there is another stone bridge over the Loire, seeing the King approaching, had sent to ask help of the Lord Duke of Mayenne; but not having had it, without waiting for the army they had sent to surrender to His Majesty, as almost all the other towns round about do, which cannot [f. 533v] hold out long; and he had received them kindly. At the same time they say that Navarre had taken Pithiviers by a ruse, and that His Majesty had set out there; he now finds himself master of all the bridges on the Loire, Orléans and Nantes apart; and they say he is resolved to go straight towards Paris. It is said that his Swiss are also on the way there, who are coming to meet him again; to whom His Majesty had sent the Duke of Longueville in place of Monsieur de la Guiche, who had first been appointed to this charge and had already set out with a good company; but two days later he had letters [from the] King ordering him to return to these parts of the Bourbonnais, saying that he would soon send him men to make war in Auvergne against those of the League. It is said from the other side that the Duke of Mayenne had retaken Montereau and also castle […], and that he was on his way to fight the King's Swiss before they could join His Majesty, and that Monsieur de Nemours was making every effort at Lyon to get money to give to the Swiss coming in the League's service, of whom they say eleven thousand have reached Chambéry, all good troops, who will not go further unless they are given money; but that as soon as [they have it] they will set out through Burgundy on the tail of the other, heretic, Swiss to fight them. The King's supporters say that His Majesty has, without the Swiss and reiters, 30,000 men in being, and that the Lord Duke of Mayenne has very few troops; and the League's supporters say that he has more than 25,000 men and the King not six thousand, and that the heretic Swiss, who others say […] well ahead, have not yet found a way to enter France. So I would not know what to affirm to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, although I [f. 534r] have spoken with one of the Duke of Nevers's men, who tells me he himself left the said Swiss at Langres many days ago; but he too might be saying what is false. At this moment Monsieur de Forges has come to see me, who left Pithiviers last Wednesday, [where] he says the King had also left the same day for Étampes, having had word from Navarre that the suburbs of that town were all for His Majesty and that they had already won the ditch and planted the artillery, so that they hoped to have the town very soon. He also says that four of the suburbs of Paris, namely Saint-Marceau, Saint-Victor, Saint-Jacques and Saint-Germain, had let His Majesty know that they held for him, and that if he wished to go that way they would receive him very gladly; and that for this reason, as soon as the enterprise of Étampes is finished, without waiting longer for the foreigners, the King will march that way with his army, it being understood that the Duke of Mayenne was at Meaux, somewhat ill. He reports further that the Count of Soissons, who was a prisoner in the castle of Nantes, had escaped by putting himself in a basket in which they used to carry his food into the castle: a thing very hard to believe. I did not want to fail to tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship what this monsieur has reported to me, although I give him little credit, being a very partial servant of the King. [?Now] certain [news] coming from the court, having brought me letters from Signor Galeazzo Fregoso, and he referring for the news to what I shall hear from the said monsieur, it did not seem to me I should fail to give an account of it to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, who will give it the consideration your singular prudence thinks fit. of Lorraine's army and the oath (Francia 18/3, ff. 233r, 234r–235v) Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription (TimB, Dec 2015, `R17_transcription_decode.txt`) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by `research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R17_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures and, where a figure itself was in doubt, on the DECODE images (crops; `R17_corrections.tsv`). No contemporary decipherment on the DECODE images: the two "cleartext" images (ff. 231r, 232r) are covering letters in clear signed by the archbishop of Nazareth (Fabio Mirto Frangipani), Paris 27 August 1586 and 27 July 1586; the cipher is not dated. Its content (the King's call to the dukes of Lorraine and Guise, revoked on Épernon's advice; Schomberg and Bellièvre sent to the Duke of Lorraine over the oath of his troops; the Queen Mother fearing war among Catholics) fits 1587 (DECODE dates the record 1585–88). The writer is the nuncio ("io non ho mancato di dar animo a la Regina Madre"). Page order: 233r, then 234r–235v. 233v is not imaged and 234r begins in mid-sentence, so 233r and 234r may not be consecutive; 235v ends in mid-sentence (the rest is not in the record). Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 116 Regina Madre, 129 duca di, 146 danari, 151 Francia, 161 quanto, 165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 217 corriere, 221 lettere, 226 catolici, 227 heretici). Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [word] supplied. ## Reading [f. 233r] […] per procurare di leuare le dificultà et difidentie et introdure l'unione, che sola può giouare ai presenti bisogni […]. […] il marsciale di Res, che teme asai questi acidenti, in un longo ragionamento che ha fato meco hogi conclude che, se N. S., come padre dela christianità, non interpone uiuamente l'autorità sua così con il Re come anco con gli altri, non uede rimedio che questo regno non si perda. Onde io, per intendere quello che egli uolese dire che potese in questo caso fare la Santità di N. S., dopo longo circuito di parole dise che questo era ricercare d'intendere le pretensioni del'una et l'altra parte, dar la ragione et il torto a che l'hauese, procurando poi con la soprema sua autorità di fare che ognuno si contenti del honesto; et che non c'era altro rimedio a questo male. [f. 234r] […] come […] quanto era stata grande l'alegreza che tuti i buoni haueano sentito dela risolutione fata dal Re di chiamare il duca di Loreno e quello di Guisa con le loro forze ad unirsi con la M.tà S., tanto anco è stato magiore il dispiacere che si è sentito dela mutatione fata da S. M.tà, la quale, per quanto si dice, haueua presa la prima deliberatione con il parere del suo consiglio, in tempo però che mons. di Epernone non c'era presente, esendo alhora andato con una grosa banda di gente per tentare di fare qualche [?danno] a' inimici. Ma esendo egli ritornato et intendendo di questo ordine già ispedito, ha saputo tanto dire che ha persuaso S. M.tà a riuocarlo, cometendo esa perciò con lettere di propria mano al marsciale di Res che, se bene per altre spedite a lui dala segretaria lo comandaua d'andare con le genti ch'ha seco ad unirsi con il duca di Guisa, nondimeno si guardi molto bene, per quanto ha cara la uita, di farlo; e per disturbare anco la uenuta del duca di Loreno spedì a la uolta sua un gentil'ho[f. 234v]mo, rinouando la dificoltà, di già acomodata, del giuramento, con dire [?che], quando egli uoglia che tute le sue genti lo prestino, deba restar sei me[si in] suo paese. Al che eso signore duca rispose che, et per il primo ordine che S. M.tà gli diede d'andarlo a ritrouare, et per il protesto mandatogli a fare dopo per mons. di Sciumbergh, che se in questo suo bisogno non andasero tute le sue genti a socorerla si saria doluta di lui, et che egli perciò, et per dimostrare ancora l'afetione et diuotione che portaua a S. M.tà, haueua con molto interese trouati danari per pagare le sue genti, come ha già fato, et per andarla a seruire; che ela non haueua ragione di domandare giuramento a le genti pagate da lui, douendole bastare quello che lui steso faria a la S. M.tà; che però egli era risoluto di uenire in ogni modo. Et esendo di questa risposta rimasto il Re malisimo sodisfato, ha con duo corieri, l'uno apreso al'altro, [f. 235r] replicato al sodeto duca che non deba entrare in Francia; ma non potendo con tuto ciò rimouerlo, stando egli fermo di uolere in ogni modo [uenire], esendo di già pasato tanto inanzi che si troua a […] leghe lontano di qu[i], gli ha di nuouo spedito S. M.tà un protesto che, se uenirà più oltre et non si ritirarà fuori del suo regno, uoltarà contra di lui tuti questi eserciti; né ancora si sa se questo haurà a bastare per fare che si ritorni. Di che [?la] Regina Madre sta con molto trauaglio, temendo [?che] non segua qualche inconueniente iremediabile, et però gli ha spedito hieri mons. di Beleure, pregandolo con grandisima instanza a uolere dare ogni sodisfatione al Re, o col fare prestar il giuramento dale sue genti a S. M.tà, ouero col ritornarsene nel suo paese; et hora si sta aspetando la sua risposta, la quale, se sarà che in ogni modo uoglia uenire [f. 235v] senza il giuramento, si tiene per sicuro che il Re sia per uoltare le sue forze contra di lui, tenendo per certo che l'intentione sua et degli altri dela lega sia uolta a leuarsi la corona; et di già si discorre da persone di molta qualità che posa uenire a Parigi con intentione di far ridure un consiglio deli tre Stati del regno per dichiarare il Re inhabile al gouerno. Il che, se bene non pare uerisimile in tempo che si trouano tanti heretici nel regno, nondimeno la Regina Madre, nel ragionamento che ho hauto hogi seco, ha dimostrato di temere asai, se continua il duca di Loreno a uoler uenire inanzi, di qualche infelice suceso. Translation R17_en.md # R17 — English (nuncio's cipher enclosure, Paris, 1586–87: the Duke of Lorraine's army and the oath) Translation of `R17_reading.md`; holes as there. ## Translation [f. 233r] […] to try to remove the difficulties and mistrust and to bring in union, which alone can help the present needs […]. […] the Maréchal de Retz, who greatly fears these events, concludes, in a long conversation he had with me today, that unless Our Lord, as father of Christendom, interposes his authority vigorously both with the King and with the others, he sees no remedy to keep this kingdom from being lost. [So] I, to understand what he meant that His Holiness could do in this case — after a long circuit of words he said that this meant seeking to understand the claims of the one party and the other, giving right and wrong to whoever had it, and then working, with his supreme authority, to make everyone content with what is fair; and that there was no other remedy for this evil. [f. 234r] […] as […] great as was the joy that all good men had felt at the resolution taken by the King to call the Duke of Lorraine and the Duke of Guise with their forces to join His Majesty, so much greater has been the displeasure felt at the change made by His Majesty. He had taken the first decision, so it is said, with the advice of his council, but at a time when Monsieur d'Épernon was not present, having then gone with a large band of men to try to do the enemy some [harm]. But when he returned and learned of this order, already sent out, he managed to say so much that he persuaded His Majesty to revoke it; and His Majesty therefore ordered the Maréchal de Retz by letters in his own hand that, although by other letters sent to him from the secretariat he had been commanded to go with the troops he has with him to join the Duke of Guise, he should nonetheless take great care, as he values his life, not to do it. And to hinder the coming of the Duke of Lorraine as well, he sent a gentleman [f. 234v] to him, renewing the difficulty, already settled, about the oath, saying [that] if he wishes all his troops to take it, he must stay six months [in] his own country. To which the said Lord Duke answered that, both because of the first order His Majesty gave him to come and join him, and because of the protest sent to him afterwards through Monsieur de Schomberg (that if in this need of hers all his troops did not go to her help she would have cause to complain of him), and also to show his affection and devotion to His Majesty, he had at great cost found money to pay his troops, as he has already done, and to go and serve her; that she had no reason to ask an oath of troops paid by him, since what he himself would give to Her Majesty should suffice; and that he was therefore resolved to come in any case. The King, very ill satisfied with this answer, has [f. 235r] sent two couriers, one after the other, to repeat to the said Duke that he must not enter France. But being unable even so to move him, since he stands firm in wishing to [come] in any case and has already advanced so far that he is […] leagues from here, His Majesty has again sent him a protest that, if he comes any further and does not withdraw out of his kingdom, he will turn all these armies against him; and it is not yet known whether this will be enough to make him turn back. [At this] the Queen Mother is in great distress, fearing [that] some irremediable mishap may follow, and so yesterday she sent Monsieur de Bellièvre to him, begging him most urgently to give the King every satisfaction, either by having his troops take the oath to His Majesty or by returning to his own country. His answer is now awaited; and if it is that he wants to come in any case [f. 235v] without the oath, it is held for certain that the King will turn his forces against him, being sure that his intention, and that of the others of the League, is aimed at taking the crown for themselves. And people of great standing are already saying that he might come to Paris intending to have a council of the three Estates of the kingdom assembled to declare the King unfit to govern. Although this does not seem likely at a time when there are so many heretics in the kingdom, nonetheless the Queen Mother, in the conversation I had with her today, showed that she greatly fears some unhappy outcome if the Duke of Lorraine goes on wishing to advance. I have not failed to encourage the Queen Mother, and if I see that things are heading towards fighting among Catholics I shall not fail to do all that is in me to prevent it, as I do not omit even now to do all those offices that I can […]

DECODE R116 is the nuncio’s copy, for the Cardinal of Como, of a letter from Philip II with two passages in figures. They read, in Italian, with the Spain nunciature’s ordinary cipher as reconstructed by Ajaydas Devadas and checked here against our own transcription, re-read against the full-resolution scans: the King on joining the Pope’s league with the Emperor, and on the affairs of Pitigliano. 1,298 of 1,324 cipher tokens (98.0%) read as sense; six single-context code groups stay open. 0̇3 2+ 10 3 20 9 6 4+ 0̇8 2̇ … o uisto il foglio mandatomi a parte soprale cose di pitigliano read · 98.0% of 1,324 cipher tokens · six code groups open Madrid → Rome (Cardinal of Como) · numerical cipher · spring 1573 Philip II’s letter to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573 from Philip II Go to the full text ↓ The nuncio’s copy of a letter from Philip II with two passages in figures, deciphered in Italian with the Spain nunciature’s ordinary cipher as reconstructed by Ajaydas Devadas; 98% of the cipher tokens fall in words, six code groups stay open, and the written-out reading builds coherent sentences but reads at 90.7% of its words, under the 95% a complete reading needs. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: partial (98% of the cipher) · On the map With Ajaydas Devadas (key or decipherment used) At a glance External key matched · partial (98% of the cipher) The letter Philip II to the nuncio Niccolò Ormanetto, bishop of Padua, spring 1573: the nuncio’s copy, sent to the Cardinal of Como and docketed 17 June 1573, with two passages in figures. Where Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 7, ff. 303r–304r and address leaf; DECODE R116, catalogued as not yet deciphered (catalogue item 259). The cipher The Spain nunciature’s cifra ordinaria : two digit signs per letter, dots and a closing zero shape the signs, a cross-stroke on 2, 4 or 5 ends a word, and a short list of code groups. How it was deciphered Ajaydas Devadas reconstructed the key and sent it on 1 October 2026. The decoder was rebuilt here and run on our own transcription, re-read against the full-resolution scans on 5 October; 20 shuffled keys read at most 32.9%. What it says The King on joining the Pope’s new league with the Emperor, sending a special envoy; and on Pitigliano, where he wants “la pace et quiete di tutta Italia”. Measured 1,298 of 1,324 cipher tokens fall in words read as sense (98.0%; passage A 97.8%, B 98.4%). Counting five single-context code values as unread too gives 95.0%. Counted by words of the written-out reading, with its doubtful and supplied words as holes, 90.7% read (24 October 2026): coherent sentences, but under the 95% a complete reading needs. Still open Six code groups with one context each: 32, 2̇88, 84, 42, 53 and 3̇22 where it stands for per (26 tokens). Credit Key reconstructed by Ajaydas Devadas (email, 1 October 2026).

f. 303r: the end of the King’s clear text (“… los puntos que de parte de Su S. en ellas me escrivis”) and the start of passage A, marked “A.” in the margin. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 7 f. 303r, via DECODE R116. f. 303r gives the King’s titles and the address to the bishop of Padua. He has received the nuncio’s letters but could not answer them sooner “por mi indispusicion, de que al presente (gracias á Dios) quedo bueno y levantado”. The nuncio may write this to His Holiness by the courier now leaving for Italy, and thank God for him. The King will answer the points raised on the Pope’s behalf. Passage A follows. An Italian slip pasted over the heading reads Della sanità ragguagliata del Re . f. 304r has three numbered clear answers. (1) Jurisdiction: the King has written to Don Juan de Zúñiga, his ambassador in Rome, and refers to that. (2) The order for dividing the Turkish slaves held in Rome has been sent. (3) He will look into the affairs of the bishop of Liège that the Pope recommends. Passage B follows, marked “B.”. The Roman summary at the head lists only the three clear points. The address leaf reads All’Ill.mo et R.mo S.r mio Col.mo Mons.r Ill.mo Cardinal di Como · à Roma · Per servitio di N. S.re , with the docket 73 / a 17 Junii . The ciphered passages are what the King or the nuncio kept out of the clear copy.

Line 1 of A: 8̇222t 40 2̇4t 0̇6 4084t 975t 32t 2̇0̇… . The cross-stroke (DECODE’s “1”) is joined to the digit before it. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 7 f. 303r, via DECODE R116. 1,098 digits in 23 lines, from DECODE’s 2020 transcription, spot-checked against the images: A 756 symbols, B 568. Dots over digits are frequent: 0̇ 148 times, 4̇ 46, 5̇ 36. A cross-stroke follows 2 (74 times), 4 (59) and 5 (51), rarely anything else. There is no word division and no pair structure: the parity of every second digit is 60/40 at both offsets, line by line. Over 31 distinct symbols the index of coincidence is 0.055. That is too low for plain substitution into Italian or Spanish.

Both passages decode with one key to Italian, written without h or doubled letters. Bracketed words are code groups. The start of passage A: [Quanto] al far [officii] a lo [Imperatore] mio fratello [perché] … nella nuova [lega] proposta da [S.S.tà], mandando io persona espressa [perché] tratti [questo] [negotio], io ho ordinato che si facino sopra [questo] particular [quelli] buoni [officii] che mi sono parsi convenienti … Sarà [bene] che [S.S.tà] [ancora] dalla parte sua facia il medesimo, [come] voi dite che si offerisce. As to making representations to the Emperor my brother to join the new league proposed by His Holiness: I am sending a special envoy to treat of this business, and I have ordered that the representations I thought fitting be made on this point … It will be well for His Holiness to do the same on his side, as you say he offers. Ho visto il foglio mandatomi a parte sopra le cose di Pitigliano, et inteso particolarmente [tutto] [quello] [che] è passato … Et io desidero [tanto] la [pace] et [qui]ete di [tutta] [Italia], il servitio di Dio, che procurarò [quanto] sarà in me, [come] ho fatto sempre, che si levi affatto ogni occasione che sia [?] alterarla; ma non [?] finora inteso, né avendomene avisato lo [Imperatore], del stato in … I have seen the sheet sent to me separately on the affairs of Pitigliano, and understood in detail everything that has happened … I so desire the peace and quiet of all Italy and the service of God that I will do all in my power, as I always have, to remove every occasion that might disturb it; but nothing has been learned so far, nor has the Emperor informed me of the state of… The passage ends there. This is Gregory XIII’s league against the Turks, which collapsed in 1573 when Venice made its separate peace; the Pitigliano business (the Orsini county in southern Tuscany) has not yet been checked against sources of 1573. The Spanish frame and the Italian passages are consistent: the King’s answers to the Pope, rendered in Italian for Rome.

The key is the one that reads R118 : the Spain nunciature’s cifra ordinaria , rules printed by Meister (1906, p. 265), table reconstructed by Ajaydas Devadas and emailed on 1 October 2026. Two signs for each letter: letter signs letter signs letter signs a 40, 4̇ i 3, 0̇8 r 0̇5, 8 b 4, 0̇2 l 80, 2̇ s 20, 9̇ c 50, 7̇ m 2, 0̇1 t 0̇7, 9 d 0̇4, 7 n 90, 6̇ u/v 10, 1̇ e 60, 5̇ o 0̇3, 6 z 0̇9 f 0̇6, 5 p 30, 8̇ g 7̈, 3̇ A dot over a lone digit is part of the sign. 0̇x is a dotted zero followed by x; x0 is x closed by an undotted zero. An undotted 0 closes the digit before it; a dotted 0 opens the next. A 2, 4 or 5 with a cross-stroke ends a word: it is the “1” that DECODE’s transcription writes after those digits. A small list of code groups covers common words: 6̇11 tutto, 2̇44 quello, 66 che, 8̇22 quanto, 4̇88 Sua Santità, 63 Imperatore, 97 officii, 87 non, 5̇11 tanto. Five or six consonant signs close each passage as nulls, and a few syllables ( 7̇2̇2 = qui) are dotted. Five of the code values are certain (they also occur in R118) and about sixteen are probable; eight are guesses and three are open.

Our own transcription. The decoder was rebuilt here from the description of the key ( dec_aj.py ) and applied to DECODE’s transcription ( r116_cipher.txt ), not to Devadas’s files. Passage B comes out as “o uisto il foglio mandatomi a parte soprale cose di pitigliano … procuraro quanto sara in me come o fato sempre”. A control. With only the sixteen well-supported code groups substituted, 597 letters score −3.02 per letter under the Italian model. The best of 200 keys with the same structure and the letters shuffled scores −6.69 (mean −8.50). The measure ( measure.py , 5 October 2026). Every cipher token is counted, digits and word-end strokes alike (1,324). A word is credited only if its letters split into words attested in Renaissance Italian (the lang/ it-renaissance and it-nunziature corpora, written as the cipher writes), or it is a code group with an adopted value, or the final nulls. On DECODE’s transcription unchanged this gives 94.3%; on the transcription re-read against the scans, 98.0%. The same measure on 20 keys with the letters shuffled gives a mean of 23.0% and a maximum of 32.9%. The sibling. The same key reads R118 (1576–77), a different ciphertext whose leaf carries the contemporary decipherment. History. The league and the Emperor fit spring 1573; Pitigliano remains to be checked.

Six code groups , each with a single context, not in R118 and on no key sheet (26 of 1,324 tokens): 32 and 2̇88 in se ben dal canto mio l’ho [32] de la buona [2̇88] havuta ; 84 and 42 in sarà [84] che S.S.tà [42] dalla parte sua facia il medesimo , where bene and ancora fit but so do other words, so they are counted unread; 3̇22 in che sia [3̇22] alterarla (it is Italia after tutta , but per is wanted here); and 53 before finora , perhaps a dittography. The King’s minute (AGS Estado, Rome papers, 1573) or the Rome decifrato would settle them. Five further values rest on one context each (62 canto , 48 essere , 4̇22 perché , 47/93 tutta , 3̇22 Italia ), grade M. Counted as unread they bring the measure down to 95.0%. The five suspect signs of the 1 October reading were checked on the full-resolution scans on 5 October. Two are the writer’s slips ( entri , particular ), one is a struck sign with a dotted 7 written above ( col Imperatore ), one is a stroke-4 ( che si oferisce ), and one, lost in a paper hole, is a dotted 0 by shape ( desidera ).

The first attempt tried the five known nunciature keys and two families of annealer. All failed because the units were wrong: the cross-stroke was taken for a digit and the zero rule was missed, so the polyphonic and homophonic models were fitted to the wrong symbols. What was tried: Keys tried Spain nunciature 1568 , Lasry’s polyphonic key (one digit stands for two letters, 0 null), which deciphers the Alessandrino letters. It gives nonsense here. Crivelli, nuncio in Spain 1561 (Meister, p. 259): polyphonic, with codes ending in 9, 3 or 5. Nonsense. “Cifra col cardinal di Como” (Meister VI.1, pp. 262–264, from Ottob. 3208–09). Its Spain nomenclator includes secretaries Zayas and Idiáquez, Cardinal Deza, Antonio Pérez and the Cruzada, and it marks codes by crossing or hooking the second digit, much like the stroke here. Letters with an odd second digit do not parse. Idiáquez and Deza date it to Sega’s nunciature after 1578. Meister VI.2 and VI.3 . VI.2 comes with the rules of “la cifra ordinaria di mons. nuntio di Spagna”: null 8 at the end of every word, a dot over the codes for che, chi, qua, que, qui, et, mente . Its letters do not parse. VI.3 (nuncio in Spain to nuncio in Flanders) uses only even digits, and this text has 330 odd ones. Ciphertext-only attacks and their controls Homophonic substitution over three symbol sets (digit; digit with dot and underline; dotted 0 and the stroke joined to the digit), solved by simulated annealing against Italian and Spanish 4-gram language models with a letter-frequency penalty. The same solver largely recovers an Italian control text of the same length with 28 symbols. On R116 no meaningful text comes out in any setting. Polyphonic “one digit, two letters”, the 1568 family, with the pairs fitted by annealing and each digit’s value chosen by a Viterbi pass. On 1,100 digits of an Alessandrino letter it recovers 7 of Lasry’s 9 pairs at −2.18 per letter. On R116 it scores −2.30 to −2.47, and five restarts give five different keys, in either language, and again with 1 as a null. A first quadgram solver failed its own control (it preferred repetitive strings to the true text), so its results were discarded. Only runs that recovered their control text are counted above.

Philip II to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573, ASV Spagna 7 ff. 303r-304r (DECODE R116) read in part A copy of Philip II's letter to the nuncio with two cipher passages. B: he has seen the separate sheet on the affairs of Pitigliano and desires the peace of all Italy, and will do all he can to remove any occasion that might disturb it. Context: Gregory XIII's league against the Turks, which collapsed when Venice made peace in 1573. Two letters printed by the HMC in 1895 with 59 figures of a numerical cipher and no decipherment. The key was recovered from the adjacent cleartext: a regular alphabet in blocks of three consecutive figures (consonants from 7, vowels from 64), nulls 91–111 and a small nomenclator. Seven of the nine code numbers were identified from Wentworth’s dispatches in Knowler’s Strafforde’s Letters (1739). 65 · 35 · 21 · 26 · 59 28 · 69 · 49 · 50 · 70 · 44 11 · 79 · 85 · 35 · 12 · 69 · 28 · 29 · 79 · 44 Ireland / England · numerical cipher with nomenclator · 1634–35 Lord Maltravers to the Earl of Ormonde from Lord Maltravers → to Earl of Ormonde Go to the full text ↓ Dorking, 13 September 1634 and Whitehall, 22 January 1634/5 · HMC, Calendar of the Manuscripts of the Marquess of Ormonde , i (1895), pp. 28–29 The letter alphabet, the nulls and the layout of the key were recovered from 59 printed figures and the cleartext around them; seven nomenclator codes were then identified from Wentworth’s own dispatches Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial The letter Two letters from Henry Frederick Howard, Lord Maltravers, to James Butler, Earl of Ormonde, reporting court news around the 1634 Irish Parliament. Where Printed by the Historical Manuscripts Commission in 1895 without a decipherment; S. Tomokiyo lists them among ciphers with no known solution. The cipher A numerical cipher, 59 figures. Consonants run in alphabetical order, three figures each from 7, vowels from 64; figures below 91 are letters, 91–111 nulls, and 112 and above a small nomenclator. How it was read The key was recovered from the printed cleartext around the figures. Wentworth’s dispatches, printed by Knowler in 1739, describe the same events in plaintext. What it says Kildare came to England “because he was angry” and the King refused to see him; in January 1635 Ormonde is to be a councellor, in exchange for Sir Piers Crosby. Still open Seven of the nine nomenclator codes are identified; the two parties in one clause about Crosby (185, 149) are not.

Maltravers (1608–1652), heir of the Earl of Arundel, sat in the Irish Parliament of 1634 and was a friend and correspondent of the young Earl of Ormonde. His letters from England report court news; the sensitive parts (the quarrel between the Earl of Kildare and the Lord Deputy, Wentworth, and what was being written about Ormonde himself) are in figures. The originals are in the Ormonde papers (now National Library of Ireland); the only witness online is the HMC calendar, whose figures were checked against the page scans. HMC Ormonde MSS, old series i (1895), p. 28: the letter of 13 September 1634. Image: Historical Manuscripts Commission, Calendar of the Manuscripts of the Marquess of Ormonde, old series i (1895), p. 28, via the Internet Archive (calmarqormonde01greauoft). 13 Sept 1634: ...he came over because he was 65, 35, 21, 26, 59, 98, 113, 186, 108, 143, refused to see him because he brought no 28, 69, 49, 50, 70, 44, 89, from 186, 99. 22 Jan 1634/5: You desire to know what 93, 185, 95, hath written unto 99, 149, concerning 98, 10, 44, 79, 47, 8, 59, for whom 270 thus hereafter ... 95, 186, 98 hath written unto 98, 218, 97 much in praise of 100, 174, 103 in general, and particularly for his good carriage in 111, 95, 221, and upon his motion 93, 31, 174 99 is to be 64, 99, 11, 79, 85, 35, 12, 69, 28, 29, 79, 44, in which courses 174 shall do well to continue.

Nulls, 91–111. Nine values (93 95 97 98 99 100 103 108 111); seventeen of their eighteen occurrences stand at the edge of a cipher run or beside a code number — 93 185 95 , 99 149 , 95 186 98 , 98 218 97 , 100 174 103 , 111 95 221 . Tomokiyo's guess is confirmed: they pad the names. Nomenclator, 112 and above. 113 143 149 174 185 186 218 221 270, each standing alone; 270 is a code being assigned ("for whom 270 thus hereafter"). Letters, below 91. The spelled runs contain 49 50 , 69 70 , 28 29 , 11 12 — doubled letters written with adjacent figures. Each letter therefore owns a block of consecutive figures, the commonest design of the period (Tomokiyo's survey of Wentworth-circle ciphers notes the same "three or six figures to each letter in regular arrangement").

Three cribs fix the grid. "brought no 28 69 49 50 70 44 89 " must be letters ; "is to be 64 [null] 11 79 85 35 12 69 28 29 79 44 " gives a councellor ; "concerning 10 44 79 47 8 59 , for whom 270 thus hereafter", the man whose fortunes were about to "go worser" in January 1635, is Crosby (Sir Piers Crosby, purged from the Irish Council by Wentworth that winter). All three fit one arrangement, and an exhaustive scan of 42 regular grids (start 1–11, block size 2–4, vowel blocks 2–6) ranks it first by English quadgram score: b c d f g h k l m n p q r s t w x y z 7–9 10–12 13–15 16–18 19–21 22–24 25–27 28–30 31–33 34–36 37–39 40–42 43–45 46–48 49–51 52–54 55–57 58–60 61–63 a e i o u nulls codes 64–… …69, 70… … 79–… 85–… 91–111 112 + (names, words) Consonants: the nineteen of the 24-letter alphabet (i = j, u = v). Attested figures: b 8 · c 10 11 12 · g 21 · l 28 29 · m 31 · n 35 · r 44 · s 47 · t 49 50 · y 59 · a 64 65 · e 69 70 · o 79 · u 85. The vowel block sizes (five each from 64, or a = 3 and the rest 6) cannot be fixed from this text; 1–6 are unattested.

Red = spelled in cipher · blue = nomenclator code, value from the documents in §05 · nulls dropped 13 September 1634. My lord of Kildare is long ago in England though I have not seen him; it is said he came over because he was angry [113 = with] [186 = the Lord Deputy] ; [143 = the King] refused to see him because he brought no letters from [186 = the Lord Deputy] . 22 January 1634/5. You desire to know what [185] hath written unto [149] concerning Crosby , for whom 270 thus hereafter; of which I can give you no account at all, only by what I hear it is like to go worser with him rather than better. [186 = the Lord Deputy] hath written unto [218 = Secretary Coke] much in praise of [174 = Ormonde] in general, and particularly for his good carriage in [221 = Parliament] , and upon his motion [174 = Ormonde] is to be a councellor , in which courses [174 = Ormonde] shall do well to continue. The history agrees with the decipherment. George FitzGerald, 16th Earl of Kildare, fell out with Wentworth over the Kildare estates during the 1634 Parliament and crossed to England that summer; Sir Piers Crosby, having opposed the Lord Deputy in the same Parliament, was removed from the Irish Council early in 1635; and Ormonde, who had backed Wentworth in the Commons debates, was sworn of the Irish Privy Council in January 1635, the month of the second letter. 186 as the Lord Deputy is used three times consistently; 174 as Ormonde ("your lordship") three times; 221 as Parliament follows "his good carriage in". The next section fixes 143, 218 and 113 from Wentworth’s own letters; 185 and 149 remain open.

Wentworth’s dispatches were printed in 1739 by William Knowler as The Earl of Strafforde’s Letters and Dispatches . Volume I covers 1634–35, and the events behind both cipher passages are in it, in Wentworth’s own words, with Secretary Coke’s answers in the margin. Wentworth to Coke, October 1634 (i. 309). “The Earl of Kildare went away from hence without the privity of this State, and in seeming displeasure against me … within an hour after, he put to sea for England. Indeed I should not have mentioned thus much, but that I hear his Majesty refuseth to admit him to kiss his hand , which I acknowledge as a respect to me.” Margin: “The Earl of Kildare shall be sent back as is advised.” That is Maltravers’s sentence of 13 September: Kildare angry [113] the Lord Deputy ; the King refused to see him because he brought no letters from the Lord Deputy. So 143 = the King , and 113 is the connective between “angry” and the Lord Deputy (“with”; Wentworth’s word is “against”). Wentworth to Coke, Dublin 22 December 1634 (i. 352–3). “In the Higher House, there is my Lord of Ormond, that hath as much advantage of the rest in judgment and parts, as he hath in estate and blood; and one, who upon my observation since I came hither, expresseth very good affections to the Crown and Government; so as I hold him a person of consequence, and fit to receive some mark of his Majesty’s favour, and humbly offer it to his Majesty’s wisdom, whether it were not seasonable to make him a Counsellor … so as I should think we had got much the better by the exchange of the Earl of Ormond for Sir Piers Crosby .” Margin: “for the Earl of Ormond, your Lordship shall receive herewith his Majesty’s warrant to swear him Counsellor, according to your advice.” Maltravers, a month later: the Lord Deputy hath written unto [218] much in praise of [Ormonde] in general, and particularly for his good carriage in [Parliament], and upon his motion [Ormonde] is to be a councellor . The match is clause for clause: 186 = the Lord Deputy , 174 = Ormonde , 221 = Parliament (Wentworth’s “Higher House”), and 218 = Mr Secretary Coke , the addressee of the dispatch. The dispatch was for the King and Coke’s marginalia are the King’s answers, so “the King” is the alternative for 218, but the King already has 143. 270 is the code Maltravers assigns to Crosby after spelling the name once. James Howell, writing to Wentworth from Westminster on 1 January 1635, has Crosby in England and “in a bravery resolved never to see Ireland while your Lordship governs”: the court gossip behind “like to go worser with him”. code value evidence 186 the Lord Deputy (Wentworth) three consistent uses; Knowler i. 309, 352–3 174 the Earl of Ormonde three uses; Knowler i. 352–3 and Coke’s marginal 221 the Parliament “good carriage in” ↔ “in the Higher House” 143 the King “refused to see him” ↔ “his Majesty refuseth to admit him to kiss his hand” 218 Mr Secretary Coke (or the King, through Coke) addressee of the 22 December dispatch 270 Sir Piers Crosby assigned in the text 113 with / against connective between “angry” and the Lord Deputy 185 unidentified party “what 185 hath written unto 149 concerning Crosby”; not the Lord Deputy 149 unidentified party same clause; not the King or the Lord Deputy

A115, Nr. 14 from Mogilev of 16 June 1942, carries the discriminator ARTTN and is in another daily key. Bletchley decrypted it at the time: it is the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre’s report of the destruction of Borki, and the reason Schmeh’s 2021 list marks the group “partially solved”. It is a different cipher with its own page, the police radiogram of 16 June 1942 , which gives the decrypt, the odd letter count and the failed key-free alignment of the decrypt to the ciphertext. That failure matters here only because the June text was the one plaintext that might have supplied the pairs a known-plaintext attack needs; even aligned, it would give the June boxes, not the February ones, and would help with 27 February only if police boxes turned out to be built from keywords.

Weierud reads the discriminator as the last three letters of the group, in any order, and cites the Bletchley note that four discriminators were issued with each daily key. Taken that way, with the O/Q confusion allowed for in one group, the seven parts of 27 February use exactly four: discriminator parts WOJ D33 ( KFWOJ ); D67 part 1 ( OWQWJ , read OWOWJ ) OSX D34 part 1 ( DNOSX ); D67 part 2 ( WNSXO ) ANR D34 part 2 ( DRANR ); E72 part 2 ( LENRA ) WYY E72 part 1 ( SBWYY ) Two parts of one message carry different discriminators, and the Mogilev and Proskurov traffic shares them. The four are therefore four names for one key, and all seven parts, 970 letters, can be attacked together. C43’s XOS is also OSX , which suggests either that it is misdated by a year or that a key ran for more than one day; Weierud already noticed the shared indicator. C43 was kept out of the pooled text.

Two manuals survive and both were consulted here: the OKH draft Schlüsselanleitung zum Doppelkastenschlüssel of 2 December 1940 and the OKW issue of December 1941. They agree. There are two 5×5 boxes. The plaintext is written in double lines of 17 letters, and the pairs are the letters that stand one under the other; a remainder too short for a double line is split in half. Each pair is enciphered twice with the same boxes. When the two letters of a pair fall in the same row, each cipher letter is taken from the right. The spelling rules are CH → Q, ß → SZ, and the hyphen written STRIQ. The reference implementation, dk.py , enciphers both manuals’ worked examples letter for letter (the 1941 manual prints tylhu on p. 5 for the tvlhu it has correctly on p. 6). The Army’s “NI” field cipher, as NSA’s Cryptologic Quarterly describes it, is the same scheme with 21 -letter lines and the left neighbour for same-row pairs; its worked examples (EU → VR → QZ, en → FL → NC, ea → HK → TT) also reproduce exactly. Which variant the police used is not documented, so every attack here was run under both. That February 1942 is the double-box period at all rests on Hanyok: the police changed from double transposition to double Playfair between September and early November 1941, and Bletchley found the new system easier to decrypt. The cross-row identity The double pass is what matters. After the first pass the first letter of a pair has been taken from box B, but the second pass looks it up in box A. So each letter is used by its position in both boxes. Write each letter as four coordinates: its row and column in A and its row and column in B. Deciphering a cipher pair (c1, c2) in the cross-row case gives the intermediate pair v1 = A[ B-row of c1 ][ A-col of c2 ] v2 = B[ A-row of c2 ][ B-col of c1 ] and the plaintext pair p1 = A[ B-row of v1 ][ A-col of v2 ] p2 = B[ A-row of v2 ][ B-col of v1 ] Every step mixes an A-coordinate with a B-coordinate. Between the two passes sits the map from each letter’s cell in box A to its cell in box B, a random permutation of the 25 cells. Section 06 shows that this permutation stops the attacks; the size of the key does not.

A failed search proves nothing without a control, so each attack on the double encipherment was first run on synthetic text: 970 letters of German text enciphered twice with random boxes by mksyn.py and dk.py , in parts of the same lengths as the real ones. The same search recovers a synthetic spelling in 35 seconds no alignment The single-encipherment results exclude that hypothesis: the pooled text is 970 letters, far more than a single-pass double box needs, and the best key found is nowhere near German. The double-encipherment results exclude nothing about the plaintext, because the same methods fail on text where the answer is known. They measure the attacks only. The alignment result is informative. A115’s repeated cipher pairs are real (section 02), and the aligner, given a synthetic text spelled in one of the ways it tries, finds it. On A115 no combination of spellings, separators, numbers, layout and length makes every repeated cipher pair fall on a repeated plaintext pair. Either the words enciphered differ from Bletchley’s rendering, through abbreviation, order or extra matter such as a longer address, or the police layout differs from both manuals.

This matches the public record. Hill-climbing solvers by Lasry, Norbert and others break single-pass double-box texts of 100 to 150 letters, and the Army’s Truppenschlüssel, a simplified one-pass relative, has been broken ciphertext-only from surviving messages. No published attack breaks a double pass through the same boxes. The synthetic runs here show where the difficulty lies. The true key is the optimum, but a narrow one. Under the unigram score the true key is the best key (−1.221). Its basin is only about eight to ten swaps wide. Under the quadgram score it is narrower still: annealing started four swaps from the true key does not climb back. Outside the basin there is nothing to climb. Random starts stall at −1.39 to −1.42. The local optima they reach share no row or column structure with the true boxes: measured as the precision of their row and column groupings against the key, they score about one in six, which is chance. Size is not the problem. Giving the solver the true permutation of cells between box A and box B, which leaves only the labelling of the letters to find, does not help: it still stalls at −1.42. The difficulty is the conjugation through a random cell permutation (section 04). The likely mechanism: a key that is partly right gives intermediate letters that are wrong, and the second pass sends those to unrelated cells, so partial correctness earns no score. Known plaintext changes this, because it removes the second pass from the scoring. kpsolve.cs enciphers each known plaintext pair once forward, deciphers its cipher pair once backward, and asks the two intermediates to agree row by row and column by column. Each half is a single pass, which gives the local search a gradient; on the synthetic controls about 80 pairs are enough.

not solved Closed; the ciphertext-only attacks failed. Two routes would reopen it. what why it would work About 80 plaintext–ciphertext pairs for one key kpsolve.exe then recovers the boxes, and the key reads all seven parts of 27 February. The source would be Bletchley’s own decrypts of that day’s traffic, which should be in TNA HW 16/17 (verbatim German police decrypts; HW 16/18 is May–June 1942), not online; or a long stereotyped preamble or address common to the messages. For A115 the pairs need the exact German wording that was enciphered. A115 aligned It would also settle the police layout, lines of 17 or 21 and the left or right neighbour, and show whether police boxes were random or built from a keyword. Keyword-built boxes would open a keyword search on 27 February. A new ciphertext-only idea for a second pass through the same boxes Nothing tried here provides one, and nothing published does.

It reports a quarrel between the captain general of the sea, the intendant and the commander of the marine guards. Where Archives nationales, AE/B/I/226, fols. 92v–93. The inventory (FRAN_IR_053989) marks the passage “[suite en chiffre, non transcrite]”. Catalogue item 541. The cipher The Cadiz consulate’s numerical table, 1 to 465 in alphabetical order, with syllables first and then words for each initial. Code words are underlined in the dispatch. How it was deciphered The table was rebuilt only from the interlinear decipherments of five neighbouring Partyet letters, frozen, and checked on held-out glossed letters of January and February 1721: about 235 numbers covered and no disagreement. What it says “On dit que ce dernier n’agit pas comme il le devroit pour le bien du service”: someone is said not to act as he should for the good of the service, and this is to be decided shortly, both sides having written to Madrid. Still open Two endings are lost in the binding ( dernie[r] , déci[dé] ), and it is not settled whom “the latter” names. The images were not seen here. Credit Brice Dudout rebuilt the table, read the passage and ran the checks, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents.

Partyet writes from Cadiz about the quarrel between the captain general of the sea, Pedro de los Ríos, the intendant Patiño and Dormay, commander of the marine guards. When he comes to judge them, he switches to cipher. The register holds no decipherment of these six lines, and the Archives nationales inventory still marks them “not transcribed”, although the neighbouring letters carry the Council’s own decipherment between the lines.

The consulate’s cipher of about 1719–1722 is a numerical table in alphabetical order: 140 da, 141 de, 142 di, 143 do, 144 du, 145 dont, 146 dans, and so on. Several numbers stand for the same letter or syllable, and code words are underlined. The table was rebuilt from the clerks’ interlinear decipherments of five Partyet letters (31 March and 4, 11, 12 and 19 May 1721, fols. 86–118v) and frozen before it was tested. Its values were then checked on held-out glossed letters of 6 and 27 January and 23 February 1721, about 280 numbers, with the contemporary decipherment compared number by number. The caveat is that the gloss sits on the same image as the numbers, so the transcription was not fully blind. One group, 392, is underlined and absent from every glossed letter of 1717–1722. It was first restored as service from the phrase “pour le bien du s…” and its place among the s words. It has since been found in three glossed letters of the same table, including the identical sequence “pour le bien du service” in a letter of 7 June 1725. We checked here on 2 November 2026 that the table and the decryption file agree; 35 of 38 numbers match their value in the line, and the exceptions are the marked alternates s/se and ci/cy and one number missing from the table.

The six cipher lines read: “On dit que ce dernier n’agit pas comme il le devroit pour le bien du service; c’est ce qui sera décidé incessamment, les uns et les autres ayant écrit amplement à Madrid sur le tout.” Who is “the latter”? Grammatically the last named is the captain general, but the reproach may be aimed at Dormay, who has just been mentioned. The cipher does not settle it.

Of 35 words, 33 are certain and two are probable: dernie[r] , whose last number is lost in the binding, and déci[dé] , cut at the edge of the binding. Group 392 ( service ) is now attested in three other glossed letters. The transcription was made by AI from the Archives nationales images and was not checked by a person against them here.

A report to the exiled King of Bohemia on Colonel Fuchs’s recruiting in Württemberg, its cipher deciphered between the lines at the time. Brice Dudout found that its letter cipher is the alphabet of the Johann Casimir–Camerarius letters moved by three, fitted the shift on one page and tested it on the next (13 of 13 letters). The content is the period decipherment; the key and the family of keys are the new part. 32 29 65 26 11 66 67 59 20 · 25 60 14 62 61 38 21 59 21 … verharret · begleitet … Carl Pawel → Frederick V · two-digit letter cipher with homophones and a code · 25 November 1624 · key identified from the period glosses Carl Pawel to Frederick V, 25 November 1624 Go to the transcriptions ↓ A Palatine agent reports to the exiled King of Bohemia on a colonel’s recruiting, in a cipher deciphered at the time; its letter key turns out to be a sibling’s alphabet shifted by three. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 6 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: complete With Brice Dudout (transcription) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (earlier solution) · Daniel Bourdeau (pointer to a source) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · complete The letter Carl Pawel to Frederick V, King of Bohemia and Elector Palatine in exile, “den 25 Novemb. 1624”, signed “741 / Carl Pawel”: a report on Colonel Fuchs’s recruiting in Württemberg. Where Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich, Clm 10382 (Collectio Camerariana 32), n. 46, digitised microfilm MDZ bsb00112117, scans 181–182. Halm (1874) dates it 15 November. Not on DECODE. The cipher Three systems mixed: a code of three- and four-digit numbers (2737 Ob. Fuchs, 3515 Stuttgart, 1732 Mansfelt, 2389 Liga), a few signs (a3 = zu, mm = so, rr = und), and runs of two-digit numbers that spell words, three numbers per letter. How the key was found The letter runs use the alphabet of the Johann Casimir–Camerarius letters with every number lowered by three. The shift was fitted on the glosses of scan 181 (0.921 of the letters, next best 0.737), frozen, and measured once on scan 182: 13 of 13 letters against 0.154 for the best shuffled key. What it says Fuchs came to Stuttgart and stayed there, accompanied; the letter speaks of the “pars victrix”, of someone who rode back, of Mansfeld and the League. The content is the period decipherment’s, not new. Still open The code groups and the clear German text are not transcribed; the held-out part is only 13 letters. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) transcribed the runs, identified and tested the key, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The decipherment is the clerk’s of 1624.

In the autumn of 1624 Frederick V, driven from Bohemia and the Palatinate, lived in exile at The Hague, and his agents reported on the armies being raised in the Empire. Carl Pawel’s report concerns Colonel Fuchs’s recruiting in Württemberg. It is part of the Camerarius collection in Munich, the papers of Ludwig Camerarius, Frederick’s councillor. The letter mixes clear German, a numerical code for names and common words, a few signs, and runs of two-digit numbers separated by commas that spell words letter by letter. A decipherment written above the lines at the time covers the code and the runs.

The runs use the same letters, in the same order and with three homophones per letter in blocks of consecutive numbers, as the Johann Casimir–Camerarius cipher of the same volume; only the origin differs. Starting from the casimir1629 key as it was frozen for that target, one parameter was fitted on the glossed runs of scan 181: the shift that best renders the glosses. A shift of 3 renders 0.921 of the letters; the next best, 4, renders 0.737, and the 22 others 0.42 or less. The shifted key was frozen before scan 182 was looked at. Scan 182 has only two letter runs, degen and brauchen : 13 letters, all rendered by the frozen key, against 0.154 for the best of 200 permuted keys. The held-out part is small, so the stronger evidence is the whole letter: over all 17 runs (102 letters), the only differences from the glosses are the clerk’s spellings ( vorharret , gunnen , scaf , uf ), a gloss written victix for victrix , and an added h in a gloss ( rückh ). One unglossed run reads geritten .

The held-out test rests on 13 letters. Numbers 1–10, 53–55 and 83 and up were not seen; by the casimir1629 key, 83 and up would be nulls. Two runs (181.14, 181.15) were re-read at high magnification after the measurement and now agree with their glosses; the frozen key and the measurement are unchanged. The code groups and the clear German text are not transcribed, so the runs are given as a word list with their glosses, not as a letter. One reader (an agent) transcribed from a 1,334-pixel microfilm; no human has checked the numbers against the images.

Despatch no. 117 of the Venetian ambassador in France (ASVe Busta 30, DECODE R1871), catalogued as an English letter of 1555: one page of continuous digits. Transcribed here (1,839 digits) and segmented into 612 three-digit groups, 211 different, from a non-alphabetical table of about 300 codes; annealing solvers with an Italian model gave no text.
