Daniel Bourdeau · posted 14 October 2026 · updated 27 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Paolo Bonavoglia (earlier solution) · Brice Dudout (pointer to a source, key corrected) · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Sebastiano Foscarini, Venetian ambassador in France, to the Doge, Paris, 11 September 1680: despatch no. 117, “P.S. Sola”, one page of cipher. Where Archivio di Stato di Venezia, IT ASVe 0045 010 Busta 30 f. 4; DECODE R1871. Catalogued as “England?”, 1555, under catalogue 264 together with R1873, a Rome despatch of 1558 in another cipher. The cipher Continuous digits that fall into three-digit groups: 612 groups, 211 different, from a table of about 300 codes. Not an alphabetical table. How it was tried Transcribed from the images, segmented, then attacked with several annealing solvers and an Italian language model. No Italian came out. Why it resisted One page is too short for a blind solution of a table this size, and the key is not on DECODE. Brice Dudout found the table is a syllabary in blocks of five consecutive codes with the blocks out of order, which an ordered-syllabary solver cannot find. What it says From Paolo Bonavoglia’s decipherment: rumoured Spanish reinforcements in the Milanese, and Louis XIV’s reported plan to raise the Pinerolo garrison to 6,000 men. Credit The decipherment is Paolo Bonavoglia’s. Brice Dudout reported his page back online; Satoshi Tomokiyo’s note on DECODE R1872 first pointed to him. Until 14 October 2026 this despatch shared an entry with R1873, Alvise Mocenigo’s Rome despatch of 1558: a different cipher, with its own page .

The two images of R1871 show one page of continuous digits under “Ser.mo Principe”, marked “#117 P.S. Sola” and signed “Sebastian Foscarini Amb.r”, dated at Paris in 1680. The dorse is addressed to the Doge and docketed “11 Sett. 1680 … n.o 117”. The record is not English and not of 1555: DECODE’s region and date seem to have been copied from the neighbouring record R1872 (Giovanni Michiel, Brussels, 1555). The DECODE images are not in the public domain and may be published only with the archive’s permission, so none are reproduced here. The strip above is from the transcription made here.

The page holds 23 lines and 1,839 digits. The rare digits 0, 7, 8 and 9 occur only in one position, and within each line that position is constant modulo 3 over long stretches: the digits are three-digit groups, and the jumps in phase are slips of the pen or of the transcription. Segmented that way the page gives 612 groups (593 of three digits), 211 of them different. The first digit runs 1–5 (6 is rare), the second 1–6 and the third 0–9, so the table holds about 300 codes between 110 and 569. The commonest groups are 156 (22 times), 517 (20), 256 (19), 152 (16) and 459 (15). Bonavoglia says Foscarini’s cipher served at both Paris and Madrid, and calls it too regular and orderly. The table here is not ordered alphabetically, though: Sukhotin’s vowel test puts vowel-like and consonant-like codes side by side (151 and 156 vowel-like, 152–154 consonant-like).

Other segmentations: two-digit pairs (the gap parity is random) and self-delimiting tokens ending in 5–0 or 6–0. Annealing gave no Italian. A monotone annealer for an ordered syllabary, 12 seeds, scored with a clean Italian 4-gram model. It recovers a synthetic ordered control only in part, and gives the same non-Italian text on every seed for the real page. Free annealers, one letter per code and letter or syllable per code, 14 seeds: fluent-looking text that changes with every seed, the mark of overfitting. 211 free code values against 612 groups is beyond what an Italian language model can pin down for a homophonic, syllabic table. The page needs the key (in the ASVe Cifre, chiavi e scontri ; the only Venetian key records on DECODE, R1788–R1790, are 16th-century tables and do not match), more ciphertext in the same key, or Bonavoglia’s decipherment.

Paolo Bonavoglia’s page on this despatch was offline during the attempt. Brice Dudout reported it back online on 27 October 2026, and its text is saved in the repository with an English translation. Bonavoglia gives the original as ASVe Senato, Dispacci Francia, filza 171A, and the Doge’s chancery decipherment as filza 166. He worked the table out from this and other despatches. It is a postscript written after the despatch was signed. Foscarini passes on a report he cannot yet confirm: the Spaniards are adding troops in the Milanese, and Louis XIV means to raise the Pinerolo garrison to 6,000 men of the old regiments and spread 16,000 men over Dauphiné and Provence. The Duke of Mantua’s illness and a feared Spanish move on Casale are given as reasons, and munitions are said to be reaching Pinerolo by way of Savoy. Bonavoglia judges it a false alarm. Brice Dudout rebuilt the table, which Bonavoglia does not publish: a syllabary in blocks of five consecutive codes, one consonant per block with the vowels in order (b 115, n 142, r 151, ch 164, f 224 …), the bare vowels on X56 (a 156, e 256, i 356, o 456, u 556), and a few words (167 con, 368 non, 200 a new paragraph). Learnt on lines 1–15 of the transcription made here and applied to lines 16–23 held out, it agrees with Bonavoglia’s text at 94.9% of the letters. The table is in the repository folder ( dudout/table_blocks.json ), with his decoding of this transcription.

Three number groups that Bonavoglia leaves open (“[Francesi?] 269?”, “114?” and the closing 202.106.100). The key is not rebuilt here, and Bonavoglia’s text is not aligned group by group with the transcription made here: his ciphertext viewer still returned an error on 27 October 2026. Dudout’s table points at two places in the transcription to re-read on the image: the group 114 at lines 18–19, and the middle of line 22, where 3/5 and 2/0 are the likely confusions. The group 269 (Bonavoglia’s “[Francesi?]”, once) stays open in his table too.

Bracketed items are his open readings, kept as he gives them. --> # R1871, Sebastiano Foscarini to the Doge, Paris, 11 September 1680, despatch no. 117, P.S. sola: English translation Most Serene Prince, After the despatch was signed, a report was sent to me. Although I cannot give it full faith, having no time to look for confirmation, the weight it carries means I must not fail to pass it on to Your Serenity. On the reports that keep coming from Italy that the Spaniards are considerably increasing their troops in the Milanese, I am told that the King, who has a great number of soldiers under arms, has resolved to reinforce the garrison of Pinerolo up to six thousand men of the old regiments, and to distribute sixteen thousand fighting men in Dauphiné and Provence, so as to be ready, should the occasion arise, stronger than the Spaniards themselves. It is not unlikely that the news written to me by a confidant of mine at court is true. These precautions may have been advised by the illness of the Duke of Mantua, by the suspicion that the abbé Morel keeps alive of some sudden accident to his life, and by the rumour that during his last illness the Spaniards had meant to push five or six thousand men into Casale. I am also given to understand that munitions continue to be carried to Pinerolo from [the French? 269?], but these will be the metals I already mentioned in my letters of [114?], which were being brought from the sea by way of Savoy, and for which passports had also been requested. I shall watch so grave a matter as closely as it needs, and shall try to sift the reports so as to give a better account of them to Your Serenity in the next post, assuring you that I spare no diligence in doing my duty. 202.106.100 Paris, 11 September 1680. Sebastiano Foscarini, Ambassador Key: table_blocks.json

A Venetian despatch in a numerical syllabic cipher, catalogued on DECODE (R1874) with sender, recipient and date unknown. The record’s own images hold the chancery’s complete contemporary decipherment, which was transcribed and checked against the cipher by paragraph marks and one repeated group run. Attempts to recover the key from the ciphertext failed, and it was not rebuilt. 672 2133 6210 2190 6219 637 2127 conte di Olivares Madrid → Doge and Senate of Venice · numerical syllabic cipher, Italian · 26 October 1628 Alvise Mocenigo to the Doge, Madrid 1628 to Doge Giovanni Cornaro Go to the full text ↓ Archivio di Stato di Venezia, IT ASVe 0045 010 Busta 30 f. 174; DECODE R1874. Catalogued as an undated ciphered letter from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient. It is a despatch of Alvise Mocenigo, Venetian ambassador in Spain, dated Madrid, 26 October 1628. The Venetian chancery’s complete decipherment of it is imaged in the same record; the text here is transcribed from that decipherment and checked against the cipher. It is calendared in CSP Venice 21 no. 515. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Alvise Mocenigo, Venetian ambassador at Madrid, to the Doge, 26 October 1628; the clear text names Spinola, La Rochelle and Monterrey. Where ASVe Busta 30 f. 174; DECODE R1874, 16 images: the despatch, a clerk’s decipherment, a second enciphered copy, and the address leaf. The cipher A syllabic nomenclator: groups of 5 or 6, an optional 1–4, then two digits, about two letters of plaintext per group. How it was read From the chancery’s own decipherment (images 8955–8959), checked against the cipher by paragraph mark 6499 and the thrice-repeated run for “conte di Olivares”. What it says The Calendar of State Papers, Venice, vol. 21, no. 515, covers it: Cottington’s journey dropped after Buckingham’s death, and Rubens negotiating a truce with the Dutch. Still open The key was not rebuilt. Ciphertext-only annealing and alignment gave nothing; it needs a group-exact transcription and more anchors.

8951–8954 : the despatch, addressed “Ser:mo Principe”. Clear news paragraphs (the Nuncio Monti, the Marquis of Vigliena, Spinola, a rumour that Monterrey had died at Genoa) alternate with long cipher paragraphs marked 8 and ‡ in the margin. 8955–8959 : the decipherment, in another hand. It gives the whole letter in clear, clear passages included, with the ciphered paragraphs numbered 6, 7, 8 and 9. 8960–8964 : a second copy, enciphered with different groups (1,405 against 840 for the same text), dated “Madrid li 26 Ott:re 1628”. DECODE’s transcription gives the year as 1606. 8965 : address leaf, numbered 74. 8966 : a deciphered page of Mocenigo’s despatch of 29 October 1628, CSP Venice 21 no. 520 (long consultations on English and Dutch trade, a licence said to have been got by a Jesuit for some 100,000 crowns). The DECODE images are not in the public domain and may be published only with the archive’s permission, so none are reproduced here.

The groups are numbers written as clusters. The looped sign that looks like b is the period’s 6, and the s -like sign is a 5, which DECODE’s transcription renders as “13” or “21”. Every group has the form 5 or 6, then an optional 1–4, then two digits. After the first digit only 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 occur. The two copies have about 2,245 groups of 355 kinds. The group 6499 marks the edges of the numbered paragraphs. Each group stands for about two letters of plaintext: paragraph 6 (“Et già si è publicato… di ogni gran Casa di Spagna”) has 386 groups for about 760 letters, and paragraph 7 (“Continuo io… in alcun tempo”) has 245 for about 445. That makes it a syllabic cipher or nomenclator, not a simple homophonic alphabet. Recovering the key from the ciphertext alone failed. Letter-by-letter homophonic annealing against a Renaissance Italian model gave gibberish, although the same solver decrypts a synthetic Italian homophonic cipher of the same size without error. Treating whole prefix classes as nulls did not help either. A monotone alignment of the groups against the decipherment, seeded with the Olivares runs, settled into even two-letter splits and gave no usable values. Rebuilding the key would need a fresh, group-exact transcription and more anchors.

The two ciphered paragraphs checked against the cipher, from the decipherment (8955–8956): [6] Et già si è publicato, che seguirà anco il Re alla giornata, persistendo l’Ecc.mo nelle prime risolutioni, che il Re ò abbracci le tregue, overo le faccia assignam.ti pronti, effettivi, et sufficienti per le imprese necessarie. Il Conte di Olivares ha desiderato con buone parole, et promesse condurlo à risolutione di ritornar in Fiandra; anco con qualche violente termine lo hà procurato, ma il Marchese constantem.te è stato ne’ primi propositi, nè hà potuto non ricever molti disgusti. Continuano quelli delli conti, che le sono dimandati, et quello che più lo affligge è haver dato sua figlia in moglie à Don Diego Messia, il quale è mantenuto dal Conte di Olivares nel posto di auttorità et gratia che haveva prima, se le diminuisse la speranza del titolo di Grande, et resta la figliola con minor fortuna di quella che senza il favore del Conte di Olivares poteva conseguire con il parentado di ogni gran Casa di Spagna. [7] Continuo io nelli affari propri con molti soldati di S. M.tà, li quali si offerseno di nuovo al servitio della Ser.ma; alcuni sono officiali di molta esperienza, et con tanto maggior affetto le corrispondo; sono la maggior parte Napolitani de’ terzi reformati… et però certa cosa, che il Re non può render tutti contenti, et molti con ragione si vegono abbandonati, et altri senza le sodisfattioni de’ proprij crediti, et desperati di poter li conseguire in alcun tempo. That is: it is given out that the King will go on campaign. Spinola holds to his first position, that the King must either accept the truce with the Dutch or give him ready and sufficient funds for the campaign. Olivares has tried fair words and harsher means to send him back to Flanders, and has failed. Spinola is also harried over his accounts, and grieved that he married his daughter to Diego Mesía, whom Olivares keeps in favour while holding back the grandeeship. Paragraph 7 reports that many soldiers of Philip IV, some of them officers of much experience and most of them Neapolitans of reformed tercios , have offered themselves anew to the service of the Republic; Mocenigo keeps to generalities with them, and the King cannot satisfy them all or pay their credits. Paragraphs 8 and 9 (8957–8959) cover Savoy’s campaign against Genoa over Oneglia and Ormea, Cottington’s cancelled journey, Rubens, Catalonia and Valencia, and Savoy’s bid for the government of Milan. Grades: the decipherment is contemporary (H). The transcription above is a first pass from the scans. Two words are doubtful (M): “prime risolutioni” and “terzi reformati”.

The key. It is a syllabic nomenclator; “conte di Olivares” = 672 2133 6210 2190 62x9 637 2127 in both copies is the only group run tied to text so far. A full transcription of the decipherment pages 8955–8959. DECODE carries only a rough one. DECODE R1862 (Busta 27 f. 354, 1628, four pages, “Ser.mo Principe”) is in the same cipher; DECODE places it at Rome, so it may be another Venetian despatch rather than Mocenigo’s. It has not been examined beyond its first page.

Il marchese Spinola, che e rimasto fin hora nella casa del marchese di Leganes, suo genero, ha fatto accomodare la sua propria, nella quale viveva Monte Rei, et pare sia habitata con tutte le circostantie che indicano dover lui trattenersi longamente in corte; et gia si e publicato che seguira anco il re alla giornata, persistendo l'eccellentissimo nelli primi risolutioni, che il re o abbracci le tregue overo le faccia assignamenti pronti, effettivi et sufficienti per le imprese necessarie. [6] Il conte di Olivares ha desiderato con buone parole et promesse condurlo a risolutione di ritornar in Fiandra; anco con qualche violente termine lo ha procurato, ma il marchese constantemente e stato ne' primi propositi, ne ha potuto non ricever molti disgusti. Continuano quelli delli conti che le sono dimandati; et quello che piu lo affligge e haver dato sua figliola in moglie a don Diego Messia, il quale e mantenuto dal conte di Olivares nel posto di auttorita et gratia che haveva prima, se le diminuisse la speranza del titolo di grande, et resta la figliola con minor fortuna di quella che senza il favore del conte di Olivares poteva conseguire con il parentado di ogni gran casa di Spagna. [7] Continuo io nelli affari propri con molti soldati di Sua Maesta, li quali si offerseno di nuovo al servitio della Serenissima Republica. Alcuni sono officiali di molta esperienza, et con tanto maggior affetto le corrispondo. Sono la maggior parte napolitani de' tercij reformati, et mi trattengo ne' generali per esser ordinariamente verbosa et legera questa natione; et pero certa cosa che il re non puo render tutti contenti, et molti con ragione si vegono abbandonati, et altri senza le sodisfattioni de' proprij crediti et disperati di poterli conseguire in alcun tempo. [9] Anco della mossa del signor duca di Savoia contro Genovesi mi viene riferito esser con concerto et de' Spagnoli et de' medesimi Genovesi, perche vi pensi Sua Altezza le terre di Oneglia, di Ormea, con li altri luochi che restavano nelle forze della Republica. Si sono mostrati Genovesi risoluti a non voler restituire la galea, come intendo, et le artegliarie; onde per questo altro camino, senza il mezo de' Francesi, carcano Spagnoli haver aggiustato quelle differenze. [10] Si sono provveduti dodeci cavalli d'ordine di Sua Maesta, li quali con altri regali di cose d'odore si preparano d'inviare a Turino in dono al signor duca. [11] Al padre Caetano, teatino, al quale sempre hanno servito li cocchi del re et si sono continuamente inviati rinfrescamenti, si da una chiesa ultimamente vacata nel regno di Napoli, et sara questo fatto confidente de' Spagnoli per ogni occasione di loro servitio. Hano il nevono di Ventimiglia et l'ambasciatore ordinario conceputo gran speranze di conseguire una grossa summa di danaro, ricercata a nome di Sua Altezza a conto de' suoi crediti con il re, di dote et altro; et pure si pensava a provedere a questo effetto di seicento mila scudi. Difficilmente pero si crede che habbia a seguire esborso alcuno nella congiontura presente, per la strettezza che ha il re, et perche carcano Spagnoli sostenere sempre con nuove speranze il duca, del quale ben sanno quanto si possono fidare et come habbino a governarsi con lui. Al tempo che Sua Maesta sara in Barcelona dicono che li principi, et forse Sua Altezza medesima, si condurra a quella volta con galee per baciarle le mani. [12] Ha il duca fatto passar ufficio dalli suoi ambasciatori di ricever nel porto Villa Franca la regina d'Ungaria in questo suo passaggio; ne da parte alcuna si tralasciano le migliori corrispondenze, per quanto si scopre sin hora. [13] Si accrescono li disgusti de' Genovesi per le operationi sinistre, come intendo, di Monte Rei et del marchese di Castagneda. Commissioni sono arrivate alli ambasciatori qui, per le quali e partito per l'Escuriale; ne possono per altra via esser pervenute che con il corriero inviato dalli ambasciatori di Spagna. [14] Doveva, come ho penetrato, passare a questi regni il secretario Cottington di ordine del re d'Inghilterra, et il passaggio suo a punto era per seguire in questo tempo che e stata sopra la costa di Francia l'armata, dalla quale si spiccavano a questo effetto doi o tre vascelli per metter il ministro in luoco sicuro; ma e svanito questo dissegno doppo la morte di Buchingam, et don Andimion Porter, che si trova qui, e senza alcuna commissione e sta aspettando che le sopragiongino nuovi ordini. Il Ruben continua le trattationi di tregue con Olandesi, et secondo le occasioni Spagnoli haveranno disposto, come si puo persuadere ognuno, la trattatione per risolvere quello le sara di maggior servitio. [15] Sempre piu si vanno essacerbando li animi di quei popoli, et nelle corti che ha da tenere il re, cosi in Barcelona come in Valentia, non e lontano che possa succedere alcun inconveniente, se il conte di Olivares non rimette del vigore et severita con che tratta quei affari. [16] Li ministri del signor duca di Savoia hano, come vengo avvisato, fatto officij perche non sia risoluta l'espeditione del duca di Feria in governatore di Milano, et gia pare che non piu si parli di lui. Dalli confidenti del duca intendo non voler Sua Eccellenza andare a quel governo senza certe promesse de assegnamenti che ricerca; se fosse vero l'avviso della morte di Monte Rei, pretenderebbe esser presidente del Consiglio d'Italia, et nella penuria de soggetti di valore puo molto avanzarsi il duca in auttorita, tutto che non sij confidente del conte di Olivares. Gratie. The clear parts of the despatch are not in the repository. --> # R1874, Alvise Mocenigo to the Doge and Senate, Madrid, 26 October 1628: the cipher paragraphs, English translation [5] Everything is being arranged for the departure of the Duke of Alcalá, Viceroy of Naples, and it is a bad omen for those who hold it doubtful, since new changes and variations keep appearing in all things; and what has been promised to one is conferred on another subject, so that, whereas in the past certain decisions were carried out at once, now no one knows what provision the resolution may have, since it changes every night. The Marquis Spinola, who has stayed until now in the house of the Marquis of Leganés, his son-in-law, has had his own house made ready, in which Monterrey used to live, and it seems to be inhabited with all the circumstances that indicate he must stay a long time at court; and it is already made public that he will even follow the King on his journey, the Most Excellent persisting in his first resolutions: that the King either embrace the truces or else make him prompt, effective and sufficient assignments for the necessary enterprises. [6] The Count of Olivares has wished, with good words and promises, to bring him to resolve to return to Flanders; he has tried it even with some violent terms, but the Marquis has stood constantly by his first intentions, nor could he avoid receiving many vexations. Those over the accounts that are demanded of him continue; and what afflicts him most is to have given his daughter in marriage to Don Diego Messía, who is kept by the Count of Olivares in the post of authority and favour that he had before, though his hope of the title of grandee has diminished, and the daughter is left with a smaller fortune than she could have obtained, without the Count of Olivares's favour, by alliance with any great house of Spain. [7] I continue in my own business with many soldiers of His Majesty, who have offered themselves anew for the service of the Most Serene Republic. Some are officers of much experience, and I respond to them with all the more warmth. Most of them are Neapolitans of the disbanded tercios, and I keep to generalities, this nation being ordinarily wordy and light; and yet it is a certain thing that the King cannot make everyone content, and many with reason see themselves abandoned, and others without satisfaction of their own credits and despairing of ever obtaining it. [9] Also concerning the move of the Lord Duke of Savoy against the Genoese, I am told that it is in concert both with the Spaniards and with the Genoese themselves, because His Highness is thinking of the lands of Oneglia and Ormea, with the other places that remained in the Republic's hands. The Genoese have shown themselves resolved not to return the galley, as I understand, and the artillery; so the Spaniards are seeking to have settled those differences by this other road, without the mediation of the French. [10] Twelve horses have been procured by order of His Majesty, which, with other gifts of perfumes, are being prepared to be sent to Turin as a present to the Lord Duke. [11] To Father Caetano, the Theatine, who has always had the King's coaches at his service and to whom refreshments have continually been sent, a church lately vacant in the Kingdom of Naples is being given, and this will make him a confidant of the Spaniards on every occasion of their service. The nephew of Ventimiglia and the resident ambassador have conceived great hopes of obtaining a large sum of money, requested in His Highness's name on account of his credits with the King for dowry and other things; and indeed it was being considered to provide six hundred thousand scudi for this purpose. It is hardly believed, however, that any payment will follow at the present juncture, because of the King's straits, and because the Spaniards seek always to sustain the Duke with new hopes, knowing well how far they can trust him and how they must conduct themselves with him. When His Majesty is in Barcelona, they say that the princes, and perhaps His Highness himself, will travel there with galleys to kiss his hands. [12] The Duke has had his ambassadors make representations offering to receive the Queen of Hungary in the port of Villafranca on this passage of hers; nor is the best correspondence neglected on any side, as far as can be seen so far. [13] The Genoese's vexations are growing because of the sinister doings, as I understand, of Monterrey and of the Marquis of Castañeda. Commissions have arrived for the ambassadors here, on account of which he has left for the Escorial; nor can they have come by any other way than with the courier sent by the ambassadors of Spain. [14] Secretary Cottington, as I have found out, was to come to these kingdoms by order of the King of England, and his passage was to take place precisely at this time, when the fleet was off the coast of France, from which two or three vessels were to be detached for this purpose to put the minister in a safe place; but this plan has vanished since Buckingham's death, and Don Endymion Porter, who is here, is without any commission and is waiting for new orders to reach him. Rubens continues the negotiations for truces with the Dutch, and, as anyone may be persuaded, the Spaniards will have arranged the negotiation according to circumstances, so as to settle what will be of greatest service to them. [15] The minds of those peoples are growing ever more exasperated, and in the Cortes that the King has to hold, both in Barcelona and in Valencia, it is not unlikely that some trouble may occur, if the Count of Olivares does not abate the vigour and severity with which he handles those affairs. [16] The Lord Duke of Savoy's ministers have, as I am informed, made representations so that the dispatch of the Duke of Feria as Governor of Milan should not be resolved, and it already seems that he is no longer spoken of. From the Duke's confidants I understand that His Excellency does not wish to go to that government without certain promises of the assignments he requests; if the report of Monterrey's death were true, he would claim to be President of the Council of Italy, and in the dearth of men of worth the Duke may advance greatly in authority, although he is not a confidant of the Count of Olivares. Thanks.

Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3053 ff. 85–87, DECODE R4248, catalogued with the eight “unknown sender (Rome)” letters of catalogue item 180. The cipher A substitution on graphic signs with nulls (30, a triple-barred cross, 22): Tomokiyo’s second fr. 3053 table, not the cardinal de Mâcon’s key. How it was deciphered From the contemporary clear decipherment on f. 86, checked against every clear connecting phrase left in the cipher on f. 85. The key was not applied. What it says The writer urged the cardinal that all affairs, the war above all, should go through Montmorency, “et que toute autre chose estoit fumee et vent”. Still open The writer, the cardinal (“Carafe”?), a few words of the secretary hand, and the key table.

DECODE files R4248 with the letters of Charles Hémard de Denonville, cardinal de Mâcon, to Montmorency in BnF fr. 3053, all catalogued with no sender. Those letters are in “Mascon’s cipher” and have their own page . This one is not: its signs are a different set, and the cardinal’s values (W = LL, ~ = null, 30 = pape) give nonsense. It is a different cipher, with its own page since 14 October 2026. The signs match the second table Satoshi Tomokiyo sketched from this volume (nulls 30, the triple-barred cross and 22; ~ for I and J; 7 and 11 for L; W for R; 3 for O; α for U; ʃ for P), and Tomokiyo noted that the fragment on f. 85 is “deciphered on f. 86”. After the clear words et partant , the cipher ꭓ m Ɛ 3 30 11 ǂ begins JE LE CO[NSEILLOIS] , as in the decipherment. The record has no date, place or signature on the DECODE images; the letter ends “Hors deux jours je seray a Rome”, and its place in the volume puts it in 1536. F. 85: cipher runs with the clear links left standing between them, et partant (line 1), et que toute aultre chose estoit fumee et vent (line 4), Je luy dys davantaige (line 5). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3053 f. 85, via DECODE R4248 (image 3).

The clear text opens: “Monsieur le cardinal Carafe [?] et moy fusmes hyer en campagne pour parler ensemble”. The legate had tried to take the writer to Rome that evening to see the Pope, and the writer asked for two days more; they talked all day, and the cardinal professed himself wholly devoted to the King’s service. Then the cipher, as f. 86 gives it: […] en toutes choses et particulierement celles de la guerre avoient a passer par voz mains, et partant je le conseilloie de s’adresser a faire fondement de vous seul … et que toute autre chose estoit fumee et vent. Je luy dys davantaige qu’il cognoistroit totallement le [Roy?] en ce jugement tant de la maniere de faire la guerre comme au lieu et du temps, par ce que en fin il falloit que tout homme feist son mestier et ceulx qui le font le mieulx sont les plus praticques. … Bien vous diray je que je trouve led. S r cardinal enclin de luy mesme a suivre ce conseil, et l’ay laissé en volunté, comme il me semble en tout persuadé. The cardinal then told him that the cardinal of Lorraine, in the capitulation he had made with the Pope, had granted things “ausquelles auparavant ilz n’avoient jamais pensé”, that they meant to undo the conditions he had passed because he had conceded more than he should, and that the whole matter would be left to Montmorency, “congnoissant ung seul fondement aux choses qui passeroient par voz mains”. The decipherment ends “Il me dist aussi” with a cue mark where the original resumes in clear. Every clear link checked on f. 85 ( et partant , fumee et vent , Je luy dys davantaige , comme , car en fin il falloit , Et seroit chose trop longue de vous racompter ) stands in the same place in the decipherment.

A few words of the decipherment in the secretary hand: Carafe , [pouvoir?] , [Roy?] , partir [?] , rompre [?] ; about 85 % of its words were transcribed securely from the DECODE images. Who wrote the letter and who the cardinal was. No signature survives on the images. The key table: it could be rebuilt by aligning f. 85 with f. 86, since the plaintext is complete, but the reading does not need it.

No date or place is visible on the downloaded crops (the letter ends on P6 "Hors deux jours je seray a Rome ..." with folio number 87 at the foot; no signature seen). ## Clear-text summary "Monsieur le cardinal Carafe [?] et moy fusmes hyer en campagne pour parler ensemble suyvant ce que vous m'avons [avez] au paravant advisé. Le Legat feist tout son effort pour me mener le soir a Rome pour parler avec le pappe, ce que je le priay differer encores deux jours pour ma plus grande commodité." They talked all day; the cardinal professed himself entirely devoted to the King's service. The writer then urged him ("je luy remonstray apres ung long discours") - here the cipher begins. The clear links inside the cipher block read "et partant", "et que toute autre chose estoit fumee et vent", "Je luy dys davantaige", "comme", "car en fin il falloit", "Et seroit chose trop longue de vous racompter toutes les ...", "Il me dist aussi qu'il" etc. Later (P5/P6) in clear: the cardinal's assurances; "je ne veulx faillir de le vous escripre"; he will be in Rome in two days to see the Emperor's (?) ministers. ## The cipher on f. 85 is NOT Mâcon's cipher The glyph set is different: "ǂ" (triple-barred cross, very frequent, often word-final), "W", "~", "α", "∞", "Ɛ", "ꝗ", "ʃ/∫ with loop", "φ", "#", "11", "z", "k", "30" (frequent, apparently a null here, not "pape"). With Mâcon's key (W = LL, ~ = null, 30 = pape) it decodes to nonsense. The signs match S. Tomokiyo's second fr. 3053 table (img/francisMacon2.png: nulls 30, ǂ, 22; I/J = ~; L = 7/11; R = W; O = 3; U = α; P = ʃ; ...) - e.g. after "et partant" the cipher "ꭓ m Ɛ 3 30 11 ǂ" starts "JE LE CO[NSEILLOIS]" as in the decipherment. I did not rebuild the table; the decipherment makes it unnecessary. About 20 cipher lines: 2 on P2 (after "apres ung long discours"), ~11 on P3, ~9 on P5 (top). ## Contemporary decipherment on f. 86 (P8-P9), transcribed f. 86 is a clear copy of the ciphered part of the letter (cipher + its clear connecting words), ending "Il me dist aussi[..]" with a "#" mark (the cue where the original resumes): "[...] en toutes choses et particulierement celles de la guerre avoient a passer par voz mains, et partant je le conseilloie de s'adresser a faire fondement de vous seul, car c'est a scavoir le premier [pouvoir?], et que toute autre chose estoit fumee et vent. Je luy dys davantaige qu'il cognoistroit totallement le [Roy?] en ce jugement tant de la maniere de faire la guerre comme au lieu et du temps, par ce que en fin il falloit que tout homme feist son mestier et ceulx qui le font le mieulx sont les plus praticques. Et seroit chose trop longue de vous racompter toutes les particularitez de ce propos. Bien vous diray je que je trouve led. Sr cardinal enclin de luy mesme a suivre ce conseil, et l'ay laissé en volunté, comme il me semble en tout persuadé. Il me dict entre autres choses c'est y digne de vous estre escripte, que le cardinal de Lorraine par la cappitulacion faicte avec le Pape avoit accordé choses ausquelles auparavant ilz n'avoient jamais pensé, comme de partir [?] et autres qu'il me nomma, adjoustant par apres ces mesmes parolles qu'ilz estoient deliberez par leurs moyens [de] rompre [?] les conditions passees par led. seigneur cardinal de Lorraine, par ce qu'ilz congnoissoient qu'il leur avoit plus concedé que n'estoit le devoir, et que eulx mesmes ne vouloient, mais que a vous seroit remise toute l'application de qui vouldroient entierement se rendre, congnoissant ung seul fondement aux choses qui passeroient par voz mains. Il me dist aussi [#]" Confidence in this transcription of the decipherment: ~85% of words (secretary hand, a few words [?]). It agrees with every clear link I checked on f. 85 ("et partant", "fumee et vent", "Je luy dys davantaige", "comme", "car en fin il falloit", "Et seroit chose trop longue ...", "en tout persuadé. Il me dict entre autres choses"). ## Key notes - Mâcon's key does not apply to this record. Cipher = Tomokiyo's fr. 3053 "table 2" type; 30 and ǂ look like nulls. - If wanted, the full key can be rebuilt by aligning f. 85 with f. 86 (plaintext is complete). The Legate made every effort to take me to Rome in the evening to speak with the Pope, which I begged him to put off for another two days for my greater convenience." [They talked all day; the cardinal professed himself entirely devoted to the King's service. The writer then urged him] "I represented to him, after a long discourse" — here the cipher begins. ## The ciphered part: the contemporary decipherment on f. 86 "[...] in all things, and particularly those of war, had to pass through your hands; and therefore I advised him to set about making his foundation on you alone, for that is, namely, the first [?power], and that everything else was smoke and wind. I told him further that he would know the [?King] entirely in this judgement, both in the manner of making war and as to place and time, because in the end every man had to do his own trade, and those who do it best are the most practised. And it would be too long a thing to tell you all the particulars of this talk. I will certainly tell you that I find the said lord Cardinal inclined of himself to follow this advice, and I have left him willing, as it seems to me, persuaded in everything. He told me, among other things, something worthy of being written to you: that the Cardinal of Lorraine, by the capitulation made with the Pope, had granted things which they had never thought of before, such as to leave [?] and others which he named to me; adding afterwards these very words, that they were resolved by their means [to] break [?] the conditions agreed by the said lord Cardinal of Lorraine, because they knew that he had conceded more to them than was his duty, and than they themselves wanted, but that to you would be left the whole application of those who would wish to give themselves up entirely, knowing one sole foundation for the things that would pass through your hands. He also told me [#]"

A young man’s letter home, its dangerous passages in a cipher from the Bavarian chancery’s own key register (R9423, block “H. Wilh. 1525”), applied once its signs were matched by shape: he was questioned about strange arts and denied everything, fears for his person, and reports the Turks coming up. About half of the cipher words are deciphered. y68TXqV H4w3ye · seltsam khinst · A = 9 · B = v · E = 6 · und = 9 a son → his father · cipher passages in a German letter · 22 March 1535 · known key applied, decoded, not read A son to his father, 22 March 1535 Go to the full text ↓ A young man writes home that he was questioned and denied everything; the dangerous lines are in a key copied in the Bavarian chancery’s key register, and the key gives phrases from them, but not sentences. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial The letter A son to his father (“gunstiger herr vater”), Monday after Palm Sunday, 22 March 1535, in German; the father and the place are not named in the clear text. Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 f. 169; DECODE R9367, part of catalogue entry 161, listed with no decipherment. The cipher Runs of invented signs inside the clear German: one sign per letter, a few signs for words ( und , auch , das ) and for ch . How it was deciphered R9423, a register in the same volume copying out nineteen keys of the 1520s and 1530s, has a block headed “H. Wilh. [15]25”; once its frequent signs were matched to the letter’s by shape, it gives German. Five values were added from the letter itself. What it says Phrases only, not sentences: he was asked about strange arts (“[?selczam] khinst”) and denied everything; he is taken for a poor writer and has learned nothing reliable yet; he fears for his person; the Turks are coming up. Still open The cipher as sentences. The re-reading of 23 October 2026 built a full reading of the letter, but four of its values rest on sense alone, two signs and the passages of lines 9–10, 14, 16, 31 and 34 stay open, and with those counted as holes the letter is still decoded, not read. Until 15 October 2026 this letter was filed on one page with thirteen other ciphertexts of the same key volume. They are different ciphers, each with its own page; the largest group is System A′ of the dukes’ agents in Hungary.

The clear German opens with the date, “Anno dni. 1535. den 22 marcij an montag nach palmarum”. From the partial reading of 23 October 2026 ( r9367/R9367_reading.md , English R9367_en.md ), with the cipher passages set in the clear text: he was summoned and questioned about strange arts and denied everything (“[?selczam] khinst gefragt, ich hab aber alles [g] verlaugnet”); he gave himself out as a poor writer, sent to learn because he is still young (“ich sey am schlechter shreiber der mainung gesent worden nach dem ich noch jung bin etwas zu lernen und erfaren”); he has learnt nothing reliable yet and will report once he reaches the place; he fears for getting himself through (“[?meinesn] leib hindurch bringen”); and many Turks are moving up (“vil Tircken [?uerauf] ziechen”). The name read earlier as Nothaft is the word botschaft . The postscript reads “Ich vernim Friderich Schmalcz vergunt euch nicht guets”: one Friedrich Schmalcz begrudges the father anything good. The back of the leaf (image P2) has no address, only two pen crosses, so the father and the place are still unnamed. Decoded, not read. Several values of this reading rest on sense alone (below), and the passages of lines 9–10 (“die [#] [?fleih] [?danck] geben worden”), 14, 16, 31 and 34 do not build sentences. Counted as holes, they leave the letter under the reading bar (check of 23 October 2026), so the reading above is partial. The DECODE image was fetched again and viewed rotated: the failures are key values, not transcription.

Block 2_4 of the key register R9423, headed “H. Wilh. [15]25”, gives A 9, B v, C Δ, D +, E 6, F ⊥, G o, H 4, I w, K ‡, L 8, M ¥, N 3, O a barred D, P two rings, Q 2, R 7, S y, T ♉, V a doubled ‡, X o-o, Y ε, Z π, with und 9, auch Z, ch t, das T. Applied with the original sign assignments it failed; it fits once the letter’s frequent signs are matched to the block by shape. The block’s name signs (for Bavaria and Duke Ludwig) do not fit the letter: here they behave as nulls or word dividers. The letter adds five values of its own (q a, Λ r, C s, H k, K z). The re-reading of 23 October 2026 re-transcribed every cipher run on the full-resolution image and added three values that hold at every occurrence (v = b or w , ‡‡ = u , boxed H = k ) and four that rest on sense alone, for review: cc = z ( zeit , ziechen , Schmalcz ), Φ = b ( bin , bringen , botschaft ), S = sch , U = ll .

The letter is decoded, not read: the four sense-only values (eleven words), the open signs and the passages of lines 9–10, 14, 16, 31 and 34 need the open signs or a second letter in this key. (The first count, 78 of 143 cipher words, 54.5%, is withdrawn as a reading figure.) Signs not in the key block: a triple-barred cross [#] (13 times, mostly where nothing is needed), an arch sign [Π] (4 times, a word or name sign), and R and d once each; the contexts do not fix them. The place name in lines 1–2; and the sign pairs in the right margin beside lines 30–33, probably a reader’s equations. The back of the letter (image P2) was examined on 23 October 2026: no address, only two pen crosses.

DECODE had Rákóczi as the sender; the clear address makes him the recipient. Where Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár, G15 Caps. C. Fasc. 39, pp. 277–279; DECODE R902, catalogued as not yet deciphered. The cipher A one-part French nomenclator of groups 10–560: homophones for letters, syllables, common words and names, with fillers at the line ends. How it was deciphered Every G15 key on DECODE was scored on the letter; R639, headed De Monsieur de Bonac et Graffei , fits and was checked on two interlinear siblings (R852, R912). Both cipher pages were then transcribed afresh from the images, group by group (30 September and 5 October 2026). What it says The Swedes’ settlement with the Emperor, their army near Poznań waiting for recruits landed at Stettin, the damage done by Ráday’s letters to Rehnskiöld, the writer’s own standing, and the Swedish complaint that Rákóczi would sacrifice himself to free Polish liberty. Measured 982 of 1,017 counted groups read as sense (96.6%, measure_tr.py ), twelve of them after a one-figure correction forced by the context (grade C). Still open Ten groups closing the first paragraph that decode to no word, and about twenty-five scattered single groups whose value gives no sense in place.

DECODE R902 describes a ciphered letter of “Pompeio Cesoni (Ferenc Rákóczi II) to unknown recipient”, dated 15 October 1707. The clear third leaf gives the recipient: A Monsieur Monsieur Pompeio Cesoni Cesoni is therefore the addressee. The hidden text also addresses the recipient with the forms expected for Rákóczi and reports work undertaken on his behalf. The catalogue entry has been corrected here to an unsigned report to Rákóczi.

The matching table is DECODE R639 , MNL OL G15 Caps. C. Fasc. 44/08. It was found by decrypting R902 with each key transcription of the Rákóczi chancery fonds (G15) on DECODE and scoring the output. Its heading reads De Monsieur de Bonac et Graffei . Rare entries as well as common letters match R902: 489 Monsieur , 491 Monseigneur , 497 les Svedois , 506 Svede , 507 Pologne , 526 le Prince Constantin , and 533 Dantzig . The key is an archival table, applied as it stands, and it can be tested directly on other documents. The remaining uncertainty lies in DECODE’s digit transcription and in the writer’s identity.

Monseigneur, Vostre Altesse aura veu par mes deux dernieres, de Gorlitz en Saxe et de Lubben en Silesie, de quelle maniere s’est denoüée l’affaire des Svedois avec l’Empereur. Il […] tout à present ici, à 8 lieues de Posnanie, où ils attendent les recrues et les munitions qui ont debarqué à Stettin. Leur confiance dans les Anglois et les Hollandois nous doit asseurer qu’ils ne s’arreste[…] point ici pour observer la conduite que ce Prince tiendra par rapport à l’execution des articles arrestez … [ten groups] J’ay aussi eu l’honneur de vous rendre compte, Monseigneur, de l’impression que […] lettres de Monsieur Ráday au general Rehnskiöld avoit faite ici sur les esprits … qu’elle vous a privé de vos meilleurs amis à la Cour de Svede, et qu’il faud[ra] bien du temps [et] beaucoup d’adresse pour reparer le tort incroyable qu’elle a fait à Vostre Altesse. C’est pourquoy je vous conseillerois, Monseigneur, … d’envoyer secretement ou de chercher une personne ici qui eust les qualitez necessaires pour y pouvoir reussir. Names as in the original. ## Translation **p. 277.** At Słupca, 15 October. Monseigneur, Your Highness will have seen from my last two letters, from Görlitz in Saxony and from Lübben in Silesia, in what manner the affair of the Swedes with the Emperor has been untangled. He [85] all at present here, 8 leagues from Poznań, where they are waiting for the recruits and the munitions that have landed at Stettin. Their confidence in the English and the Dutch must assure us that they will not stop[8] here to watch the conduct this Prince will keep as to the execution of the articles agreed, they aforesaid. I persuade [120] that the Court of Vienna will not break a word confirmed and strengthened by a guarantee as accredited in the league, and with them, as that of these two powers into whose hands it seems they have put the fate of affairs [224 264 174 226 37 / 324 125 104 589 4]. I have also had the honour of giving you an account, Monseigneur, of the impression that [297] letters of Monsieur Ráday to General Rehnskiöld had made on minds here. I [363]s that perhaps in [129 436] said as frankly in April, as I owe it, that it has deprived you of your best friends at the Court of Sweden, and that it will take [860] and much time [95] much skill to repair the incredible harm it has done Your Highness. That is why I would advise you, Monseigneur, if you believe [120] that it were also in your interest to remedy this, to send secretly, or to seek here, a person who had the qualities needed to succeed in it. I confess in good faith that I lack them, [9] besides which the misfortune I have had of being suspected by Your Highness, or by those [?who may] belong to you, makes me understand that the continuation of my services would not be agreeable to you. I have nevertheless not yet slackened, up to now, in my zeal towards you, and I have made every effort of which I have been [194]pable, both at the Swedish chancellery and at the Court of Poland, **p. 278, lines 1-9.** [121] to destroy at once the rumour that was going about, or rather the opinion people had, that Your Highness had had arrested the children of the Palatine of Russia and the envoy of the King of Poland, who was coming back from Prince Constantine [27] (?Constanti)nople, [129] and was bringing with [264 89] a deputy of the Porte to the King of Sweden. I do not know whether my efforts, joined to this information, more exact than what people had had, have effaced that opinion; but I can say that if it is not yet entirely dispelled, it will not be denied that too much faith was lightly given to reports and prejudices which **p. 278, lines 10-18.** gave rise to it. For the present they confine themselves to complaining of Your Highness's conduct with regard to the affairs of Poland, and of certain remarks you are said to have made in the presence of people who have reported them, asserting that you had said that, taking the interests of Poland as much to heart as those of Hungary, you were resolved to sacrifice yourself if need be to free Polish liberty, oppressed by the Swedes in favour of King Stanislas. I am, with a very deep respect, …

Decrypted by Lasry. R191 98r–101r 6 Riario to the Secretary, mid-January 1581: the Smerwick massacre, the “distruttione di quelli poveri Italiani”, Alba’s report on the 700 Italians, two ships to Ireland, the soldiers’ pay. Decrypted by Lasry. Card.le Riario R194 281 2 Riario (by hand and subject); undated. The Irish captains, money, Flanders first, the truce The key is Lasry’s reconstruction: fixed two-digit homophones ( a 00 81, e 07 83, i 05 85, o 03 87, l 25 75, u/v 01 27, one number for each other letter), a few words (78 che , 84 per , 24 quell , 14 quest , 44 ancora , 28 M.tà ) and the single digit 9 as a word separator. No group begins with 9, so a digit string splits in only one way. Numbers are left as plain numerals between separators (“4 mesi”, “1300”).

R192, Riario. Riario spoke with the King “sopra il negotio di Piamonte”. Philip II was very pleased with the avvertimento and much obliged to His Holiness. Idiáquez then came to report that the King had taken the warning in good part. Cipher passages name the Marquis of Ayamonte, formerly governor of Milan, the Anselmi, and Ugonotti of the Dauphiné who were to help them in Italy. The King promised that nothing would disturb Italy. Further on: the Italian soldiers were to be sent with artillery, munitions and four months’ pay under the name of S.S.tà . Going on in plain danger, they would all be killed, because the Queen of England’s ships and men were waiting. The appended copy of 29 November 1580 answers the King’s ministers. The English enterprise must wait until Flanders is pacified. The Italians are embarked on the river at Lisbon with victuals for three months and are to be sent back toward Italy. R193, Riario to the Cardinal of Como, Badajoz. The impresa d’Inghilterra : the King lacks the means and wants Flanders subdued first. It also covers galleys, Italian infantry, and 1,300 badly armed soldiers in need of “aiuti, armi et munitioni”. The third page, a clean decipherment from Elvas, says of the President that he “è pietra scandali et mal sodisfatto della Corte romana”. R194. The Irish captains; the King needs a “gran provisione di denari” and must settle Flanders before “questa impresa”; the truce; what he has spent “per mantenimento la religione cattolica in Fiandra”. R190 and R191. Riario writes to the Earl of Desmond about the papal soldiers in Ireland, and to the Secretary in mid-January 1581 about the massacre at Smerwick (the “distruttione di quelli poveri Italiani”), the Duke of Alba’s report on the 700 Italians, two ships to be sent to Ireland, and the Duke of Sora. Per-passage digit strings, decrypts and glosses are in the repository ( transcription_R192.md , transcription_R193_R194.md ); the readings of 22 October 2026, with the clear text and the decipherments in full, are texts/R190_reading.md to R194_reading.md , with English in texts/R19*_en.md .

The five records, their 22 page images and DECODE’s attachments were fetched. The attachments are Midas’s 2017 transcription of R190–R191, Lasry’s key and his decryption. That decryption covers only ff. 92–101, so R192–R194 had key but no text. Two image-reading passes transcribed the digits of each cipher passage on those eleven pages and copied the interlinear gloss. A table decoder applied Lasry’s key. Where a digit was ambiguous in this hand (3/5/8, 0/6, 1/7), the value that gives Italian was kept. That makes the decrypt a check on the gloss rather than an independent decryption. Groups that decrypted to nothing in the key were lined up with their glosses to recover code words.

20 and 28 are hard to tell apart in this hand. One is glossed S.M.tà and the other Italiani , probably 28 and 20 respectively; not settled. 82 is navi , settled on the re-reading (R191 f. 99r “dui navi” twice; R192 “la Regina d’Inghilterra navi”): Lasry’s “Hune” came from a misreading of the gloss. 72 has two glossed senses, Regina (R190, R192) and denari (R191, the R192 copy, R194); 60 is Duca and 77 9 00 il Marchese . The four-digit prefixes 6371, 7771, 7361 and 7761 and the code for religione cattolica (R194) have no gloss word. 10 is glossed Italia three times, but once apparently V.S. Ill.ma , which may be a misread 18. Four-digit groups 6371, 7771, 7361 and 7761 stand before several phrases in R193–R194 and are never glossed. They may be nulls or a code. Religione cattolica in R194 p. 2 is enciphered by a short group that could not be made out. On R192 p. 1 the tail after “dubbio che ha S.S.tà” (“0?9 32 0 9 75 71 63”) has no gloss and was not decrypted. Letter dates: R193 p. 1’s month and R194’s date are not established; R190 and R191 were re-transcribed from the images on 22 October 2026 (Midas’s 2017 draft corrected on the image); Lasry’s decryption of ff. 92–101 stands.

Ho inteso con molto contento mio con quanto valore V.S. To the Earl of Desmond, Elvas, 12 January 1581 I have heard with great satisfaction how valiantly Your Lordship bears the charge there {of His Holiness's soldiers}, and how you do not cease to take the best care of them and to make what progress is possible. Thanking you warmly for this, for the service of God, which is pursued with infinite zeal {by His Beatitude}, I tell you that here no effort has been spared to obtain {strong aid} for you; and it has been held back because of the news that has come to this court {that the fort held by your force has been lost, and part of those soldiers too}. And so I commend myself to you, praying God for your health and that he always prosper all your holy actions. From Elvas, 12 January 1581. ## 2. News from court (f. 93r) While writing this I am told how {a captain from Ireland came to tell the Queen of England that all His Holiness's soldiers} who were {in the fort} ... {the viceroy had cut them to pieces} ... [?without] their having made {any resistance}, but letting themselves {be killed like beasts}; and although he does not give the day, {the celebration} that {the Queen} has made of it makes it held {for true}. And it is not possible that they managed well, since after {the viceroy} had resolved not {to attack them}, for this [...] the second time to take them. ## 3. Memorial to Philip II (ff. 94r-95r) In the last {payment} His Majesty made to the {Italian infantry} he paid {3,037 foot}, and as to the number of the {men fit for service, they come to a thousand} and a little more; and so His Majesty offers to make them up {to 2,000 with Spaniards, victualled and paid for 4 months}, on condition that the {legate takes charge of them} from now, caring to provide for them and to give them [...] intention for when the said {4 months} have passed; or His Majesty will give {the Italians such as they are and as many as} there are, but under {His Holiness's name, paid and victualled for 4 months}, with orders to come back once the three months have passed if they have no other orders, so as to have that month free to {return to their homes}; and if {Signor Prospero Colonna} will not go as {their commander}, His Majesty wants the {legate} to provide {a commander to go}, the said {legate} dealing with that {commander}, who within eight days should take up {the men at Lisbon}. True or not {the report}, I am of opinion, and beg His Majesty for the service of God, of His Majesty himself and the satisfaction of His Holiness, that {the aid or relief} should go [?in any case] as strong as possible, {with arms, munitions, victuals, money and artillery}, for as many {months} as can be, so that there is time to arrange greater {aid}, and meanwhile to hearten {the Catholics of the island} and gain a foothold {in a port, which Pietro Ortiz} says can be done easily in any case, even if it were the port {of Smerwick}, which was the worst {port} of all; and he says that even if {the Queen's fleet} were there and met them, they would overcome it and take {the port}; and since the other is not lost, {those poor men} would be relieved so that they are not {lost}, and would rather make progress. It does not seem good to send {a commander} who could rival the {Earl of Desmond}, who already holds the title {of General} in the {island}, but to send {a commissary} to hand these {men to the said Earl}, someone not inexperienced in {war}, so that he can {command} on the way if need be; and this will be a smaller {expense} for His Majesty, making only a {colonel} to serve {under the Earl}, to which officers His Holiness's {patents} will be given; it being right in every respect to do as soon as possible what must be done, to the praise of God. And if His Majesty thought fit, it would be good to send {an escort with a zabra} so as to inform {these men} of the state of things, and also to send with these {soldiers the English and Irish} who have served {in Flanders} and are here, with some gift {to the Earl of Desmond}; and everything is left to His Majesty's prudence and piety. The writer is the legate at Philip II's court ("le dico che qui ...", "nel tempo che starò qui"); he encloses "the copy" of his letter to the Earl of Desmond and his brother, which is R190 f. 92r, dated Elvas 12 January 1581, so this letter belongs to the same days. It reports the destruction of the papal force at Smerwick (November 1580). ## Letter (ff. 98r-99v) Doppo l'haver scritto a V.S. Ill.ma, questi ministri di S.M.tà m'hanno portato l'aviso {secondo de la distruttione di quelli poveri Italiani}, che è alligato et segnato A, {scritto dalo} Ambasciator di S.M.tà {che sta in Inghilterra}; et in nome di S.M.tà quasi in un medesimo tempo mi fu data per ultima risolutione in questo negotio l'oblationi che saranno alligate, alle quali diedi la risposta che V.S. Ill.ma vedrà nel medesimo foglio signato B, conforme a quello che Mons. Nuntio m'ha scritto et mandato a trattar qui per uno {chiamato Ortiz} a posta. Et nel istesso quasi tempo si sono ricevute dua lettere del s.r Prospero alligate, una al s.r Duara signata C et una a me signata D, et Idiaquez me n'ha portato una originale {del Duca d'Alva a S.M.tà, che dice che li Italiani imbarcati erano 700}, et che tutti se n'andavano {fuggendo per terra, et ancora deli imbarcati scappavano}, che erano in gran parte {amalati} et tutti senza {armi et vestimenti}, et che erano così {mal ridutti} che non li giudicava atti a alcuna sorte {d'impresa}, et domandava licentia di rimandarli {in Italia}; et che essendo {sudditi} la maggior parte del {Gran Duca, li capitani} facevano difficultà d'andare a {alcuna impresa} senza {sua licenza}. Et mi disse il suddetto Idiaquez che per {questi avvisi}, et non accettando io la oblatione simplicemente, et conoscendo che si mandavano chiaramente {a degollar tutti} nelli termini che hanno, che a S.M.tà pareva metterne della conscientia {a mandar a perdere questa natione} che l'haveva servito tanto bene, et che teneva bonissimo animo et risolutione {a questa impresa}, ma con le debbite preparationi et considerationi, mostrando che ci bisognavano maggior {forze di quelle} che forse meno [...] a S.S.tà, et per questo si risolveva {non poter mandar gente per hora}. Ill.ma vedrà dal contenuto della copia che con questa viene, tutto per tenerli {animati} per ogni buon effetto; et ho mandato {dui frati di quelli che} mandò già Mons. In conclusion I believe His Majesty has ordered {that they return}, and is about to send {two ships} {to get information on the state of that island} so as to inform His Holiness; and perhaps, as I hope from the words of His Majesty and his ministers, to make some good and well-founded decision, which God grant, for the service of God and His Majesty and the satisfaction of His Holiness; and while I am here I shall miss no occasion to pursue all this. Ma al sicuro {S.M.tà ha preso l'avvertimento in ottima parte, et il Piemonte credo sia vero, ma credo non succederà con intera sodisfattione di S.M.tà}, la quale facilmente ha il medesimo {dubbio che ha S.S.tà}. In questo punto la sera delli 5 è venuto il s.r Idiaquez a nome di S.M.tà a dirmi {che è vero che il Marchese d'Ayamonte, già Governatore di Milano,} cominciò et mantenne {la prattica et fomento} con alcun mezzo {con quelli Anselmo}, ma che sempre gli ha dispiaciuto {a S.M.tà}, la quale nel tempo che morì {il Marchese} li scriveva liberamente l'animo suo, ch'era che li dispiaceva; et che S.S.tà stia sicura che non solo procurarà o consentirà {a cosa che possi perturbare l'Italia}, premendoli tanto quanto la {quiete di Castiglia} propria, ma che dove li bisognarà per impedire {ogni perturbatione} che li potesse succedere s'impiegarà potentissimamente {con tutte le forze sue}, soggiungendomi {che il fomento che diede il Marchese a quelli Anselmo} era con questa ragione, che vedendosi abandonato non tirasse {in suo aiuto in Italia una furia d'Ugonotti del Delfinato}, et che in questo negotio ci haveva {mano il Duca di Savoia morto}, qual era amicissimo {del detto Marchese}; et di nuovo S.M.tà bacia li piedi a S.S.tà di questo amorevole {avvertimento}, mostrando {che tal prattica sia cessata}. Passages that were in cipher are in { }; holes as in the Italian. --> # R192, Portogallo 8 ff. 195-197: Cardinal Riario to the Cardinal Secretary, [Elvas], 4-5 January 1581, with a copy of 29 November 1580 ## Letter Today, the 4th of January, I spoke to His Majesty {about the Piedmont business}, so that His Majesty was very content and showed himself much obliged to His Holiness, whose feet he kisses a thousand times for this kind {warning}, {telling me that there is something in it concerning those Anselmi, putting their men into Italy}; and that he would have {the letters they had on this business} searched for, and would send Idiáquez to me to inform me of everything, so that I could {report to His Holiness}; so I shall wait and report what happens. But certainly {His Majesty has taken the warning in very good part, and the Piedmont affair I believe is true, but I believe it will not turn out wholly to His Majesty's satisfaction}, who readily has the same {suspicion as His Holiness}. At this moment, on the evening of the 5th, Signor Idiáquez came in His Majesty's name to tell me {that it is true that the Marquis of Ayamonte, formerly Governor of Milan,} began and kept up {the dealings and encouragement} by some means {with those Anselmi}, but that it always displeased {His Majesty}, who at the time {the Marquis} died wrote him his mind frankly, which was that it displeased him; and that His Holiness may be sure that he will not only not procure or consent {to anything that might disturb Italy}, it mattering to him as much as the {peace of Castile} itself, but that wherever needed to prevent {any disturbance} that might arise he will employ himself most powerfully {with all his forces}; adding that {the encouragement the Marquis gave those Anselmi} was on this reasoning, that if they found themselves abandoned they would not draw {to their aid into Italy a fury of Huguenots from the Dauphiné}, and that in this business {the late Duke of Savoy had a hand}, who was a great friend {of the said Marquis}; and again His Majesty kisses His Holiness's feet for this kind {warning}, showing {that such dealings have ceased}. I pressed {the English business}, as I wrote to Your Lordship, and referred to the decision I sent you before, which was an answer in writing to Idiáquez, of which he has now sent me the duplicate. Seeing the {general enterprise} all but excluded, I sought {the aid of 4 or 5 thousand men} with the other necessary provisions, since this had been promised to Monsignor Nuncio; and others say {that because of the release of Don Antonio such a promise was revoked}; so that, {His Majesty's army} being much reduced, which I do not think reaches {5 or 6 thousand men or more}, and this {kingdom} needing a great part of it, the business was finally brought to this, that His Majesty would send {all the Italians with artillery, arms and munitions, victualled and paid for 4 months}, who at the {muster were 3,000 in the pay}, but [...] little more than {[...] thousand}; and although His Majesty wanted me to take charge of providing for them from now once {the 4 months} were over, or that Monsignor Nuncio should, having however reduced His Majesty to this, that having sent them {with the said munitions, victuals and pay, about 2,000 foot}, if within three months they had no other orders they should come back, without our taking any other care; now that His Majesty wanted {a commander found, and that they go under His Holiness's name}, and while they held this {relief} certain in this form, to inform His Holiness, so that in the said term {new aid} could be procured and meanwhile {the enemy} harassed, and {the soldiers} sent there not left {to perish}, and {the Catholics} heartened, the report came that Your Lordship will see, which has upset everything and seems to be confirmed by way {of France and England}, at which His Majesty's ministers seem to have {cooled}, and now offer {the Italians such and as many as} there are, but say they will not get involved in sending or appointing any {commander}, believing rather that none will be found, since they would be going into {clear danger} of all being {cut to pieces, the Queen of England having ships and men} there in strength, as they say; Otto di sono venne il s.r Secretario Idiaquez in nome di S.M.tà a dirmi che, havendo fatto io instanza a S.M.tà {per l'impresa d'Inghilterra} in nome di S.S.tà, mi diceva che S.M.tà desiderava molto compiacere S.S.tà in quello ch'era sodisfattione sua et servitio della Christianità, ma che non si trovava in termine per {questa impresa}, che haveva bisogno di grandissimi {apparati et genti}, et che li aiuti et gratie che l'erano stati offerti a nome di S.S.tà, volendo inferire da Mons. Nuntio, che da me non s'è mai disceso a particolari in questo, erano deboli {per tale impresa}, la quale [?S.M.tà] doveva differirla fin che fusse {impadronito della Fiandra}, che saria più sicura et facilità; et in tanto {per la Fiandra} S.S.tà li doveva dare larghi aiuti, dolendosi che hora sotto pretesto che le galere fossero in Portogallo, ho che non era finito il tempo, S.S.tà differiva la confirmatione del sussidio delle galere; et che io doveva in questo far buoni offitii, mostrando di credere haverli fatti in contrario; et con tutto ciò a nome di S.M.tà mi offeriva {per Irlanda li Italiani} nel modo vedrà V.S. Ill.ma nella pollizza signata A. Io li risposi la speranza che teneva S.S.tà in S.M.tà {per questa impresa} con molte raggioni, et le speranze che S.M.tà ne haveva dato et a me in particolare; li mostrai che li {aiuti} che li dicevano, se bene io non li haveva in commissione, erano di maggior consideratione di quello li facevano, et che quando S.S.tà havesse visto {li felici progressi di S.M.tà} in questo negotio, si poteva credere che S.S.tà haveria fatto quello havesse potuto in sodisfattione di S.M.tà. Quanto alli gratie, non era mio negotio, et che io non ci haveva fatto ne bene ne male, et che S.S.tà era prudentissimo et inspirato da Dio santo, sapeva quel che faceva. Quanto all'offerta {per questa d'Irlanda} non era stata mia negotiatione, massime quando non si havesse havuto mente a tirar avanti {in Inghilterra}, et che ne scriveria a Mons. Nuntio, se mi davano tempo; et così spedirno loro un corriero, havendoli fatto mettere in scritto come si vede nella pollizza signata A, et risposto in scritto come nella mia signata B, et scrissi a Mons. Nuntio come nella lettera signata C, che mi rispondi con la signata D, che arrivò hiersera, dove come vedrà V.S. Ill.ma discorre prudentemente in questo negotio; ma non si vole pigliar carico alcuno {di questi soldati}, li quali mi dicono non arrivano {a 1300, et mal armati}. Et a me è parso pigliar tal offerta, ma si bene pregar S.M.tà col mezzo d'Idiaquez che aspetti questo ordinario fra otto dì, acciò si veda meglio la mente di S.S.tà, mostrando che S.M.tà dice si fa da incaricarmi {di questi fanti} doveria aiutare {quelli meschini} suoi vassalli {mandati là}, massime havendo fatto qualche profitto, et dando buone speranze, mandandoli li {aiuti, armi et munitioni}, come ne doverà haver avisato Mons. Nuntio V.S. Ill.ma, alla quale humilmente bacio le mani, et Dio la sana. Di Badajoz li 2 di [?ottobre] 1580. Di V.S. Ill.ma et Rev.ma humilissimo et devotissimo servitore A. Card.le Riario. ## 2. Ill.ma quanto si vadi avanzando per la parte loro nel pretendere in questo negotio per ridursi al mio giuditio a lasciar l'agenda a S.S.tà senza giurisditione et da pigliarsi dalle mano sua senza intervento di Ministri di S.S.tà; et li temperamenti offerti da Mr. Montio non erano da metter fuori se in un medesimo tempo non si concludevano; anzi dicono (che non credo) che veniva in quelli del Presidente, eccetto che nel preambulo che si dechiarava che durassero sinchè piacevano a S.M.tà; et questo mi disse il suddetto Consigliero. Badajoz, 2 [October?] 1580 Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord. Eight days ago the Secretary, Signor Idiáquez, came in His Majesty's name to tell me that, as I had pressed His Majesty {for the English enterprise} in His Holiness's name, His Majesty greatly wished to please His Holiness in what was his satisfaction and the service of Christendom, but was in no position for {this enterprise}, which needed very great {preparations and men}; and that the aids and graces offered to him in His Holiness's name, meaning by Monsignor Nuncio (for I have never gone into particulars on this), were weak {for such an enterprise}, which he had to put off until he was {master of Flanders}, which would be safer and easier; and meanwhile {for Flanders} His Holiness should give him generous aid, complaining that now, on the pretext that the galleys were in Portugal, or that the term had not ended, His Holiness was delaying the confirmation of the galley subsidy; and that I ought to do good offices in this, showing I believed I had done the contrary; and with all that, in His Majesty's name, he offered me {the Italians for Ireland} as Your Lordship will see in the note marked A. I answered with the hope His Holiness had in His Majesty {for this enterprise}, with many reasons, and the hopes His Majesty had given, to me in particular; I showed him that the {aids} they spoke of, although I had no commission for them, were of greater weight than they made out, and that when His Holiness had seen {His Majesty's happy progress} in this business, one could believe His Holiness would have done what he could to His Majesty's satisfaction. As for the graces, that was not my business, and I had done neither good nor harm in it; His Holiness, most prudent and inspired by God, knew what he was doing. As for the offer {for this Irish matter}, it had not been my negotiation, especially if there was no intention of going on {into England}, and I would write of it to Monsignor Nuncio if they gave me time; so they sent a courier, having had it put in writing as seen in the note marked A, and answered in writing as in mine marked B; and I wrote to Monsignor Nuncio as in the letter marked C, who answered me with that marked D, which arrived last night, where, as Your Lordship will see, he reasons prudently on this business, but will not take any charge {of these soldiers}, who they tell me do not reach {1,300, and badly armed}. And I thought it right to accept that offer, but to beg His Majesty through Idiáquez to wait for this post in eight days, so that His Holiness's mind can be better seen, pointing out that if His Majesty means to put me in charge {of these foot}, he ought to help {those poor wretches}, his vassals {sent there}, especially as they have made some gain and give good hopes, by sending them {aid, arms and munitions}, as Monsignor Nuncio will have told Your Lordship, whose hands I humbly kiss, and God keep you well. From Badajoz, 2 [?October] 1580. Your Lordship's most humble and devoted servant, A. Cardinal Riario. ## 2. Elvas, 1[?0] December 1580 (deciphered copy) Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord. After sending the dispatch for Monsignor Marco at Madrid I received the attached note from Councillor Vázquez, from which Your Lordship will understand how far they are advancing on their side in their claims in this business, to bring it, in my judgement, to leaving the business to His Holiness without jurisdiction, to be taken from his hands without the intervention of His Holiness's ministers; and the compromises offered by Mr. Montio were not to be put forward unless they were concluded at the same time; indeed they say (which I do not believe) that he came into those of the President, except that the preamble declared they should last as long as His Majesty pleased; and this the said Councillor told me. And from what I know and hear from good quarters, this {President is a stone of scandal and ill disposed to the Roman Court, and whoever defends and covers him does so out of friendship and perhaps with good intent, but I think it right to report what I discover and hear, leaving the truth to be found later}. Having just dismounted at Elvas, I found the enclosed from the Archbishop of Évora with the possessions [...] of Your Lordship's servant; and with this I end, humbly kissing your hands. 1[?0] December 1580. A. Cardinal Riario. A long Italian letter entirely in about 60 graphic signs from the Sforza chancery box in Milan. Shuffled-token controls give Italian, a sign reader and a key estimated from the ciphertext alone reach 24% dictionary-word coverage, and a hand correction of the sign boxes adds only a point: the DECODE scans are too small (signs 15–25 px) for a reading. The 115 key sheets in the box are 19th-century reconstructions and do not fit. Milan, Sforza chancery · homophonic substitution in graphic signs · 1450s–60s · attempted, not read A Sforza chancery letter in graphic signs A two-leaf cipher letter in the Milan archive's box of ciphers: the controls say Italian and a key was estimated from the signs alone, but the scans are too small for a reading. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 7 November 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The document A letter entirely in cipher from the Sforza chancery, no word division, undated; no sender or recipient is named. Where Archivio di Stato di Milano, Carteggio Visconteo-Sforzesco, Potenze sovrane, Cancelleria segreta, Chiavi e cifrari, cart. 1597, stamped leaves 158–159 (the pencil stamps suggest the leaves may belong to two letters, nos. 158/159 and 165; not yet checked); DECODE R5464. The cipher A homophonic substitution with about 60 graphic signs for the Italian alphabet. Dots separate look-alike signs. How it was tried A sign reader built for these scans, then a homophonic solver (Lasry's CTTS) with period Italian text, controls on shuffled and simulated ciphers, key refinement from words, and a hand correction of the sign boxes. Why it resists The DECODE images are 1,671 px wide and a sign is 15–25 px tall; about one sign in ten is misread, which is enough to stop the solver from locking onto sentences. Still open The whole reading. Better images from the archive are the next step; the key sheets tested so far do not fit this hand, and some in the box are 19th-century reconstructions.

Cart. 1597 holds 174 DECODE records: 115 key sheets (nos. 1–114 and 169–171) and 59 ciphertexts. The key sheets are neat copies headed with correspondents' names (Cosimo de' Medici, Roberto de' Malatesti, Antonio da Pistoia, 1458–68) and the Naples inventory shows they are later reconstructions, so they are not a key to the letters. The letters use a dozen or so different sign alphabets, so every alphabet needs its own key; the catalogue lists them separately (items 2399–2413, one key per entry). This page covers one letter, R5464, which is long enough for a statistical attack: 3,279 signs, 60 distinct.

The solver's score on the real signs is compared with the score on the same signs shuffled. For Italian the ratio is 1.65; for Latin 1.38, Spanish 1.36, French 1.32, German lowest. Simulated Italian ciphers with 0, 8 and 15% sign noise were run the same way to see how much a misread sign costs. The letter families that come out are coherent by shape: the V-shaped signs fall on e , the φ-shaped on o , the hooked-stroke signs on n , the R-shaped on s .

The CTTS sign detector failed on these scans, so a reader was written here: deskew, straightened line strips, connected components merged by overlap, dots attached to the sign they belong to, then Ward clustering on shape features. Dictionary-word coverage of the decryption (5–12 letter words from a period corpus) measures it: first reader: 10.9% sensitive ink detection, key refined from words: 19.9% and 27.1% refined ring merging: 21.6%; with token pair rules: 23.2% hand correction of every line of the first leaf and the first three of the second: 24.2% to 25.0%, within the run-to-run noise. The last row is the answer to "can the boxes be fixed by eye": a little, and it stops paying off after about 30 lines. Resolution is the ceiling.

Short stretches build Italian words ( dele letere , gravisima , stamatina tornare , molte cose , sempre desiderat amici , porta dela bona ) but nothing builds a sentence, so by the project's standard the letter is not read. The sign transcription (3,279 signs, labelled s00–s59) is in the repository; the page images are not reproduced here because the DECODE copies are not ours to republish.

Which of the 60 sign classes are one letter written two ways, and which look-alikes are one sign: 40 of 60 homophone assignments agree across runs. Every other letter of the box: R5465, R5463 and one more family show signals only. The date, the writer and the recipient: nothing in the letter names them. The next step is better images. A request to the Archivio di Stato di Milano for 400 dpi photographs of the stamped leaves 158, 159, 164 and 165 is drafted, not sent.
